Issue #98008: Add profile-guided optimization (PGO) to improve mobile app startup performance

## Proposal

Add profile-guided optimization (PGO) to Android and iOS release builds to improve mobile (app startup) performance, covering app-owned native code and relevant native dependencies built from source, including React Native, Hermes, JSI, Nitro, and Expensify native modules.

### Background
Android and iOS compilers optimize native code by guessing which functions and branches run most frequently. PGO gives the compiler a recording of how the app was actually used — analogous to a traffic report — so it can make the busiest paths faster and spend less space on rarely-used ones. PGO optimizes compiled native code; it does not compile our JS into native code, but JS benefits indirectly because Hermes is native (faster Hermes init, bytecode loading, JSI communication, and native modules let NewDot become ready sooner).

### Problem
Release builds currently use generic compiler heuristics with no knowledge of which native paths matter during startup and normal authenticated usage. Startup passes through many native components quickly: RN runtime init, Hermes VM startup and bytecode loading, JSI communication, Nitro/other native module init, native storage/networking/image/document integrations, and app-owned Kotlin/Java/Obj-C/Swift/C/C++ code. Some dependencies are consumed as prebuilt artifacts and cannot be further optimized with actual NewDot-usage info.

### Solution
Add PGO to Android and iOS release builds. The representative workload focuses on cold startup of the HybridApp into NewDot. NewDot authenticated flows, OldDot, and hybrid transitions are not optimization targets (initially).

### Benchmark results (directional local proof)

**Android — faster phone (20 measured cold starts):** Avg improved 4.75% (2951 → 2811 ms, −140 ms), P90 −166 ms (5.39%), P95 −185 ms (5.87%). Up to ~5–6% on mid-to-high-end devices.

**Android — slower phone:** Avg improved 1.85% (2721 → 2671 ms, −50 ms), P90 −45 ms, P95 −55 ms. Up to ~2% on low-end devices.

**iOS — iPhone 14 Pro (10 measured cold starts):** Avg improved 3.21% (1409 → 1364 ms), with P90 2.49% and P95 11.54%. Larger iOS gains likely because more code is compiled by the same toolchain than on Android.

### How the PGO workflow works
1. **Identify a representative workload** — cold authenticated startup plus (as the workload expands) opening/scrolling chats, sending messages, opening a workspace and changing reversible settings, uploading receipts/images/documents, viewing attachments, and search. Same logical journey on both platforms; OldDot/hybrid transitions excluded.
2. **Collect a profile** — build with instrumentation counting native function/branch execution, run the journey on a physical device. Android writes `.profraw` explicitly (process is killed without exit callbacks), pulled via `adb` and merged with `llvm-profdata` from the same NDK. iOS uses Xcode to generate a profile on a physical device (not Simulator). Instrumented builds are never shipped.
3. **Build using the profile** — recompile app + relevant native deps in release mode with the profile so the compiler can inline hot small functions, arrange hot branches, co-locate hot machine-code blocks, and trade speed vs. size appropriately. Android and iOS share the journey but each produces its own profile artifact.

### Implementation, profile lifecycle, CI, and safeguards
- **Android** tooling supports three modes: `release`, `instrumented`, `optimized`. Relevant native dependency graph built from source; tooling verifies LLVM instrumentation and profile-writing APIs, pulls/merges per-library `.profraw` into one `.profdata`, and archives APKs separately.
- **iOS** will expose the same three logical modes; RN/Hermes/JSI/Nitro/app-owned native targets built from source with the right Xcode/Clang profile settings, mirroring the app-ready startup boundary. Finish the local iOS proof and collect equivalent numbers before enabling for production.
- **Profile lifecycle & CI** — initially manual; once validated, automate per release: build instrumented app → install on physical device → run representative journey → persist/merge profiles → build optimized release from same revision/toolchain → benchmark release vs. optimized → reject stale/incompatible profiles and surface warnings → publish optimized artifact only if perf and functional checks pass. Regenerate profiles every release; keep each profile tied to platform, source revision, build config, compiler/toolchain version, and architecture assumptions. Keep the perf marker/benchmark automation separate from the PGO implementation, and use the same measurement code for both builds.
- **Risks & safeguards** — workload must represent normal usage (avoid over-training one path); never ship or benchmark instrumented builds; native deps must be built from source; use compatible NDK/`llvm-profdata` (Android) and Xcode/Clang (iOS); never share profiles across platforms; monitor APK/IPA size, build time, crash rate, and non-startup interactions; confirm OldDot/hybrid transitions still work via functional regression tests; record device model, OS version, thermal state, source revision, and build order, and counterbalance test order. If a release shows no meaningful improvement or a regression, the regular non-PGO release remains the fallback.

### Follow-up ideas raised in discussion
- Measure impact on flows not covered by PGO (e.g. startup combined with the "last visited path" feature).
- iOS: combine PGO with order-file / temporal-instrumentation generation to further optimize main-binary layout for startup (temporal profile support for Swift landed in Xcode 26.4). Order files may also help on Android.
- Android complementary optimization: generate Baseline Profiles and Startup Profiles to precompile startup-critical Java bytecode and improve dex layout (with a workaround for prior HybridApp blockers).

## Product outcome

Ship the native front door to Extra Chill's Online Music Scene: discover what is happening, participate in Community, find shows, read timely coverage, create, manage meaningful artist/venue relationships, and use Roadie for authorized work.

The app is not a native blog wrapper. It is not Roadie-only. It is not a generic engagement feed.

## Product hierarchy

- **Home:** default cross-network Online Music Scene composition.
- **Community:** discussions and human participation.
- **Calendar:** events, venues, artists, dates, and locations.
- **Stories:** publication and Festival Wire coverage; a peer surface, not Home.
- **Roadie:** ambient operating interface and peer surface, not the whole app.
- **Work and Inbox:** runs, approvals, questions, completions, and artifacts.
- **You:** identity, explicit relationships, owned resources, privacy, and settings.
- **Create:** domain-aware creation with GutenbergKit for rich editing.

## Non-negotiable architecture

- One authenticated shell and refresh lifecycle serves the multisite network.
- Derived site clients use exact approved REST roots.
- WordPress core REST and domain-owned abilities are canonical.
- Server owners enforce authorization, visibility, validation, authorship, notifications, side effects, and persistence.
- No app-owned parallel API, feed store, chat store, transcript store, approval store, or notification substrate.
- Roadie tools, prompts, roles, workspaces, sessions, runs, and approvals remain server-owned.
- GutenbergKit is the rich editor; WordPress core autosaves are the draft primitive.
- Browser handoff is an explicit escape hatch, not the primary architecture.

## Product guardrails

- Extra Chill is a scene, not an audience leaderboard.
- No generic follower graph, follower counts, popularity mechanics, engagement-ranked feeds, or synthetic participation.
- Prefer chronology, location, subscriptions, ownership, membership, and user-selected context.
- Optimize for genuine participation, retention, cross-site traversal, direct relationships, and recurring utility.

Issue #410: Track OpenCode explore access to DMC-managed worktrees

## Problem

A DMC-managed workspace root is granted through generated `opencode.json` as:

```json
{
  "permission": {
    "external_directory": {
      "/path/to/dmc-workspace/**": "allow"
    }
  }
}
```

The parent coding session can use its native file tools in a worktree below that root. An OpenCode `explore` subagent, explicitly asked to inspect that same worktree, can still return an external-directory access denial. This makes delegated exploration unreliable and shifts duplicate investigation back to the parent.

## Audit Result

The current integration already writes the root allow during OpenCode config generation and reconciliation. The effective native `explore` agent policy also contains the configured workspace allow. The failure is therefore not a missing DMC workspace discovery value or an absent top-level grant.

OpenCode owns the final subagent/session permission evaluation. Its native `explore` policy adds its own external-directory rules, and its platform history includes subagent permission inheritance and external-directory evaluation defects. This repository cannot safely compensate by broadening unrelated tool permissions or duplicating an allow that the effective policy already reports.

## Required Contract

Define and verify a compatibility contract for an OpenCode runtime used by this integration:

- A top-level `permission.external_directory` allow for a DMC workspace root must apply to native delegated agents, including `explore`.
- The grant must cover descendants such as `/path/to/dmc-workspace/repository@branch`.
- The integration needs a deterministic regression check that proves the delegated read/search path succeeds, or a version/capability guard that reports the unsupported runtime clearly.
- Keep the grant scoped to the configured workspace root and preserve the existing installed-source edit restrictions.

## Upstream Context

Related upstream history: anomalyco/opencode#30529 and anomalyco/opencode#41991. This tracker remains the integration owner for detecting the runtime capability and documenting the supported contract.

Issue #736: feat(api,db): service principals — let apps call the API as themselves, and retire the env-var secrets

## Overview

Today, when one of our apps needs to call the F3 API as *itself* rather than as a logged-in person, we solve it by inventing a new password, pasting it into an environment variable, and shipping it. We've now done this five separate times, most recently in PR #693.

This doesn't scale, and it's brittle in ways that matter:

- **Adding an app means changing and redeploying the API.** Every new consumer needs a new environment variable in the shared API service. One app's new feature forces a deploy of the thing every app depends on.
- **There's no way to turn a key off.** If a key leaks, someone has to edit a secret and redeploy the API — again, affecting every app at once.
- **Keys never expire and nobody can see who's using them.** We can't answer "which app made this change?" or "is this key still in use?"
- **It's all-or-nothing.** A key either works or it doesn't; we can't say "the Slackbot may read Slack settings, and nothing else."

Two things need to be true to fix this. An app needs to be able to **be somebody** in our system — to have an identity of its own, the way a person does. And there needs to be a way to say **what that somebody is allowed to do**.

[ADR 0002](docs/adr/0002-permission-based-authorization.md) already answers the second one. **This issue is about the first**, plus cleaning up the environment- variable passwords we've accumulated along the way.

## Relationship to ADR 0002

ADR 0002 (permission-based authorization) establishes the model: code checks permissions, humans are granted roles, and the org hierarchy scopes the grant. This issue does **not** propose a competing mechanism, and deliberately does not define its own vocabulary of permissions or its own middleware.

What it adds is the piece ADR 0002 assumes but doesn't provide:

> API keys authenticate through the same role tables (`roles_x_api_keys_x_org`, resolved in `packages/api/src/shared.ts`), so a permission layer must cover both principal types.

That's true for database-backed API keys. It is **not** true for the env-var secrets below — they bypass the role tables entirely, so a permission layer built per ADR 0002 cannot see them at all. Once the ADR lands, these become the only paths in the API that don't check permissions. The exception gets more conspicuous, not less.

There's also a gap on the identity side: [shared.ts](packages/api/src/shared.ts#L218) inner-joins `users` on `api_keys.owner_id`, so every key must belong to a person. A service role is not much use if no key can represent a service.

**Sequencing:** ADR 0002's permission helper and middleware come first — they are the seam this work plugs into. The hashing work (#360) is independent of both and can go any time.

## Why now

PR #693 (Slack settings routes) needed the Slackbot to read Slack bot tokens from the API. With no primitive for "an app is calling," the PR added a `SLACKBOT_SERVICE_API_KEY` env var, compared it by hand, and left the route out of the public `/docs` listing.

**PR #693 is shipping as-is.** Technical leadership made that call deliberately, with the drawbacks understood — the feature is worth more right now than the delay it would take to build a general answer first. This issue is not a request to revisit that decision.

What it does mean is that the pattern now has one more instance to migrate, and the underlying question raised in the review thread (#693 discussion r3661806908) and at standup still needs an answer:

> "Consider a future where we have a dozen apps that each want to do their own thing. How do we manage API routes that need to be restricted to a certain user or use case?"

## What we have today

Five different shared-secret environment variables, each with its own convention:

| Secret | Used by | How it's sent | Guards |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `SUPER_ADMIN_API_KEY` | `packages/api` → map revalidate | `x-api-key` header | `revalidateAuthProcedure` ([shared.ts:139](packages/api/src/shared.ts#L139)) |
| `SUPER_ADMIN_API_KEY` | `packages/auth` → OTP send | JSON request **body** | [send-otp-verification-request-server.ts:50](packages/auth/src/lib/send-otp-verification-request-server.ts#L50) |
| `SUPER_ADMIN_API_KEY` | `apps/map` revalidate route | `x-api-key` header | [apps/map/src/app/api/revalidate/route.ts:49](apps/map/src/app/api/revalidate/route.ts#L49) |
| `F3_MAP_API_KEY` | `apps/map` → API | `Authorization: Bearer` | normal API-key path |
| `API_KEY` | `apps/auth` → API register | `Authorization: Bearer` | normal API-key path |
| `SLACKBOT_SERVICE_API_KEY` | Slackbot → API (Slack settings) | `x-slackbot-service-key` header | hand-rolled compare in [slack.ts](packages/api/src/router/slack.ts) |

Four different header/body conventions, one secret reused across three unrelated purposes, and no revocation path for any of them. The bottom four rows are the ones that bypass the role tables; `F3_MAP_API_KEY` and `API_KEY` already ride the normal database-backed path and need no migration.

That makes it the highest-value of the set to migrate — not because anything is wrong today, but because it's the one where a revocable, permission-checked key buys the most. It's also the shape ADR 0002 flags for extra scrutiny: middleware-only, with no org-scoped check behind it.

Issue #855: feat(db,api,admin): add "territory" org level and make hierarchy depth-agnostic (epic)

## Overview

F3 is adding a new level to its organizational hierarchy. Today an F3 org is one of five kinds — **nation → sector → area → region → AO**. Going forward there will be six, with **territory** sitting between sector and area:

**nation → sector → territory → area → region → AO**

The good news is that our database was designed for this. Every org lives in one `orgs` table and simply points at its parent, so the database does not actually care how deep the tree goes. Adding "territory" is, at the database level, one new value in a list plus moving some rows to point at a new parent.

The bad news is that several parts of our application code did **not** trust that design. In five places we wrote code that assumes the tree is exactly five levels deep, by hand-writing one step for each level. When the tree becomes six levels deep, that code does not crash and does not log an error — it just quietly returns incomplete results. Two of those five places control **who is allowed to edit what**, and a third quietly drops AOs out of list endpoints across six routers, so the failure shows up as administrators mysteriously losing access to regions they own.

**The fourth is not in this repo.** `org_type` is a published API value, and `f3-org-map` reads it from `/v1/org-chart`. It has the same hardcoded-depth assumption — and because it deploys independently of this repo, nothing holds it back when the migration runs. That makes the cross-repo work a rollout ordering constraint, not a follow-up. See "Cross-repo impact" below.

So this Epic is deliberately not "add territory." It is: **fix the places that hardcoded the depth, then add territory.** Once that is done, adding the *next* level (F3 keeps growing, so there will be a next one) becomes roughly a one-line change plus a data migration, instead of this whole project again.

There is a second, related cost. Our admin site currently has a separate page, table, and edit dialog for each kind of org — one for sectors, one for areas, one for regions, and so on. These files are near-identical copies of each other. Adding "territory" the naive way means copying roughly 700 more lines of code that we then have to maintain forever. This Epic folds that duplication into shared components driven by a single configuration, so a new level shows up in the admin site automatically.

---

## The five silent breakages

These are the reason this cannot ship as a single "add an enum value" PR. None of them throw an error; all of them return quietly wrong results.

| Location | What it does today | What happens when `territory` is inserted |
|---|---|---|
| [`packages/api/src/check-has-role-on-org.ts:54`](https://github.com/F3-Nation/f3-nation/blob/main/packages/api/src/check-has-role-on-org.ts#L54) | Five aliased self-joins climbing AO → region → area → sector → nation to find inherited permissions | The chain is now six deep, so the walk stops at sector. **Nation admins silently lose implicit admin rights over AOs.** |
| [`packages/api/src/get-editable-org-ids.ts:65`](https://github.com/F3-Nation/f3-nation/blob/main/packages/api/src/get-editable-org-ids.ts#L65) | Three aliased self-joins descending from the user's own org to find what they may edit | A sector admin's descent now ends at area. **Regions disappear from their editable set.** |
| [`packages/api/src/get-descendant-org-ids.ts`](https://github.com/F3-Nation/f3-nation/blob/main/packages/api/src/get-descendant-org-ids.ts) | Five aliased self-joins descending, documented in its own docstring as *"up to 5 levels deep"* | From a nation, today's chain is exactly five and fits with nothing to spare. Six needs six joins, so **AOs drop out of every descendant set** — across 8 call sites in `location.ts`, `event.ts`, `position.ts`, `user.ts`, `org.ts` and `map/event.ts`. Surfaces as events and locations going missing from list endpoints, not just as a permissions bug. |
| [`apps/admin/src/app/regions/regions-table.tsx:65`](https://github.com/F3-Nation/f3-nation/blob/main/apps/admin/src/app/regions/regions-table.tsx#L65) | Rolls a sector selection up to areas via `areas.filter(a => selectedSectorIds.includes(a.parentId))` | Once areas hang off territories, that predicate matches **zero rows**. The sector filter returns an empty region list with no error. |
| **[`f3-org-map` `src/orgChart.ts:38` and `:86`](https://github.com/F3-Nation/f3-org-map/blob/main/src/orgChart.ts#L38)** *(different repo)* | `normalizeOrgType` whitelists the five type strings and **falls back** on anything else; `hierarchyTypes = ['area','sector','nation']` then indexes our `hierarchy` array **by position** | `"territory"` is not rejected — it is coerced into a valid-looking `'sector'` or `'area'`, and every positional index shifts by one. **The map renders a plausible but wrong hierarchy.** Tracked in [F3-Nation/f3-org-map#47](https://github.com/F3-Nation/f3-org-map/issues/47). |

**Why these fail silently rather than loudly:** a `LEFT JOIN` that runs out of tree returns `NULL`, and both authorization functions `.filter()` nulls away before use. A truncated ancestor chain is therefore indistinguishable from a legitimately short one.

The fourth is a distinct — and worse — variant of the same instinct. Nulls are at least recognizable as missing data. A defensive fallback that coerces unrecognized input into a *valid* value destroys the evidence that anything went wrong, so the failure is not merely silent but actively disguised. Worth noting because "make unknown input safe by substituting a default" is a pattern we have elsewhere, and the lesson generalizes: unknown org types should fail loudly.

Issue #12: MASTER CONTROL BUS — FIEZEL 7-agent orchestration

# FIEZEL MASTER CONTROL BUS

Issue #12 is the permanent coordination bus for concurrent AI work on this repository.

**Master Control:** the coordinating ChatGPT session acting for the owner. Master Control is outside the seven agent slots below. It owns scheduling, conflict resolution, lane reassignment, promotion decisions, and the final go/no-go call. Master Control does not silently bypass verifier gates.

## Seven agent slots

1. **A1 — Coordinator / Scheduler** — read-only by default. Maintains work graph, dependencies, lane state, ownership map, and handoff quality. Never edits product code unless Master Control explicitly reassigns it.
2. **A2 — Evidence Analyst / Diagnostics Worker** — read-only by default. Parses device diagnostics, reproduces timelines, distinguishes observed facts from hypotheses, and produces the smallest next experiment.
3. **A3 — Neural Runtime Worker** — code-writing lane for Kokoro/ONNX/WebKit neural inference, neural core/bootstrap, generation lifecycle, and runtime instrumentation specifically required to isolate inference failure.
4. **A4 — PWA / Service Worker Worker** — code-writing lane for `sw.js`, cache invalidation, standalone navigation headers, asset delivery, and deployment freshness. Must not change neural runtime logic.
5. **A5 — Puter / Auth Worker** — code-writing lane for Puter auth/popup/token restoration only when current evidence supports an auth defect. Must not touch neural inference logic.
6. **A6 — Test / CI Verifier** — independent verifier. Owns regression design, test adequacy, CI interpretation, stale assertions, and exact-head verification. Read-only on worker branches unless Master Control explicitly requests a test-only patch.

## Mandatory protocol

Every agent session MUST read Issue #12 and the relevant lane issue immediately before any mutation/push. No product-code mutation is allowed without a current `CLAIM`.

Allowed control messages:
- `CLAIM` — agent ID, branch/PR, exact base SHA, files/subsystem leased, intended change, acceptance test.
- `OBSERVATION` — read-only evidence with source/commit/request IDs; explicitly separate fact from hypothesis.
- `REQUEST` — asks another lane for a bounded deliverable without transferring ownership.
- `HANDOFF` — completed result with commit/PR, changed files, tests, residual risks, and what the next agent must do.
- `VERIFY` — independent verifier result: PASS / FAIL / INCONCLUSIVE with exact evidence.
- `BLOCKER` — external/device/owner dependency or unresolved conflict.
- `RELEASE` — lane finished/abandoned; file leases are free.

- One file may have only one active code-writing lease at a time.
- A1, A2, A6, and A7 are read-only by default and therefore do not reserve product files.
- A3/A4/A5 use their own branches: `agent/a3-*`, `agent/a4-*`, `agent/a5-*`. Never push into another agent's branch.
- A worker must state exact base SHA in its CLAIM. If `main` moves materially before push, re-read #12 and rebase/recreate before continuing.
- Shared-file changes require Master Control to serialize ownership; parallel edits to the same file are prohibited.
- Draft/legacy PRs are not merged merely because CI is green. Their base and scope must be revalidated against current `main`.

A worker cannot self-certify a release. Promotion requires:
1. worker HANDOFF;
2. A6 independent `VERIFY: PASS` for tests/CI/regressions;
3. A7 independent `VERIFY: PASS` for integration/deployment/merge safety;
4. Master Control go/no-go decision.

For diagnostic deployments, A7 must label the result as diagnostic rather than production-success until physical evidence passes.

## Parallel execution policy

Parallel work is allowed only when scopes do not overlap. Preferred topology:
- A2 investigates evidence continuously without writing code.
- A3 investigates/fixes neural runtime.
- A4 audits cache/PWA freshness independently.
- A5 audits Puter/auth independently and should remain read-only unless fresh evidence shows an auth failure.
- A6 validates each worker's tests and exact-head CI.
- A7 integrates only verified branches.
- A1 maintains dependencies and alerts Master Control to collisions/stale bases.

Maximum simultaneous code-writing lanes: **3** (A3, A4, A5). Everything else is analysis/verification.

Every HANDOFF must contain:
- agent ID and lane issue;
- branch/PR and exact head SHA;
- exact base SHA;
- changed files;
- observed problem addressed;

This issue is the **durable, addressable home for every finding packet awaiting analyst adjudication.**

**"not yet adjudicated" never means "lost"**.

## Why this is needed — measured, not assumed

`findings-and-filing.md:42` says a finder records a packet as *"an ordinary issue or PR comment under
the `fsgg:finding-packet` anchor"*. It names the anchor and nothing else. There is no queue, no board
column, and no index — so a pending packet is discoverable only by remembering which pull request it
was posted on, which survives exactly one session.

Measured on 2026-08-15, against a real, well-formed 3896-character packet posted on
[PR #2686](https://github.com/FS-GG/.github/pull/2686#issuecomment-5304065011):

| query | returns |
|---|---|
| `repo:FS-GG/.github "fsgg:finding-packet"` | #2675, #2676, #2688 |
| `repo:FS-GG/.github "fsgg:finding-packet" in:comments` | #2675, #2676 |

**The packet itself appears in neither.** Every hit is a row that *discusses* the anchor. The comment
was confirmed to exist by direct fetch, so this is a discoverability failure, not a posting failure.
Whether the cause is search-index lag or a systematic gap is **not established** and is deliberately
not claimed here.

One comment per packet, each carrying the `fsgg:finding-packet` anchor, recording what

hand, and the narrow `Paths:` it would propose.

A packet whose natural home is a pull request may stay there; **cross-link it here** so it is reachable

- **Not a board row.** Created through `gh api`, never `fsgg-coord add`. No `Status`, no `Class`, no

  re-derives it, and it never fills in evidence the packet omits."* A thin packet stays thin.

A maintainer on the project FalkorDB/FalkorDB (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #2400: Unbounded recursion in expression evaluator: nested GRAPH.QUERY expression exhausts stack

Reported to `security@falkordb.com` by `firewok137` / "JerryGW", who reports it against v4.20.1. Filing publicly with corrected severity.

**Maintainer note on the reported framing.** The report states no authentication is required. That is not accurate for any deployment with `requirepass` or ACLs configured — `GRAPH.QUERY` is subject to normal Redis authentication. Scored below as `PR:L`. PoC payload details are intentionally omitted here.

## Problem

`_AR_EXP_Evaluate` in `src/arithmetic/arithmetic_expression.c` (line 574) walks the arithmetic expression tree by recursion with no depth limit:

- `_AR_EXP_Evaluate` → `_AR_EXP_EvaluateFunctionCall` for `AR_EXP_OP` nodes
- `_AR_EXP_EvaluateFunctionCall` → `_AR_EXP_Evaluate` for each child (line 460)

Expression tree depth is a direct function of query text nesting, which the client controls. A query with deeply nested parenthesised arithmetic produces a correspondingly deep tree; the reporter reached `SIGSEGV` at ~50,000 levels against the default 8MB stack.

There is no depth counter, no configured maximum, and no stack headroom check anywhere on this path.

Because the stack is fully exhausted, the `SIGSEGV` handler cannot run and no `REDIS BUG REPORT` is emitted — the process simply disappears. That makes this materially harder to diagnose in production than a normal crash, and it is worth noting for triage that several of these reports share that property.

### Relationship to #2330

#2330 covers unbounded mutual recursion in `src/ast/param_parser.c` (`parse_array` ↔ `parse_value`). This is the same class of defect at a different stage: #2330 is reached while parsing parameters, this one while evaluating the expression tree. They are separate call graphs and need separate bounds, but a single shared "maximum nesting depth" configuration would sensibly govern both.

Worth checking as part of the same pass: the AST is also built and validated by recursive descent, so a nesting limit is probably best enforced once at parse time rather than separately in each consumer.

## Suggested fix

1. Enforce a maximum expression nesting depth at parse/build time and reject queries that exceed it with a normal error response. This is the cheapest fix and it protects every consumer of the tree at once, not just the evaluator.
2. Failing that, thread a depth counter through `_AR_EXP_Evaluate` / `_AR_EXP_EvaluateFunctionCall` and return `EVAL_ERR` past the limit.
3. Make the limit configurable, defaulting to something well under what an 8MB stack tolerates. The evaluator's frame is not tiny, so the safe depth is likely in the low thousands rather than tens of thousands — worth measuring rather than guessing.

## Impact

- **Requires an authenticated connection** on any server with `requirepass`/ACLs.
- Process termination; all in-memory graph data lost, service unavailable until restart.
- A single query is sufficient and the payload is trivially generated. No memory-corruption expertise needed.
- No crash report is produced, so operators see an unexplained process exit.

`CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` (6.5 Medium)

## Affected files

- `src/arithmetic/arithmetic_expression.c` — `_AR_EXP_Evaluate` (line 574), `_AR_EXP_EvaluateFunctionCall` (line 460)

A maintainer on the project FalkorDB/FalkorDB (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #2601: [Rust] CALL {} subquery relationship scan is incorrectly anchored to the outer-scope imported variable (silent wrong results)

## Summary

On the Rust engine, a `CREATE` that writes a **relationship**, followed by `WITH *` and a `CALL {}` subquery containing a relationship traversal, makes the subquery yield **zero rows**. The query succeeds and returns `0`, so nothing indicates an error.

The C engine returns the correct result, so this is a **regression in the Rust implementation**.

Found while verifying #2374 on `main`.

## Reproduction

Setup (8 nodes, 32 edges):

```cypher
UNWIND range(0,7) AS i CREATE (:l10:l5 {id:i});
UNWIND range(0,7) AS i
MATCH (a {id:i})
UNWIND [1,2,3,4] AS d
MATCH (b {id:((i+d)%8)})
CREATE (a)-[:R]->(b);
```

Repro:

```cypher
CREATE (a:Seed)-[:R]->(b:Seed)
WITH *
CALL { MATCH p=(n3:l10)-[]-(n4:l5) RETURN 1 AS z }
RETURN count(*) AS c
```

| | result |
|---|---|
| C 4.20.4 (`falkordb/falkordb:latest`) | `64` ✅ |
| Rust `main` (`falkordb/falkordb:edge`) | **`0`** ❌ |

Deterministic: 3/3 runs on each engine, fresh graph per run.

## Controls — all of these agree between C and Rust

| Variant | C | Rust |
|---|---|---|
| `CREATE (a:Seed)` (node only) + same `CALL {}` | 64 | 64 ✅ |
| no `CREATE` at all, `CALL {}` alone | 64 | 64 ✅ |
| `CREATE (a:Seed)-[:R]->(b:Seed) WITH * MATCH p=(n3:l10)-[]-(n4:l5)` (same traversal, **no subquery**) | 64 | 64 ✅ |
| relationship `CREATE` + `CALL {}` with a **variable-length** `-[*0..1]-` traversal | 72 | 72 ✅ |

So the failure needs **all three** of: (a) the `CREATE` writes a *relationship* (a node-only `CREATE` is fine), (b) the traversal is inside a `CALL {}` subquery (the same traversal outside it is fine), and (c) the traversal is a fixed-hop `-[]-` (the variable-length form is fine).

That combination points at the newly written relationship invalidating the matrix the subquery's fixed-hop traversal operator reads, without the subquery seeing a synced/flushed version — the traversal then matches nothing at all, including the 32 pre-existing edges.

## Impact

Silent wrong results — zero rows instead of 64, with no error. Any read-after-write in a `CALL {}` subquery in the same query as a relationship `CREATE` is affected.

## Also seen in the original #2374 shape

With the reporter's 8-label dataset and bounded path lengths (where C survives instead of being OOM-killed):

Issue #12: Workers cannot perform nested orchestration: resident connection profile is not projected into the private worker runtime

## Problem

A worker inside its private runtime cannot start a bounded child Run (the recursive-successor / nested-task-set pattern). Repository discovery succeeds (`baton doctor`: `connection: ready` via `.git/baton/connection.json`), but `baton run start` fails with `cli_config_invalid: user connection profile is unavailable` — the connection profile lives in the owner's `~/.config/baton/connections/`, which is deliberately not projected into the worker's private HOME.

Phase 77/85 recursive run authority (RUN_ORCHESTRATOR_CAPABILITIES: run.context/run.start/run.status/run.stop, maxDepth 4, bounded children) and issue #9's live acceptance (a recursive successor) both presuppose a worker that can reach the resident with bounded authority. Today that path only works if the worker happens to share the owner's profile store, which private-runtime isolation forbids.

## Options

- Project a **bounded, run-scoped connection profile** into the worker runtime at spawn: resident-published, lease-bound (capabilities = the worker's orchestrator lease), revocable, mode-0600, digested into the spawn receipt. Never the owner's full profile.
- Or a resident-issued **nested session token** (capability-attenuated to the lease) delivered through the spawn envelope, with discovery in the worktree.

- A worker on an orchestrator-leased run can start exactly the bounded child runs its lease allows, with requested/resolved/observed authority, and nothing more.
- The projected profile/token is revocable and appears in spawn receipts and stop/reap evidence.
- Owner profile store is never read by the worker.
- Red tests cover lease bounds, revocation, replay, and zero residue.

Issue #1080: Security: freeze and guard free-text dispatch inputs interpolated into run: bodies (34 workflows, 20 gated on write)

## Problem

**34 gated workflows interpolate a free-text `workflow_dispatch` input directly into a `run:` script
body. 20 of them touch a write environment.** GitHub substitutes `${{ }}` as raw text before any
shell or PowerShell sees it, so the value is parsed as *code*, not data.

This is not theoretical and it does not require breaking out of quotes. Two live instances,
reproduced locally before filing:

**`.github/workflows/720-create-repo.yml:193`** — double-quoted PowerShell, so `$( )` runs as-is:

```
Description = "${{ inputs.Description }}"

$ Description = "$(Write-Host 'INJECTED-PWSH: ran with the job credential')"
INJECTED-PWSH: ran with the job credential      <- executed; Description ends up empty
```

**`.github/workflows/720-create-repo.yml:274`** — same input, bash half of the same workflow:

```
repo_input="${{ inputs.RepoName }}"

$ RepoName='$(echo INJECTED-BASH: command substitution ran)'
repo_input=[INJECTED-BASH: command substitution ran]
```

720 runs on `github-prod`.

## Why this matters here specifically, given dispatch needs write access

The usual dismissal — "only someone with write access can dispatch, and they could edit the workflow
anyway" — **does not hold for a gated workflow**, and that is the whole point of this issue.

`environment:` approval is a trust boundary between the *dispatcher* and the *approver*. The approver
sees `run-name`, the input values, and the workflow's committed source, and decides whether to spend
a production credential. Interpolated inputs let the dispatcher supply code that runs **after** the
approval, inside the job, with `cloudflare-prod-write` / `whmcs-prod` / `github-prod` / `m365-prod`
credentials — none of which are in the dispatcher's hands beforehand. Editing the workflow instead
would be visible in the diff the approver reads; an injected input is not, because it is not in the
repository at all.

That is also why the burn-down should be ordered by environment, not by file.

## The repo already knows the right pattern and documents it

`.github/workflows/105-manage-record.yml:178-184` passes user-supplied values via `env:` with a
comment saying exactly why:

> Untrusted/user-supplied values are passed via env (never interpolated directly into the script
> body) so they cannot break out of the string and inject PowerShell.

105 is the exception. The other 34 are the house pattern. Nothing enforces 105's rule, so it is a
comment in one file rather than a property of the repo — which is the tier this should move up from.

`boolean` and `choice` inputs are excluded throughout: GitHub constrains those values, so they cannot
carry a payload. Only `type: string` inputs are counted below.

One PR. Add the detector and freeze the current set; fixing the 34 call sites is follow-on work,
ordered by environment.

**Create `scripts/check-workflow-input-interpolation.py`**, following the conventions of its
neighbours (`scripts/check-pwsh-workflow-invocations.py` is the closest structural match):

- Parse every `.github/workflows/*.yml`. For each, collect `workflow_dispatch.inputs` whose `type` is
  `string` (or absent — the default is string).
- Flag any occurrence of `${{ inputs.X }}` or `${{ github.event.inputs.X }}` inside a `run:` block, or
  inside an `actions/github-script` `script:` block, where `X` is one of those free-text inputs.
- Record, per finding, the workflow's `environment:` values, and whether any is a write environment
  (does not end in `-read`).
- Carry a `KNOWN_UNGUARDED` allowlist of the current 34, **asserted exactly** — same shape #825 uses,
  so an entry that gets fixed must be removed and a new instance cannot be added silently. Exit 1 on
  any finding not in the list, and also on a stale list entry.

**Wire it into `.github/workflows/722-ci.yml`** as its own step in the guard roster, next to
`Validate every pwsh invocation of a repo script can bind` (`:158-172`); copy that step's shape.

**Tests in `tests/workflow-logic/test_workflow_input_interpolation.py`**, picked up by
`tests/workflow-logic/run_all.py`'s roster convention.

3. Adding a synthetic workflow with a free-text input interpolated into `run:` makes it exit 1 —

Both signals are therefore worthless here, and a conclusion drawn from either is wrong.

Decide per branch on **content**: does `main` today already contain the change? Read the branch's actual hunks and check the corresponding lines in `main`. `conductor/948-claim-vs-citation` is the clearest example of why — 737/claim-sync work did land (ledger L33/L34, via #939), so that branch is very likely already-applied despite reading as 1-ahead.

Issue #230: Power-button SOS trigger fires on ~2 screen toggles instead of 3 presses

## Summary
The power-button SOS gesture counts **screen transitions** instead of **button presses**, so locking → waking → locking the phone (3 transitions within 2 s) starts an SOS countdown. The feature is documented and implemented as "press the power button 3 times rapidly", but as wired it fires on ordinary screen usage.

## Location
- `apps/mobile/android/app/src/main/java/network/reticulum/emergency/SosPlatformCoordinator.java:45` — forwards **both** `ACTION_SCREEN_ON` and `ACTION_SCREEN_OFF` as SOS screen events
- `crates/reticulum_mobile/src/sos_detector.rs` (`screen_event`) — triggers when `power_events.len() >= 3` within `POWER_WINDOW_MS` (2 s)

## Impact
Each power-button press produces one transition (off→on or on→off). Locking the phone, waking it, and locking it again — a completely normal gesture — generates 3 events in well under 2 s and starts the SOS countdown. In an emergency-management app, false distress broadcasts erode trust in real ones and spam the whole team.

The feature is opt-in (`triggerPowerButton`, default off), but once enabled the false-positive path is very reachable.

## Suggested fix
Count full presses rather than transitions, e.g.:
- forward only `ACTION_SCREEN_OFF` events (one per press), or
- keep both edges but require `power_events.len() >= 6` (3 complete off→on cycles), or
- detect an off→on pair in the Java coordinator and submit a single "press" event.

Issue #744: perf(screach): Avoid computing distances for returns that will not reach target

SDSE assigns each pending path a distance to the requested target, then explores the shortest one first. For call instructions, `isTarget` consults the call graph and only considers a call if its callee could reach the target. But for every return instruction it unconditionally says that it may lead to the target.

https://github.com/GaloisInc/grease/blob/504eed88cb2c87a5ed5fbcfb57038483fde5760d/screach/src/Screach/ShortestDistanceScheduler.hs#L114-L127

That matters because a return reaches the target only through its caller, after the current function returns. For example:

```
A() -> calls B() -> returns to A(), which cannot reach target()
```

When SDSE is analysing `B`, it still treats return from B as a potential route to `target` and runs interprocedural distance computation through the return stack. Eventually it can discover that `A` cannot reach the target, but it has already done that work.

We should apply an equivalent reachability check for returns: inspect the return destination/caller in reverse through the call graph or use the symbolic return stack, and only mark a return as an `InterTarget` when returning there could lead to the target.

Issue #793: [Security] Apply a four-day rolling inactivity window to authentication sessions

## Problem

Revalidated against backend `master` at `f082fd84f07f840c60b81d50346cc281c4f655e1` on 2026-08-20.

Authentication sessions currently have one absolute seven-day expiry. Login stores `expires_at = issued_at + 7 days`; refresh rotates the verifier but deliberately reuses the original deadline. Consequently, activity never extends a session, while a completely inactive browser can still refresh until the seventh day.

The approved product policy is different: keep the existing 12-hour access token, but expire a session after approximately four days without use. Extend that four-day window only when refresh succeeds, not on every API request. Active students may therefore remain signed in, while inactive students must authenticate again.

Before: a student signs in Monday at 10:00 and is logged out the following Monday at 10:00 whether or not they used the service.

After: a successful refresh on Thursday at 09:00 moves the inactivity deadline to Monday at 09:00. If no refresh succeeds for four days, the next refresh is rejected and the frontend clears authentication state.

## User story

As a student,
I want my session to remain active while I regularly use Quizzence but expire after several inactive days,
So that I avoid unnecessary daily logins without leaving an abandoned browser authenticated for a full week.

## Scope

- Keep access-token validity at 12 hours.
- Set the refresh/session inactivity window to exactly four days (`345600000` ms).
- Set each new session deadline to four days after successful authentication.
- During refresh, retain the existing JWT validation, session ownership check, pessimistic row lock, refresh-verifier comparison, replay revocation, and fail-closed store behavior.
- Only after every refresh check succeeds, calculate `next_expires_at = now + 4 days`.
- Issue the replacement refresh JWT with that exact deadline and atomically update the existing session's refresh-token hash, `refreshed_at`, and `expires_at` in the current transaction.
- Keep access-token authentication read-only. Ordinary API requests must not update `refreshed_at` or `expires_at` and must not add a database call.
- Preserve the existing cleanup scheduler, logout behavior, replay handling, metrics, and RFC 7807 errors.
- Apply the approved compatibility transition to sessions issued before deployment: retain their existing seven-day deadline until their first successful refresh or existing expiry. Their first successful refresh adopts the four-day rolling window. Full convergence therefore takes no more than seven days.
- Keep session duration backend-authoritative; the frontend continues to clear credentials when refresh or `/auth/me` rejects the session.

## Out of scope

- A hard maximum lifetime for continuously active sessions.
- Per-request or browser-activity writes.
- A frontend-only idle timer.
- Changing JWT storage, cookie policy, OAuth providers, roles, permissions, password policy, or account linking.
- Changing access-token validity from 12 hours.
- Revoking all existing sessions during deployment.
- Adding a schema migration, new table/column, dependency, endpoint, or manual-testing document.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Given a new login, when the session and refresh JWT are issued, then both use a deadline exactly four days after issuance and the response reports `refreshExpiresInMs = 345600000`.
- [ ] Given a valid current refresh token, when refresh succeeds, then the replacement refresh JWT, stored `expires_at`, and response all use exactly `now + 4 days`.
- [ ] Given repeated successful use, when refresh occurs before each inactivity deadline, then the session may remain active beyond four total days without an absolute cap.
- [ ] Given no successful refresh for four days, when refresh is attempted at or after the boundary, then it is rejected with the existing generic `401`, no replacement tokens are issued, and the deadline is not extended.
- [ ] Given an invalid, expired, wrong-owner, replayed, revoked, or persistence-failed refresh, when it is processed, then it never extends the inactivity deadline.
- [ ] Given two concurrent requests using one refresh token, when they race, then the existing lock/replay policy remains intact: only one rotation can succeed and all hash/deadline changes are atomic.
- [ ] Given ordinary bearer-authenticated API requests, when they succeed, then they perform the existing active-session read and never write session activity.
- [ ] Given a pre-deployment seven-day session, when it has not yet refreshed, then its existing deadline remains valid; its first successful refresh adopts a four-day deadline.
- [ ] Given an expired rolling session, when cleanup runs, then the existing indexed cleanup path can remove it without a new scan or relationship traversal.
- [ ] Public request/response field names, status shapes, logout behavior, and password/OAuth login UX remain compatible.

## API changes

- No endpoint, method, request field, response field, or status-code shape changes.
- `JwtResponse.refreshExpiresInMs` now reports four days for a new session and resets to four days after every successful refresh.
- `/api/v1/auth/refresh` retains its current single-use rotation, `401` rejection, replay behavior, and bounded store-failure response.
- No pagination, filtering, sorting, OpenAPI group, authorization, or iOS-specific wire change is introduced.

## Data changes

- Reuse `auth_sessions.created_at`, `refreshed_at`, and `expires_at`; no migration or backfill is required.
- A successful refresh updates the existing row under its current pessimistic lock. It does not insert a new session row.
- Existing rows are intentionally grandfathered until their first successful refresh or current expiry.
- `expires_at` remains indexed and continues to own bounded cleanup.

## Permissions and privacy

- No permission or ownership rule changes.
- Continue binding a session to the user and opaque session ID already validated from the JWT.

Issue #872: feat(architecture): add executable invariant ownership and cross-layer conformance gates

### 📋 Pre-flight Checks

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand this issue needs `status:approved` before a PR can be opened

### 🔍 Problem Description

Engram already has strong technical boundaries and a clear local-first model: SQLite is authoritative, cloud is optional replication, and MCP, HTTP, CLI, TUI, setup, and plugins act as interfaces around the same memory core.

The remaining architectural risk is not a missing feature or an unclear package map. It is that the same domain fact can still be accepted, normalized, projected, or reported differently across layers.

Several open issues show this pressure from different surfaces:

- #814: an observation accepted locally can produce a mutation that cloud rejects, poisoning the sequential push queue.
- #785: a delete can lose its operation semantics and be materialized as an upsert during chunk ingestion.
- #704 and #778: persisted repair/retry state and running autosync state can diverge until restart or stop retrying.
- #614, #698, #749, #750, and #659: project identity can be normalized, detected, displayed, merged, or validated differently.
- #684, #711, #717, #753, and #754: the runtime MCP contract, plugin expectations, tool profiles, and protocol conformance can drift.
- #737: documentation currently has no complete authority map for generated, embedded, and runtime contracts.

Each issue is independently valid and should remain actionable. The architectural gap behind this family is that critical invariants do not yet have an explicit executable owner plus a conformance gate proving that every adapter and projection preserves them.

This tracker proposes that architecture without changing Engram's product model, adding a new service, or weakening the existing issue-first process.




### 💡 Proposed Solution

Adopt two related rules:

1. **Invariant ownership:** each critical semantic rule has exactly one owning bounded context/package.

2. **Published-contract conformance:** every adapter, persistence path, projection, and integration proves that it preserves the owner's contract.

This is an incremental hardening of the current architecture, not a rewrite.

### Proposed ownership map

| Context | Existing owner | Examples of owned invariants |

|---|---|---|

| Memory lifecycle | `internal/store` | Valid observations, sessions, prompts, relations, and atomic durable writes |

| Project identity | `internal/project` | Canonical identity, normalization, ambiguity, and source/path metadata |

| Replication | `internal/sync` and `internal/cloud/*` | Operation preservation, ordering, idempotency, tombstones, retries, and recovery |

| Agent contract | `internal/mcp` | Tool inventory, profiles, schemas, envelopes, and error codes |

| Integration capability | `internal/setup` and thin `plugin/*` adapters | Installed capabilities, hook compatibility, and effective protocol behavior |

The owning package should expose constructors, commands, and results that are valid by construction where repeated issue evidence justifies it.

Downstream layers should translate the published result instead of independently re-deriving the rule.

### Transactional integrity for local writes

For sync-visible changes, the target flow should be:

```text

command

  -> validate owner invariants

  -> write local state

  -> append typed mutation

  -> commit one SQLite transaction

```

If a valid mutation cannot be produced, the sync-visible local change should not commit as if it were safely replicable.

This preserves SQLite as the local authority while preventing records that are valid locally but impossible to replicate.

All observation creation paths should cross the same validation boundary before persistence and mutation enqueue.

Project detection should produce one canonical result that interfaces display and validate without independently renormalizing it.

A sync mutation should carry an explicit operation so a delete is never inferred back into an upsert.

### Versioned mutation semantics

Define a backward-compatible mutation envelope owned by the replication context.

The exact Go representation remains a design decision, but the semantic contract should include:

```text

contract_version

mutation_id

entity_type

entity_id

operation: upsert | delete

canonical_project

occurred_at

payload

checksum

```

Required properties:

- Existing supported chunks and mutations remain readable.

- `delete` remains `delete` through materialization, cloud ingestion, and pull.

- Duplicate delivery is idempotent.

- Invalid payloads are rejected before entering the durable push queue.

- Contract changes are intentional, versioned, and covered by fixtures.

This proposal does not require Event Sourcing, a broker, another service, or a non-Go runtime dependency.

### Recoverable autosync state

Make autosync behavior an explicit and testable state machine:

```text

ready -> materializing -> pushing -> awaiting_ack -> applied

retryable_failure -> backoff -> ready

invalid_mutation -> quarantined

repair_applied -> reload -> ready

failure_ceiling -> degraded, but not permanently dead

```

Required properties:

- A retry ceiling reduces retry pressure but does not silently kill replication forever.

- A permanently invalid mutation is identifiable and cannot invisibly block unrelated work.

- A safe repair invalidates or reloads stale in-memory materialization without process restart.

Issue #1973: feat(review): scope the RDD kill switch per worktree and announce its blast radius

## Pre-flight Checklist

- [x] I have searched [existing issues](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/gentle-ai/issues) and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I understand that PRs will be rejected if the linked issue does not have `status:approved`

## 🔍 Affected Area

CLI (commands, flags)

## 💡 Problem Statement

The RDD kill switch has exactly two scopes, `global` and `clone`. There is no worktree scope, and **linked worktrees silently share the clone-local override** because it is stored under the Git common directory, which every linked worktree shares.

This makes the switch unusable for the multi-agent workflow the product otherwise encourages: several agents working in parallel, one worktree each, off a single clone. Turning reviews off for one of them turns them off for all of them, and nothing says so.

### Reproduction (verified on `main` @ `f25647d4`)

```bash
git init clone-a && cd clone-a
git commit --allow-empty -m init
git worktree add ../wt-b -b featb

# Disable in clone-a ONLY, using the narrowest scope available
gentle-ai review mode disable --scope=clone --cwd clone-a --json
#   "clone_local": "off"
#   "effective":   "off"
#   "source":      "clone_local"
#   "revision":    "sha256:abadcd392ac5189b49c99bdc9963b314d8d8099de11bc569fbd6ed5d07119ef1"

# Now read the sibling worktree, which was never touched
gentle-ai review mode status --cwd ../wt-b --json
#   "clone_local": "off"
#   "effective":   "off"
#   "source":      "clone_local"
#   "revision":    "sha256:abadcd392ac5189b49c99bdc9963b314d8d8099de11bc569fbd6ed5d07119ef1"   ← identical
```

A separate `git clone` is correctly unaffected (`effective: on`, `source: default`). The blast radius is precisely "one clone, all of its worktrees".

### Why it happens

`cloneLocalRDDModeRoot` derives the override directory from `identity.GitCommonDir`:

- `internal/reviewtransaction/rdd_mode.go:528` — `base := filepath.Join(identity.GitCommonDir, ...)`
- Stored at `<git-common-dir>/gentle-ai/review-transactions/rar-authority/v1/rdd-mode/gen-NNNNNNNNNN.json`

Linked worktrees resolve to the same `--git-common-dir`, so they read the same record. This is correct and deliberate for the *authority* store; it is the *policy* switch inheriting that placement that produces the surprise.

### Two aggravating factors

**1. `--scope` defaults to `global`.** `internal/cli/review_mode.go:57` — `flags.String("scope", reviewModeScopeGlobal, ...)`. A plain `gentle-ai review mode disable` writes to `os.UserHomeDir()` and disables RDD for **every repository, clone and worktree of that user**. The narrowest thing a hurried operator can type is also the widest thing the product can do.

**2. The reach is never announced.** `review mode status` reports `source` faithfully, but only if you go and read it *from the other worktree*. Neither `disable` nor `enable` says how far the write it just performed actually reaches.

Precedence (`ResolveRDDMode`, `internal/reviewtransaction/rdd_mode.go:215-231`) is `any off wins, a repository can never force on`. The clone-local override is off-only, so a worktree that needs RDD **cannot opt back in** while its sibling holds the switch off.

### Not in scope for this issue

The consent decline path is correct and should not change. `internal/cli/review_mode.go:619-628`: answering "not now" writes nothing, does not latch, and does not touch the mode — the next candidate is asked again. Only acceptance latches. That asymmetry is deliberate and documented, and it is working.

## 📦 Proposed Solution

Something along these lines, in rough priority order:

**1. Announce the blast radius on write.** Every `enable`/`disable` should state what it just reached — at minimum whether the clone has linked worktrees, and how many. Cheapest fix, closes the silent-surprise hole on its own.

```
Disabled review-driven development for clone /path/to/clone-a.
This reaches all 4 linked worktrees of this clone (wt-b, wt-c, wt-d).
```

**2. Add a `worktree` scope.** Stored per-worktree rather than under the common dir — `git rev-parse --git-dir` resolves to the per-worktree directory (`.git/worktrees/<name>`), which is the natural home. Precedence would extend to `worktree > clone > global`, keeping the off-only rule at every level so no scope can force RDD *on*.

**3. Reconsider the `--scope` default.** Either require `--scope` explicitly for the mutating operations, or default to the narrowest scope rather than the widest. Defaulting a policy write to "everything this user owns" is a sharp edge.

Whichever combination lands, `review mode status` should keep reporting the deciding source, extended to name the deciding *scope* when a worktree-level record exists.

## 🔄 Alternatives Considered

**Document the behavior and stop there.** Cheap, and item 1 above is most of the value. But it leaves the parallel-agent workflow with no way to isolate a single agent, which is the actual user need behind this report.

**Tell users to use separate clones instead of worktrees.** This works today and is the only current answer. It costs a full checkout per agent and gives up the shared object store, which is most of why worktrees are used for this in the first place.

**Make the clone-local override support an allow-list of worktrees.** More flexible than a worktree scope, considerably more state to reconcile, and it puts policy for worktree B inside a record that worktree B does not own. A per-worktree record is simpler to reason about.

6. Begin one narrower read-only re-verification objective against the corrected untracked inventory.

- Both passed and interrupted settlement returned `candidate_unavailable` because one acquire-bound path no longer existed.
- Temporarily materializing the two obsolete paths from the native begin tree allowed the interrupted settlement to commit with `state: proceed`.
- Reset at exact runtime revision was then refused because the objective was open, zero-drift, and still had an attempt available.
- The provider-directed narrower rescope committed only while the obsolete paths were temporarily materialized.
- After removing those temporary obsolete paths, beginning the narrower objective with the corrected untracked selection was rejected as an objective change.
- Beginning with the exact published objective retains the obsolete untracked binding, so it cannot represent the corrected candidate.

Safe opaque runtime references:

- Interrupted objective revision: `sha256:d19b238fbb3460b6706493a384f3feb20d6ee83c7e6fa4d4ec4e18fc91a6c2d3`
- Narrower objective revision: `sha256:dab632c415602a63e4e08c6a760d4049cc477eb07362ade07004319fe47c3a7f`
- Interrupted result: `state: proceed`
- Narrower objective state: open, `next_action: begin`, one-attempt / 400-line bounds

1. Start with untracked files `A` and `B` and acquire an SDD attempt selecting both.

- The corrected candidate remains uncommitted and unchanged after the failed lifecycle operations.
- No delivery, reset, source checkout, or repository publication occurred.

Open and closed issue search completed before this write. ## Three things that will make this gate lie if we skip them

**1. Model + spec pinning.** Selection accuracy is model-dependent — a regression on a small model may not exist on a large one. **2. Blast radius.** Editing tool A's description changes whether A steals traffic from B. So re-eval scope is **changed tools ∪ their confusable neighbors** — and the analyzer's confusable-pairs check is exactly what supplies that neighbor set. Re-evaluating only the changed tools will miss the regression those changes caused elsewhere.

## Default posture

Default to the `manual` provenance subset — human-written queries are the trustworthy signal. Generated cases are reported but shouldn't block a merge by default.

Issue #2436: cluster-only prints "graph.json updated" when to_json refused to write

## What happens

`graphify cluster-only <path>` on a large existing graph computed a clustering, declined to persist it, and then reported success:

```
[graphify] WARNING: new graph has 794784 nodes but existing graph.json has 794903 (net -119).
  Refusing to overwrite. Possible causes: missing chunk files from a previous session, or
  fuzzy dedup collapsed same-named symbols across files during an --update on an already-current
  graph. Run a full rebuild (/graphify .) to be safe, or pass force=True only if you have
  verified the reduction is legitimate.
Loading existing graph...
Graph: 794784 nodes, 1766987 edges
Re-clustering...
Done - 27088 communities. GRAPH_REPORT.md and graph.json updated.
```

Exit code **0**. `graph.json` was **not** written — its mtime was unchanged and only 1.1% of nodes carried a `community`. The guard did its job; the final line contradicts it.

`.graphify_labels.json`, its `.sig`, and `GRAPH_REPORT.md` **were** written, for the clustering that was discarded. So a successful-looking run leaves labels and report describing a clustering the graph does not contain. Anything downstream keyed to community ids is then silently wrong.

We only caught it because our runbook says to verify community coverage after clustering rather than trust the exit code — that habit exists because this cost us a full clustering run once before.

## Suggested fix

Either is enough, both would be better:

1. When `to_json` returns falsy, say so and exit non-zero — `graph.json NOT written: refusing to overwrite (net -119 nodes)` — rather than printing `graph.json updated`.
2. Don't persist labels, `.sig` or `GRAPH_REPORT.md` when the graph write was declined, so the outputs stay consistent with each other.

## Second, separate finding: the -119 is unexplained

The guard's own explanation does not fit our case, and we could not account for the reduction:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Duplicate node ids in `graph.json` | **0** (794,903 nodes, 794,903 distinct, all `str`) |
| `networkx.node_link_graph(raw, edges="links")` | **794,903 nodes, 1,768,522 edges** — no loss |
| `graphify.paths.load_node_link_graph` | same call, so also lossless |
| `prune_dangling_edges` | removes edges only, never nodes |
| graphify's own report after "Loading existing graph..." | **794,784 nodes, 1,766,987 edges** |

So 119 nodes and 1,535 edges disappear between reading the file and reaching the writer, inside graphify, on a graph that plain networkx round-trips intact. We did not use `force=True`, because "verify the reduction is legitimate" is not something we could honestly claim.

Workaround, in case it helps anyone else: load the graph yourself and drive the public API — `load_node_link_graph`, `cluster`, `remap_communities_to_previous`, `label_communities_by_hub`, then `to_json(G, communities, path, community_labels=labels)`. The node count reaching the writer then equals the count on disk, the guard has nothing to fire on, and the output keeps graphify's exact format (`community`, `community_name`, `norm_label`). That produced 100% community coverage on all 794,903 nodes.

Also worth noting for anyone using `cluster-only` to refresh an existing store: it clusters from scratch with no reference to previous membership. Ours renamed 22,507 of 28,004 communities by hub. Community ids are what authored per-cluster content is keyed to, so that is a total loss of that content unless you pass the old membership through `remap_communities_to_previous` yourself. Driving the API with that step gave us 88% retention on the same change.

Versions: graphify 0.9.30, networkx 3.6.1, Python 3.13, macOS.

Issue #2713: T-SQL: a bracketed FOREIGN KEY can drop the child table entirely and emit a self-referencing edge tagged EXTRACTED

## Summary

For some bracket-quoted T-SQL, a `FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES` clause causes the **child table to be
dropped from the graph entirely** and produces a **self-referencing edge on the parent, tagged
`EXTRACTED`**.

`EXTRACTED` means "explicit in the source". There is no `Customer → Customer` reference anywhere in
the input. So this is not a missing edge — it is a **fabricated edge carrying the highest confidence
grade**, which is worse, because the grade is what a reader uses to decide whether to trust it
without checking.

The identical input with brackets removed is extracted correctly.

## Repro

`s.sql`, alone in a directory:

```sql
CREATE TABLE [dbo].[Customer] (
    [CustomerId] INT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    [Name]       NVARCHAR(100) NULL
);
GO

CREATE TABLE [dbo].[Invoice] (
    [InvoiceId]  INT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    [CustomerId] INT NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT [FK_Invoice_Customer] FOREIGN KEY ([CustomerId])
        REFERENCES [dbo].[Customer] ([CustomerId])
);
GO
```

```
graphify . --code-only --force
```

## Actual

```
labels: ['s.sql', 'dbo].[Customer']
edges : [('s', 'contains',   's_dbo_customer', 'EXTRACTED'),
         ('s_dbo_customer', 'references', 's_dbo_customer', 'EXTRACTED')]
```

`[dbo].[Invoice]` is **absent from the graph**. The FK it declares appears as `Customer → Customer`.

## Expected

The same file with brackets removed gives the right answer, so this is the behaviour to match:

```
labels: ['s.sql', 'dbo.Customer', 'dbo.Invoice', ...]
edges : [..., ('s_dbo_invoice', 'references', 's_dbo_customer', 'EXTRACTED')]
```

## What I could and could not isolate

Reproduces deterministically, including with `--force` in a fresh directory, so it is not an
incremental-cache artefact.

I could **not** isolate the trigger. Four plausible causes were each tested and **refuted** — nearby
variants all extract correctly:

| Hypothesis | Test | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Objects after the first are dropped | three bracketed `CREATE TABLE`, no FK | **all three extracted** — refuted |
| A bracketed FK breaks extraction generally | `[dbo].[Beta]` FK → `[dbo].[Alpha]` | **correct edge** — refuted |
| FK column name matching the referenced column name | `AlphaId` → `AlphaId` vs `AlphaId` → `Id` | **both correct** — refuted |
| A parameterised column type (`NVARCHAR(100)`) breaks statement boundaries | with and without | **both correct** — refuted |

So the minimal failing case above is the smallest input I have that fails, and structurally similar
inputs succeed. I did not want to guess further at a mechanism in someone else's parser — the repro
is deterministic, so hopefully it is quicker to bisect from inside.

## Why this matters for schema corpora

The stated value of the SQL path is that **declared foreign keys become high-confidence edges**, and
that is exactly the case failing here. A schema with many FKs is the corpus where the tool should be
strongest; instead some tables vanish silently and some relationships are replaced by self-loops
that look authoritative. Both failures are invisible in the build log — the run exits 0 and reports
a node and edge count that looks reasonable.

For scale, the schema we are indexing declares ~1,365 foreign keys.

## Environment

- graphify **0.9.39**, `tree_sitter_sql` present (confirmed importable)
- Python 3.14.2, Windows 11
- `--code-only`, so this is the local AST path with no LLM involved

## Related

The bracket-quoted identifier label mangling (`dbo].[Customer`) is filed separately. It is visible
in the output above but does not appear to share a trigger with this — every bracketed case mangles
labels, only some drop nodes.

Issue #1796: Inconsistent role gating on delete/restore: Moderators can permanently delete core content

**Describe the bug**

Three related inconsistencies in how `RightService` group checks are applied across delete/restore controllers. Roles are **not hierarchical** (`PERMISSION_SYSTEM.md`), so which group a controller checks decides exactly who can act — and the checks were not applied uniformly.

Grouping these together because they share one root cause and one fix decision: pick the intended rule per operation, then make every controller match.

---

### 1. Permanent deletion of core content is gated on Moderator, not Administrator

For 10 of 13 soft-deletable entities the `isPermanent` branch is reached after **only** a `MODERATOR` check, with no Administrator re-check before the irreversible hard delete.

`api/controllers/v1/cave/delete.js` is representative — `MODERATOR` at line 11, then `deletePermanently` read at line 47 and acted on at line 55, no further gate:

| Gate before hard delete | Controllers |
|---|---|
| `MODERATOR` only | `cave`, `comment`, `description`, `document`, `entrance`, `history`, `location`, `massif`, `organization`, `rigging` |
| Re-checks `ADMINISTRATOR` | `device` (line 13), `sensor-configuration`, `guideline` (line 38) |

`device/delete.js` shows the intended shape: Moderator to soft-delete, Administrator required to escalate to permanent.

Consequence: a Moderator can irreversibly destroy caves, entrances and documents. `PERMISSION_SYSTEM.md` claimed permanent deletion was Administrator-only until this audit; the doc has been corrected to match the code, but the code is likely what's wrong.

### 2. Restore is Moderator-only for every entity except guidelines

12 of 13 restore controllers check `MODERATOR` alone. `guideline/restore.js` (lines 10-14) accepts Moderator **or** Administrator.

So guideline is the outlier here — either it should drop to `MODERATOR` only, or the other 12 should accept both.

### 3. `device`/`sensor-configuration` and `guideline` disagree on restore

A narrower instance of #2 between entities modelled almost identically: `device/restore.js` (line 9) and `sensor-configuration/restore.js` check `MODERATOR` only, while `guideline/restore.js` accepts either role. Their `delete.js` counterparts *all three* accept either role — so within the same entity, delete and restore use different rules.

---

**To Reproduce** (case 1)

1. Authenticate as a user holding **only** the Moderator group.
2. `DELETE /api/v1/caves/<id>?isPermanent=true`
3. The cave is hard-deleted. No Administrator role required.

**Expected behavior**

To be decided as part of this issue — the point is that these should be uniform. Suggested:

- **Permanent deletion** → require `ADMINISTRATOR` in all 10 core-content controllers, matching `device`/`sensor-configuration`/`guideline`.
- **Restore** → settle on one rule and apply it to all 13.

Note that in practice Administrators are usually granted every group, so cases 2 and 3 are mostly latent rather than actively blocking anyone. Case 1 is the one with real exposure, since it grants a destructive power to the lower-privilege role.

**Additional context**

- `api/services/RightService.js` — `G.ADMINISTRATOR`, `G.MODERATOR`, `G.LEADER`; no inheritance between them
- `PERMISSION_SYSTEM.md` → "Known Permission Inconsistencies" documents all three as current observed behaviour, and the permission matrix now reflects the code rather than the intent
- Deliberately **out of scope**: the missing role check on `v1/observation/import` is intentional (observation upload is a core contributor workflow) and should not be changed

Core entities: Portfolio node (hierarchical grouping container); Project (schedule-bearing container with calendars, defaults, codes, baselines, security context); Work breakdown node; Activity (duration, dates, status, logic, calendar, percent complete, assignments); Relationship (directed dependency with type and lag); Milestone (zero-duration checkpoint); Calendar (working-time definition for projects, resources, activities); Baseline snapshot (frozen copy of key schedule fields).

Dependency logic: FS, SS, FF, SF; positive/negative lag; optional comments; batch editing. C

# Improve job filters frontend and backend

Trellis task: `.trellis/tasks/07-28-improve-job-filters`
Priority: `P2`

## Goal
Make the Jobs Filters workflow readable, predictable, and efficient on desktop,
while giving every visible structured filter one coherent frontend-to-backend
contract.

## Requirements
### Filter interaction and layout

- Redesign only the currently visible filter set: Source, Source
  Classification, Employment Type, Canonical Job Taxonomy, Company Industry,
  explicit posted-date range, experience range, and Posting Window presets.
- Replace native multi-selects with collapsible inline selector cards. A closed
  card shows selected count and removable summaries; an open card provides
  search and checkbox selection.
- Use source-grouped paths for Source Classification, a flat checkbox list for
  Employment Type, and hierarchical browsing for Job Taxonomy and Company
  Industry. Keep date, experience, and Posting Window directly visible.
- Make hierarchical selectors parent-first. Major categories are visible before
  collapsed children. Selecting a parent includes all descendants, removes
  redundant selected descendants, and prevents covered descendants from being
  selected until the parent is cleared.
- Optimize for desktop: simple fields use at most two columns and complex
  selectors use the full row. Narrow widths collapse to one usable column; a
  separate mobile drawer is not required.

### Draft and layered-search workflow

- Filter edits are drafts and never request Jobs merely because a selector is
  opened, searched, or changed. Pending state and a discard action must be
  explicit.
- With no applied layers, `Search all jobs` applies the draft as the root
  search. With applied layers, users can either replace all layers with
  `Search all jobs` or append the draft with `Refine current results`.
- Show applied layers as a human-readable stack covering every visible filter.
  A user can inspect, edit in place, remove, or clear all layers. Editing saves
  back to the same position rather than appending.
- `Discard changes` exits draft/edit mode without a request. `Clear all layers`
  clears draft and applied scope, immediately loads unfiltered Jobs, and clears
  restoration state.
- Persist only normalized applied scope in the current tab's `sessionStorage`.
  Refresh restores and reruns it from page one. Closing the tab clears it;
  unapplied drafts, pagination, and the URL are not persisted.

### Backend facets and contracts

- A successful applied search returns Jobs and contextual facet data derived
  from the same validated scope. Draft edits leave displayed facet counts
  unchanged until a successful apply/reset.
- Each facet is calculated from the applied text and other filter dimensions
  while excluding that facet's own field(s) across all layers.
- Return complete active governed catalogs for Source, Employment Type,
  Canonical Job Taxonomy, and Company Industry with distinct available-Job
  counts. Parent counts include descendants without double-counting a Job.
- Keep zero-count governed nodes visible but disabled, except that an already
  selected zero-count value remains visible and removable.
- Source Classification is data-backed until a complete governed hierarchy
  exists: return only source-qualified paths represented by retained searchable
  Jobs, with distinct contextual Job counts.
- Preserve governed stable codes as authority, OR semantics within a filter
  field, AND semantics across fields/layers, the existing legacy adapters, and
  the rule that unspecified experience represents 0–1 years.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] At the demonstrated width, labels, values, help, and actions neither
      overlap nor become unintelligibly clipped; desktop uses at most two
      columns and narrow layouts remain usable in one column.
- [ ] Complex selectors support local search, checkbox selection, removable
      summaries, parent-first browsing, and ancestor/descendant de-duplication.
- [ ] Pending drafts do not fetch Jobs; discard restores the prior state; replace,
      refine, edit, remove, and clear-all each issue the intended normalized
      scope and keep visible results synchronized.
- [ ] Applied layers have complete human-readable summaries and can be edited in
      place, removed individually, or cleared together.
- [ ] Refresh restores only applied layers in the same tab, starts at page one,
      and does not restore drafts or change the URL.
- [ ] Facet counts exclude their own dimension, respect every other applied
      layer/filter, count distinct Jobs, aggregate descendants correctly, and
      stay stable while a draft is pending.
- [ ] Complete active governed catalogs retain zero-count nodes as disabled;
      selected zero-count nodes remain removable; Source Classification remains
      limited to retained source-qualified paths.
- [ ] Existing GET/POST search consumers and current-taxonomy consumers remain
      compatible, and all visible filters retain explicit validated semantics.
- [ ] Frontend and backend automated tests cover the new selectors, state
      transitions, session restoration, layered scope operations, facet
      contracts, date/experience behavior, and compatibility paths.
