source plus opaque revision. It uses typed fields rather than generic facet/tag maps.

- [ ] Parent and superseded chains are axis-explicit, bounded, cycle-safe, and queryable.
- [ ] Repository, authorized REST, and bundle lineage expose run refs separately from sources.
- [ ] Two identical-content runs produce one proposition/source grounding and two run links.
- [ ] Every lookup, join, inverse query, chain, page, and aggregate fails closed across tenants.

Issue #371: @odata.context omits the nested projection under $expand (and drops the expanded nav entirely with no top-level $select)

## Summary
`@odata.context` omits the nested projection under `$expand` — a request combining `$select` with a nested `$select` inside `$expand` (e.g. `$select=Name&$expand=Parts($select=Sku,Price)`) emits the flat context suffix `#Set(Name,Parts)` where §10.9/§10.10 require the nested form `#Set(Name,Parts(Sku,Price))`. When there is no top-level `$select` at all, the context drops the expanded navigation from the suffix entirely rather than reflecting it.

## Evidence
```
REQ: GET http://localhost:5099/v2/Movies?$select=Title&$expand=Studio($select=Name)&$top=1
STATUS: 200
BODY: {"@odata.context":"http://localhost:5099/v2/$metadata#Movies(Title,Studio)",...}
  -> context says (Title,Studio); expected (Title,Studio(Name)). The payload itself IS correctly projected — only the context URL is wrong.

Collection nav, same shape:
GET /v2/Studios?$select=Name&$expand=Movies($select=Title,Year)&$top=1
  @odata.context = http://localhost:5399/v2/$metadata#Studios(Name,Movies)

Single entity:
GET /v2/Movies(1)?$select=Title&$expand=Studio($select=Name)
  @odata.context = http://localhost:5399/v2/$metadata#Movies(Title,Studio)/$entity

$expand without a top-level $select drops the expansion from the context entirely:
GET /v2/Movies?$expand=Studio($select=Name)&$top=1
  @odata.context = http://localhost:5399/v2/$metadata#Movies   <-- no mention of Studio at all
```
**Code**: `OhDataEndpointFactory.cs:3852-3853` (`AppendSelectSuffix`, a flat comma-join, structurally incapable of nesting); `:2554-2583` (`ExtractSelectedProperties` appends the nav as a bare name, discarding `ensi.SelectAndExpand`); call sites `:4467, 4980, 5151, 5349, 3967`.

## Spec
Part 1 §10.9 (Collection of Projected Expanded Entities) / §10.10 (Projected Expanded Entity) — the context URL for a projected expanded entity/collection carries the nested suffix, e.g. `#Movies(Title,Studio(Name))`.

## Suggested fix
Rework `AppendSelectSuffix`/`ExtractSelectedProperties` to recursively include each expanded navigation's own `$select`/`$expand` suffix (`ensi.SelectAndExpand`) rather than flat-joining bare navigation names, and ensure a navigation with a nested `$select` but no top-level `$select` still appears in the context suffix.

Issue #409: Report parent reconcile jobs as active when descendant work is leased

## Summary

Floecat reports parent reconcile jobs as `WAITING` even when they have active
descendant work leased to an executor. This makes the top-level job list imply
that no work is occurring.

## Motivation

Operators use the top-level job listing to determine where Floecat is actually
sending work and which connector/table is consuming executor capacity.

If a parent remains displayed as `WAITING` while its child file groups are
leased and running, the listing hides the active workload. In particular, it
is not possible to identify which job tree is occupying Floescan ingest slots
without recursively inspecting individual job trees.

The top-level listing should make active work visible so an operator can see
where execution is landing, identify starvation or imbalance, and make
informed cancellation or scheduling decisions.

## Observed behavior

A snapshot-plan job for `floedb.obs.floe_prod_otel_metrics@813631` is shown as
`WAITING`:

- Job: `6b44f595-fdad-4d9f-97fd-7c4e9135b206`
- Kind: `plan_snapshot`

At the same time, it has 15 descendant `exec_file_group` jobs in `RUNNING`
state, all leased to `floescan_ingest`.

The root and connector-parent job list therefore shows `WAITING` while ingest
is actively scanning files for that job tree.

## Expected behavior

A job with no active descendant work should remain `WAITING`.

A job with one or more leased or running descendants should be reported as
active in user-facing status output. This applies recursively to snapshot,
table, and connector parents.

The internal lifecycle state can remain unchanged where necessary. The change
is to the effective, aggregate state presented by job APIs and CLI output.

## Proposed effective-state rules

- `RUNNING` or `ACTIVE`: any descendant is leased or running.
- `QUEUED`: no descendant is running and work is queued but not yet leased.
- `WAITING`: no descendant is running or queued for execution; the job is
  awaiting planning, dependency completion, retry time, or an external event.
- Terminal: all descendants are terminal and the parent has reached its final
  outcome.

The output should preserve the underlying job state when useful, for example:

```text
STATE    EFFECTIVE_STATE
WAITING  ACTIVE
```

Alternatively, present `ACTIVE` as the primary state with detail that the
parent planner itself is waiting.

## Acceptance criteria

- A snapshot parent with one or more running file-group children is displayed
  as active.
- Table and connector parents inherit active status from running descendants.
- A parent with queued but no leased descendants is not displayed as active.
- Terminal and cancelled children do not keep a parent active.
- CLI and job-list APIs use the same effective-state calculation.
- Tests cover a waiting snapshot parent with running file-group children.

### Summary
After upgrading from `2.0.0` to `2.1.0`, it seems like composition `nodes` fragment is being truncated to a fixed depth, omitting nested child nodes. The issue persists on `2.2.0`.

### Context
We bind a shared Optimizely Forms container (`_section` base type, `OptiFormsContainerData`) into page experiences via composition. Our React component resolves it through the standard registry binding:

```ts
initReactComponentRegistry({
  resolver: { OptiFormsContainerData: OptiFormsContainerData },
});
```

and reads its child tree from `content.nodes` (populated by the SDK's own generic composition query — we don't author that query ourselves for this path).

After upgrading `@optimizely/cms-sdk` from `2.0.0` to `2.1.0`, the `nodes` array returned for this container is silently truncated. Deeply nested structural nodes (Form `step` > `row` > `column` > form-field `component`) now stop at `column` — the `column` nodes report `nodes: undefined`/omitted, so the actual field elements (`OptiFormsTextboxElement`, `OptiFormsSubmitElement`, etc.) never reach our component at all.

### Root cause (as far as we can tell from `dist`)
In `2.0.0`, the generic `ICompositionNode` fragment used the `@recursive` directive for structural nodes:

```
fragment ICompositionNode on ICompositionNode { ... ...on CompositionStructureNode { nodes @recursive } ... }
```

In `2.1.0`+, this was replaced with a fixed-depth, hand-unrolled fragment generated by `buildNestedCompositionNodes(depth)` (currently called with `depth = 4`), per [this comment](https://github.com/episerver/content-js-sdk/blob/d79e697e91e7a1822ba79fe5fa932b6359b9bc9e/packages/optimizely-cms-sdk/src/util/baseTypeUtil.ts#L70):

```js
// NOTE: Temporary workaround for Graph issue with @recursive directive.
// This function will not be used once Graph properly supports @recursive.
```

### How to deal with this?
- A minor version (`2.0.0` → `2.1.0`) shouldn't silently reduce the queried composition depth for existing consumers — this should at minimum be called out as a breaking change in the changelog.
- Is there any way to configure the maximum depth? If not, is our only option to manually re-fetch the content tree until the `@recursive` directive is implemented?

### Reproduction example
Minimal reproduction: any `_section` content type with a composition >4 structural levels deep (e.g. Forms' `step > row > column > component`) rendered via a component bound in `initReactComponentRegistry`, comparing the resolved `content.nodes` before/after the `2.0.0` → `2.1.0` upgrade. Issue #2249: Guest access to random tables and card decks in host/guest VTT sessions

Follow-up to #2247 (random roll tables and custom card decks, spec `157-random-tables-decks`).

Tables and decks ship **host-only**. Guests in a VTT session cannot see, roll, or draw from them. This is a deliberate deferral recorded in the spec's Out of Scope and in `research.md` R11 — not an oversight — but it should not be forgotten.

## Why they're absent today

- `GuestExporter.export` takes an explicit allow-list of content kinds (entities, maps, canvases, assetManifest), so a new kind simply isn't published into the guest snapshot.
- `GuestVaultStore` is a read-only snapshot, and the P2P protocol carries vault mutations host→guest only (`ENTITY_UPDATE`, `GRAPH_SYNC`, `MAP_SYNC`). Guests have no vault write path at all.

Shipping without this degrades cleanly: guests just don't see tables or decks.

## The design is already settled

Tables and decks need **different** mechanisms, and both patterns already exist in the codebase.

**Tables — stateless, use the dice pattern.** `vtt-chat-manager.svelte.ts` resolves `/roll` locally on the sender's machine via `diceEngine.evaluate` and broadcasts only the result. Rolling a table consumes nothing shared, so it can work the same way: publish tables into the guest snapshot and let guests resolve locally.

The wrinkle is nested references — a guest can only resolve `{creature}` if that table was published too. The export needs to include the reference closure of every published table, or mark unresolved fragments.

**Decks — mutate shared state, use the token pattern.** A guest sends `TOKEN_ADD_REQUEST`; the host validates, mutates, and broadcasts `TOKEN_STATE_UPDATE`. Guests request, the host decides.

Draws must work this way. The discard pile is shared mutable state and only the host has a vault to persist it to. If guests resolved draws locally, two guests could draw the same card and the host's `state.json` would learn of neither.

```
guest → DECK_DRAW_REQUEST { deckName, count }
host  → draws against its own deck state, writes state.json
host  → broadcasts the result to all participants
```

This is the genuine concurrency case for this feature — two guests pressing draw in the same second. It's resolved by host authority, not by a merge.

## Scope sketch

- [ ] Extend `GuestExporter` to publish tables (with reference closure) and deck definitions
- [ ] Add `DECK_DRAW_REQUEST` / deck state broadcast to `p2p-protocol.ts`
- [ ] Add a deck handler alongside `vtt-handler.ts`, following the token request/broadcast shape
- [ ] Guest-side UI for rolling a published table and requesting a draw
- [ ] Decide whether guests may roll host tables that were not explicitly published (probably no — Fog of War already governs what guests can see)

## Prerequisite

Land #2247 first. Guest support is only worth building once decks have proven themselves in single-player use.

Issue #9: Vulnerable transitive dependencies via react-scripts@5.0.1 (nth-check ReDoS, postcss, webpack-dev-server advisories)

## Summary
The frontend depends on `react-scripts@5.0.1`, which pulls in a well-known set of transitively vulnerable packages. A fresh `npm install` in `frontend/` produces multiple high-severity `npm audit` findings that ship with the build tooling and, in some cases, into the bundle.

## Evidence
- `frontend/package.json` — `"react-scripts": "5.0.1"`.
- Known advisories reachable via CRA 5.0.1's dependency tree:
  - `nth-check` < 2.0.1 — inefficient regex complexity / ReDoS (GHSA-rp65-9cf3-cjxr), via `svgo` → `@svgr/webpack`.
  - `postcss` < 8.4.31 — line-return parsing (GHSA-7fh5-64p2-3v2j), via `resolve-url-loader`.
  - `webpack-dev-server` <= 5.2.0 — source code exfiltration advisories (GHSA-9jgg-88mc-972h, GHSA-4v9v-hfq4-rm2v).

## Why this matters
CRA 5.0.1 is effectively unmaintained and cannot be patched without overrides/ejecting. The `webpack-dev-server` advisories matter if the dev server is ever exposed on a non-loopback interface; the `nth-check` ReDoS ships through the SVG pipeline.

## Attack or failure scenario
A developer runs `npm start` on a shared/exposed network; the vulnerable `webpack-dev-server` can leak source to a malicious page the developer visits. In build tooling, the ReDoS path can be triggered by crafted SVG assets.

## Root cause
Reliance on the deprecated Create React App toolchain with pinned vulnerable transitive dependencies.

## Recommended fix
- Run `npm audit` and apply `overrides` to bump `nth-check`, `postcss`, and `webpack-dev-server` to patched versions, or
- Migrate off CRA to a maintained toolchain (Vite).
- Bind the dev server to loopback only.

## Acceptance criteria
- `npm audit` reports no high/critical advisories, or documented overrides pin patched versions.
- Dev server is not exposed beyond localhost.

## Suggested labels
dependencies, security

## Priority
P2

## Severity
Medium — dev-time/tooling exposure; not a direct production-runtime RCE.

## Confidence
Likely — based on CRA 5.0.1's known dependency tree; confirm with `npm audit`.

Issue #322: [BUG] ImportError: cannot import name 'TrainedQuantizationThresholdPass' from 'esp_ppq.quantization.optim.training' due to circular import

### Checklist

- [x] Checked the issue tracker for similar issues to ensure this is not a duplicate.
- [x] Provided a clear description of your suggestion.
- [x] Included any relevant context or examples.

### Issue or Suggestion Description

**Describe the bug**

When trying to import `TrainedQuantizationThresholdPass` from `esp_ppq.quantization.optim.training`, an `ImportError` occurs. However, after calling `importlib.reload(training)`, the class becomes available. This suggests a circular import issue within the module.

**To Reproduce**

1. Install `esp-ppq` in a clean environment.
2. Run the following Python code:

```python
from esp_ppq.quantization.optim.training import TrainedQuantizationThresholdPass
```

3. Observe the error:

```
ImportError: cannot import name 'TrainedQuantizationThresholdPass' from 'esp_ppq.quantization.optim.training'
```

**Expected behavior**

The import should succeed directly without needing to reload the module.

**Actual behavior**

The class is not defined on first import. `dir(training)` does not contain `TrainedQuantizationThresholdPass`. After `importlib.reload(training)`, the class becomes available.

**Temporary workaround**

```python
import esp_ppq.quantization.algorithm.training  # preload dependency first
from esp_ppq.quantization.optim.training import TrainedQuantizationThresholdPass
```

Or:

```python
import esp_ppq.quantization.optim.training as training
import importlib
importlib.reload(training)
from esp_ppq.quantization.optim.training import TrainedQuantizationThresholdPass
```

**Root cause analysis**

The issue appears to be a circular import between:
- `esp_ppq.quantization.optim.training` (which contains `TrainedQuantizationThresholdPass`)
- `esp_ppq.quantization.algorithm.training` (which is imported via `from ...algorithm.training import *` at the top of `optim/training.py`)

When `optim.training` is first imported, it attempts to import `algorithm.training`, which in turn references `optim.training` (which is still being initialized). This results in an incomplete module where the class definition at line 1128 is never executed.

**Environment**

- Package version: `esp-ppq` (please specify version)
- Python version: 3.10
- PyTorch version: 2.1.0
- OS: Linux (Huawei Cloud)

**Additional context**

The file `esp_ppq/quantization/optim/training.py` clearly contains the class definition:

```python
class TrainedQuantizationThresholdPass(TrainingBasedPass):
    ...
```

And `esp_ppq/quantization/optim/__init__.py` exports it:

```python
from .training import BiasCorrectionPass, LearnedStepSizePass, RoundTuningPass, TrainedQuantizationThresholdPass
```

However, the circular dependency prevents the class from being defined during the initial import.

**Suggested fix**

Consider restructuring the imports to avoid the circular dependency, e.g.:
- Move shared base classes to a separate module
- Use lazy imports inside methods rather than at module level
- Refactor `algorithm.training` to not depend on `optim.training` at import time

Issue #2301: Sandbox flatten commits per-task scratch (/tmp, .venv, caches) into permanent images — 16.36 of 18.01 GiB in one snapshot, paid twice

## Measured, not inferred

Host forensics on aios-hil-01 (2026-08-28, read-only, ledger closed on two independent substrates to 0.01 GiB).

The per-session sandbox flatten — `GET /containers/{id}/export` piped to import, producing `aios-sbx-default-sess_<session_id>:latest` — is the producer of 98.6% of in-window disk allocation.

Dominant event, 01:38:27Z, snapshot `1915877`:

```
snapshot 1915877   19,336,183,808 B = 18.01 GiB  (847,791 inodes)
blob 3ade623b9185   6,377,786,117 B              (same commit, compressed half)
```

**Inside that snapshot, `/tmp` is 16.36 GiB of the 18.01.** Contents: 245 accumulated per-task scratch directories, including **42 full `eumemic-company` clones at ~400 MB each**, `pytest-of-root` (with four copies of a 52 MB fixture), `.mypy_cache/cache.db`, `.venv` trees, and `~/.cache/ms-playwright` webkit builds.

Never cleaned between tasks. The flatten then persists all of it into an image permanently.

**The cost is paid twice** — once as a compressed content blob, once as an unpacked overlayfs snapshot.

## Why this is the highest-leverage fix

Excluding ephemeral scratch from the flatten recovers **16.36 of 18.01 GiB in the worst observed case, and saves it twice** (blob + snapshot). No reclaimer can match that, because a reclaimer runs after the bytes have already been written twice and must then argue about what is safe to delete.

Note the ordering: **there is currently no gate on this host** (the build freeze is a declared posture agents re-assert, not an enforced threshold — growth continued straight through it). So until a gate exists, a reclaimer races an unbounded producer. Fixing the producer is the only change that reduces the rate rather than the backlog.

## Fix direction

Either:

1. **Exclude ephemeral paths from the export** — `/tmp`, `.venv`, `.mypy_cache`, `pytest-of-*`, `~/.cache/ms-playwright`, `.git` clones under scratch roots; or
2. **Clean sandbox `/tmp` before the flatten**, not just during the session's life.

(1) is preferable: it is enforced at the commit boundary and cannot be defeated by a task that writes scratch after the last cleanup.

**Caution against a naive exclusion list.** A session may legitimately keep working state under `/tmp`. The exclusion must be by *recognised throwaway shape* (a directory containing `.git` that is a re-clonable remote, a pytest tmpdir, a package cache), not by path prefix alone — the same discipline `scratch_reaper.sh` already uses: anything unrecognised is kept and reported, never silently dropped.

## Acceptance criteria

- A flatten of a session with a deliberately-populated scratch `/tmp` produces an image whose size is within a stated bound of the same session with an empty `/tmp` — **measured, not asserted**.
- The exclusion **discriminates**: prove it drops a pytest tmpdir / repo clone **and** preserves an unrecognised user directory under `/tmp`. An exclusion seen only excluding is indistinguishable from one that excludes everything.
- A session whose real working state lives under an excluded path must still resume correctly — or the exclusion must refuse and report rather than silently lose it.

## Related

- Storage lives in `/var/lib/containerd` (116 GB) on this host, not `/var/lib/docker` (989 MB) — dockerd runs with `--containerd=/run/containerd/containerd.sock`. Any tooling that inspects `/var/lib/docker` is looking at 0.8% of the data.
- `patterns/disk-control-loop.md` in eumemic-company documented this class ("du the fs, docker df is blind to /srv, /var") two months ago; it was not consulted before this incident.
- Companion issues: sandbox-image GC, and the missing host-level gate.

### 1. Summary (Required)

New holon lineages acquire `OwnedBy → current HolonSpace` from their bound `TransactionContext`; ordinary commit materializes the inverse `HolonSpace ─Owns→ Holon` SmartLink. ---

### 2. Problem Statement (Required)

`AllHolonNodes` is a storage-owned global-discovery index. It duplicates a semantic topology already defined in the MAP Core Schema:

    Holon --OwnedBy--> HolonSpace
    HolonSpace --Owns--> Holon

The schema already defines `HolonSpace`, `OwnedBy`, and its `Owns` inverse; `OwnedBy` is an `InstanceRelationship` of `HolonType`. The missing behavior is runtime materialization and lifecycle policy, not a new query model.

Today:

- `MutationFacade::new_holon` creates a transient holon without `OwnedBy`.
- `GuestHolonService::get_all_holons_internal` reads `get_all_holon_ids()` from `AllHolonNodes`.
- Guest commit processing already persists a declared relationship and its descriptor-resolved inverse as ordinary SmartLinks.
- Version-producing commits replay their full relationship scope, so membership must be protected from becoming one link per historical version.
- Existing count fixtures include the local-space bootstrap holon because it is persisted; this issue intentionally changes `GetAllHolons` to return owned members rather than the space anchor.

      → TransactionAction::GetAllHolons

Issue #661: [sub issue] Storage SL5b-V1 — Holon space membership

### 1. Summary (Required)

**What is the enhancement?**

Make `Holon --OwnedBy--> HolonSpace` and its `HolonSpace --Owns--> Holon` inverse real, persisted
relationships, correct across the whole holon lifecycle: a new lineage acquires membership when it
is published, a new version inherits its lineage root's rather than acquiring its own, and a deleted
holon has its membership retracted.

Membership becomes queryable through ordinary relationship traversal — ask a holon which space owns
it, ask a space what it owns — with no new read API and no change to `GetAllHolons`.

---

### 2. Problem Statement (Required)

**Why is this needed?**

The MAP Core Schema declares `OwnedBy` / `Owns` in `schema-src/core/relationship-types.tdl`, and
`root.tdl` puts `OwnedBy` in `HolonType`'s `InstanceRelationships`, so every holon's effective
contract already includes it. Nothing writes or reads it. `CoreRelationshipTypeName::OwnedBy` and
`::Owns` exist in `relationship_names.rs` purely so the names are spellable.

The consequence is that a holon cannot answer which space it belongs to, and a space cannot
enumerate its members, even though the schema says both should be possible. Whole-space discovery is
served instead by `AllHolonNodes`, a storage-owned global index that duplicates this topology
(#642 §2).

This slice closes the gap between the declared schema and the persisted graph. It does **not** touch
discovery — that is [SL5b-V2](storage_sl5b_v2_issue.md).

---

### 3. Dependencies (Required)

**Does this depend on other issues or features?**

- Depends on PR #637 (Storage SL5a): the `HolonNodeUpdates` revision index is retired.
- Depends on the bootstrap `LocalHolonSpace` anchor existing, which
  `dance_adapter::init_guest_context` guarantees before any dance body runs.
- Does **not** depend on `QueryExpression` / `QueryDance` (#642 §3).
- Does **not** depend on, and is not blocked by, V2 or the `AllHolonNodes` teardown.

Nothing depends on this slice landing except V2.

---

### 4. Proposed Solution (Required)

**How would you solve it?**

**4.1 Author membership when a lineage is published.** `commit_holon`'s `ForCreate` arm calls
`stage_space_membership` (`commit_functions.rs`), which stages `OwnedBy → current HolonSpace` on the
staged holon. The ordinary relationship pass then persists it and materializes the `Owns` inverse
through the existing `save_smartlinks_for_collection`. This mirrors the adjacent
`stage_predecessor_relationship`, which already mutates a staged holon mid-commit for the same
reason.

It is called *after* `persist_holon` returns, so the new lineage's own id is available to the
self-ownership guard below.

**4.2 A space does not own itself.** `stage_space_membership` returns early when the holon being
published is the space itself. The `LocalHolonSpace` anchor is exempt in practice because
`create_local_space_holon` publishes it through `persist_holon` directly and it never reaches
`commit` — the guard makes the rule hold on its own terms rather than as a consequence of that
routing.

**4.3 Do not re-anchor membership on a new version.** A version-producing commit replays the full
relationship scope against the *new* version's id, which would make the space own the lineage root
and every version after it separately (#642 §8 rejects this). `RelationshipCommitScope` gains a
`FullExceptMembership` variant, set by `prepare_new_version_relationship_commit_scope()` and used by
the `ForUpdateNewVersion` arm. It is a commit *scope* rather than a check on staged state because by
the time the relationship pass reads it the holon is already `Committed` and its version-producing
origin is no longer visible.

**4.4 Write membership before anything that can fail.** The relationship pass stops at a source
holon's first failing relationship, and undescribed holons with freeform relationships fail there by
design (`simple_add_remove_related_holons_fixture` is the canonical case). `OwnedBy` is therefore
ordered first under `Full` scope, so a failing user relationship cannot preempt membership.

**4.5 Resolve the inverse structurally.** `resolve_inverse_relationship_name`
(`inverse_resolution.rs`) short-circuits `OwnedBy → Owns` without descriptor resolution. The general
path goes through the source holon's `DescribedBy`, which membership cannot rely on twice over:
undescribed holons commit successfully today, and on the first core-schema load the `OwnedBy`
descriptor is itself among the holons being staged. The TDL header already describes this
relationship as infrastructure-supplied.

**4.6 Retract membership on delete.** `delete_holon_node` deletes only the `LocalHolonSpace` path
link and the entry; every SmartLink survives it. `delete_holon_internal` gains
`retract_space_membership`, which deletes the `Owns` link on the space and the `OwnedBy` link on the
holon. The space's inverse view is retracted first, since that is the side a future discovery
implementation reads. It lives in `guest_holon_service.rs` rather than `persistence_layer`, which is
deliberately descriptor-unaware.

**4.7 Do not skip quietly.** `stage_space_membership` warns when no space is bound to the
transaction. That branch should be unreachable, which is exactly why silence there would hide a
regression.

**No new read code is required.** `related_holons("OwnedBy")` and `related_holons("Owns")` are
already served by `fetch_related_holons_internal` via `expand_from_source`. That is what makes this
a vertical slice rather than a write-only layer: the capability is observable the moment the writes
land.

| `happ/crates/holons_guest/src/guest_shared_objects/commit_functions.rs` | `stage_space_membership` + its `ForCreate` call site |

Issue #37: libvirt-vm-pool generates cloud-init network config for eth0 only

## Summary

`@evrardjp/libvirt-vm-pool` generates NoCloud `network-config` with the guest interface hardcoded as `eth0`. Arch cloud images commonly use predictable interface names such as `ens3` or `enp1s0`, so the configured static address may never be applied and downstream SSH readiness times out.

The generated `user-data` already installs OpenSSH and runs `systemctl enable --now sshd`. The observed failure therefore does not show that the SSH startup command is absent; it shows that the guest cannot be reached at the configured address when the seed targets a nonexistent interface.

## Evidence

The VM-pool implementation currently renders:

```yaml
network-config:
  version: 2
  ethernets:
    eth0:
      addresses: [<static-address>/<prefix>]
```

In the same seed, it renders:

```yaml
packages:
  - openssh
runcmd:
  - systemctl enable --now sshd
```

The related `@evrardjp/arch-cloud-init` extension already supports `networkInterfaceMatch` and defaults it to `en*`, specifically to match common predictable libvirt interface names.

## Reproduction

1. Define an Arch VM in `@evrardjp/libvirt-vm-pool` with a static address and `bootstrapSSHUser`.
2. Run the pool `sync` method.
3. Observe that libvirt successfully defines and starts the domain and the pool reports `currentState: running`.
4. Run `@keeb/ssh/host.waitForConnection` against the configured address.
5. The SSH readiness check times out after 360 seconds.

Concrete observed VM configuration:

```yaml
name: development-vm
desiredState: running
ipAddress: 192.168.164.40
prefixLength: 24
gateway: 192.168.164.1
bootstrapSSHUser:
  username: admin
  publicKeyPath: ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
```

Observed failure:

```text
SSH not reachable on 192.168.164.40 after 360s
```

## Expected behavior

The generated network configuration should match the actual guest interface, allowing cloud-init to configure the static address and making the bootstrap SSH service reachable.

## Proposed fix

- Add a VM option such as `networkInterfaceMatch`, consistent with `@evrardjp/arch-cloud-init`.
- Default it to `en*` for Arch/libvirt cloud images.
- Render cloud-init v2 matching configuration rather than a literal `eth0` key.
- Include seed inputs in an artifact fingerprint, or otherwise regenerate the cloud-init ISO when network/bootstrap settings change. The current implementation only creates the ISO when the path is absent, which can preserve stale seed configuration.

## Additional note

Changing `desiredState` from `running` to `reachable` does not solve this. In the current VM-pool implementation, `reachable` performs the same substrate actions as `running` and only publishes reachability intent for downstream models.

Issue #14: Implement the unified Subagent lifecycle and communication protocol

## Problem Statement

Static `interactive`/`auto-exit` modes and parent-relayed results cannot represent explicit settlement/completion, direct durable collaboration, capability-scoped authority, crash-safe obligations, bounded operational recovery, or passive human visibility. One consolidated contract is required so implementation does not infer completion, duplicate Agent payloads, lose Requests, report uncertain work as successful, or split authority across incompatible interfaces.

## Solution

Implement one Pi-extension-owned collaboration protocol. An Agent is a durable Pi session; each Subagent activation has explicit work and terminal state. Agent Control provides discriminated messaging, explicit activation with Activation Intent, Delegated Activation Approval, lifecycle controls, and durable Human Interrupt. Recipient Inbox Routers accept direct Agent payloads; a live Owner hosts workflow control without brokering them; Workflow-scoped SQLite stores coordination pointers and fences, not copied Agent-authored payloads.

The protocol enforces Workflow membership, Addressability, Child Control, Request/approval authority, ownership fencing, completion gates, obligation-preserving cancellation, one Automatic Recovery activation, state-based deadlock detection, incident-scoped moderation, and passive attention/Direct Children projections. Herdr remains only the terminal surface. The integrated body, [issue #9](https://github.com/ewgdg/pi-herdr-subagents/issues/9), [#39 and resolved #40–#43/#45](https://github.com/ewgdg/pi-herdr-subagents/issues/39), and synchronized `CONTEXT.md` supply the settled contract; this body and current `CONTEXT.md` control conflicts.

## User Stories

Users need one predictable lifecycle, unchanged Owner behavior, durable direct collaboration, honest passive visibility, and focused UI. Owners need one nested Workflow and workflow-wide control; Spawners need atomic kickoff, bounded child authority, policy and approval context; Agents need durable identity, explicit activation/wait/completion, correlated messaging, cancellation/recovery, and ownership safety; Moderators need scoped incidents and Owner Handoff; maintainers need one state model and black-box contract tests.

## Implementation Decisions

### 1. Normative scope and precedence

The following are normative requirements unless explicitly listed under **Reserved implementation choices**.

- The redesign MUST be implemented entirely in the Pi extension. Herdr MUST remain unchanged.
- This integrated specification and the synchronized current `CONTEXT.md` MUST override conflicting earlier ticket text, including the issue #9 baseline where a later listed amendment has deliberately superseded it.
- Core support for current `interactive` and static `auto-exit` behavior MUST be removed rather than retained through compatibility adapters.
- The implementation MUST NOT introduce backend-less operation, alternative execution backends, global cross-Workflow discovery, or new token/cost instrumentation.
- The Cooperative Trust Model MUST be preserved: protocol capabilities prevent accidental routing and authority transfer; they are not an adversarial filesystem or process sandbox.

### 2. Normative architectural seams

The implementation MUST preserve five deep seams:

1. **Agent Control** — the model-facing interface for actionable messaging, durable Human Interrupts, self-completion, Request/activation cancellation, interruption, and read-only inspection.
2. **Workflow Control Plane** — hosted by the live Workflow Owner Pi process; owns Workflow membership, capability checks, ownership fences, Request and Operational Incident state, recovery, deadlock detection, pending-input metadata, and workflow-wide attention.
3. **Recipient Inbox Router** — one per live recipient; validates and finalizes ordinary message acceptance, owns recipient ordering, rebuilds pending delivery, and commits Inbox Batches to that recipient's transcript.
4. **Workflow coordination store** — Workflow-scoped SQLite for coordination state, metadata, ordering, pointers, and fences, but never duplicate Agent-authored payloads.
5. **Observability projection** — derives status, attention, roster, and diagnostics without creating model turns or mutating lifecycle state.

The Workflow Control Plane MUST be a control plane, not a message broker. Agent-authored payloads MUST travel directly from sender-side Agent Control to the addressed Recipient Inbox Router over local IPC. The Workflow Owner MUST NOT relay peer payloads or write peer transcripts.

When the Workflow Owner process is not running:

- durable coordination state MUST remain intact;
- direct communication between reachable Recipient Inbox Routers MAY continue;
- Workflow-wide recovery, deadlock detection, incident creation, and attention automation MUST pause;
- Owner-directed runtime Protocol Notices MUST remain durably pending until the Owner is resumed.

### 3. Identity, membership, visibility, and authority

#### Identity and visibility

- An Agent MUST be exactly one durable Pi session identified by UUID. Resume preserves identity; create/fork/clone creates another Agent.
- A Subagent is any non-Owner Agent governed by activation lifecycle, including Moderator.
- One permanent Owner identity roots each Workflow; every descendant remains in it at every depth. Owner stays a normal user-driven Pi session with no activation lifecycle, typed waiting, `agent_complete`, or Automatic Recovery.
- Knowing an in-Workflow Agent ID grants only direct actionable messaging, minimal identity/projected-status inspection, and read-only discovery of its complete transcript path. Sharing the ID delegates only those capabilities—never enumeration, transcript mutation, lifecycle/Request authority, Spawner/Child Control, ownership, or cross-Workflow access.
- A child initially knows its direct Spawner. Owner ID MUST NOT be injected into every descendant; escalation SHOULD follow the Spawner chain

Issue #6876: [Infisical] Recursive find overwrites duplicate SecretKey values within one selected subtree

**Describe the bug**

After #6821, a non-empty `dataFrom.find.path` scopes the Infisical list request, so the sibling-folder case in #6230 (`/app/FOOBAR` and `/crons/FOOBAR`) arrives in separate responses and resolves correctly. A different case is still open: two secrets with the same `SecretKey` inside one selected recursive subtree, for example `/app/FOOBAR` and `/app/sub/FOOBAR`. `GetAllSecrets` returns `map[string][]byte` keyed on `SecretKey`, so both rows land under the same `FOOBAR` key and one overwrites the other. Which one wins is not stable across reconciles.

**To Reproduce**

1. An Infisical project seeded with:

```
/app/FOOBAR      = root-value
/app/sub/FOOBAR  = nested-value
/app/ONLY_ROOT   = root-only
```

2. A store pointing at that project with `recursive: true`, and one ExternalSecret:

```yaml
dataFrom:
  - find:
      path: /app
```

3. Reconcile and read the `FOOBAR` key in the target Secret.

Measured against Infisical `v0.158.0`, ESO built from `main` after #6821. Twelve reconciles with `SkipUniqueValidation` disabled returned `nested-value` all twelve times. Twelve reconciles with `SkipUniqueValidation` enabled (the change proposed in #6349) returned:

```
FOOBAR=nested-value   10
FOOBAR=root-value      2
```

Nothing changed in Infisical between reconciles.

**Expected behavior**

A recursive find should not silently or nondeterministically pick one of several source secrets that map to the same Kubernetes Secret key. The behavior should be explicit. Options, in rough order of how much they change:

1. Fail with a deterministic error that lists the colliding source paths.
2. Define and document a deterministic precedence rule.
3. Carry the source path into the result so `rewrite` can separate the values.

Failing on collision is the safest near-term behavior, since the current flat `map[string][]byte` cannot represent both values.

**Additional context**

- #6821 fixed the request-shape half of #6230 by scoping each `find.path` at the Infisical API.
- #6349 sets `SkipUniqueValidation: true`, which keeps both rows in the SDK output but does not change the map overwrite a step later, so it does not resolve this on its own.
- #6873 tracks the broader loss of source-path information in `GetAllSecrets`.

A maintainer on the project fabiandistler/aRchtest (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #2: Declare and enforce architectural dependency rules in testthat

## Problem Statement

R codebases — packages, Shiny apps, plumber APIs — have no way to declare and enforce architectural boundaries. A team can agree that "UI code never talks to the database directly" or that "`domain/` must not depend on `infra/`", but nothing checks it. The agreement lives in a README, a code review habit, or someone's head.

The result is architectural drift that stays invisible until it hurts: a `dbGetQuery()` call slipped into a Shiny module, a domain function reaching into an infrastructure helper, a layering violation that only becomes obvious when someone tries to swap the database or test the domain in isolation. By then the violation is load-bearing and expensive to unwind.

The R ecosystem has no analogue to ArchUnit (Java), import-linter (Python) or dependency-cruiser (JS). `flow` (call graphs) has been stale since 2023, `dupree` is dead, and `pkgnet` visualises dependencies but enforces nothing. Visualisation shows you drift after the fact; it does not stop the commit that causes it.

This problem has sharpened with coding agents. Agents produce architectural drift fast, and they respond to deterministic, machine-readable feedback far better than to prose conventions. A rule that fails in CI is a guardrail an agent can act on; a paragraph in CONTRIBUTING.md is not.

## Solution

`aRchtest` lets a developer declare architectural rules as data and enforce them as ordinary `testthat` tests.

A rule is built with a small pipe-friendly DSL: name the rule, select the modules it applies to, state the constraint, and check it. Running it in the test suite turns an architectural agreement into a failing test with concrete findings — file, line, and the offending call — the moment someone crosses the boundary.

```r
test_that("UI never touches the database directly", {
  rule("layering") |>
    modules_matching("R/ui_*.R") |>
    must_not_call(packages = c("DBI", "RPostgres")) |>
    arch_expect()
})
```

The analysis is purely static: the package parses source files and never sources, loads, or evaluates the code under analysis. That makes it deterministic, safe to run in CI, fast, and usable on a project that does not currently load — including a half-finished refactor.

Crucially, the checker resolves *unqualified* calls, not just `DBI::dbGetQuery()`. A bare `dbGetQuery(conn, ...)` is attributed to `DBI` by consulting the project's declared dependencies. A tool that only catches namespace-qualified calls is trivially evaded and would miss most real drift.

## User Stories

1. As an R package author, I want to declare that my UI layer must not call database packages, so that presentation logic cannot quietly acquire a data-access responsibility.
2. As an R package author, I want those declarations to run as `testthat` tests, so that architecture is enforced by the tooling I already have rather than a new command to remember.
3. As a Shiny developer, I want to enforce layering in an app that has no `DESCRIPTION` file, so that the tool works on projects that are not R packages.
4. As a plumber API developer, I want to enforce that route handlers do not call infrastructure packages directly, so that my API surface stays thin.
5. As a developer, I want to select the modules a rule applies to with a familiar glob pattern, so that I do not have to learn a new path language.
6. As a developer, I want to select modules by regular expression when globs are not expressive enough, so that irregular file naming does not block me.
7. As a developer, I want a rule to state which packages the selected modules must not call, so that I can forbid an entire dependency from a layer.
8. As a developer, I want a rule to state which specific functions the selected modules must not call, so that I can forbid `system()` or `setwd()` without banning their whole package.
9. As a developer, I want a rule to state which of my own modules the selected modules must not depend on, so that I can enforce `domain/` not reaching into `infra/`.
10. As a developer, I want a failing rule to report every violation, not just the first, so that I can fix a boundary in one pass instead of iterating one error at a time.
11. As a developer, I want each violation to name the file and line, so that my editor can jump straight to it.
12. As a developer, I want each violation to show the calling function and the called symbol, so that I understand the violation without opening the file.
13. As a developer, I want each violation to show the source text of the offending call, so that the failure message is self-explanatory in CI logs where I cannot browse the code.
14. As a developer, I want a bare `dbGetQuery()` to be attributed to `DBI`, so that a rule cannot be bypassed by dropping the `::` prefix.
15. As a developer, I want a locally defined function that shadows a package export to be attributed to my project, so that I do not get a false violation for my own helper.
16. As a developer, I want calls the tool cannot attribute to be reported separately from violations, so that unresolved symbols do not masquerade as architectural problems.
17. As a developer, I want to know how many calls went unresolved in a check, so that I can judge how much confidence to place in a passing result.

Issue #80: recursive action in action position overflows the stack

Follow-up from the walker engine work (#76, #77 item 4).

A parseable but ill-founded action such as `Foo == Foo \/ Bar`, or mutually
recursive `A == B` / `B == A`, makes `walk()` in `src/eval/walk.rs` recurse
without bound; the process crashes with a stack overflow (SIGBUS/SIGSEGV) where
the legacy inference engine and TLC report an error instead.

A clean fix is non-trivial:
- A plain recursion-depth limit risks false errors on legitimately deep specs,
  and the safe limit depends on stack size (test threads have a smaller stack, so
  a limit safe in the CLI can still overflow under `cargo test`).
- A visited-operator set false-positives because the continuation discharges
  later conjuncts INSIDE an earlier operator's walk scope, so `Foo /\ Bar` where
  `Bar` legitimately references `Foo` would be misflagged as a cycle.

Needs a design that distinguishes a true resolution cycle from ordinary reuse
across the continuation (e.g. tracking the operator-resolution chain distinctly
from the continuation discharge), or running the walk on a large-stack thread
with a generous depth backstop. Robustness on malformed input; priority low
(it crashes rather than producing a wrong answer).

Issue #178: Close completed umbrella issues after AFK validation

## Problem

AFK work can complete every child of a tracking umbrella while leaving the parent issue open indefinitely. The stale umbrella then requires manual bookkeeping, obscures whether the original contract is complete, and may continue to appear as an open blocker for later work.

Closing children is necessary but not sufficient: a parent criterion may be shared across children, amended in trusted comments, or accidentally left uncovered. The AFK workflow therefore needs a small parent-level validation round rather than closing an umbrella solely because its sub-issues are closed.

## Future capability

When the AFK workflow completes the last child of an eligible Overmind umbrella, identify the parent as a closeout candidate and validate the original parent contract against durable child and pull-request evidence.

The validation should:

- read the parent body and trusted contract-amending comments;
- verify that every original acceptance criterion maps to completed child evidence;
- inspect final PR closure tables and unresolved follow-ups rather than inferring completion from issue state alone;
- verify that relevant blockers are resolved and account for criteria implemented by a child attached under another parent;
- leave the umbrella open and report exact gaps when coverage is missing, ambiguous, or unverified;
- post a concise child/PR coverage summary before closing a completed umbrella;
- behave safely when a child is reopened or concurrent closeout activity changes the dependency graph.

This behavior belongs in the Overmind AFK workflow while that tool is repository-local. It is a deferred feature and does not authorize closing any existing umbrella as part of this issue.

## Design questions

- How is an eligible tracking umbrella distinguished from a roadmap, Wayfinder map, or intentionally long-lived parent?
- Should closeout be opt-in through a label, durable parent marker, or decomposition metadata?
- Does the AFK worker close automatically after a fully tested mapping, or prepare an `afk-review` artifact for maintainer approval?
- How are shared criteria represented when GitHub allows a child issue to have only one native parent?
- What happens when parent wording is ambiguous even though every child closed successfully?
- How should reopening a child affect an already closed umbrella?

## Completion condition

- Eligible umbrellas have an explicit, testable identification rule.
- A parent-level closure gate maps every authoritative criterion to durable completed evidence exactly once or explains valid shared coverage.
- Missing, inferred, or ambiguous coverage leaves the umbrella open with a precise report.
- Successful closeout posts a readable coverage summary and closes the umbrella with the completed reason.
- Repeated execution is idempotent and safe under reopened children or concurrent state changes.
- Non-eligible maps and long-lived parent issues are never closed by inference.
- Repository AFK documentation and tests cover successful closure, incomplete coverage, ambiguous criteria, shared-child coverage, and reopening behavior.

Issue #363: Reconcile the Work domain model before the desktop UI overhaul

## Objective

Reconcile Falcon Dash's persisted Work/domain model before the desktop-web UI overhaul so the database, semantic commands, agent contract, and Stitch-led interface all describe the same product.

This issue is the working decision log and implementation tracker. It does not make the existing Work UI a behavior reference.

## Authorities and boundaries

- The Project Governance Portal Stitch project and `docs/DESIGN.md` are the sole visual authority.
- The redesign is desktop-web first. Dedicated mobile product work remains in #349.
- Product behavior starts with the domain: every persisted concept must have a concrete purpose, invariant, and presentation need.
- OpenClaw owns agents, sessions, transcripts, messages, tool activity, approvals, and native runtime state.
- Falcon Dash owns Work state and durable contextual links to OpenClaw sessions. It must not create a parallel transcript store.
- The current v3 contract is implementation/history evidence where this issue explicitly replaces it; the current UI is not normative.

## Agreed decisions

### Project, Milestone, and removal of Phase

- Remove Phase as a domain object.
- Project represents a bounded outcome.
- Milestone represents an ordered exit gate or meaningful outcome checkpoint.
- Tasks, Questions, Decisions, and Change Requests are the Work used to reach a Milestone.
- Milestones retain explicit order and may have an optional display label when language such as "Phase 2" is useful.
- Milestones remain Project-local; they do not need a global navigation surface.
- Work is associated semantically with Milestones rather than placed inside another containment hierarchy.

### Project lifecycle

- Agents do not directly set ordinary Project status.
- Project completion is automatic when its required Milestones are achieved.
- Remove archive as a Project domain state. Completed Projects leave the default open list through filtering.
- Replace cancellation with abandonment.
- Abandonment is reversible: an agent can abandon a Project with a reason and later resume it.
- The Event Log must preserve every abandoned-at and resumed-at event.
- A direct `complete_project` command must not exist in the target model.

### Conversational transitions

- Consequential transitions use an intent -> requirements -> commit interaction.
- An agent may first express intent, for example "achieve this Milestone", without supplying every required field.
- Falcon returns a structured `input_required` result describing missing fields, prompts, input types, limits, and relevant context.
- The agent can gather or provide the missing information over multiple OpenClaw conversation turns.
- Once the complete payload is supplied, Falcon validates and commits one atomic domain transition.
- No database transaction remains open between conversation turns.
- Incomplete negotiation belongs to OpenClaw conversation state, not a half-created Work-domain transition.
- Falcon persists the successful transition, bounded rationale, actor, timestamp, and optional related Work/source references.
- Falcon does not impose explicit human confirmation for ordinary Milestone or Project transitions. Whether an agent consults its user belongs to the user-agent contract.

### Milestone achievement

- A Milestone has an observable success condition.
- Achieving it records a bounded explanation of why that condition is met. "Achievement basis" is the current working term.
- Relevant Tasks, Questions, Decisions, Change Requests, Findings, and source references may support that explanation.
- Merely being associated with a Milestone does not automatically prove the success condition.
- Project completion follows automatically when the final required Milestone is achieved.
- Reopening a Milestone makes a previously completed Project open again while preserving its earlier completion event.

Issue #38: infra: retention/cleanup policy for GHCR container images

## Problem description / value add

Once #25 lands, every push to `main` publishes a new commit-SHA-tagged image for both `finops-backend` and `finops-frontend` to GHCR, and each build additionally produces untagged manifests as SBOM/provenance attestation byproducts. Without a cleanup process, GHCR storage grows unbounded, and there's no defined rule for what's safe to delete. GHCR has no built-in retention policy for non-Enterprise-org repositories, so this has to be built explicitly rather than configured in the UI.

## Proposed solution

Add a separate, scheduled GitHub Actions workflow (e.g. weekly cron, plus `workflow_dispatch` for manual runs) that prunes old package versions from `ghcr.io/felikowski/finops-backend` and `ghcr.io/felikowski/finops-frontend`, using an existing action such as `dataaxiom/ghcr-cleanup-action` or `actions/delete-package-versions`:

- Delete untagged image versions immediately — these are attestation/manifest byproducts, never referenced by a running deployment
- Keep only the most recent N (e.g. 20) commit-SHA-tagged images per package
- Always keep semver release tags and `latest`
- Log what was deleted for auditability

Out of scope: registries other than GHCR, retention for non-image artifacts, tuning the exact N (start with a sane default, adjust later).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A scheduled workflow runs on a defined cadence (e.g. weekly) and can also be triggered manually via `workflow_dispatch`
- [ ] Untagged image versions are deleted
- [ ] Commit-SHA tags beyond the configured retention window/count are deleted
- [ ] Semver release tags and `latest` are never deleted
- [ ] The workflow uses least-privilege permissions (`packages: write` scoped to this job only)
- [ ] Deleted/kept versions are visible in the workflow run log
- [ ] Retention policy and rationale are documented in the README

## Deutsche Fassung

## Problembeschreibung / Mehrwert

Sobald #25 umgesetzt ist, veröffentlicht jeder Push auf `main` ein neues, mit der Commit-SHA getaggtes Image für `finops-backend` und `finops-frontend` in GHCR. Zusätzlich erzeugt jeder Build untagged Manifeste als Nebenprodukt der SBOM-/Provenance-Attestierungen. Ohne Cleanup-Prozess wächst der GHCR-Speicherbedarf unbegrenzt, und es gibt keine definierte Regel, was gefahrlos gelöscht werden kann. GHCR bietet für Nicht-Enterprise-Org-Repositories keine eingebaute Retention-Policy — das muss also explizit gebaut statt in der UI konfiguriert werden.

## Vorgeschlagene Lösung

Einen separaten, geplanten GitHub-Actions-Workflow hinzufügen (z.B. wöchentlicher Cron, plus `workflow_dispatch` für manuelle Läufe), der alte Package-Versionen aus `ghcr.io/felikowski/finops-backend` und `ghcr.io/felikowski/finops-frontend` entfernt, z.B. mit `dataaxiom/ghcr-cleanup-action` oder `actions/delete-package-versions`:

- Untagged Image-Versionen sofort löschen — das sind Nebenprodukte der Attestierungen, nie von einem laufenden Deployment referenziert
- Nur die letzten N (z.B. 20) SHA-getaggten Images pro Package behalten
- Semver-Release-Tags und `latest` immer behalten
- Gelöschte/behaltene Versionen protokollieren, für Nachvollziehbarkeit

Nicht im Scope: andere Registries als GHCR, Retention für Nicht-Image-Artefakte, Feintuning von N (erst ein sinnvoller Default, später anpassbar).

## Akzeptanzkriterien

- [ ] Ein geplanter Workflow läuft in einem festen Rhythmus (z.B. wöchentlich) und lässt sich zusätzlich manuell per `workflow_dispatch` auslösen
- [ ] Untagged Image-Versionen werden gelöscht
- [ ] SHA-Tags jenseits des konfigurierten Retention-Fensters/-Limits werden gelöscht
- [ ] Semver-Release-Tags und `latest` werden nie gelöscht
- [ ] Der Workflow nutzt minimale Berechtigungen (`packages: write` nur in diesem Job)
- [ ] Gelöschte/behaltene Versionen sind im Workflow-Log sichtbar
- [ ] Retention-Policy und Begründung sind im README dokumentiert

Hängt von #25 ab (Images müssen erst in GHCR veröffentlicht werden, bevor es dort etwas zu bereinigen gibt).

A maintainer on the project felixefelip/steep (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #53: Precondition contracts: known gaps (false positives, unsoundness, non-inference)

Follow-up to the precondition-contract work (#51 explicit-receiver + attribute-write narrowing, #52 transitive closure). This tracks the scenarios where the mechanism does **not** hold, so we can prioritize closing them.

Legend: ✅ = reproduced empirically; the rest reasoned from the implementation.

## 🔴 Unsound — `steep check` passes but runtime raises

**U1. Aliasing** ✅
```ruby
a = Column.new; b = a
a.board = Board.new
b.board = nil          # same object as `a`
a.board.user_name      # runtime NoMethodError — Steep: "No type error"
```
Attribute-write narrowing (like the existing pure-call cache) is flow-local per node; it can't see that `b` aliases `a`. #51 extends this known Steep unsoundness to attribute writes. Lowest priority (inherent to the flow model).

**U2. Transforming/custom writer**
```ruby
def board=(v); @board = v || Board.default; end
x.board = nil          # narrowed to `nil`, but runtime stores a Board
```
`narrow_attribute_write` narrows to the *assigned value's* type, assuming the writer stores it faithfully (true for `attr_accessor`). A custom `def x=` that filters/transforms breaks it. **Cheap fix: gate the narrowing to real `attr_writer`/`attr_accessor` members (not arbitrary `def x=`).**

**U3. Mutation via an opaque call between write and read**
```ruby
x.board = b; x.reset!; x.board.user_name   # if reset! nils @board and x.board isn't invalidated
```

## 🟡 False positives — `steep check` errors but runtime is safe

**F1. Receiver set inside a factory/builder** ✅
```ruby
def self.build; c = Column.new; c.board = Board.new; c; end
column = build   # type is just Column (board: Board?)
column.save      # precondition unsatisfied
```
Very common (factory, `find_or_create`, `dup` + setup). The "board is set" fact doesn't cross the method-return boundary.

**F2. Conditional set** ✅
```ruby
column.board = x if cond
column.save          # column.board merges to Board? across branches
```

**F3. Precondition established by a method call**
```ruby
column.setup!   # sets self.board internally
column.save     # Steep doesn't know setup! guarantees board
```
Needs a *postcondition* on `setup!` connected to the precondition check.

**F4. Non-narrowable receiver**
```ruby
columns[0].board = b; columns[0].board.user_name   # receiver is `[]`
find_column().board = b; ...                       # receiver is a method call
```
`narrow_attribute_write` only handles lvar/ivar/self/pure-send receivers.

## ⚪ Mechanism doesn't apply — no contract inferred / not checked

**N1. Deref via a local copy** ✅
```ruby
def set_default_user_name
  b = board                    # copy
  self.user_name = b.user_name # NoMethod is on `b` (lvar), not self.board
end
```
`Contracts::Inferrer` only maps a `NoMethod` whose receiver is a `self` path → no contract inferred at all, so nothing can discharge the body error even at safe call sites.

**N2. Nil-deref that isn't `NoMethod`** — e.g. `render(self.board)` where `render` expects `Board` → ArgumentType error, which the inferrer doesn't harvest.

**N3. Dynamic dispatch** — `public_send(:save)`, `send`, `method_missing`, `define_method`: no static call node → enforcement never observes it.

**N4. Untyped receiver** — `x = untyped; x.save` → `precondition_target_type_name` is nil → skipped.

**N5. Call inside a block/iterator with a fresh receiver** — `columns.each { |c| c.save }`: `c`'s board is unknown per iteration.

## 🔵 Convergence / typing edges

**E1. Deep or mutual recursion** beyond `Runner::MAX_PASSES` (20) → falls back to the last flags, possibly incomplete.

**E2. Inheritance/polymorphism** — contract inferred on a superclass method, overridden in a subclass; or static type is the superclass while the runtime is a subclass. Enforcement decides on the static type.

**E3. Multi-hop chains** — the contract expr supports `self.a.b.c`, but attribute-write narrowing of a 2-hop `x.a.b = ...` isn't tracked.

## Suggested priority

1. **U2 — writer gate** (cheap, closes an unsoundness): only narrow for real `attr_writer`/`attr_accessor`, not arbitrary `def x=`.
2. **F1/F3 — method-boundary facts**: infer a *postcondition* (return type / `self` state) so a factory's returned object or a `setup!` call carries the established attribute forward. Kills the largest, most common class of false positives — and matches the project goal (improve inference, don't push guards onto users). Out of scope stays only for the genuinely undecidable (U1 aliasing, N3 dynamic dispatch).

Issue #71: [High] Preserve the complete spec-owned resource graph during full-replace restore

## Severity

High — launch blocker for `full_replace`

## Problem

`full_replace` carries the live `api_specs` section into `/restore`, but constructs the resource arrays only from the repository's desired `GatewayConfig`. Spec-owned proxies, upstreams, and plugin configs are deliberately absent from desired state, so the restore body contains API-spec documents without the resources that those specs own.

Ferrum Edge restore validates the ownership graph and requires each referenced owner/resource relationship to be present. A namespace with API specs therefore cannot be safely carried through as advertised; restore fails unless the operator explicitly deletes the API specs.

## Evidence

- Apply keeps the actual resource config and backup extras in separate maps at [`src/main.rs:1379-1393`](https://github.com/ferrum-edge/ferrum-edge-git-forge-ops/blob/491d838e569e566280cf572bb62858885952ff57/src/main.rs#L1379-L1393).
- [`apply_full_replace` passes only `desired` plus the opaque extras](https://github.com/ferrum-edge/ferrum-edge-git-forge-ops/blob/491d838e569e566280cf572bb62858885952ff57/src/apply/api_target.rs#L365-L405).
- [`build_restore_body` serializes desired resource arrays and splices in only `api_specs` and trust bundles](https://github.com/ferrum-edge/ferrum-edge-git-forge-ops/blob/491d838e569e566280cf572bb62858885952ff57/src/http_client.rs#L1115-L1146).
- Ferrum Edge's restore validation requires the owning proxy to exist with the matching `api_spec_id`: https://github.com/ferrum-edge/ferrum-edge/blob/b96cfaadd41a676d39a409d47b48e0b0588fa86e/src/admin/backup.rs#L739-L755
- The documented backup/restore contract describes the ownership validation: https://github.com/ferrum-edge/ferrum-edge/blob/b96cfaadd41a676d39a409d47b48e0b0588fa86e/docs/admin_backup_restore.md#L109-L126

## Impact

`full_replace` fails for namespaces using OpenAPI ingestion, despite the CLI reporting that API specs are being carried through unchanged. This blocks a documented apply strategy and can pressure operators toward the destructive `--confirm-api-spec-deletion` escape hatch.

## Suggested implementation

1. From the authoritative live backup, identify the complete set of resources carrying `api_spec_id` and merge that graph into the restore payload unchanged.
2. Preserve API specs, their owning proxies/upstreams/plugin configs, and any required associations as one opaque consistency unit.
3. Detect ID conflicts between repo-owned desired resources and spec-owned live resources before any mutation and fail with actionable details.
4. Keep preserved spec-owned rows out of the repo-managed state ledger and apply counts.
5. Refuse full replace when the backup is cached/incomplete or the ownership graph cannot be proven complete.
6. Retain `--confirm-api-spec-deletion` as the only path that intentionally omits the graph.

## Verification

- Add an integration fixture containing an API spec plus its spec-owned proxy, upstream, and plugin config, alongside repo-owned resources.
- Assert the generated restore body contains a complete, unchanged spec-owned graph and passes Ferrum Edge restore validation.
- Assert repo-owned rows are replaced as requested and preserved rows are not added to managed state.
- Assert an ID conflict or incomplete/cached graph fails before credential allocation or `POST /restore`.
- Assert explicit API-spec deletion still requires the existing confirmation flag.

Issue #2437: gate: run the DOM half by impact analysis (vitest --changed) in check:pr, with the guards always forced

## Where this stands

After #2431 and #2433, `check:pr` runs everything cheap: static checks, the bot fast lane (91 files), and the whole node project (692 files, 30s). What it still does **not** run is the DOM half — 252 files, 133s at the light tier's 2 workers.

That gap is real, not theoretical: #2339 was a `convex/cards/**` refactor touching no `src` file that turned 102 tests across 12 `src` suites red, first seen at the merge-train. `scripts/__tests__/convex-cards-barrel-mock.test.ts` now catches that specific class statically, but it is one class.

## The idea

`vitest --changed <merge-base>` selects test files whose module graph reaches a changed file. For a `src`-only diff that is a handful of suites; for a `convex/cards` diff it may be most of them (everything imports the barrel), which is correct — those are the ones that can break.

## Why it needs a decision first

Impact analysis changes the gate's **coverage contract** from "these files always run" to "the files the tool believes are affected run". Three known ways that belief is wrong here:

1. **`vi.mock` string literals are not import edges.** #2339's dependency was `vi.mock("@convex/cards", …)` — a string, invisible to the module graph. `--changed` would not have selected those 12 files.
2. **Guards that read the filesystem have no edges at all.** `divergenceMarkers`, `identity-only-card-tests`, `check-guards-scope`, the census guards — they `readdirSync` their subject. A diff that breaks them touches nothing they import.
3. **Fixture/data files** (JSON catalogues, lockfiles) may or may not be edges depending on how they are loaded.

So the design is not "add `--changed`", it is **what is always forced on top of it**. The node lane (30s) already covers 1 and 2 for the backend; the question is the `src` side.

## To decide

- Forced set: the whole node project (already) + which `src` suites? "Every suite that mocks a module the diff touched" is computable — `convex-cards-barrel-mock.test.ts` already parses those `vi.mock` specifiers and could be generalised into a selector.
- Base ref: `origin/main` merge-base, or the last known-green SHA (`.claude/telemetry/green-sha`)?
- What the full gate still runs unconditionally — the merge-train must stay a total run, or this becomes a hole one level up.
- Whether the saving is worth it at all: for a typical `src` diff, `--changed` cost vs the 133s it replaces has not been measured. **Measure that before designing anything** — if the median diff selects 80% of the suites, there is nothing here.

## Prior art in-repo

`vitest.config.ts` deliberately chose deny-lists over allow-lists twice (bot fast lane, `HEAVY_BOT_GLOB`) on the grounds that a hand-maintained selection silently stops covering what is added after it. Impact analysis is the same shape with the maintenance moved into a tool — the failure mode is identical if the tool's model of "affected" is wrong.

## Parent

- #111
- Review finding from PR #121

## What to build

Make one successful signed Folder deletion converge as a hard deletion on every affected durable Brain Working Tree, including clients that were offline and ordinary collaborators whose live Folder Access disappears with the subtree. ## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The minimum signed deletion record is available to every principal that held a materialized or syncing relationship to the deleted subtree at deletion time, even after live access is removed.
- [ ] Principals with no prior or current relationship to the subtree cannot enumerate or read its deletion record.

Issue #32: [P1] setup --remove recursively deletes files not owned by Finterm

## Summary

`finterm setup --remove` recursively removes the entire `.agents/skills/finterm` and `.claude/skills/finterm` directories instead of removing only the files installed by Finterm. User or tool-created files in those directories are destroyed without confirmation.

## Evidence

- Installation writes one owned `SKILL.md` file at each location in [setup.ts](https://github.com/finterm-ai/finterm-cli/blob/b71457426a37740ddee3ddc4c3e3474cea908207/packages/finterm-cli/src/cli/commands/setup.ts#L42-L49) and [setup.ts](https://github.com/finterm-ai/finterm-cli/blob/b71457426a37740ddee3ddc4c3e3474cea908207/packages/finterm-cli/src/cli/commands/setup.ts#L84-L88).
- Removal passes each file's parent directory to recursive `rm` in [setup.ts](https://github.com/finterm-ai/finterm-cli/blob/b71457426a37740ddee3ddc4c3e3474cea908207/packages/finterm-cli/src/cli/commands/setup.ts#L189-L203).
- There is no ownership manifest, directory-content check, backup, or interactive confirmation before deletion.

## Why this matters

Skill directories are extension points and can contain supporting references, scripts, user notes, or files added by another installer. An uninstall command should not erase data it did not create.

## Attack or failure scenario

1. Setup installs `.agents/skills/finterm/SKILL.md`.
2. A user or agent adds `.agents/skills/finterm/references/policy.md`.
3. The user runs `finterm setup --remove` expecting only Finterm's integration to be removed.
4. Recursive deletion removes `SKILL.md`, `references/policy.md`, and every other file under the directory.
5. The CLI reports successful removal with no warning or recovery path.

## Root cause

The uninstall implementation derives a directory from the owned filename and recursively deletes that directory, conflating file ownership with directory ownership.

## Recommended fix

Remove only the exact files and hook entries installed by Finterm. Prune parent directories only when they are empty, and preserve unknown files. If legacy cleanup requires broader deletion, enumerate it and require explicit confirmation.

## Acceptance criteria

- `setup --remove` deletes the installed Finterm `SKILL.md` files and owned hook entries only.
- Unrecognized sibling and descendant files remain byte-for-byte unchanged.
- Empty Finterm directories may be removed after owned files are deleted.
- Tests cover extra files, nested directories, read-only files, missing owned files, and partial installation.
- Dry-run lists every exact path that would be removed.

`bug`, `priority:P1`, `data-loss`, `setup`

High

A maintainer on the project flashtrace/flashtrace (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #36: Impact analysis: ask "what is affected if I change this item?" before bumping

Revision matching is deliberately exact (`#2.4` never equals `#2.5`), so bumping an item's revision breaks every exact `Needs`, `Covers` and forwarding reference to it. Today flashtrace reports that damage only *after* the edit, as `uncovered`/`orphaned` defects. The question you actually have *before* editing — "what is affected if I change this item?" — has no answer yet, even though the whole trace graph is already in memory.

## Proposal

```
flashtrace --impact <ref> [directory-or-file ...]
```

- `<ref>` is a full ID (`impl:auth/login#2.4`) or a bare key (`impl:auth/login`) meaning "all defined revisions" — the natural form when planning a bump.
- Scanning and `--tags` work as today; `--impact` replaces the coverage report with the impact report. It is a query, not a check: exit `0` when the ref exists (even with empty impact), `1` when nothing matches it, `2` on usage errors (including combining with `-v` for now).

## Semantics

An item directly depends on `X` when it *needs* something `X` satisfies (exact or wildcard), *covers* `X`, or *forwards to* `X`. The impact set is the transitive closure of these edges in reverse, cycle-safe like deep coverage.

Each **direct** edge gets classified for the bump question:

- **exact** — names the revision itself; breaks when the item is bumped/removed.
- **tolerant** — a wildcard need (e.g. `#2.x`) that another existing revision also satisfies; survives the bump.
- **wildcard-last** — a wildcard need whose only match is this item; breaks too, but a same-pattern replacement revision heals it.

Transitive members are listed without classification — they are affected because a direct dependent sits on their coverage chain.

## Output sketch

Reuses the verbose report's visual language:

```
impact of impl:auth/login#2.4  login.ts:3   (2 direct, 1 transitive)

  direct
    req:auth/login#1 "Login"  spec.md:12
        needs impl:auth/login#2.x (→ #2.4)   tolerant (also matched by #2.5)
    test:auth/login#3  login.test.ts:7
        covers impl:auth/login#2.4           exact — breaks on bump
  transitive
    req:auth#1 "Authentication"  spec.md:2   via req:auth/login#1
```

No dependents prints `no items depend on <id>` (the `unwanted` condition seen from the other side); an unmatched ref prints `no item matches <key>` with the usual revision hint.

## Scope notes

- Zero new dependencies; the reverse graph falls out of `buildResolver` plus the `wantedBy` map the `-v` report already builds (extended with covers/forwarding edges and moved out of the renderer so both share one source of truth). Effort roughly comparable to the verbose report (#27).
- Deliberately out of scope, as follow-ups: the downward slice ("what does X rest on?"), rendering impact in JSON/HTML (belongs to #31/#33 once their envelope exists), and any auto-rewriting of stale references after a bump.

A fuller write-up lives in [`docs/proposals/impact-analysis.md`](https://github.com/flashtrace/flashtrace/blob/claude/new-feature-proposal-c2fecm/docs/proposals/impact-analysis.md) on the `claude/new-feature-proposal-c2fecm` branch.

## Goal

| User story |
|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| As a Fleet administrator managing Windows hosts via fleetd,
| I want Fleet to enroll a Windows host into Fleet MDM without requiring an interactive user to sign in,
| so that I can send MDM commands (configuration profiles, disk encryption, scripts) to freshly imaged, headless, kiosk, and shared devices immediately.

Today fleetd enrolls a Windows host into Fleet MDM by calling the Windows user-enrollment API `RegisterDeviceWithManagement`. orbit runs as the SYSTEM account, and this API needs an interactive user security context. When no user is signed in, the call fails with `0x80070525` (ERROR_NO_SUCH_USER) and orbit retries on every config poll without ever enrolling. The host reports "MDM: Off", and any queued Windows MDM commands (including the disk encryption profile) stay pending until a user finally signs in, at which point the same call succeeds within about 30 seconds.

Fleet's MDM server advertises the OnPremise authentication policy, but its WSTEP handlers only accept a `<wsse:BinarySecurityToken>` (the orbit node key for programmatic fleetd enrollment, or an Entra AAD JWT for Entra-joined or Autopilot devices). The industry-standard userless path on Windows is a provisioning package (Microsoft bulk enrollment), applied by `Install-ProvisioningPackage` as SYSTEM with no user. That path presents a `<wsse:UsernameToken>` under the OnPremise policy, which Fleet explicitly rejects.

## Goal

| User story  |
|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| As a Fleet administrator managing a large fleet of Android devices,
| I want the Android device reconciliation cron to have explicit bounds on its Google API pagination
| so that I can avoid unbounded memory growth, indefinite loop execution, and excessive database pressure from a malformed or unexpectedly large API response.

## Context

`server/mdm/android/service/reconcile_devices.go:50-64` contains a `for {}` loop that pages through the Android Management API (`EnterprisesDevicesListPartial`) at 100 devices per page. The loop continues until `resp.NextPageToken == ""`. There is no maximum iteration guard.

This runs as a cron job every 1 hour (see `cmd/fleet/cron.go:2417-2431`), and all fetched device names are accumulated into an in-memory `map[string]struct{}`.

**Risks:**
- **Malformed API response**: If Google ever returns a non-empty `NextPageToken` that cycles (e.g. due to a bug or proxy issue), the loop will never terminate.
- **Memory pressure**: For very large enterprises, all device names are held in memory simultaneously. At 100 devices/page with no cap, a 100K-device enterprise would accumulate ~100K map entries before any reconciliation begins.
- **No progress logging**: There is no periodic logging during pagination, making it hard to diagnose a slow or stuck reconciliation.

A maintainer on the project flix/flix (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #13159: Open questions in relation to constraint-based monomorphization replacing the demand-driven one

If the constraint-based monomorphization phase (i.e. the `monomorph2` phase) is to replace the existing monomorphization phase there are a couple of things that could and probably should change:
**1. Proper polymorphic recursion error-message**
Programs with polymorphic recursion currently crashes the compiler with an `OutOfMemoryError` (see https://github.com/flix/flix/issues/7181).
The new monomorphization phase "improves" on this already by throwing an `InternalCompilerException`.
But we probably want a proper compiler error message. In relation to this there are two issues (1) the backend part of `Flix.scala` (understandably) does not accumulate compiler error-messages and (2) the information we have currently from the strong-connected-components is not enough to point out the actual offending "cycle" (though this should be doable by performing BFS in the offending cases).

**2. Remove type variables in `MonoAst`**
The old monomorphization phase did not specialize enums/structs and therefore still needed type-variables in `MonoAst`.
The new monomorphization phase does specialize enums/structs and there should never be a case where type-variable makes it into the `MonoAst`. This should be guaranteed structurally by removing `Type.Var` from `MonoAst` entirely.
We can't (currently) erase type parameters since we don't specialize the built-ins (e.g. `Array` and tuples) as they are first addressed by Eraser.

**3. Simplify enum/struct specialization in Eraser.scala**
Eraser specializes enums/structs per-instantiation based on use-site type args, since the old monomorphization phase leaves them generic.
The new phase already specializes them so every use-site has empty type args, and Eraser's `specializeEnums`/`specializeStructs` end up walking every case through a substitution that's always empty, rebuilding symbols that are already identical.
This can be skipped whenever there are no type parameters left to substitute.
