Issue #790: fix(tailwind): scope native CLI runtimes to the build host

## Problem

`ForgeTrust.AppSurface.Web.Tailwind` selects the standalone Tailwind CLI for the current build host, but its package metadata declares every supported platform runtime package as an unconditional dependency. Restore therefore resolves Linux ARM64/x64, macOS ARM64/x64, and Windows x64 assets even though one build can execute only one of them.

Those native runtime assets are normal transitive runtime dependencies, so they are also copied into the outputs of project-reference consumers that do not import or execute the Tailwind MSBuild target. This can substantially increase restore traffic, output size, CI disk pressure, and artifact-transfer cost.

## Desired behavior

- Acquire and expose only the native Tailwind CLI compatible with the current build host.
- Keep the native CLI build-time scoped so it does not propagate through downstream project references.
- Preserve the managed Tailwind integration for applications that use `AddTailwind`.

Issue #877: Reduce initial frontend payload by 71% and release binary size by 48%

## Summary

En Croissant currently ships its frontend as one large eagerly loaded JavaScript bundle, and the Rust release binary retains symbols. A local proof of concept produced substantial reductions by enabling supported route-level code splitting and tightening the Cargo release profile.

## Measured impact

Measured locally on **Ubuntu 26.04** with a Tauri release build:

| Measurement | Before | After | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Initial JavaScript, gzip | 1,403.03 KiB | 405.80 KiB | 71.1% lower |
| Initial JavaScript, minified | 4,656.47 KiB | 1,425.88 KiB | 69.4% lower |
| Initial CSS, gzip | 43.87 KiB | 39.95 KiB | 8.9% lower |
| Rust release binary | approximately 46 MiB | 23.9 MiB | approximately 48% lower |

The optimized build's median time from process launch to the existing `React app started successfully` log was **370 ms** across three valid samples. Median summed idle RSS for the Tauri and WebKit process group was **579.5 MiB**. There is no pre-change startup/RSS sample, so these two values are a baseline, not evidence of improvement.

## Proposed changes

- Enable TanStack Router's `autoCodeSplitting`.
- Replace an accidental `@tiptap/react` import used only for numeric clamping with a local clamp.
- Load PostHog asynchronously after the React application has started.
- Configure the Cargo release profile with:
  - `lto = true`
  - `codegen-units = 1`
  - `panic = "abort"`
  - `strip = true`

Route-specific code remains available in on-demand chunks; the total application JavaScript is not expected to fall by the same amount as the initial payload.

- React Compiler is already enabled, so speculative memoization was avoided without React Profiler traces.
- Progress, engine, clock, and database-search updates are already event-driven.

## Tradeoffs

The first release rebuild after changing the Cargo profile took **149 seconds** because the release dependency graph was invalidated. Development and test profiles are unaffected. LTO may improve optimization across crate boundaries, but no CPU-heavy workflow was benchmarked, so this proposal makes no runtime-speed claim.

## Validation

- `npm run build-vite`: passed
- `npm run lint`: zero errors, 52 existing warnings
- Frontend tests: 40/40 passed
- Complete `npm run build` Tauri release build: passed
- Rust tests: 27 passed; 8 existing chess-evaluation/database-search assertions failed in code untouched by this proposal

Issue #41916: [Bug] Sidebar editor crashes when adding a nested sidebar item (TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined reading 'indent')

Frappe version: 16.31.0

## Bug
Adding a NEW nested item to a workspace sidebar through the UI (Workspace page -> sidebar dropdown -> "Edit Sidebar" -> "Add Nested Items" under a section break) throws an uncaught TypeError:

```
sidebar_item.js:93 Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'indent')
    at SidebarItem.make (sidebar_item.js:93:64)
    at new SidebarItem (sidebar_item.js:12:8)
    at Sidebar.make_sidebar_item (sidebar.js:576:10)
    at ... nested_items.forEach ...
    at SectionBreakSidebarItem.add_items (sidebar_item.js:178:21)
```

## Root cause
In `frappe/public/js/frappe/ui/sidebar/sidebar_editor.js`, the `primary_action` handler for `opts.nested`:

```js
if (opts && opts.nested) {
    values.child = 1;
    ...
    me.new_sidebar_items[index].nested_items.push(values);
}
```

sets `child = 1` but never sets `values.parent`. The `parent` reference is normally populated only for server-loaded items by `sidebar.js find_nested_items()`; it is never attached to items created in the dialog.

The renderer then evaluates `sidebar_item.js:93`:

```js
if (!this.item.icon && !(this.item.child && this.item.parent.indent)) {
```

Since `item.child` is truthy, it reads `item.parent.indent`, but `item.parent` is `undefined`, so JS throws.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Open a workspace page (e.g. `/app/hr-setup`).
2. In the left sidebar header dropdown choose "Edit Sidebar".
3. Click "+ Add Sidebar Item", OR click a section break -> "Add Nested Items".
4. Fill the dialog and save.
5. Observe the TypeError; the new nested item is not added.

## Expected behaviour
A newly added nested sidebar item should render correctly (and ideally inherit the parent section break) without throwing.

## Suggested fix
- `sidebar_item.js:93`: guard with optional chaining `(this.item.child && this.item.parent?.indent)`.
- `sidebar_editor.js` (`opts.nested` branch): set `values.parent = me.new_sidebar_items[index]` before pushing into `nested_items`.

## Workaround
Edit the `workspace_sidebar/<title>.json` file directly and sync to the DB; avoid the sidebar editor for nested items.

## Impact
Sidebar editor for nested items is unusable on this version.

Issue #5407: ci: rule-lint #1 misses unqualified Instant::now(), so the DST ban depends on spelling

## Problem

`.github/scripts/check_banned_patterns.py` enforces rule-lint #1 ("`std::time::Instant::now()` — use TimeSource instead") with a single literal regex:

```python
re.compile(r"std::time::Instant::now\(\)")
```

That matches only the fully-qualified spelling. Production code written as

```rust
use std::time::Instant;
...
let t = Instant::now();
```

is the identical banned construct and passes the lint untouched.

## Evidence

Observed on PR #5403, which added three production uses of `std::time::Instant::now()` in `crates/core/src/conformance/`:

| Site | Spelling | Rule Lint |
|---|---|---|
| `capture.rs:920` | `std::time::Instant::now()` | **flagged** (CI red) |
| `status.rs:162` | `Instant::now()` (via `use std::time::Instant;` at :52) | not flagged |
| `status.rs:391` | `Instant::now()` (same import) | not flagged |

`mod tests` in `status.rs` begins at line 395, so both unflagged lines are production code, and both were added by that PR — the linter is diff-scoped, so they were in scope and simply did not match.

The same hole applies to rule #2 (`rand::thread_rng()` / `rand::random()`) if imported and called unqualified, and plausibly to rule #3.

## Why it matters

The lint is the automated half of the DST guarantee described in `.claude/rules/testing.md`. A guard that depends on which of two equivalent spellings an author happens to use is not enforcing the rule — it is enforcing a coding style, and silently. The failure is invisible in the direction that matters: CI goes green, so nobody looks.

There is a second-order effect worth naming. When the lint fires on the qualified spelling only, the path of least resistance for the author is to add an import and shorten the call — which makes CI pass while leaving the banned construct in place. The lint currently teaches the bypass.

## Suggested fix

Match the call irrespective of qualification, e.g. a pattern along the lines of `\bInstant::now\s*\(\s*\)` combined with a check that the file imports `std::time::Instant` (so `tokio::time::Instant`, which is pausable under `tokio::time::pause()` and is the accepted alternative in async code, is not falsely flagged). The distinction between the two `Instant` types is the substance of the rule, so the linter needs to resolve which one is in scope rather than pattern-match the prefix.

Whatever shape the fix takes, it should come with a test case per rule asserting that the **unqualified** form is flagged — the existing self-tests in that script cover the qualified form only (see the `prod Instant::now call — must flag (rule #1)` case, which uses `let t = std::time::Instant::now();`).

## Scope note

Filing rather than fixing inline: this affects every PR touching `crates/core/src/`, not just the one that surfaced it, and pre-existing unqualified uses elsewhere in the tree may need triage before the stricter pattern can go green. #5403 itself will be fixed on its own merits by moving to `tokio::time::Instant`, which is already the convention in that module (`shadow.rs:41`).

Issue #142: Security sub-agent: add workflow_call permission inheritance checks

## What happened

On [PR #1611](https://github.com/fullsend-ai/fullsend/pull/1611), the review bot's initial review (May 27 17:38 UTC) found only medium/low findings: protected-path detection, incorrect prioritize path resolution, and a stale comment. Within 50 minutes, human reviewer waynesun09 [found a CRITICAL bug](https://github.com/fullsend-ai/fullsend/pull/1611#discussion_r2112346789): `permissions: {}` at workflow level blocks OIDC token minting in all per-org stage jobs because reusable workflows called via `workflow_call` cannot elevate beyond the caller's permission grant. waynesun09 also found HIGH issues: `secrets: inherit` exposing all repo secrets to the prioritize workflow, and `prioritize.yml` missing `secrets:` declaration under `workflow_call`. The bot's security sub-agent has detailed guidance for GHA workflow command injection and permission-expansion detection, but nothing about how permissions propagate (or fail to propagate) through `workflow_call` chains. The bot ran 3 more review cycles and never flagged these issues.

## What could go better

The security sub-agent (`skills/pr-review/sub-agents/security.md`) covers permission expansion and role escalation in workflow files, but lacks specific knowledge about GitHub Actions' permission inheritance model for `workflow_call`. This is a well-documented platform behavior: called workflows inherit the caller's effective permissions as a ceiling, and cannot request elevated permissions. When a caller sets `permissions: {}`, all called workflows get zero permissions regardless of their own `permissions:` blocks. This pattern is distinct from issues [#1275](https://github.com/fullsend-ai/fullsend/issues/1275) (correctness-focused workflow_call chain tracing), [#2658](https://github.com/fullsend-ai/fullsend/issues/2658) (verifying tool permission requirements), and [#2933](https://github.com/fullsend-ai/fullsend/issues/2933) (CI security anti-patterns like verbose scanning). High confidence this is a systematic gap: the bot had 4 review cycles and never caught it, and #898 documents the same class of gap on another large PR.

## Proposed change

Add a 'workflow_call permission inheritance' section to `skills/pr-review/sub-agents/security.md` with these checks: (1) When a workflow sets `permissions: {}` or restrictive permissions at the workflow level, verify that all jobs calling reusable workflows via `uses:` have explicit `permissions:` blocks granting what the called workflow needs (especially `id-token: write` for OIDC). (2) Document that the caller's effective permissions are the ceiling — called workflows cannot exceed them. (3) Flag `secrets: inherit` as a least-privilege violation when explicit secret passing is feasible, with medium severity. (4) When a `workflow_call` trigger declares `inputs:` but not `secrets:`, and the caller passes explicit secrets, flag the missing declaration as a runtime failure.

## Validation criteria

Run the security sub-agent against a test diff containing: (a) a workflow with `permissions: {}` at the workflow level and stage jobs calling reusable workflows without explicit permission blocks, and (b) `secrets: inherit` on one job while others pass secrets explicitly. The sub-agent should produce at least one high-severity finding about the permission inheritance gap and at least one medium finding about `secrets: inherit`.

Issue #3900: Review agent should not post findings on files outside the PR diff

## What happened

On [PR #82](https://github.com/redhat-developer/rhdh-agentic/pull/82), the review agent posted an inline comment on `.fullsend/agents/review.md` flagging a skill-count mismatch (stated three skills but lists four, frontmatter lists five). However, this file is not among the PR's 20 changed files — it is upstream content materialized from the `base:` composition URL in `review.yaml`. The [PR diff](https://github.com/redhat-developer/rhdh-agentic/pull/82/files) shows the deleted file was `.fullsend/customized/agents/review.md` (different path). The review agent itself correctly noted the content was inherited from upstream v0.30.0 but still posted it as a PR review comment.

The finding appeared in review run [29022640678](https://github.com/redhat-developer/rhdh-agentic/actions/runs/29022640678) (13:47-13:53 UTC). The APPROVED verdict and inline comment were posted at 13:53 UTC.

## What could go better

When the review agent posts findings on files outside the PR diff, it creates noise the PR author cannot address. In this case, the skill-count mismatch is an upstream issue in the fullsend framework's review agent prompt — the repo maintainer would need to fix it upstream, not in their migration PR.

This wastes reviewer attention and dilutes the signal from legitimate findings. The other 3 findings (on `code.yaml` and `debug.yaml`) were on files actually changed in the PR and were genuinely useful.

Confidence: High that the file was outside the diff (confirmed via the GitHub Files API). Moderate confidence on the root cause — the review agent may be reviewing all materialized harness files rather than scoping to the PR diff, or it may have confused the deleted `.fullsend/customized/agents/review.md` with the materialized `.fullsend/agents/review.md`.

## Proposed change

In the review agent's file-selection logic, filter findings to only files present in the PR diff (as returned by the GitHub API's `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{number}/files` endpoint). If the agent discovers issues in files outside the diff (e.g., upstream-inherited content), it should either:

1. Suppress the finding entirely, or
2. Include it in the review summary as an informational note (not an inline comment) with a clear label like 'upstream issue — not addressable in this PR'

The change likely belongs in the review agent's skill definition or the harness's diff-fetching logic.

## Validation criteria

On a PR that uses `base:` composition and only modifies harness config files (not the materialized agent prompts), the review agent should produce zero inline comments on files outside the PR diff. Specifically, re-running review on a PR like rhdh-agentic#82 should not produce a finding on `.fullsend/agents/review.md` when that file is not in the changed files list.

Issue #19: epic(workflow): add end-to-end change delivery

## Authority and purpose

This is the **umbrella/epic issue** for Aerstello’s end-to-end change-development and delivery system.

The current body and the linked child issues are authoritative. They supersede conflicting detail in the issue’s earlier body and design-discussion comments. Those comments remain useful history, but agents should implement from this epic, the relevant child issue, current `main`, and the repository’s canonical workflow documentation.

Do not implement this epic in one pull request.

## Objective

Provide one repository-local workflow entry point that lets a main agent durably orchestrate a change from source request through planning, implementation, pull request, official Codex review, remediation, matching full CI/full E2E, final-head acceptance attestation, optional guarded merge, and source-issue reconciliation.

The intended lifecycle is:

```text
request / GitHub issue / accepted plan
→ $change-development
  → planning and immutable task graph
  → bounded specialist implementation workers
  → central integration
  → targeted validation
  → exact-HEAD specialist review
  → development integration verification
  → pushed PR and immutable exact-SHA handoff
→ $pr-review-cycle
  → official Codex review
  → bounded remediation workers
  → repeated review rounds until clean by default
  → matching full CI and full E2E
  → no open Codex threads
  → PR-review Done
→ $change-delivery completion
  → review-done, or
  → final-head criterion-by-criterion acceptance attestation
  → explicitly authorized guarded squash merge
  → source-issue checklist reconciliation and closure/progress
```

## Core architectural decisions

### One user-facing orchestrator

The main agent that starts or resumes `$change-delivery` is the sole lifecycle orchestrator.

- One operator invocation is sufficient to start the normal lifecycle.
- The operator must not be required to invoke `$change-development` or `$pr-review-cycle` separately.
- The main orchestrator performs every permitted stage transition and owns central integration, pushes, PR updates, official review requests, GitHub thread mutations, acceptance-evidence persistence, authorized merge, and issue reconciliation.
- Workers, planning helpers, specialist reviewers, acceptance verifiers, and final verifiers never own lifecycle transitions and never write GitHub.
- Human input is requested only for a genuine unresolved product decision, material scope change, policy conflict, destructive decision, or missing merge authorization.
- The system is durable and resumable, not an external background daemon. A later session resumes from state when the runtime ends.

### Separate workflow ownership

Keep separate mutable states and responsibilities:

| Capability | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `aerstello-specialists` | Reusable domain profiles, planning-helper routing, risk-review routing, supplemental guidance |
| `$scope-review` | Stateless implementation-minimality and material-scope assessment; no lifecycle or GitHub authority |
| `$acceptance-review` | Stateless positive criterion-by-criterion assessment for one exact final head; no lifecycle or GitHub authority |
| `$change-development` | Accepted plan, task graph, bounded implementation, integration, targeted local verification, PR preparation, exact-SHA handoff |
| `$pr-review-cycle` | Official Codex review, review findings, remediation, threads, full CI/full E2E evidence, Done |
| `$change-delivery` | Child-workflow coordination, acceptance-evidence enforcement, completion target, optional merge, live source-issue reconciliation |

The workflows communicate through guarded interfaces and immutable exact-SHA evidence. Do not combine them into one mutable state document.

`$pr-review-cycle` has no configured review-request count cap by default. It repeats exact-commit review and remediation until clean unless an operator explicitly configures a durable finite limit. Stale review evidence must receive an exact disposition or a human gate without rewriting prior request history.

### Reuse specialist profiles

Reuse the existing profiles:

```text
web
api
contracts
data-integrity
behavior-tests
ops-workflow
```

Do not create one write agent per profile.

Add exactly the workflow roles required by the child issues:

```text
implementation_worker
development_integration_verifier
delivery_acceptance_verifier
```

Keep existing PR-review roles PR-specific:

```text
review_fix_worker
integration_verifier
```

Reuse `behavior_mapper`, `security_reviewer`, and `offline_realtime_reviewer` across workflows after routing becomes workflow-neutral.

A profile provides knowledge only. Immutable task packets remain authoritative for paths, dependencies, criteria, and validation. A verifier result provides evidence only and never grants lifecycle or GitHub authority.

### Targeted local validation

Workers run only exact task-level validation. Orchestrators run the exact integrated union and related E2E selections.

GitHub Actions remains authoritative for:

```text
npm run check:full
npm run test:e2e:full
```

Unknown related-test selection is a planning error. It never authorizes a full local-suite fallback.

### Completion targets

`$change-delivery` supports:

```text
review-done
merged
```

- `review-done` is the safe default and terminates when `$pr-review-cycle` is Done for one exact Review commit.
- `merged` is opt-in only and requires explicit durable authorization, a positive receipt-valid final-head acceptance attestation where issue criteria are targeted, and a separate guarded merge stage.
- PR-review Done and acceptance satisfaction never authorize merge by themselves.
- Initial merge support is squash-only and must inspect current repository/branch policy at merge time.
- Merge never implies release or deployment.

### Live source-issue consistency

For issue-backed work:

- the accepted plan is immutable implementation authority;
- the live GitHub issue is progress/lifecycle

A maintainer on the project fxreichl/eSLIM (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #2: Non-topologically-sorted BLIF input fails silently and yields a plausible but non-equivalent circuit

Thanks for eSLIM — it built and ran on a 2026 toolchain with only `-DCMAKE_POLICY_VERSION_MINIMUM=3.5`.

This is a request to **detect and reject** a precondition violation that currently fails silently, not a report of an undocumented bug: the README does state that input must be topologically sorted, and even notes that the EPFL best-results files violate it. The problem is what happens when someone misses that clause.

### Mechanism

`blifIO.SpecificationBuilder` normalises every gate to `f(0,…,0) = 0`, records the flipped ones in `negated_gates`, and compensates by flipping those literals in the *consumers*:

```python
input_indices_to_negate = {i for i, x in enumerate(inputs) if x in self.negated_gates}
```

`negated_gates` is built incrementally **in file order**. A gate that appears before its driver is therefore built without the compensating flip, and gets a wrong truth table. Nothing raises.

This is not an exotic input. ABC's `write_blif` emits the primary-output blocks first, so **every** BLIF produced by a standard ABC flow — including the EPFL best-results files the README points at — trips it.

### Why it is worth a hard error

The failure is invisible to every cheap check. On the `cavlc` size champion, the first run returned a netlist with 49 LUTs, depth 7, 10 PIs and 11 POs — an exact shape match for its input, entirely plausible, and passing a legality check. It was `NOT_EQUIVALENT` on 7 of 11 outputs under `abc`'s `cec -n`. Topologically sorting the same input first turned the identical run into `Networks are equivalent`.

So the cost of missing one clause in the README is a wrong result that looks right, and the only thing that catches it is a full equivalence check against the original — which is exactly the expensive step a user is likely to skip while iterating.

### Suggested fix

A single pass over `.names` blocks before building the specification, erroring out if any block references a signal that is neither a primary input nor already defined. That is O(n), needs no new dependency, and converts a silent wrong answer into an actionable message. Sorting the input automatically would also work, though rejecting is arguably better since it keeps the tool's input contract explicit.

We work around it with an unconditional topological sort in our own driver, so this is not blocking us — but the silent-wrong-answer property seemed worth reporting given how the tool is typically used.

```
specs sealed TWICE                 547   (module-name key AND path-derived key)
```

Deleting the twins wholesale. Some of the 547 may be the only seal a downstream reader knows by name, and a seal that vanishes is indistinguishable from a spec that was never sealed.

Either `seal --save` updates every seal whose `spec_path` matches, or the gate refuses a spec that has more than one seal — one truth per spec, chosen deliberately, with the 31 disagreements resolved by re-sealing rather than by picking.

A maintainer on the project garvys-org/rustfst (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #316: Document (or expose) the contract for assembling lookahead composition

## Summary

rustfst ships a complete label-lookahead stack (`LabelReachable`, `IntervalSet`,
`StateReachable`, `LabelLookAheadMatcher`, `LookAheadComposeFilter`, `MatcherFst`,
…), but `compose()` cannot select it: `ComposeFilterEnum` has no lookahead
variant and `compose_static::create_matcher` always builds a `SortedMatcher`.

Assembling it by hand works and is fast — we measured ~3.8x over plain `compose` (14.4 ms -> 3.8 ms per input)
on a 187k-state grammar — but every step of the setup is an undocumented
invariant, and getting one wrong yields a **silently empty composition** rather
than an error. The only worked example is `do_test_compose_lookahead` in
`src/tests_openfst/algorithms/compose.rs`, which is `#[cfg(test)]` and therefore
invisible to users.

## The invariants we had to reverse-engineer

For `compose(fst1, fst2)` where the lookahead FST is `fst2`:

1. **Which side gets relabeled.** `MatcherFst::new` internally calls
   `LabelLookAheadRelabeler::init`, which relabels `fst2`'s **input** labels.
   Composition matches `fst1.olabel` against `fst2.ilabel`, so `fst1` must be
   relabeled with `relabel_input = false`.
   Passing `true` produces no matches at all — an empty result, no diagnostic.

2. **Flags also gate table construction.** `MatcherFlagsTrait::flags()` is not
   only a capability declaration: `LabelLookAheadMatcher::create_data` checks
   `INPUT_LOOKAHEAD_MATCHER` / `OUTPUT_LOOKAHEAD_MATCHER` to decide whether to
   build the reachability table for that match type at all. With the wrong bit,
   `create_data` returns `None`, `flags()` degrades to the inner matcher's flags,
   and the filter silently never performs lookahead — composition still succeeds,
   just with no pruning.

3. **Sortedness.** `LabelReachable::reach_init` requires the lookahead FST to be
   label-sorted on the side given by `reach_input`, and errors with
   `Properties are not known: FstProperties(O_LABEL_SORTED | NOT_O_LABEL_SORTED)`
   if it is sorted on the other side. This one at least fails loudly, but the
   message does not say which FST or which side is expected.

4. **Selector ↔ match type.** `SMatchInput` maps to `Selector::Fst1Matcher2`,
   i.e. *matcher2* is the lookahead matcher and it looks ahead into *fst1*. The
   naming reads the opposite way at first glance.

## Suggestions

Any subset would help, roughly in order of value:

- A public convenience entry point: a `ComposeFilterEnum::LookAhead` variant, or
  a `compose_lookahead(fst1, fst2)` helper, or public type aliases equivalent to
  OpenFST's `StdILabelLookAheadFst`.
- A doc example on `MatcherFst` or in `algorithms::compose` showing the full
  assembly (the existing test body is already almost this).
- Doc comments recording invariants 1–3 on `LabelLookAheadRelabeler::relabel`,
  `MatcherFlagsTrait`, and `LabelReachable::reach_init`.
- Optionally, a debug assertion when a lookahead filter is constructed but the
  matcher reports no lookahead flags — that would turn the silent
  no-pruning case into a visible one.

## Note on filter stacking

One doc line that would have saved us time: stacking
`PushWeightsComposeFilter` / `PushLabelsComposeFilter` on top of
`LookAheadComposeFilter` can change *which* of several equally-weighted paths
`shortest_path` returns. We confirmed that total path weight is preserved (so
this is correct behaviour, not a defect) — but for callers who compose and then
take the shortest path over an ambiguous grammar, the visible output can change.
Using `LookAheadComposeFilter` alone over `AltSequenceComposeFilter` (pruning
only) reproduced plain `compose` exactly across our 184-case corpus.

Since the only worked example in the tree uses the full four-layer stack, a note
that the pushing layers are aimed at incremental/pruned decoding rather than
"compose then shortest-path" would be helpful.

Happy to send a PR for any of the above.

Context: this came out of getting lookahead working for a text-normalization
workload; the one-line export it also needed is #314.

Issue #4120: Pattern across recent incidents: effects assumed rather than verified (evidence + contributed fixes)

We run gascity edge hard in production (multi-rig, compound-build factory, ~24/7). Over 72h of incident archaeology we kept finding the same shape underneath otherwise-unrelated bugs, and we think it's worth naming as a design doctrine rather than continuing to patch instances piecemeal — so this issue consolidates the pattern, the evidence, and the fixes we've already contributed, instead of us filing more one-off PRs.

## The pattern

**An action is performed and its effect is assumed, not verified.** Each instance is invisible in normal operation and surfaces as a silent stall/wedge under production load:

| Assumed | Reality | Consequence | Fix contributed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Recorded `work_dir` exists | reconcile re-derivation clobbered the launcher's real path; and worktrees get reaped | control beads hard-quarantine / gates chdir-fail | #4021 (consolidated: recording + resolution) |
| `send-keys` == delivered | TUI composer can swallow every Enter; delivery reported **ok** on failure | sessions freeze 9-12h looking `active`; 95 nudges queued | #4119 |
| Migration applied == committed | crash in the fallible tail leaves working set dirty; retries never converge | managed towns stuck at old schema | beads#4611 (merged — thank you) |
| Schedule evaluated == evaluated in the right clock | catch-up scan ran on the store's UTC-located timestamps | ET crons fire at UTC readings + double-fire | #4080 |
| Deployed binary == running binary | adopted sessions keep executing the old build | deployed fixes silently not in effect (bit us twice) | *(no PR — see ask below)* |
| Routed == claimed-by-the-right-dispatcher | static preference overrode rig-scoped ownership | compound builds stall at first control gate | #4006 |

(Two sibling instances live in gascity-packs: slack adapter registers once then dies on the boot-race 404 (packs#182); review loop iterates without an actionable delta (packs#188).)

## The doctrine we'd propose

_Re-filed into the template; the original body omitted the required fields._

## Gas City version

v1.4.0 (`/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew/Cellar/gascity/1.4.0/bin/gc`). Script verified unchanged on `main` via the contents API on 2026-08-03. `bd` 1.1.2 (Homebrew).

## Environment

Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, Linux 7.0.0-28-generic x86_64, bash 5.3.9. Single-workstation city, one HQ store plus one rig.

## Reproduction

`internal/bootstrap/packs/core/assets/scripts/wisp-compact.sh` selects the beads it will act on with:

```bash
ALL=$(gc bd list --json --all -n 0 2>/dev/null) || exit 0
EPHEMERALS=$(echo "$ALL" | jq '[.[] | select(.ephemeral == true)]' 2>/dev/null) || exit 0
if [ -z "$EPHEMERALS" ] || [ "$EPHEMERALS" = "[]" ]; then exit 0; fi
```

Wisps are infra beads, and `bd list` excludes infra unless `--include-infra` is passed:

```console
$ bd list --json --all -n 0                 | jq '[.[]|select(.ephemeral==true)]|length'
0
$ bd list --json --all -n 0 --include-infra | jq '[.[]|select(.ephemeral==true)]|length'
144
```

Then add `--include-infra` to that first line — the obvious repair — and dry-run the delete branch. On this city it selects **139 beads, every one `issue_type: message`**:

```
bl-wisp-dcey4  HANDOFF: PRODUCTION IS DEPLOYED AND HEALTHY. The ETL dry run now reach…
bl-wisp-063ou  BLOCKED: ta-2yl7 needs an architecture decision before any polecat can…
bl-wisp-rs8c0  ESCALATION: two blocked beads need routing decisions, not polecats [ME…
```

Because mail is stored as ephemeral `issue_type=message` beads and a **read** message is a **closed** one, so it satisfies "closed + past TTL + no comments" and falls through to `bd delete "$id" --force`.

Grouping every ephemeral bead by type shows there is nothing here the script should be deleting at all:

```console
$ # HQ store
message/closed: 142
message/open: 2
$ # rig store
molecule/in_progress: 1
molecule/open: 10
```

A second defect compounds it: one invocation only reads the store its cwd resolves to, so from the city root it never sees a rig's wisps. `gc bd --rig <name>` is not the fix on its own — it returns nothing for the HQ, which holds 144 of the 155 ephemeral beads here.

## Expected behavior

The order compacts genuine wisp churn — closed patrol/heartbeat wisps past TTL — across every store, and never treats the user's mail archive as automation churn.

## Actual behavior

It has never compacted anything, in any city: the selector returns `[]` every time, the guard trips, and the order exits 0 hourly reporting success. Neither the TTL cleanup nor the stuck-detection promote path has ever executed.

And the no-op is the only thing preventing data loss. Fixing the visibility bug alone arms the deletion of every read mail past TTL on the next hourly tick — on this city, every mayor handoff and every `ESCALATION:`, including the handoff the investigating session had been resumed from.

**The promote path can strand the agent it protects.** For non-closed wisps past TTL the script does `bd update "$id" --persistent`. 1. Add `--include-infra` to the list call — **but not without 2.**
2. Exclude `issue_type == "message"` from deletion unconditionally. Mail retention is a separate policy from wisp retention and shouldn't be governed by a wisp TTL table.
3. Iterate stores explicitly (`gc rig list --json` → per-rig path) rather than depending on cwd.
4. Consider whether the promote path should skip a live agent's current signal.

Issue #10: Laberinto: difficulty spikes hard by level 6 + subtitle wraps mid-word on mobile

## Summary

Reviewed **Laberinto** (`laberinto.html`, added in commit `8ad0aaf`, game #11 in the plan), the latest game published to the arcade and already merged to `main`. Overall it's a strong addition — the recursive-backtracker maze generation is solid, the flashlight/fog-of-war visual effect reads well, pause works correctly, and there were no console errors or crashes. Found one real balance issue and one visible rendering bug worth fixing, plus a couple of smaller suggestions.

## How I tested

Served the file locally and drove it with Playwright (Chromium headless): played through the start/pause/move flow, held vs. tapped movement keys to check input responsiveness, and screenshotted the header at several mobile viewport widths (375/414/430/500/768px). Separately, I extracted `generateMaze`/`braid`/`levelConfig` into a standalone Node script and ran 200 trials per level to measure actual shortest-path length vs. the time/vision budget the game gives you.

## Balance issue: full difficulty hits by level 6, then flatlines while the clock and vision keep shrinking

`levelConfig(n)`:
```js
const size = Math.min(9+(n-1)*2, 19);
const time = Math.max(16, 42-(n-1)*2.5);
const visionRadius = Math.max(1.5, 2.6-(n-1)*0.07);
```

Simulated shortest path (BFS) vs. budget, averaged over 200 mazes/level:

| level | size | time budget | vision radius | avg shortest path |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 9×9 | 42s | 2.60 | 24.9 |
| 4 | 15×15 | 34.5s | 2.39 | 48.3 |
| **6** | **19×19 (max)** | **29.5s** | 2.25 | **63.1** |
| 8 | 19×19 | 24.5s | 2.11 | 60.4 |
| 11 | 19×19 | 17s | 1.90 | 61.0 |
| 14 | 19×19 | 16s (floor) | 1.69 | 61.9 |

By **level 6** the maze is already at max size (19×19) with an average ~60-step shortest path, while the flashlight only reveals a ~2.25-cell radius — the player physically cannot see the route and must explore/backtrack under a 29.5s (and shrinking) timer. Movement is also strictly one-step-per-input: holding an arrow key does nothing after the first step (confirmed empirically — holding `ArrowRight` for 1.5s left the player in the exact same cell as a single tap; the code explicitly ignores repeat keydowns via `if(e.repeat) return;`), and the D-pad buttons only fire on `pointerdown`, not on hold. So clearing a ~60-cell blind maze requires ~60 accurately-aimed individual key presses/taps inside a shrinking window, with no further increase in maze size after level 6 to justify the still-tightening clock. Net effect: difficulty spikes abruptly around level 6 and most runs likely end there regardless of skill, rather than escalating smoothly like earlier levels do.

**Repro:** play to level 6 (or briefly set `level=6` in devtools and call `setupLevel(6)`) and try to reach the goal within 29.5s using only the flashlight radius — very hard to do consistently even for a spirited attempt.

## Bug: header subtitle wraps mid-word on common mobile widths

The subtitle `P U Z Z L E   ·   L I N T E R N A   N E Ó N` fakes letter-spacing with literal (breakable) spaces between individual letters, on top of `letter-spacing:5px` in CSS. On narrow viewports the browser wraps inside a "word" instead of only at the ` ` word boundaries:

- 500px wide: `NEÓN` splits into `NEÓ` / `N` on its own line.
- 375px wide (iPhone SE-class): `LINTERNA` splits into `LINTERN` / `A`.

This reproduces consistently on load, no interaction needed — just open `laberinto.html` at ≤500px width. Screenshots taken at 375/414/500px all show it; 414px happens to wrap only at the `NEÓN` boundary but 375/500 both break mid-word.

## Suggested improvements

1. **Fix the subtitle wrap**: swap the letter-by-letter regular spaces for ` ` between every character (or drop the manual spacing entirely and rely on CSS `letter-spacing` alone), so the line only breaks at the intended word gaps.
2. **Rebalance levels 6+**: either keep growing maze size a bit further before capping (so the time/vision squeeze has a matching size increase to justify it), or ease the time-per-level floor once size caps out, so the mid-game doesn't spike into "keeps getting harder for no new reason."
3. **Consider inertia-free continuous movement**: let holding a direction (keyboard or D-pad) repeat moves after a short delay, the way most maze/roguelike games do — would meaningfully help with the ~60-step traversals without changing the core blind-exploration challenge.
4. *(Minor, arcade-wide)* No sound effects anywhere in this game (consistent with the rest of the arcade so not a regression, but reaching the goal/losing on the clock both currently land silently).

If none of these are worth prioritizing right now, the maze generation/rendering/core loop is solid and the game is otherwise ready to ship as-is; the balance issue mainly affects players who get past the first few levels.

Issue #4: Prototype pollution via __proto__/constructor.prototype paths (CWE-1321)

# Prototype pollution via `__proto__.xxx` / `constructor.prototype.xxx` paths (CWE-1321)

## Summary

`object-set` writes nested path values with zero key filtering. Because path traversal does `nested = nested[key]` without guarding `__proto__` / `constructor` keys (index.js:33-53), a path like `__proto__.polluted` or `constructor.prototype.polluted` walks onto `Object.prototype` itself and **pollutes the global prototype**:

- `__proto__.polluted` → `nested` becomes `Object.prototype` (via `nested['__proto__']`), then `assignValue(Object.prototype, 'polluted', value)` sets a global property on `Object.prototype`
- `constructor.prototype.polluted` → same result through the `constructor` chain
- `toString` / `hasOwnProperty` etc. as leaf keys overwrite methods on the target object (method override)

No `hasOwnProperty` check, no deny-list, no `Object.create(null)` anywhere in the write path (`assignValue` at index.js:9-18 is a bare `object[key] = value`).

## Reproduction

```js
const objectSet = require('object-set');

// Global prototype pollution
objectSet({}, '__proto__.polluted', 'yes');
console.log({}.polluted);        // 'yes' — EVERY plain object is affected
console.log(Object.prototype.polluted); // 'yes'

// Same via constructor chain
objectSet({}, 'constructor.prototype.polluted', 'yes2');
console.log({}.polluted);        // 'yes2'

// Method override on target
const t = objectSet({}, 'toString', 'hacked');
console.log(typeof t.toString);  // 'string' (was: function)
```

Verified on object-set@1.0.1 (latest), Node.js v24.

## Impact

Classic **CWE-1321 prototype pollution** (the same class as lodash's set CVE-2019-10744 / dot-prop CVE-2020-8141):

- **Application-level DoS / logic corruption**: once `Object.prototype` carries attacker keys, property lookups across the whole process are poisoned (e.g. option objects silently gain keys like `admin: true`, status maps inherit unexpected entries).
- **Potential RCE in real apps**: in codebases that later use polluted keys in sinks (template engines, `child_process` option objects, `require` paths — see prior research on prototype-pollution-to-RCE chains), this escalates beyond DoS.
- **Method override**: `toString`/`hasOwnProperty` leaf writes break template interpolation and common checks.

Attack surface: any app that passes **user-controlled path strings** to `objectSet()` — e.g. `objectSet(config, req.query.key, value)`, dot-notation form keys, JSON path from client payloads.

## Suggested Fix

Reject prototype-chain keys during traversal:

```js
const FORBIDDEN = new Set(['__proto__', 'constructor', 'prototype']);
// in the walk loop: if (FORBIDDEN.has(key)) return object;
```

(and/or use `Object.create(null)` intermediates + `Object.hasOwn` reads before `nested = nested[key]`).

## Environment

- object-set 1.0.1 (published 2016-04, last repo commit 2016-12)
- Node.js v24.15.0
- npm registry

- Editing the original comment.
- Hiding all comments authored by a banned user.
- Redesigning the public comment-thread UI.
- User-facing appeals.

Issue #1889: [Design] Bind provider-native sessions to governed runtime executions

## Status

Retargeted under #1980. `RuntimeExecution` is the portable governed unit; a
Codex, Claude, or other provider session is an opaque origin/binding of that
execution, not a second universal governance resource.

This issue owns the provider-native binding and thin-adapter design. #1980 owns
the shared execution contracts, #1970 owns credential requirements and
host-local bindings, and #1859 owns MoltNet-native conversations and detach.

## Outcome

Bind provider-native thread/session identifiers to a governed runtime execution
without requiring a MoltNet task, copying the provider transcript, or pretending
provider hooks are an operating-system sandbox.

The binding must identify the provider and adapter version, attach the opaque
provider reference to one execution epoch, expose enforcement coverage and
unsupported paths, and preserve the execution snapshot, lease, evidence, and
revocation semantics defined by #1980.

## Retained Codex evidence

PR #2013 proves a private Codex 0.149.0 / Gondolin 0.12.0 compatibility path:

- Codex App Server, authentication, model traffic, MCP, and host tools remain on
  the trusted host.
- One Codex exec-server runs inside Gondolin for each remote-environment
  WebSocket connection.
- Model-requested shell execution uses the selected Gondolin environment.
  `thread/shellCommand` is host-local and is not valid remote-execution proof.
- The environment transitions from `pending` to `ready`; the guest command
  completes on Linux with exit code zero.
- A host-only sentinel and credential-shaped environment names are absent from
  the guest.
- Closing the VM prevents detached delayed work from surviving.
- The retained evidence excludes prompts, transcripts, opaque thread and
  environment identifiers, machine paths, tokens, and credential values.

The Codex remote-environment API, `deferred_executor`, and `externalSandbox`
path are experimental. This evidence proves compatibility and boundary shape;
it does not prove MoltNet signing, exact-origin credential delivery, Docker
support, or a production adapter.

## Binding decisions

- Store only an opaque provider reference plus provider/adapter identity and
  version. Do not make provider transcript semantics canonical MoltNet state.
- Attach provider start/resume/fork operations to runtime-execution origins and
  execution epochs. Provider lifecycle never widens the pinned authority.
- Declare which operations execute on the host and which execute through the
  selected sandbox environment. Host tools/MCP and sandbox controls remain
  separate enforcement surfaces.
- Re-evaluate execution authority and local bindings at the #1980 lifecycle
  boundaries. A stale or revoked binding must fail closed.
- Represent experimental, advisory, unsupported, degraded, and failed-open
  behavior explicitly and feed it into #1888.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An ADR defines the provider-binding identifier, lifecycle, invariants, and
      privacy boundary over `RuntimeExecution`.
- [ ] One Codex thread binds to a deterministic governed execution without a
      MoltNet task ID.
- [ ] Adapter/version identity and the opaque provider reference are recorded
      without copying the provider transcript.
- [ ] Host App Server/tools/MCP and guest execution coverage are declared and
      evidenced separately.
- [ ] Start, resume, fork, revoke, expire, and close cannot retain or widen stale
      execution authority.
- [ ] Unsupported and experimental Codex/Claude paths are excluded from product
      claims rather than silently treated as governed.
- [ ] The minimum value-free decision/evidence envelope is reusable by Codex,
      Claude, and future provider adapters.
- [ ] #1888 exercises direct shell, hosted tools, MCP, nested agents,
      resume/fork, inherited environment, and degraded-service paths.

- #1970 — separate credential requirements and trusted host-local bindings.
- #1927 — declaration and attestation for host-versus-guest tool egress.

- #1888 — adversarial validation after provider bindings and execution contracts

Issue #421: Google Drive (DWD scoped): index documents with effective permissions from drive & folder ACLs

## Problem

The Google Drive connector indexes shared-drive content in "scoped" (DWD) mode with an ACL that only contains the syncing principal, because the Drive API does not return a `permissions` array on shared-drive items in list responses. Consequences:

- Documents in selected drives/folders are only searchable by one person, even though they are shared with the whole drive.
- Files inside limited-access folders can end up with too-broad or too-narrow ACLs (inherited drive-wide access is not truncated at the boundary).
- Drive membership and folder-grant changes are not detected by the incremental changes feed, so wrong ACLs persist in the index indefinitely.

The SA-direct path already solves this with an "effective permission model" (drive ACL as baseline + folder-level grants + limited-access boundaries); the DWD scoped path does not have it.

## Proposed solution (high level)

- Index each document in a scoped drive with its **effective permission set**: drive membership as baseline, plus directly-assigned folder grants, respecting limited-access folder boundaries.
- Detect ACL changes (drive membership, folder grants) that `changes.list` does not deliver, and re-traverse affected drives so the index converges to correct ACLs.
- If a drive's ACL is unreadable for the principal (not a manager), degrade gracefully for that drive instead of failing the whole source sync.
- On deploy, run one full re-traversal so previously indexed documents get corrected ACLs.

A working implementation exists on branch `fix/drive-folder-permission-inheritance` (pending review); this ticket tracks the remaining review feedback, merging, and the deferred per-user (My Drive) path, which needs live-API verification first.

## Out of scope (for now)

- Per-user unfiltered (My Drive) path — requires verification of Google's `permissionDetails` semantics against the live API before designing.

Issue #27180: ggml-openvino: frontend compiled-model cache import loads but cannot compute — exported port names embed pointer-derived hash suffix (map::at on first inference)

### Summary

The frontend compiled-model cache introduced in #26952 (`GGML_OPENVINO_COMPILED_MODEL_CACHE_DIR`) exports a `CompiledModel` whose Parameter/Result friendly names embed the `#N` suffix produced by `get_tensor_ov_name()`. That suffix is `ggml_hash_find(&cgraph->visited_hash_set, tensor)` — a slot index derived from the tensor's **pointer value** (`ggml_hash` is `(uintptr_t)p >> 4`). It therefore changes from process to process. On import in a fresh process, the decoder recomputes names from the new cgraph, gets different suffixes, and the very first input binding lookup throws `std::out_of_range ("map::at")`. The cache HIT loads fast but every inference fails. This is deterministic and affects any model whose graph has suffixed port names (KV-cache / recurrent-state inputs, i.e. every stateful LLM graph).

### Environment

- llama.cpp master, b10428 (`885c5bbe8e`), `GGML_OPENVINO=ON`, `BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF`
- OpenVINO 2026.4.0 (`openvino-git` r263.g0f453eb8dca), GPU plugin, intel-compute-runtime 26.27.39122.11
- Intel Core Ultra 7 356H (Panther Lake) iGPU, Arch Linux
- Model: qwen35-arch GGUF (GatedDeltaNet linear attention, 9B Q4_K_M), `-ngl 99`, `-c 16384`

### Repro

```bash
# 1. fresh cache dir: first start compiles + exports the blob
env GGML_OPENVINO_DEVICE=GPU \
    GGML_OPENVINO_COMPILED_MODEL_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/ov-test \
    llama-server -m model.gguf --port 18100 -c 16384 -ngl 99 -dev OPENVINO0
# log: "ggml-openvino: model cache WROTE /tmp/ov-test/<fp>.blob"
# /completion works. Stop the server.

# 2. second start: cache HIT, fast load
env GGML_OPENVINO_DEVICE=GPU \
    GGML_OPENVINO_COMPILED_MODEL_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/ov-test \
    llama-server -m model.gguf --port 18100 -c 16384 -ngl 99 -dev OPENVINO0
# log: "ggml-openvino: model cache HIT /tmp/ov-test/<fp>.blob"
curl localhost:18100/completion -d '{"prompt":"1+1=","n_predict":8,"temperature":0}'
# => HTTP 500 "Compute error", every time
```

Note: the backend's cache lines are `GGML_LOG_INFO` and are suppressed at the
server's default log verbosity — pass `-lv 5` (as in the invocations above) to
see the WROTE/HIT lines.

Server log on the HIT path:

```
I ggml-openvino: model cache HIT /tmp/ov-test/<fp>.blob
E GGML OpenVINO backend std::exception: map::at
E graph_compute: ggml_backend_sched_graph_compute_async failed with error -1
E srv  decode: Compute error. off = 0, n_batch = 2048, ret = -3
```

### Root cause (gdb-confirmed)

Backtrace of the throw on the import path (first inference after HIT,
RelWithDebInfo build, `catch throw` on `std::out_of_range`):

```
std::__throw_out_of_range
std::map<std::string, ggml_tensor*>::at(__k="cache_k_l11#55152")   stl_map.h:611
GgmlOvDecoder::get_input_ggml_tensor(name="cache_k_l11#55152")     ggml-decoder.h:218   <- m_inputs.at(name)
convert_ggml_input_to_ov                                           utils.cpp:1028
get_ov_input_tensor                                                utils.cpp:1069
ov_graph_compute_dynamic  (binding loop over cm.inputs())          utils.cpp:506
```

The imported model's input port friendly name is `cache_k_l11#55152`. The
suffix is appended by `get_tensor_ov_name()` (`ggml-decoder.cpp`):

```cpp
const size_t hash_pos = ggml_hash_find(&cgraph->visited_hash_set, tensor);
if (((tensor->flags & GGML_TENSOR_FLAG_COMPUTE) || is_kvcache(tensor, nullptr)) && ...) {
    return std::string(tensor->name) + "#" + std::to_string(hash_pos);
}
```

`hash_pos` is a slot in a pointer-keyed hash set; across two runs of the same
binary + model we observed `cache_k_l11#2940` and `cache_k_l11#55152`. The
compile path works because both the ov::Model and the decoder are built from
the same cgraph in the same process. The import path compares names baked at
*export* time against names recomputed in a *different* process, so `m_inputs`
has no such key and `.at()` throws.

This means the feature could not have worked across processes for any graph
with KV-cache/recurrent-state inputs — only same-process round-trips or graphs
without suffixed port names would survive.

### Proposed fix

Make the disambiguation suffix deterministic across processes: use the
tensor's index in the cgraph `nodes`/`leafs` arrays (build order is
deterministic for a given model + graph params) instead of the pointer-hash
slot:

```cpp
static std::string get_tensor_ov_name(const ggml_cgraph * cgraph, const ggml_tensor * tensor) {
    if (tensor == nullptr) {
        return "";
    }
    if ((tensor->flags & GGML_TENSOR_FLAG_COMPUTE) || GgmlOvDecoder::is_kvcache(tensor, nullptr)) {
        const size_t hash_pos = ggml_hash_find(&cgraph->visited_hash_set, tensor);
        if (hash_pos != GGML_HASHSET_FULL && ggml_bitset_get(cgraph->visited_hash_set.used, hash_pos)) {
            for (int i = 0; i < cgraph->n_nodes; i++) {
                if (cgraph->nodes[i] == tensor) {
                    return std::string(tensor->name) + "#" + std::to_string(i);
                }
            }
```

Issue #237: Preliminary design: side chats

## Status

Preliminary proposal for discussion. This is not a finalized product or implementation spec.

## Summary

Side chats are lightweight sessions attached to a parent session. They let a user branch into a focused conversation while keeping the main session active and uncluttered.

Core characteristics:

- A side chat belongs to exactly one parent session.
- A side chat inherits the parent session worktree.
- A side chat is archived when its parent session is archived.
- Side chats do not appear in the global sessions list.
- Side chats remain discoverable from the parent session.

## Proposed model

Conceptually, sessions could distinguish primary sessions from side chats:

```ts
type SessionKind = "primary" | "side"

type Session = {
  id: SessionId
  kind: SessionKind
  parentSessionId?: SessionId
  worktreeId: WorktreeId
  archivedAt?: Date
}
```

A side chat would have its own message history, title, agent state, and lifecycle, but share the parent session worktree.

Suggested lifecycle behavior:

- Archiving a parent archives all of its side chats.
- Archiving a side chat does not affect the parent.
- Unarchiving a parent should probably not automatically unarchive side chats; users can restore individual side chats if needed.

## Creation flow

While a parent session tab is active, users can create a side chat via:

- `/side`
- `/side <prompt>`
- Command palette action, for example `Start Side Chat`

Potential context sources for creation:

- The typed `/side` prompt.
- Current file, selection, or focused UI context.
- A compact summary of relevant parent-session context.

The side chat should not automatically receive the full parent transcript unless there is a deliberate product reason to do so.

## UI proposal

A side chat opens as a popover over the active parent session. The popover should feel like a lightweight session surface, not a blocking modal.

Suggested popover affordances:

- Compact header with side chat title, status, close button, and overflow menu.
- Closing the popover keeps the side chat alive.
- Running side chats show activity somewhere in the parent session chrome.
- Completed or inactive side chats are available from a parent-local side chat picker.

One possible parent-session affordance:

```text
[Session Title]        [Side Chats 3] [⋯]
```

The side chat picker could show recent attached chats:

```text
Side Chats
- Investigate failing auth test       running
- Draft migration notes               done
- Explore SDK parity issue            archived
```

Global session lists should exclude side chats by default. Search can either exclude side chats globally or include them only through an explicit “include side chats” option.

## Worktree implications

Because side chats share the parent worktree, concurrent edits are possible. The UI should make that visible.

Possible affordances:

- Show `Shared worktree` in the side chat header.
- Surface parent timeline events when a side chat modifies files.
- Show an activity indicator if a side chat is currently running against the shared worktree.

Example parent event:

```text
Side chat “Fix lint error” modified 2 files.
```

## Other characteristics to consider

- **Send result to parent:** allow a side chat to send a summary, selected message, changed-files summary, or recommended next step back to the parent session.
- **Permission inheritance:** decide whether side chats inherit the parent permission mode exactly or start with a safer default for file edits.
- **Purpose presets:** lightweight creation modes such as Ask, Investigate, Draft, Review, or Implement could tune context and permissions without creating separate product concepts.
- **Notifications:** when a side chat continues after the popover closes, show subtle parent-tab activity and completion indicators.
- **Naming:** auto-title side chats from their first prompt, with fallback names like `Side chat` or `Investigate test failure`.
- **Promotion:** consider, but probably defer, a way to promote a side chat into a top-level session. This complicates ownership, listing, and archive semantics.
- **Limits and organization:** consider how the parent UI behaves if a session accumulates many side chats.

## Suggested MVP

A narrow first version could include:

- Create side chat from `/side` and command palette.
- Open side chat as a popover.
- Share the parent session worktree.
- Store `parentSessionId` or equivalent relationship.
- Hide side chats from the global sessions list.
- Reopen side chats from a parent-local picker.
- Keep a side chat running when its popover is closed.
- Archive side chats when the parent session is archived.

Deferrable items:

- Promotion to top-level session.
- Advanced permission customization.
- Global search integration.
- Automatic side-chat summary injection into the parent session.
- Rich purpose presets.

## Open questions

- Should side chats be allowed to modify files by default when the parent session can?
- Should side chats inherit full parent context, a summarized context packet, or only explicit launch context?
- Should side chats appear in any global search result by default?
- Should unarchiving a parent expose archived side chats automatically, keep them hidden, or restore them?
- Do we need a conflict model for simultaneous parent and side-chat edits in the same worktree?

Issue #220: [bug] Soft-delete makes FK/restrict constraints never fire, leaving live rows referencing API-404 parents

### What happened

`gorm.Model` gives every model a `DeletedAt`, so admin/generated deletes are
soft (they set `deleted_at`; the row physically remains). But Atlas still emits
real `ON DELETE NO ACTION` foreign keys for associations. Because no physical
DELETE ever happens, the restrict constraint **never fires**, and a child row is
left pointing at a parent the API now reports as 404.

So a schema that looks referentially safe is not: deleting a referenced parent
"succeeds", and you silently have a live row referencing an API-invisible parent.

Expected: soft-delete and FK/restrict semantics should be coherent, either the

Issue #109: feat(router): policy-driven tiered LLM routing, failover, and recovery

## Summary

Add a policy-driven routing layer that selects among cloud and local LLM execution profiles according to:

- Task capability requirements.
- Model quality tier.
- User-defined provider priority.
- Provider availability and quota state.
- Tool, context-window, and protocol compatibility.
- Security, privacy, and data-egress policy.
- Cost and latency preferences.
- Verification strength.

The primary objective is **continuity without silently sacrificing code quality**.

This feature is not intended to make a local model as fast or capable as a frontier model. It should allow CCT to continue making safe, useful progress when the preferred model is unavailable, while preventing weaker or incompatible models from taking work they are not trusted to perform.

Example priority chain:

1. Anthropic Sonnet through Claude Code.
2. DeepSeek V4 Pro through Claude Code's Anthropic-compatible endpoint.
3. GPT-5.6 Sol through the Codex backend.
4. Qwen3-Coder-Next on a local DGX Spark for explicitly bounded Tier-2 work.

When the preferred Anthropic profile becomes available again, CCT should detect recovery automatically and return to it at the next safe task boundary.

---

## Problem

CCT currently has several pieces of the required infrastructure, but no unified execution router:

- `auto-build-loop.sh` selects one build backend—currently Claude or Pi—for the complete run.
- `cooldown-supervisor.sh` detects a usage-limit message, sleeps for a fixed interval, and relaunches the same backend.
- `providers.toml` supports fallback chains for peer reviewers, not build execution.
- The benchmark harness correctly separates backend and model, but runtime auto-build does not yet preserve the complete backend/provider/model identity.
- Provider health checks primarily establish that a CLI or endpoint is reachable; they do not prove that a real inference and tool-use request succeeds.
- Switching models by redirecting Claude Code does not provide a quality policy, task eligibility rules, checkpointed handoff, or primary-model reconciliation.

Claude Code's native fallback chain does not solve this problem. It does not trigger on rate-limit failures, and Anthropic subscription session and weekly limits are shared across models. Switching from Sonnet to another Anthropic model therefore usually does not restore access. See [Claude Code fallback behavior](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config#fallback-model-chains) and [subscription-limit behavior](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/errors#youve-hit-your-session-limit).

### Benchmark evidence

The 2026-08-09 Sonnet-versus-Qwen smoke benchmark proved that the local path is viable:

- Both implementations passed all 31 canonical tests.
- Sonnet completed the task in 57.7 seconds.
- Qwen completed it in 1,075.2 seconds—approximately 18.6× slower.
- Sonnet used 6 agent turns and one successful test run.
- Qwen used 20 turns and eight test runs, seven of which failed.
- Qwen produced approximately three times as much code and left redundant/dead logic.

This was one run, so it is not a statistically valid model-quality comparison. It does establish the architectural point:

> A capable local model can continue implementation, but it should receive smaller work packets and stronger externally enforced controls than the preferred frontier model.

---

## Goals

1. Continue building when the preferred provider reaches a usage limit, rate limit, outage, or temporary capacity failure.
2. Support an ordered chain of profiles spanning different backends, providers, and models.
3. Use Tier-2 models for explicitly bounded tasks, either by preference for simple work or when no Tier-1 model is available.
4. Prevent Tier-2 models from receiving architecture, security, migration, or other high-risk work.
5. Preserve task state through durable, backend-neutral checkpoints.
6. Keep verification, landing authority, and quality policy outside the model.
7. Detect provider recovery and fail back to the preferred profile at a task boundary.
8. Produce an explainable audit trail for every routing decision.
9. Use benchmark results to improve routing policy over time, without making learned routing a prerequisite for the initial implementation.

### Success definition

Success is not equivalent speed across models. Success means:

- Useful work continues during preferred-provider downtime.
- Final verifier quality does not materially regress.
- Tier-2 work remains bounded and provisional.
- Primary/Tier-1 reconciliation catches or simplifies weak local changes.
- No provider switch bypasses security, verification, or review policy.
- The final repository state remains the source of truth.

---

## Terminology

These concepts must remain separate:

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Backend** | The coding harness that executes the task, such as `claude-code`, `codex`, or `pi`. |
| **Provider** | The service or endpoint supplying inference, such as Anthropic, DeepSeek, OpenAI, or local vLLM. |
| **Model** | The requested model identifier, such as `sonnet`, `deepseek-v4-pro[1m]`, `gpt-5.6-sol`, or `qwen3-coder-next`. |
| **Execution profile** | A validated combination of backend, provider, model, tool profile, authentication mode, tier, roles, and policy constraints. |
| **Capability tier** | The class of work a profile is trusted to perform. This is unrelated to an API provider's billing or usage tier. |
| **Priority** | The order in which otherwise eligible profiles are attempted. |
| **Quota pool** | Profiles that share the same underlying usage allowance. |
| **Task route class** | The routing policy attached to one bounded task. |
| **Availability** | Whether a profile can successfully execute a real request now. |
| **Landing authority** | Whether verified work from that profile may satisfy a phase/landing gate without additional reconciliation. |

A backend is not a provider. For example:

- Claude Code is a backend.
- Anthropic, DeepSeek, and a LiteLLM/vLLM gate

Issue #1410: Embed dependency metadata in the Java agent JAR

## Problem

The built `grafana-opentelemetry-java.jar` is an uber JAR containing the upstream OpenTelemetry Java agent and its shaded dependencies. When the JAR is copied into a Docker image and scanned with JFrog Xray, those components are not reliably identified because the JAR does not contain machine-readable dependency metadata. This can lead to incomplete vulnerability attribution and scan coverage.

## Findings

An initial approach embedded Maven `pom.xml` and `pom.properties` metadata for `com.grafana:grafana-opentelemetry-java`. This allowed JFrog to identify the Grafana distribution itself, but not the shaded dependencies.

The CycloneDX Gradle plugin can generate a standards-compliant SBOM for this project, but it works from Gradle's resolved dependency graph. Gradle sees `io.opentelemetry.javaagent:opentelemetry-javaagent` as one pre-shaded artifact, so the plugin cannot discover the libraries already bundled inside that upstream JAR.

OpenTelemetry publishes an official SPDX 2.3 SBOM alongside each Java agent artifact in Maven Central using the `spdx` classifier. For example:

`io.opentelemetry.javaagent:opentelemetry-javaagent:2.31.1:spdx@json`

That upstream SBOM contains the real bundled component inventory, including package URLs and checksums for shaded Maven dependencies.

## Proposed change

Embed two complementary SBOMs in the final JAR under `META-INF/sbom/`:

- `grafana-opentelemetry-java.cdx.json`: generated by the CycloneDX Gradle plugin from this project's `javaagentLibs` and `upstreamAgent` configurations. It identifies the Grafana distribution and its direct dependencies.
- `opentelemetry-javaagent.spdx.json`: resolved from the official upstream `spdx` classifier. It describes the OpenTelemetry agent's bundled and shaded components.

The SBOMs should be generated or resolved automatically by `:agent:shadowJar`, use the current distribution and upstream versions, and replace the earlier embedded-POM proposal.

## Expected outcome

JFrog Xray and other SBOM-aware scanners can identify both the Grafana distribution and the dependencies shaded into the upstream OpenTelemetry agent when scanning the JAR directly or as part of a Docker image. This also avoids maintaining a duplicate dependency inventory in this repository.

Issue #754: No limit in nested selection sets

## Summary
graphql-go's public parser can be made to exhaust the Go runtime stack while parsing a syntactically valid, deeply nested GraphQL selection set. The issue is in the recursive selection-set parser path under `language/parser/parser.go`: the parser descends through nested fields before validation or execution depth limits can run, so a single large document can terminate the hosting process. This may have some security-relevant effects but we were not able to find any means of contact for private report.

## Affected
- Project: graphql
- Repo: https://github.com/graphql-go/graphql
- Pinned ref: 7cd8e416df5584b863584033651b658e0098b3a7

## Root cause
The exported `Parse` entry point accepts caller-controlled input and wraps string sources into the parser's `source.Source` at `language/parser/parser.go:56`. It then immediately calls `parseDocument` at `language/parser/parser.go:69`; a document beginning with `{` is treated as an anonymous operation at `language/parser/parser.go:143`, and `parseOperationDefinition` hands that selection directly to `parseSelectionSet` at `language/parser/parser.go:178`. `parseSelectionSet` parses `{ Selection+ }` through `reverse(..., parseSelection, ...)` at `language/parser/parser.go:317`, while `reverse` repeatedly calls the supplied parse function at `language/parser/parser.go:1582` without tracking nesting depth. Issue #2529: bug: recursive struct check E3061 is bypassed through a type alias, leaking a C compiler error

### Description

A struct that contains itself by value is rejected with `E3061`. Routing the self-reference through a type alias skips that check entirely — the typechecker emits no diagnostic, codegen produces a struct with a field of its own incomplete type, and the user sees a raw C compiler error.

This affects both direct self-reference and mutual recursion between two structs.

### Expected behavior

`E3061: struct 'Node' cannot contain itself by value; use a pointer field '^Node' for recursive types`, the same as the direct form.

### Actual behavior

Compilation reaches `cc`, which fails:

```
/tmp/gray_run-1.c:15:21: error: field has incomplete type 'GrayStruct_Node' (aka 'struct GrayStruct_Node')
   15 |     GrayStruct_Node next;
      |                     ^
/tmp/gray_run-1.c:14:8: note: definition of 'struct GrayStruct_Node' is not complete until the closing '}'
   14 | struct GrayStruct_Node {
      |        ^
1 error generated.
gray: C compilation failed
```

### Minimal reproduction — direct self-reference

```gray
const Node struct {
    next NodeAlias
    v int
}

alias NodeAlias = Node

do main() {
    println("hi")
}
```

### Minimal reproduction — mutual recursion

The same bypass defeats the cycle check between two structs:

```gray
const A struct {
    b BAlias
}
const B struct {
    a AAlias
}

alias AAlias = A
alias BAlias = B

do main() {
    println("hi")
}
```

```
/tmp/gray_run-1.c:16:18: error: field has incomplete type 'GrayStruct_B' (aka 'struct GrayStruct_B')
   16 |     GrayStruct_B b;
      |                  ^
/tmp/gray_run-1.c:13:16: note: forward declaration of 'struct GrayStruct_B'
   13 | typedef struct GrayStruct_B GrayStruct_B;
      |                ^
1 error generated.
gray: C compilation failed
```

### Contrast — both forms are caught without aliases

```gray
const Node struct {
    next Node
    v int
}

do main() {
    println("hi")
}
```

```
error[E3061]: struct 'Node' cannot contain itself by value; use a pointer field '^Node' for recursive types
  --> repro.gray:1:7
   |
  1 | const Node struct {
   |       ^
```

```gray
const A struct {
    b B
}
const B struct {
    a A
}

do main() {
    println("hi")
}
```

```
error[E3061]: struct 'A' cannot contain itself by value through 'B'; break the cycle with a pointer field '^B'
error[E3061]: struct 'B' cannot contain itself by value through 'A'; break the cycle with a pointer field '^A'
```

And the pointer form works as intended:

```gray
const Node struct {
    next ^Node
    v int
}

do main() {
    println("hi")   // compiles and runs
}
```

Issue #9: Roadmap: the generic Ignatius PostgreSQL blockchain and HAL client

## Direction

Ignatius is the authoritative, application-neutral PostgreSQL blockchain and its portable HAL client/workflow layer.

```text
Hestia and other applications
  -> application-owned canonical operation packs
  -> Ignatius HAL client
  -> postgres.core
  -> gw_ledger transaction execution and block commit
  -> canonical generic receipt
```

The chain owns HCV1/HCP1 state, accounts/controllers, signed transactions, deterministic execution, ordering, blocks, heads, snapshots, roots, scoped refs and generic receipts.

The HAL client owns transaction construction, local evaluation/conformance, signing payloads, direct `postgres.core` submission, synchronization, receipt verification, outbox handling and reusable workflow management.

Applications own domain meaning and policy.

## Application boundary

### Hestia

Owns the private authority office: human/agent profiles, delegations, rooms, membership epochs, mandates, exact-root approvals, source mandates, room application grants, documents, negotiation, continuity and Hestia-specific projections/receipts.

Hestia records are ordinary application operation packs submitted through Ignatius. Ignatius public contracts must not contain Hestia room/profile/document types or evaluate Hestia policy.

### Greenways OS

Owns local installation, local app approval, key/provider custody, routes and effects. It may submit or verify ordinary Ignatius transactions but does not make device authority a chain primitive.

### Tahto and other applications

Own their semantic records, merge policy and projections. Ignatius commits exact accepted operations and roots without becoming the application model.

## Non-negotiable implementation rules

- `gwdb.ledger.*` remains the Clojure Foundation PostgreSQL DSL source for the authoritative engine and generated SQL.
- Do not port the authoritative ledger engine to `.hal`.
- Portable execution is planning, local evaluation and conformance—not admission, ordering or block commitment.
- Do not introduce an Ignatius HTTP/evidence microservice or a second application ledger.
- PostgreSQL credentials and handles remain inside `postgres.core`.
- Generated public contracts remain application-neutral.
- Exact accepted history, roots, signatures and receipts remain stable across application migrations.

## Roadmap

### Chain release contract — #76

- [ ] Freeze cross-runtime HCV1/HCP1, signing, transaction, state, receipt and block fixtures.
- [ ] Publish the stable versioned `postgres.core` surface and atomic general submission.
- [ ] Add ordered additive schema upgrades, backup/restore and rollback evidence.

### HAL client and workflow layer

- [ ] Generate request/result descriptors from the stable chain surface — #64.
- [ ] Submit signed transactions directly through `postgres.core` — #65.
- [ ] Complete synchronization and receipt verification — #66.
- [ ] Prove the reference workflow manager and client loop — #41, #48.
- [ ] Keep provider inputs, capabilities, outbox and workflow adapters generic — #44–#47, #53.

### Hestia integration

- [ ] Integrate the private authority office directly through ordinary application packs — greenways-ai/hestia#28.
- [ ] Preserve all existing Hestia canonical roots during migration.
- [ ] Rebuild only Hestia projections from accepted Ignatius records.
- [ ] Remove copied ledger paths after parity, replay, backup/restore and rollback gates.

### Generic data structures and evidence

- [ ] Keep HPT1, portable VM and attestation work application-neutral — #14, #16, #19.
- [ ] Define generic merge transaction/evidence support without owning Hestia/Tahto/document policy — #17.
- [ ] Keep query/projection infrastructure rebuildable and root-preserving — #18, #43.

## Acceptance

- One atomic submission verifies pack, signer, sequence, manifest and cost; executes; commits a block; and returns exact canonical roots/receipt.
- Exact replay returns the existing receipt; collisions and invalid input do not advance the head.
- No public Ignatius schema or generated contract names Hestia rooms, profiles, documents, mandates or Greenways local clients.
- Hestia can evolve room/source/application authority without an Ignatius protocol change.
- Greenways OS, Tahto and other consumers can use the same chain without importing each other's domain models.
- Existing canonical history survives coordinated Ignatius/Hestia releases unchanged.
