Issue #1487: lint:cycles silently omits a file from madge's graph, so a real server cycle goes unreported

`bun run lint:cycles` (`madge --circular --extensions ts,tsx packages`) reports `No circular dependency found!` while a genuine two-file cycle exists in `packages/server`. The cause is not that madge mishandles the cycle — it is that **madge omits one of the two files from its dependency graph entirely**.

Found while implementing [#1430](https://github.com/ms2sato/agent-console/issues/1430), when `dependency-cruiser` (with `tsPreCompilationDeps: true`) reported a cycle that `lint:cycles` does not.

## The cycle is real

Both import statements read directly from the source:

```
packages/server/src/services/session-manager.ts:72
    import { SessionPauseResumeService } from './session-pause-resume-service.js';   // value import

packages/server/src/services/session-pause-resume-service.ts:24
    import type { WebSocketCallbacks } from './session-manager.js';                  // type-only import
```

## The general mechanism is healthy — a synthetic control proves it

The obvious hypothesis is "madge strips `import type`". **It does not.** Two synthetic file pairs, one run:

```
a1.ts <-> b1.ts   (value <-> value)              -> reported   [positive control]
a2.ts  -> b2.ts   (value out, `import type` back) -> reported   [the shape in question]
=> Found 2 circular dependencies!
```

The second pair is exactly the shape of the real cycle, and madge reports it. So the defect is **specific to this file**, not to the edge kind — which is the single most useful fact for narrowing the investigation, and the reason this control belongs in the report rather than only in the notes.

(Consistent with [#1473](https://github.com/ms2sato/agent-console/pull/1473), where a type-only edge *did* turn CI red via this same check.)

## What the graph actually contains

Dumping madge's own `--json` graph for `packages/server`:

```
src/services/session-manager.ts                -> 44 deps, and NONE of them is
                                                  session-pause-resume-service.ts
                                                  (12+ other src/services/ siblings ARE listed)
src/services/session-pause-resume-service.ts   -> not present as a key at all
```

So madge does not merely miss the back-edge; it never records the **value** import either, and never processes the file as a node.

madge's own skip report names two skipped items and neither is this file:

```
✖ Skipped 2 files
bun:test
bun:sqlite
```

**The omission is silent.** Nothing in the tool's output indicates a file was dropped.

## Cause: not established

Deliberately not guessed at. The drop happens at graph-construction time, so the candidate families are a parse failure (something syntactic in this file) or a resolution failure. Which one is unknown.

## The blast radius is bounded, and by when

**#1430 closes the exposure even though it does not fix this.** That PR enables `tsPreCompilationDeps: true`, at which point dependency-cruiser's `no-circular` rule sees this cycle — that is precisely how it was found — and baselines it in `.dependency-cruiser-known-violations.json` with a comment pointing here.

So the state "a cycle exists in `main` that no check reports" **ends when #1430 merges**. After that, `lint:deps` is the backstop for `lint:cycles`'s blind spot, and this Issue is about restoring the primary check rather than about an unguarded defect. That is the relevant input to prioritising it.

## Suggested first step: reduce, do not hypothesise

The failure is deterministic, local to one file, and free to re-run — the conditions where delta-debugging converges and hypothesis generation does not (`workflow.md` Sub-pattern 6). **Bisect the file's contents until the drop disappears**, and let the minimal difference name the cause. Generating candidate explanations for what madge dislikes about an 18KB TypeScript file, and testing them one at a time, is the strategy that predictably costs more.

Whatever the cause turns out to be, the second question is the one that matters for the check: **how many other files does this silently drop?** One known instance says nothing about the size of the class, and `lint:cycles` gives no way to ask — a file it omits is indistinguishable, in its output, from a file with no cycles.

Issue #113: Design durable child-step resume for composite external effects

## Summary

A single Mycelium ledger entry represents one effect transition: one effect identity, one side-effect boundary, one external-operation reference, and one terminal outcome.

When a ledgered function performs multiple independently observable external effects, those distinct outcomes are compressed into one transition. After a crash, Mycelium can safely fail closed, but it cannot represent which internal effects completed or automatically resume at the first incomplete effect.

## Illustrative example only

The following generic sequence illustrates the failure shape; it is **not** the domain or intended scope of this issue:

```python
def composite_operation():
    external_effect_a()
    external_effect_b()
    external_effect_c()
```

If execution crashes after `external_effect_b()`, the outer ledger knows that `composite_operation()` did not complete. It does not have independent durable state for effects A, B, and C.

## Current guarantee

Mycelium does the safe thing: an ambiguous retry of the composite function can hard-block instead of blindly replaying every internal effect.

What it cannot currently provide is automatic partial-progress recovery. Doing that requires each independently observable effect to have its own durable identity, outcome, provider reference, and reconciliation decision.

This is a recoverability and modeling gap—not a claim that Mycelium currently duplicates effects under ambiguity.

## Why this matters

- Hidden multi-effect functions are common integration boundaries.
- A single `external_operation_ref` cannot describe multiple provider outcomes.
- Safe hard-blocking preserves correctness but can unnecessarily stop progress.
- The runtime and documentation need an explicit, honest definition of effect granularity.
- Any first-class composition feature affects identity, persistence, fencing, reconciliation, replay, migrations, and public API design.

## Current safe pattern

Each independently observable effect should be a separately ledgered operation with a stable identity:

```text
Ledger effect A -> record outcome
                -> Ledger effect B -> record outcome
                -> Ledger effect C -> record outcome
```

On deterministic replay, completed child effects should return their stored results, while execution proceeds from the first unresolved child effect. Each child independently owns its provider reference, reconciliation strategy, terminal state, and retry policy.

## Design decision needed

Decide whether Mycelium should:

1. Treat this strictly as an effect-boundary/documentation concern;
2. Formally support composition through existing nested ledgered operations; or
3. Add a small first-class parent/child operation primitive.

The decision must answer:

- How are stable parent and child identities derived and versioned?
- Are children ordinary linked `LedgerEntry` records or a new persisted shape?
- What are the exact semantics when orchestration code or step order changes?
- How are concurrent resumes fenced?
- How are child outcomes aggregated without erasing ambiguity or overstating parent completion?
- How does reconciliation operate independently per child effect?
- Where is the boundary that keeps Mycelium from becoming a general workflow engine?
- What compatibility and migration behavior is required for existing ledgers?

## Candidate minimal capability—not a decided design

- Durable parent operation identity and definition version.
- Stable child effect identities.
- One normal ledger entry and external-operation reference per child effect.
- Explicit dependency or ordering metadata.
- Deterministic replay that reuses completed child results.
- Resume from the first unresolved child effect.
- Per-child reconciliation and retry decisions.
- An aggregate parent view derived from, but never replacing, child evidence.

Mycelium must not imply that arbitrary function bodies are transactional or that it can infer hidden effect boundaries.

## Good-first-issue scope

The first contribution is a design/RFC plus an executable spike, not a production protocol rewrite:

- [ ] Document current nested-ledger identity and context behavior.
- [ ] Add a provider-neutral three-effect crash example.
- [ ] Demonstrate whether deterministic replay safely skips completed, separately ledgered child effects.
- [ ] Compare documentation-only, nested-ledger, and first-class parent/child approaches.
- [ ] Propose the smallest persisted metadata and API surface needed.
- [ ] Record non-goals and rejected alternatives.
- [ ] Split any chosen implementation into independently reviewable follow-up issues.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A reviewed design explicitly chooses one of the three approaches above.
- [ ] The design defines identity, version changes, ordering, fencing, concurrency, reconciliation, and aggregate outcomes.
- [ ] Failure semantics are specified before, during, and after each child effect.
- [ ] Required deterministic, process-kill, redispatch, and durable-backend tests are enumerated.
- [ ] Documentation states that one ledgered transition should represent one independently reconcilable external effect until stronger composition semantics ship.

## Relevant implementation areas

- `sdk/mycelium/action_ledger.py`: `LedgerEntry`, `ActionLedger`, ledger decorators, and active-transition context
- `sdk/mycelium/transition.py`: effect identity, effect boundary, outcomes, capabilities, and causation metadata
- `sdk/mycelium/reconcile.py`: reconciliation of one ledger entry
- `sdk/mycelium/verify/proof/crash_sweep.py`: crash-point proof machinery
- `sdk/tests/test_handoff_identity.py`: existing parent/child causation foundations
- `sdk/tests/test_effect_protocol_proof.py`: effect-protocol invariants

## Non-goals

- Inferring effect boundaries inside arbitrary user code.
- Providing atomic transactions across unrelated external systems.
- Building a scheduler, queue, or general-purpose workflow product.
- Weakening fail-closed

A maintainer on the project nanobpm/nano-workforce (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #209: merge-loop wedges forever when a pr_dependencies row references an issue (non-PR) instead of a PR

## Summary

A merge-loop instance can be **permanently wedged** at `wait-deps` when a `pr_dependencies` row points at a GitHub **issue** (or any non-PR / not-yet-existing PR) instead of a merged/mergeable **pull request**. Nothing ever publishes `deps-cleared`, and the operator gets **no signal** that the run is stuck.

## Live example (found in production)

- Instance `8451` (`merge-loop` v4) for PR `nanobpm/nano-workforce#206` ("Overview panel", issue #205) sat at `wait-deps` indefinitely.
- Its single dependency was `nanobpm/nano-ide#227` — which is an **open issue**, not a PR (it's the upstream "showCount" enhancement the panel needs; no implementing PR existed yet).

## Root cause

`pollMerges` block 1 (`app/service.ts:786`) only advances a PR in `waiting_deps` once **every** dep satisfies `isDepMerged`:

```
isDepMerged(depKey)
  → fetchPrState(repo, number, token)   // app/github.ts:274 — runs `gh pr view <n>`
```

For an issue number, `gh pr view 227` errors ("Could not resolve to a PullRequest"), so `fetchPrState` **throws**. The throw propagates to `isDepMerged`, is caught by the `try/catch` in `pollMerges`, logged (`[poller] deps <prKey>: <err>`), and the loop moves on — **without ever publishing `deps-cleared`**. On every subsequent pass the same throw recurs. The instance waits forever with no incident and no escalation.

## Why it's bad

- A single mis-recorded dependency (issue ref, typo'd number, or a PR that will never be opened) **silently** wedges the merge-loop.
- There is no distinction between "dep is a real PR that hasn't merged yet" (legitimate wait) and "dep can never be satisfied" (operator error / data bug).
- The only symptom is a log line; nothing surfaces in the UI or escalates.

## Proposed fix

1. In `isDepMerged` / `fetchPrState`, distinguish **"not a pull request" / 404** from a transient transport error. A non-PR ref should not throw-and-silently-retry-forever.
2. When a dependency cannot be resolved to a PR (issue ref, non-existent number), **escalate** (surface a blocker to an operator) rather than looping silently — this dep will never clear on its own.
3. Consider validating dep refs at the point they are recorded (`pr_dependencies` insert): warn/reject when the ref resolves to an issue rather than a PR.

## Immediate remediation applied

The stale `pr_dependencies` row (`nanobpm/nano-workforce#206 → nanobpm/nano-ide#227`) was deleted so the poller could publish `deps-cleared` and release instance `8451`.

Issue #604: WP-060 / WP-L110: an absent table_states entry is weaker than every authored state, and the helper documents the opposite

## What

An absent `table_states` entry is strictly weaker than any value that entry could hold. It bypasses SAFE-005's planner guard **and** emits a plan carrying zero PART-013 protection obligations.

## Measured

```
  table_state = Indeterminate{Unreadable}   Wipe plan(): refused TableStateIndeterminate
  table_state = Indeterminate{Ambiguous}    Wipe plan(): refused TableStateIndeterminate
  table_state = Present{checksum}           Wipe plan(): Ok, obligations = ["ParseBackup"]
  table_state = Absent                      Wipe plan(): Ok, obligations = ["JournaledDetermination"]
  table_state = <no entry>                  Wipe plan(): Ok, obligations = []
```

Absence is below the floor of the vocabulary. `Present` demands a parse backup, `Absent` demands a journaled determination, `Indeterminate` refuses outright — and *no entry* demands nothing and refuses nothing.

## Mechanism

Both readers key on `Some(TableState::...)` and fall through on `None`:

- `indeterminate_table_guard` (`crates/planner/src/lib.rs:707-721`) — `matches!(facts.table_states.get(&device), Some(TableState::Indeterminate { .. }))` is false when the entry is absent, so the guard passes.
- `protection_obligations` (`crates/planner/src/lib.rs:741-743`) — `let Some(state) = ... else { continue; }`, so an absent entry yields no obligation for that device.

## The documented claim this contradicts

`services/helper-linux/src/capture.rs:33-35` states the helper's policy verbatim:

> A device whose geometry cannot be stated, whose node cannot be bracketed by device number, or whose read falls short gets no `table_states` entry — **honest absence, which fails closed at the closure** — with the refusal recorded in the envelope.

That claim is **vacuously true and materially false**. `table_states` appears in `crates/domain/src/model/protection.rs` at exactly two places: the field declaration at `:100`, and `validate_facts` at `:321`, which only checks that fact keys name entries of the right kind. **The protection closure never reads table state when computing a verdict.** The layer that does read it — the planner — fails open on absence.

So two devices in the identical physical situation get opposite answers: the one stamped `Indeterminate` refuses; the one whose read fell short, and which therefore got no entry at all, plans — with no backup obligation.

## Why it is masked today, and when it goes live

`crates/adapter-linux/src/devices.rs:230` returns `TransportClass::Unrecognized` unconditionally, so on a real Linux capture every device's own arm is `Indeterminate { MissingFact }` and every mutating operation is gated before the planner is reached. The defect is masked by an unrelated temporary condition and goes live exactly when ADR-0018's transport discrimination rows land — which the helper's own module doc already flags as outstanding.

## Suggested resolution

Decide what an absent entry means and make one layer enforce it. The options are to make absence refuse at the planner guard (treating it as at least as strong as `Indeterminate`), or to require the helper to author an explicit state for every captured device so absence is unreachable. Either way, correct the `capture.rs` claim — it is the fourth doc comment in this area asserting a safety property its code does not have.

Issue #1: No way to propagate shared domain logic to subdomains

## Problem

Currently, there is a way for a subdomain to selectively export its public API to a parent domain. However, there is no way to express logic that is shared by both a domain and its subdomains.

In other words, the current structure only allows dependencies to flow from subdomains upward to parent domains. It does not provide a mechanism for defining common domain-level logic that can be shared downward with subdomains.

## Why this matters

Issue #62: Inheritance resolution: merge parent and child content with child priority

## Motivation

Inheritance is the core promise of Frames: a team Frame extends an org Frame and refines it. The resolver in `backend/internal/frames/resolver.go` currently walks the `extends` graph, honors `excludes`, detects cycles, dedupes diamonds - and then merges by **concatenating** bodies, ancestors first and the child's body last.

Concatenation is only a proxy for merging. The resolved Frame reads as a pile of documents rather than one document: a parent's rule and a child's contradicting rule both survive, and the reader (a model) has to infer that the later one wins from ordering alone. As inheritance chains get deeper, resolved output gets longer and more self-contradictory - the opposite of what a Frame is for.

## Proposal

Make resolution a real merge where the child has priority and parent content is carried forward rather than duplicated:

- Merge on structure within the body rather than treating it as an opaque blob: content under the same heading merges, with the child's version taking precedence; content only the parent has is inherited; content only the child has is added.
- Child content overrides the corresponding parent content instead of appending after it. Where a genuine conflict cannot be resolved structurally, the child wins.
- Preserve the existing guarantees: `excludes` still prunes ancestors, diamonds still contribute once, cycles still error, unreadable ancestors still fail closed.
- Keep the resolved output attributable enough to debug - an author looking at a resolved Frame should be able to tell which ancestor a piece of content came from (the web app's hierarchy view and `ResolvedPreview` are the consumers here).

## Open questions

- What is the merge key? Markdown headings are the obvious candidate, but that makes heading text load-bearing and needs a defined answer for un-headed prose and for a child that renames a parent's heading.
- Should a child be able to explicitly *remove* an inherited section, as opposed to overriding it? `excludes` prunes whole ancestors, not parts.

## Acceptance criteria

- Overlapping content between a child and its ancestors resolves to the child's version, not both.
- Non-overlapping ancestor content is still inherited.
- Deep chains and diamonds resolve without duplicated content.

Issue #26: [Bug] Iterate element-set keys when resolving integral attachment dependencies

## Summary

`SWEP:GetDependentIntegralSlots` attempts to remove elements that are still supplied by another attachment slot, but it iterates the values of the element set instead of its keys. Because `SWEP:GetElements()` returns `{ [elementName] = true }`, the current loop repeatedly removes `eles[true]` and leaves every real element name unchanged.

This can make valid attachment changes appear to enable/disable integral slots even when another installed attachment continues to provide the same element.

**Suggested severity: Medium attachment-system correctness.**

## Evidence

Reviewed at `main` commit `0f51e3236948c5f00fcd15f4dcd27e3efb1b69d7`.

- `lua/weapons/arc9_base/sh_elements.lua` — `SWEP:GetElements`
- `lua/weapons/arc9_base/sh_attach.lua` — `SWEP:GetDependentIntegralSlots`, `SWEP:GetSlotMissingDependents`, `SWEP:CanAttach`

`GetElements` converts its list into a set:

```lua
local eles2 = {}
for _, ele in pairs(eles) do
    eles2[ele] = true
end
return eles2
```

The dependency code then does:

```lua
local othereles = self:GetElements({[addr] = true})
for _, e in pairs(othereles) do
    eles[e] = nil
end
```

Here `e` is the value `true`, not the element-name key.

## Impact

With two or more slots providing the same element, ARC9 can incorrectly:

- consider an integral slot newly enabled when it was already enabled;
- consider an integral slot affected by a detach even though another provider remains;
- require the player to own an unnecessary dependent attachment;
- reject `CanAttach` through `GetSlotMissingDependents`;
- produce inconsistent behavior depending on attachment order and duplicate element providers.

## Suggested change

Iterate set keys:

```lua
for e in pairs(othereles) do
    eles[e] = nil
end
```

Add a regression test or test fixture covering duplicate providers for both `ActivateElements` and slot `InstalledElements` / `UnInstalledElements`.

## Acceptance criteria

- Elements supplied by any non-excluded slot are removed from the set of elements affected by the proposed change.
- Attaching/detaching one of two equivalent providers does not report dependent integral slots as newly enabled/disabled.
- `GetSlotMissingDependents` blocks only when the proposed change truly creates an unfillable integral slot.
- Single-provider behavior remains unchanged.
- Cache invalidation still refreshes dependency decisions after attachment changes.

## Validation notes

Create a test weapon with two independent slots that provide the same element and an integral slot gated by that element. Test attaching and detaching each provider in both orders, with and without a compatible integral attachment in inventory. Static GLua review only; live customization validation is required.

Issue #36: Table / BufferPtr use-after-free across compile and perform_ksmps


`Table` and `BufferPtr` are views into engine memory, not copies. Csound frees and reallocates that memory during ordinary operation. Both paths below are confirmed `heap-use-after-free` under AddressSanitizer, reachable from **safe code** (no `unsafe` in the caller).

Came up while working on #35. `reset()` taking `&mut self` closes one related case; these two remain because `compile_orc` and `perform_ksmps` still take `&self`.

## 1. Recompiling resizes a function table while a `Table` handle is alive

```rust
let cs = Csound::new().unwrap();
cs.set_option("-n").unwrap();
cs.set_option("-d").unwrap();
cs.compile_orc("sr=44100\nksmps=32\nnchnls=1\n0dbfs=1\n\
                gi1 ftgen 1, 0, 16, 2, 1\ninstr 1\nendin\n", 0).unwrap();
cs.start().unwrap();

let table = cs.get_table(1).unwrap();
cs.compile_orc("gi2 ftgen 1, 0, 1024, 2, 2\n", 0).unwrap(); // reallocates table 1
let _sum: f64 = table.as_slice().iter().sum();               // UAF
```

## 2. An `f` statement in the score reallocates one during `perform_ksmps`

```csound
<CsScore>
f 1 0.05 1024 2 2
i 1 0 0.5
e
</CsScore>
```

```rust
let table = cs.get_table(1).unwrap();
while !cs.perform_ksmps() {}        // score replaces table 1 partway through
let _sum: f64 = table.as_slice().iter().sum(); // UAF
```

Both report:

```
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free
```


## Proposed fix

Take `&mut self` on `perform_ksmps` and the compile family. That is the same rule as `reset(&mut self)` in #35: if a call can free or reallocate the memory a handle points into, it must conflict with the handle's borrow.

`while !cs.perform_ksmps()` still works; callers just need `let mut cs`. The breaking part is anyone who hoists a `Table` or `BufferPtr` out of the performance loop — which is the unsound pattern, so rejecting it at compile time is the point.

A generation counter on each deref would catch this at runtime without a signature change, but it adds a branch on the audio path (`BufferPtr`). Leaving it documented keeps the UAF in safe code. Neither matches what `reset` already does.

If this is the direction, it is worth doing before more handle types land, since it would touch the same call sites.

Issue #316: obsidian_run_command's opaque-command denylist misses broad-blast-radius (but fully inspectable) commands

## The gap

`obsidian_run_command`'s safety guard (`OPAQUE_ACCEPT_COMMAND_IDS` in `mcp/cli-policy.ts`, currently `["quickadd:*", "js-engine:*"]`) denies-by-default only commands that execute **arbitrary, uninspectable code** — the reasoning being "the acceptance guard can't see what these will do, so refuse them." Every other registered command is allowed by default, on the assumption that it's "bounded by the plugin that registered it" — implicitly, a small, well-defined action.

That assumption is false for at least one real, currently-installed command, and probably others: **a command's code being fully inspectable (readable, not a macro/script sandbox) says nothing about its blast radius.** A command can be perfectly ordinary, well-documented, non-opaque plugin code, and still rewrite the content of every note in the vault in one call.

## The concrete incident

The `automatic-linker` community plugin (installed, id `automatic-linker`) registers a command `automatic-linker:format-vault` ("Format vault"). Its handler (`modifyLinksForVault()`) calls `app.vault.getMarkdownFiles()` and iterates over **every markdown file in the vault**, rewriting each one's content via `vault.process()`, with **no exclusion check of any kind** — not even the plugin's own `excludeDirsFromAutoLinking`/`excludeNotesFromAutoLinking` settings, which only govern link *targets*, not which files get rewritten.

This command is not in `OPAQUE_ACCEPT_COMMAND_IDS` (doesn't match `quickadd:*` or `js-engine:*`), so any agent connected via Governor's MCP can call it right now via `obsidian_run_command` with zero special approval — same as calling any harmless single-note command.

On 2026-08-19/20, a vault-wide text-substitution pass (the Assent→Governor rename) resulted in this command actually running against the vault, and it walked straight through a live symlink (`00.89 obsidian-governor/Build/vault-mcp README.md` → the obsidian-governor repo's real `README.md` on disk) and mangled the repo's actual README file — twice, since the underlying cause wasn't understood the first time. Exact mechanism of what invoked the command that night is not fully confirmed (deliberate step vs. side effect of a broader script), but the command itself is confirmed reachable, ungated, and vault-wide-destructive by inspection of its source.

## The underlying question

The guard's current test is "can we see what this command will execute?" A second, independent test — "how much of the vault can this command touch, regardless of whether we can read its code?" — is missing entirely. `format-vault` passes the first test (it's ordinary compiled plugin code, not a macro) and fails the second one badly (unconditional, vault-wide content rewrite, no dry-run, no undo beyond git/backup).

This is filed to capture the gap and the reproduction, not to prescribe a fix — deliberately not proposing allowlist-vs-denylist or any other specific design here.

## Related, separate, not blocking this issue

The `automatic-linker` plugin itself (Nelson's fork) has no way to exclude a specific note's *content* from being rewritten by `format-vault` — only from being a link *target*. That's a plugin-level fix, independent of whatever Governor decides about command-reachability policy.

# Bug: async-delegation wakeup turns persist without `_source` and render as raw user bubbles

## Summary

When a background `delegate_task` fan-out completes and its `[ASYNC DELEGATION COMPLETE — …]` / `[ASYNC DELEGATION BATCH COMPLETE — …]` summary is delivered to an idle WebUI session, the delivery is persisted as a plain user-role message **without** the `_source: "process_wakeup"` stamp. The frontend gates the collapsed background-wakeup card on that stamp, so the transcript renders the full multi-kilobyte raw envelope as a normal user bubble instead of the intended collapsed wakeup card.

Two independent faults contribute:

1. **Server — the wakeup turn loses its provenance during turn settlement.** When the session runs in the default deferred save mode, no eager checkpoint row exists when the agent turn settles, so `_settle_current_turn_boundary` takes the adoption branch in `api/streaming.py` that marks the agent-returned user row with `_mark_active_turn_checkpoint`. That helper historically wrote only `_active_turn_token` and never routed through `stamp_message_source`, so `_source` (and the `_wakeup_meta` display metadata that rides along) is silently dropped before the row is promoted into the display transcript. The materialize branch of the same settlement does stamp, so only the adoption path is affected — which is exactly the path the default save mode takes.
2. **Client — no display grammar for the async-delegation envelope.** Even a correctly stamped async-delegation delivery gets no collapsed card, because `_parseProcessWakeupBody` in `static/ui.js` only recognizes the two `[IMPORTANT: Background process …]` grammars, and the server's `wakeup_display_meta` deliberately returns `None` for the async-delegation shape. The delivery then falls through to the raw process-wakeup notice dump.

## Environment

- WebUI: `exp-v0.52.263` (Experimental) — observed on a live deployment
- Fault verified unchanged through current `master` (`exp-v0.52.264`): `git log exp-v0.52.263..exp-v0.52.264 -- api/streaming.py static/ui.js` is empty and the faulty helper is byte-identical across both tags
- The faulty adoption helper dates to the turn-ownership settlement change first released in `exp-v0.52.155`
- Session save mode: default (`deferred`)

## Observed behavior

1. Dispatch a background `delegate_task` (single or fan-out) from a WebUI chat.
2. Let the batch complete while the origin session is idle.
3. The completion is injected as a user turn starting with `[ASYNC DELEGATION BATCH COMPLETE — deleg_…]`.

Actual: the transcript shows the entire envelope (header, per-task results, raw output) as a fully expanded user bubble. Inspecting the persisted session shows the message is `role: "user"` with `_active_turn_token` set but **no `_source` key at all** — unlike correctly stamped process wakeups, which carry `_source: "process_wakeup"` plus `_wakeup_meta`.

Expected: the delivery renders as the collapsed background-wakeup card (compact semantic summary, full raw body preserved in the expanded section), like other background-process wakeups.

## Evidence from a captured delivery

A persisted delivery was captured and replayed through the turn-settlement path with the captured timestamp, token, and agent-returned row. With no eager checkpoint row present (the deferred-save default), the settlement output reproduces the captured record exactly: `_source= None` while everything else matches byte-for-byte. With the adoption path fixed to apply the same provenance as the materialize path, the same probe yields `_source= process_wakeup`.

The same settlement branch has a sibling effect: turns with `source: "fork"` also lose their `_fork_child_turn` marker, which regeneration authorization relies on for forked sessions.

## Notes for triage

- Restoring the stamp at the turn-adoption chokepoint fixes classification for all non-`webui` turn sources, including the fork marker, and requires no data migration for the rendering path only if the client also recognizes persisted unstamped rows (they exist in every transcript saved since `exp-v0.52.155`).
- Client-side, the collapsed-card pipeline needs to learn the two formatter-owned async-delegation envelope headers; status aggregation should read only formatter-owned structural markers so that status-like text inside subagent-authored goal/summary prose cannot forge an outcome.

Issue #84: Recompute per-checkpoint LM loss on a fixed Pile slice, then test λ_ca-vs-loss collapse

Prerequisite for the collapse test, and it is **not a download — it is a computation**.

## Pythia per-checkpoint loss is not obtainable

The eval JSONs at `github.com/EleutherAI/pythia/tree/main/evals/pythia-v1` (831 files, 21
variants × {zero-shot, five-shot} × 27 steps) carry only `acc`, `acc_norm`,
`likelihood_difference` and `lambada_openai.ppl` — **no loss** — and contain **no 14m or 31m
directories at all**.

Loss exists only in the maintainers' self-described *"(messy!)"* W&B project
`wandb.ai/eleutherai/pythia`, with no CSV or JSON export path.

## Recompute it instead

LM loss on a **fixed held-out Pile slice**, same slice for every model and every checkpoint.
Cheap at these sizes, covers 14M and 31M which the published evals do not, and — the actual
reason to prefer it — it evaluates on **exactly the token distribution driving the λ_ca
lattice**, rather than on downstream task accuracy.

> Note: `experiments/loss_baseline.py` already does this shape of computation against a fixed
> **WikiText-103** slice (`results/loss_baseline.json`). That was deliberately scoped as a
> shape-only comparison because WikiText is not the training distribution. This issue is the
> Pile version — same machinery, correct corpus — and should extend that script rather than
> start over.

## The test

Does λ_ca **collapse** when plotted against loss rather than against step? If it does, the
transition is a property of *how good the model is*, not of *how long it trained*, and the LR
confound in C20 dissolves as a side effect.

## Hold it to the right standard

arXiv:2507.02119 (Qiu et al., "supercollapse") sets the bar: **the collapse residual is measured
against a per-model seed noise floor, not eyeballed.** Anything less will read as curve-fitting.

Getting that noise floor needs multiple seeds per configuration — **scope that cost into the
issue rather than discovering it mid-run**. PolyPythias (arXiv:2503.09543) provides 9 seeds ×
14M–410M and may supply the floor without new training; check whether its checkpoint spacing is
compatible.

## Frame it as an extension, not an invention

arXiv:2403.15796 (Du et al.) already owns loss-reparameterisation collapse for *task metrics*.
Our contribution would be extending it to a **dynamical** observable — a quantity measured from
the model's own generation dynamics rather than from its outputs on a benchmark. State it that
way or a reviewer will state it for us, less charitably.

**Post-tag.** Writes to `results/`.

Issue #18: Incident Record: Markdown Content Accidentally Materialized as Git Tree Path (2025-10-23)

## Incident Summary

**Title:** Markdown Content Accidentally Materialized as Git Tree Path  
**日本語タイトル:** Markdown本文がGitパスへ実体化した事例  
**Discovery date:** 2026-07-19  
**Incident date:** 2025-10-23  
**Commit:** to be confirmed from tree containing anomalous path  
**Severity:** Repository integrity / CI reproducibility

---

## Provenance (Reconstructed Sequence)

```
2025-10-23
    │
    ▼
GitHub Web UI (web-flow)
    │
    ▼
Create new file
    │
    ▼
Filename欄へ README / Notion本文が貼り付く
    │
    ▼
"/" を Git がパス区切りと解釈
    │
    ▼
巨大ディレクトリ生成
    │
    ▼
Blob 追加
    │
    ▼
Git tree へ永続保存
```

This sequence is consistent with all commit, tree, and patch data retrieved during the investigation.

---

## Key Evidence

The most decisive finding was the **filename field containing Markdown body text**:

```
filename:
# BananaMoon Quantum NFT...
...
### Title
...
### Subtitle
...
```

The filename contains `### Title`, `### Subtitle`, `### Overview` — these are **Markdown headings, not a file name**.

This means:

```
Content  →  Path
README   →  filename
```

Markdown body text was entered into the **path field** rather than the content field. Git interpreted every `/` as a directory separator, materializing the document structure as a real directory tree in the repository.

---

## Impact

- An abnormally long, structured path was registered in the Git object store
- The path contains what appears to be a full Markdown document as its filename
- `actions/checkout` encountered this path during CI runs, causing failures
- The anomalous tree entry persists in Git history and cannot be removed without history rewriting

---

## Classification of Claims

### Verified facts
- The anomalous path exists in the Git tree
- The path structure matches Markdown heading syntax (`# ...`, `### ...`)
- The commit was made via GitHub Web UI (web-flow committer)
- `actions/checkout` failed on affected branches
- The sequence above is consistent with all retrieved API data

### Reasonable hypotheses
- The content was pasted into the filename field of the GitHub Web UI "Create new file" dialog
- The source material was a README or Notion document
- The paste occurred during a routine file creation operation

### Unsupported speculation (explicitly excluded)
- Whether a human or a tool performed the paste
- Whether the action was intentional or accidental
- The exact source document

GitHub API data alone cannot distinguish human paste from automated tool input.

---

## Why This Is Noteworthy

This is an unusual case study for several reasons:

1. **Git allows arbitrarily long paths** — there is no filename length validation at the object store level
2. **GitHub Web UI does not prevent** entering multiline or slash-containing content into the filename field
3. **The resulting tree is valid Git** — it can be cloned on most systems but breaks tools with path-length limits (Windows, some CI runners)
4. **Provenance archaeology was required** to identify the root cause — standard CI logs alone were insufficient

---

## Research Boundary

This issue marks the **end of the investigation phase**.

The question *"why did actions/checkout fail?"* has been answered with sufficient evidence:

- An abnormally long, Markdown-structured path exists in the Git tree
- That path originates from Markdown body text entered as a filename
- That path caused `actions/checkout` to fail

Further byte-level or UTF-8 analysis is not required.

---

## Next Steps (Separate Issue)

Repair strategy is tracked separately to keep diagnosis and remediation distinct.

See: *(to be linked once remediation issue is opened)*

Repair must be:
- non-destructive to provenance records
- reviewed before execution
- documented with before/after SHA evidence

Issue #166: Support following/parsing Nix import expressions recursively

### Describe the feature request

Currently, `nixdoc`'s static analysis parser only reads and parses the single file passed via the `-f` flag. If the target file imports other files containing the actual doc-comments (e.g. `default.nix` imports `a.nix` which imports `b.nix` containing the functions and doc-comments), `nixdoc` does not resolve or follow these imports. As a result, no function documentation is generated when running `nixdoc` on the entrypoint file.

It would be highly beneficial if `nixdoc` could follow and parse standard Nix `import` expressions (e.g., `import ./path.nix`), resolving the referenced files and extracting their doc-comments recursively.

This feature request is a more general version of and supersedes the specific `callPackage` tracing issue described in #21.

### Minimal Reproducible Example

Consider three files:

**`b.nix`**:
```nix
lib:
{
  /**
    This is helperFunc defined in b.nix.
  */
  helperFunc = x: x;
}
```

**`a.nix`**:
```nix
lib:
import ./b.nix lib
```

**`default-test.nix`**:
```nix
{ lib }:
import ./a.nix lib
```

If we run `nixdoc` on the entrypoint `default-test.nix`:
```bash
nixdoc -c test-deep -d "Deep Category" -f default-test.nix
```

The output contains no function documentation for `helperFunc` because `nixdoc` does not follow the import chain:
```markdown
# Deep Category {#sec-functions-library-test-deep}
```

### Proposed Behavior

It should trace the `import` statements recursively and extract the documentation from `b.nix`:
```markdown
# Deep Category {#sec-functions-library-test-deep}

## `lib.test-deep.helperFunc` {#function-library-lib.test-deep.helperFunc}

This is helperFunc defined in b.nix.
```

Issue #1297: bug: Memory commit accepts malformed revisions and search can return text that entries() rejects

### Describe the bug

RFC 0014 and the Memory protocol name the backend as the final trust boundary: `commit()` must validate and atomically persist one complete Revision in the same transaction, and search must filter every candidate through the authoritative head manifest. The current implementation does not honor that contract.

This is not a default HTTP/MCP remember, revise, retire, or flush incident. Those paths go through `MemoryService`, which currently fills predecessor, hash, and projections itself. The gap is the public SPI: `MemoryCommit`, `MemoryWritePlan`, and `MemoryBackend` allow a writer to bypass the service and call `backend.commit()` directly. Tests and a later writer can already take that seam.

**What the contract says, and what the code does**

1. The protocol requires `MemoryUnitOfWork.commit()` to validate and atomically commit one complete Revision. `_validate_commit()` only checks family, the whole-document `content_hash`, revision +1, base identity, and equality of the active/projection version-id sets.
2. The RFC sequence diagram requires the backend to validate identity, predecessor, manifest, hash, and vectors. The implementation does not recompute the entry body hash, validate the direct predecessor, or require projections to match the authoritative entry.
3. The RFC schema draws a self-referencing foreign key on `previous_version_id`. `pc_memory_entry_versions.previous_version_id` is a plain string column.
4. The RFC requires search to revalidate active membership, exact version, and canonical bytes against the authoritative manifest. The implementation only confirms that the target is still the current head, so the index can act as a second content authority.
5. The RFC describes projections and indexes as rebuildable, non-authoritative copies. Hit text can come from an unrevalidated index/body and no longer line up with the manifest hash.

**What has already been reproduced**

1. A revision-1 entry with `previous_version_id="does-not-exist"` commits and reads back.
2. A body replaced with `tampered searchable body.` while keeping the hash of `User prefers black tea.` also commits.
3. In that corrupted state, `search()` returns the tampered body, while `entries()` raises `InvalidMemoryCitationError` for the same revision.
4. `entries()` also omits the `version.entry_content_hash` comparison that `_validate_anchor()` already performs.

Closing only the write path or only the read path leaves the loop open. Both sides should be fixed in one PR.

**What this gap can cause later**

Official product paths almost never construct a bad envelope today, so normal use usually does not show the damage. If the seam is taken, or if the service or a second writer later emits a bad commit, the likely consequences are:

1. Illegal history becomes durable authority. A hash is then a label written with the envelope, not a commitment.
2. A fake predecessor has almost no current read consumer, but later lineage, offline validation, or citation code that walks `previous_version_id` will not be able to rebuild history reliably.
3. After a body / declared / manifest hash mismatch, remember, revise, forget, and organize fail with `hash-mismatch`. The Memory can still be recalled but can no longer be governed.
4. If a projection or `searchable_text` diverges from the canonical row, search and automatic `POST /v1/context/prepare` injection can hand a different body to the model.
5. Context Pack and Handoff can consume text the authoritative manifest never committed.
6. A new adapter, migration script, or homemade `MemoryWritePlan` will copy the current thin checks as the contract, and the gap will spread.
7. Fixing only one side still lets dirty data in, or still lets search return it after it is in.

Issue #7250: Dependency-tree walk enqueues every child twice and propagates parents before their children

**Version:** `dev-2026-08:a7c8a4b94`, x86-64 Linux

## Summary

`check_update_dependency_tree_for_procedures` (`src/checker.cpp`, the live `#else` branch):

1. every child is enqueued twice, so task count grows as `2^depth` in procedure-literal nesting;
2. a parent propagates its dependencies upward without waiting for its children, so dependency sets come out nondeterministic and short.


## Origin

Both lines arrived together in 629777b98 ("Multithread `check_update_dependency_tree_for_procedures`", 2025-09-10); the region has not been touched since. That commit redefined `check_walk_all_dependencies` to be nothing but `thread_pool_add_task(...)`, and kept the sequential version's loop body verbatim:

```cpp
for (DeclInfo *child = decl->next_child; child != nullptr; child = child->next_sibling) {
	thread_pool_add_task(check_walk_all_dependencies_worker_proc, child);
	check_walk_all_dependencies(child);   // <- now the same enqueue, not a recursion
}
add_deps_from_child_to_parent(decl);      // <- no longer runs after the children
```

One line broke two things. In the sequential form, `check_walk_all_dependencies(child)` *returning*
meant the subtree was complete, which is what made the following `add_deps_from_child_to_parent`
correctly ordered. As a non-blocking enqueue it guarantees nothing, and that merge is only correct
bottom-up. The `#if 0` block directly above still shows the intended shape.

Issue #70: [BUG] Invalid Dependency Fallback in Planner Step Reset Allows Out-of-Order Execution

Labels: bug, security, medium, cwe-670 / aether-planner

1. Description & Location

  - File Location: crates/aether-planner/src/lib.rs -> PlannerManager::uncheck_step -> Lines 405-415
  - Severity: MEDIUM
  - Classification: Logic Breakdown / Dependency Invariant Inversion (CWE-670 / CWE-703)
  - Summary: In `PlannerManager::uncheck_step` within `crates/aether-planner/src/lib.rs`, when re-evaluating whether pending steps become `Ready` after a step uncheck, `plan.steps[i].depends_on.iter().all(...)` uses `.unwrap_or(true)` when searching for a dependency step in `plan.steps`. If a plan step specifies a dependency ID that does not exist in `plan.steps` (or was removed), `find` returns `None`, and `unwrap_or(true)` treats the missing/invalid dependency as satisfied (`Done`). This causes steps with unresolvable or invalid dependencies to automatically transition from `Pending` to `Ready`, leading to out-of-order step execution and plan corruption.

2. Forensic Root Cause & System Impact

  - Root Cause: In `uncheck_step`, when `.find(|s| s.id == *dep_id)` fails to find a dependency step, `.map(...)` returns `None`. `.unwrap_or(true)` defaults to `true`, treating non-existent dependencies as satisfied (`Done`) instead of unsatisfied (`false`).
  - System Impact: Steps with broken or invalid dependency references are falsely marked as `Ready` for execution despite their prerequisite steps not being completed. This bypasses planner execution guarantees and causes out-of-order execution in the media pipeline.

3. Steps to Reproduce / Irrefutable Proof (PoC / Trace)

Deterministic Step-by-Step Execution Trace:
1. Create an AETHER plan where step `S2` depends on an invalid step ID `"S99"`.
2. Initially `S2` is `Pending`.
3. Perform an uncheck operation on any step in the plan (e.g. `uncheck_step(plan_id, "S1")`).
4. `uncheck_step` evaluates `S2`'s dependencies: `plan.steps.iter().find(|s| s.id == "S99")` returns `None`.
5. `.map(...).unwrap_or(true)` evaluates to `true`.
6. `all_deps_done` becomes `true`.
7. `S2.status` is set to `PlanStepStatus::Ready`, illegally bypassing dependency validation.

4. Suggested Remediation

Provide high-level guidance and the concrete code fix required to eliminate the issue:

```rust
// In crates/aether-planner/src/lib.rs (PlannerManager::uncheck_step):
for i in 0..plan.steps.len() {
    if plan.steps[i].status == PlanStepStatus::Pending {
        let all_deps_done = plan.steps[i]
            .depends_on
            .iter()
            .all(|dep_id| {
                plan.steps
                    .iter()
                    .find(|s| s.id == *dep_id)
                    .map(|s| s.status == PlanStepStatus::Done)
                    .unwrap_or(false) // Fix: Missing/invalid dependency must evaluate to false
            });
        if all_deps_done {
            plan.steps[i].status = PlanStepStatus::Ready;
        }
    }
}
```

5. Acceptance & Verification Criteria

- [ ] Deterministic Proof of Fix: `uncheck_step` evaluates invalid dependency IDs as unsatisfied (`false`), keeping dependent steps in `Pending` state.
- [ ] Blast Radius Validation: Validate plan step status state transitions in `aether-planner` unit tests.
- [ ] Standards Compliance: Strict adherence to dependency validation rules and state machine integrity.

The same failure occurred on the three most recent boots (Aug 19, Aug 21,
Aug 23). Two distinct error signatures appear depending on how far Docker
Desktop got:

1. `reploy service-container error: ... inspect Docker endpoint: exec: "docker": executable file not found in $PATH`
   — `/usr/bin/docker` is a dangling symlink; the `cli-tools` mount does not exist yet.
2. `reploy service-container error: ... failed to connect to the docker API at unix:///var/run/docker.sock; check if the path is correct and if the daemon is running: dial unix /var/run/docker.sock: connect: no such file or directory`
   — CLI tools mounted, socket bind-mount not yet.

## Expected

An installed service survives a host reboot without manual intervention when
Docker becomes available a normal amount of time into boot.

## Cause

Two independent contributing defects.

**1. Backend selection ignores the Docker runtime.**
`hostPlatform.installBackend` (`internal/dockerdeploy/platform.go`) dispatches on
`GOOS` alone:

```go
case "linux":
    return installBackendLinuxSystemd
```

So WSL + Docker Desktop gets the systemd backend, which assumes a
`docker.service` exists, rather than the Docker Desktop backend whose
reboot-resistance story is Docker's own restart policy (as recorded in
`docs/archive/WINDOWS_PORT.md` and `docs/archive/MACOS_PORT.md`). The codebase
already detects Docker Desktop — `dockerRuntimeDockerDesktop` in the same file —
but that detection never reaches backend selection.

**2. Absence of `docker.service` is treated as "no gating needed".**
`inspectProviderInstallHostToolsWithV1`
(`internal/dockerdeploy/provider_install_host_tools.go`) decides whether to emit
an ordering dependency by shelling out:

```go
result.IncludeDockerUnit = tools.run(
    CommandSpec{Name: systemctlPath, Args: []string{"cat", "docker.service"}},
    RunOptions{Context: ctx},
) == nil
```

That command exits 1 here, so `providerInstallSystemdFileV1`
(`internal/dockerdeploy/provider_install_systemd.go`) emits an empty ordering
block:

```go
dockerUnit := ""
if includeDockerUnit {
    dockerUnit = "Requires=docker.service\nAfter=docker.service\n"
}
```

The detection is technically correct — there genuinely is no `docker.service` to
depend on — but the fallback should be "Docker readiness must be established
some other way", not "no gating needed".

**Amplifier: the restart policy is off by an order of magnitude.**
`Restart=on-failure` with systemd defaults gives `RestartSec=100ms`,
`StartLimitBurst=5`, `StartLimitIntervalSec=10s` — a ~1 second total retry budget
against a ~22 second wait. That converts a transient unavailability into a
permanent failure.

There is also no readiness wait in the service path. `--docker-timeout` (default
5s) is a daemon *responsiveness* timeout, it is not passed in the generated
`ExecStart`, and it would not help signature 1 regardless — that fails at
`exec.LookPath` before any daemon contact.

## Note for whoever picks this up

The obvious narrow fix — `After=` on the Docker Desktop WSL mount units — does
**not** work. Those units are synthesized from `/proc/self/mountinfo` and have no
unit file:

```console
$ systemctl show 'mnt-wsl-docker\x2ddesktop-cli\x2dtools.mount' -p FragmentPath -p SourcePath
FragmentPath=
SourcePath=/proc/self/mountinfo
```

systemd does not know about them at dependency-resolution time, so the ordering
constraint is silently a no-op and the unit proceeds anyway.

## Suggested fix

Either or both:

- Add a bounded Docker readiness wait in `_service-container` before the first
  Docker call, covering both the missing-executable and missing-socket cases.
- Scale the restart policy to real Docker Desktop startup time (e.g. a longer
  `RestartSec` with a `StartLimitIntervalSec`/

Issue #271: ORDER BY / LIMIT / OFFSET (and window functions) over set-operation (UNION/UNION ALL) results

**Refocused.** This issue originally asked for "CTE (WITH) + UNION ALL combinator". On re-check those DO
exist on 1.10.x (`orm.withCte(name)`, `q1.unionAll(q2)` / `.union` / `.intersect` / `.except`) — see the
earlier close note. But the actual remaining gap in the same area is real, so reusing this issue for it rather
than minting a new one.

## The gap

Set-operation results cannot be **ordered, limited, paginated, or windowed** in SQL. `q1.unionAll(q2)` returns
a terminal `SetOperationBuilder` that only exposes `.all()` / `.dump()` — no `.orderBy()`, `.limit()`,
`.offset()`. And there's no builder path to wrap the union in a CTE/subquery and order the outer SELECT
(`orm.withCte` is unnest-only; `CteQueryBuilder` is likewise terminal). So
`(SELECT … UNION ALL SELECT …) ORDER BY … LIMIT … OFFSET …` and `… COUNT(*) OVER() … FROM (union)` are
inexpressible.

## Reproduction (compile-only, 1.10.x)

```ts
const q1 = orm.from(calls).where(eq('edge_type', 'call')).columns(['caller_id', 'call_line']);
const q2 = orm.from(calls).where(eq('edge_type', 'ref')).columns(['caller_id', 'call_line']);
q1.unionAll(q2).orderBy('caller_id')   // ❌ orderBy not a method on SetOperationBuilder
q1.unionAll(q2).limit(50)              // ❌ limit not a method either
```

## Desired

`ORDER BY` / `LIMIT` / `OFFSET` (and window functions) on a set-operation result, e.g.
`q1.unionAll(q2).orderBy('group_id').orderBy('call_line').limit(50).offset(0)`.

## Impact (astix)

- `getCalleesBatch` (aggregate branch) — converted with a JS-side sort of the (bounded) returned rows as a
  workaround; ideally DB-side.
- `checkHardcodedValues` — `WITH findings AS (… UNION ALL …) SELECT … ORDER BY category, file, line
  LIMIT $ OFFSET $` with `COUNT(*) OVER()`; needs outer ordering/pagination/window over a union → stays raw
  on this issue rather than a fetch-all JS rewrite.

Issue #3717: Enhancement: make the edge probe's shape cues language-aware in the engine (deterministic — not the #652 LLM classifier)

## Pre-submission checklist

- [x] Improves existing behavior — does not add a new command, workflow, or concept.
- [x] Searched existing issues — not already proposed.
- [x] Read CONTRIBUTING.md; will wait for `approved-enhancement` before any code.
- [x] Can describe a concrete benefit, not just "nicer."

## What existing feature or behavior does this improve?

`SHAPE_CUES` / `classifyShape` in `src/edge-probe.cts` — the deterministic prose→shape classifier the spec-phase Step 5.5 edge-completeness probe uses to decide which of the closed 8-category edge taxonomy applies to each requirement.

## Current behavior

`SHAPE_CUES` is five English word-boundary regexes. A project running with `response_language` set writes its SPEC requirements in that language, so every requirement matches no cue, classifies to zero shapes, and surfaces as the `unclassified` sentinel (#1110). The taxonomy contributes nothing and `--auto` resolves nothing.

**#2773 shipped the stopgap the triage approved** (PR #3713, merged): spec-phase Step 5.5 now feeds the probe a faithful **English translation** of each requirement's `text` while the SPEC keeps its original language. That works — measured against the compiled engine:

| Requirement text handed to the probe | `classifyShape` | categories raised |
|---|---|---|
| `O sistema mescla intervalos sobrepostos em uma lista ordenada` | `[]` | none |
| `The system merges overlapping intervals in a sorted list` | `["collection"]` | `adjacency`, `empty`, `ordering` |

But it is a **documented instruction, not an enforced contract**. The engine still cannot read anything but English, so the correctness of every non-English spec's edge coverage rests on the model following a prose instruction, with no machine check that it did. The triage on #2773 said so explicitly:

> Option 1 is a two-line markdown change and removes the silent no-op today; **option 2 is the durable fix.**

and closed with:

> **The durable engine fix is a separate follow-up, not blocked by this** … worth a follow-up enhancement issue once the doc stopgap lands.

This issue is that follow-up.

## Proposed behavior

Make the engine itself language-aware, **staying fully deterministic**. Three candidate forms, in rough order of cost:

1. **Scan an English `text_en` field when present.** `Requirement` becomes `{ id, text, shapes?, text_en? }`; `classifyShape` reads `text_en ?? text`. Smallest change; makes the current translation step an explicit, validatable field instead of an invisible convention, and lets a contract test assert that a `response_language` project actually populated it.
2. **A `lang` hint + per-language cue sets.** `SHAPE_CUES` becomes `Record<lang, Record<Shape, RegExp>>` with `en` as the default. Genuinely reads the author's own prose — no translation step at all — at the cost of maintaining a cue table per supported language.
3. **Both** — `lang` where a cue set exists, `text_en` as the universal fallback.

Whichever form is chosen, the acceptance bar should include a **parity assertion** that the shape vocabulary stays single-sourced across the cue table and `VALID_SHAPES` (the `DEFECT.GENERATIVE-FIX` class), and a fixture pair proving a non-English requirement classifies identically to its English equivalent.

## Reason and benefit

The probe exists to catch domain-boundary edges the author never wrote down — the failure mode it targets is precisely a *silent* one. Leaving the language handling as prose reproduces that shape one level up: if the instruction is not followed, coverage silently degrades to `unclassified` and nothing fails.

The concrete gap the stopgap cannot close is the **partly-classified** case. Step 5.5's `$APPLICABLE = 0` warning fires only when *every* requirement is unclassified, so a spec where a few requirements happen to carry English loanwords (`API`, `upload`) classifies partially and raises **no signal at all**. An engine that knows the input language can fail closed there; a prose instruction cannot.

## Scope of changes

- `src/edge-probe.cts` — `SHAPE_CUES`, `classifyShape`, and (for forms 1/3) `Requirement` + `validateRequirement`.
- `CONTEXT.md` — the `EdgeCompletenessProbeModule` glossary entry records the export surface as locked, so a new field or a re-shaped `SHAPE_CUES` is a glossary update and likely an **ADR-550 amendment** rather than a silent change.
- `gsd-core/workflows/spec-phase.md` + `gsd-core/references/edge-probe.md` — the #2773 translation instruction becomes redundant or changes shape.
- `docs/FEATURES.md` §144, `docs/how-to/probe-edges-in-a-non-english-project.md` — both currently describe the translation workaround.
- Fixtures under `gsd-core/references/edge-probe-fixtures/` and `tests/edge-probe*.test.cjs`.

## Breaking changes

None intended if `en` stays the default and `text` keeps its current meaning — both proposed forms are additive. Worth stating explicitly in review, since `CONTEXT.md` records the edge-probe export surface as **locked**: adding `text_en` or re-shaping `SHAPE_CUES` changes that surface even when no existing caller breaks.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep the #2773 doc stopgap and do nothing further.** Viable — it works today. The cost is that non-English edge coverage stays unenforced, and the partly-classified case above stays silent.
- **An LLM-assisted classifier.** ⚠️ **Explicitly NOT what this proposes, and out of scope here.** ADR-550 records it as REJECTED (#652, closed 2026-06-04), on the grounds that the existing taxonomy plus the prohibition probe already capture most of the value *"without adding a separate model-dependent surface to maintain"*, with the re-open condition *"only if a classifier demonstrably beats both probes on a held-out battery."* @davesienkowski built and ran exactly that pre-registered battery in August 2026 and reported it **did not meet the bar**. Nothing here seeks to re-open that.

Issue #844: Separate zero-edge LSP symbol inventory from the traversal graph

## Goal

Keep repository-specific LSP symbols queryable without forcing large zero-edge inventories into every structural traversal graph and resident query process.

## Context

Profiling the cold exact-tree Django cache for #839 showed that its 301,300 persisted nodes are fully accounted, but not all are structural graph entities. The extractors produced 111,442 nodes and LSP consumers added 189,229 virtual nodes. Two zero-enrichable-node languages dominate the expansion:

- gettext / babel-lsp: 81,150 virtual nodes, 0 edges;
- plaintext / cohort language server: 6,290 virtual nodes, 0 edges.

Other contributors include Python (93,987 virtual nodes / 71,584 edges), CSS (1,618 / 0), TypeScript (1,398 / 0), and JSON (1,586 / 23).

These can be legitimate searchable repository entities (for example translation keys), so deleting them blindly would violate RNA's context-assembly purpose. But loading zero-edge inventory into the petgraph traversal projection costs startup time and resident memory even when an agent asks for one exact code node.

Discovered and dispositioned during #839; #839 fixes the unrelated unbounded diagnostics path and documents these counts.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Classify each LSP virtual-node producer by provenance, entity semantics, query value, and graph-edge participation.
- [ ] Measure cache bytes, graph-load time, and resident memory by producer on the retained Django cache.
- [ ] Define separate persisted/query projections when an entity is useful for search but has no structural graph role.
- [ ] Exact search continues to find useful non-code entities such as gettext keys after projection changes.
- [ ] Exact-node graph traversal does not hydrate zero-edge search-only inventories.
- [ ] Nodes with real LSP relationships remain available to neighbors/impact/path traversal.
- [ ] Add regression fixtures for high-cardinality gettext/plaintext inventories and mixed code/non-code roots.
- [ ] Demonstrate lower large-cache startup/RSS without weakening source identity or provenance.

## Non-goals

- Treating raw node count alone as a defect.
- Dropping non-code repository knowledge.
- Folding resident multi-request runtime work from #838 into this issue.

Issue #10324: Courses: optional course prerequisites and progression tracks

Another topic related to the discussion in #10255

### Relationship to #10255 & #10265
This proposal complements the learner progression and curriculum structure discussed in #10255 (`Courses: course-pipeline overhaul`) and #10265 (`Courses: centralized myProgress learner dashboard overhaul`).

### Current Problem
- **Unrestricted, Out-of-Order Course Enrollment**: In Planet Learning, all courses in the catalog can be joined independently with no sequential requirements or curriculum tracks.
- **Missing Curriculum Dependencies**: Educators creating progressive multi-part subject tracks (e.g., *Introductory Algebra* → *Calculus*, or *Foundational Literacy* → *Advanced Reading*) have no mechanism to require that foundational coursework be completed before learners attempt advanced material.
- **Fragile Link Integrity on Renames**: Relying on course titles or textual descriptions breaks whenever a prerequisite course is renamed, updated, or translated into another language.
- **Orphaned Dependency Traps on Deletion**: If a prerequisite course is deleted or archived, learners could become permanently blocked from taking advanced courses if the system lacks graceful dependency resolution.

### Proposed Solution: Optional Course Prerequisites & Progression Tracks
We want to introduce configurable course prerequisites with referential ID tracking, circular dependency safeguards, and intuitive learner-facing unlock states:

1. **Course Authoring & Prerequisite Configuration (`CoursesAddComponent`)**:
   - **Multi-Select Prerequisites (`prerequisiteCourseIds: string[]`)**: Add an optional multi-select chip/autocomplete control in `src/app/courses/add-courses/courses-add.component.html` allowing educators to select one or multiple prerequisite courses.
   - **Circular Dependency Guardrails**: Prevent a course from selecting itself as a prerequisite or forming circular dependency loops (e.g., Course A → Course B → Course A).
   - **Immutable ID Referencing**: Store immutable CouchDB `_id` values on the course document so that **renaming a course title** never breaks existing prerequisite links (titles and metadata are resolved dynamically).

2. **Resilient Deletion & Sync Handling**:
   - When evaluating course prerequisites, if a referenced prerequisite `_id` is missing from the database (due to course deletion or selective offline sync), the system gracefully skips the missing ID and treats the requirement as satisfied/waived, preventing learners from being permanently locked out by orphaned IDs.

3. **Learner-Facing Prerequisites Overview & Lock States (`CoursesViewComponent`)**:
   - **Prerequisites Status Card**: On the course overview page (`courses-view.component.html`), display a dedicated **"Prerequisites"** card listing all required courses:
     - ✅ **Completed** (green badge / checkmark)
     - 🔒 **Required** (clickable course link directing the learner to enroll and take the prerequisite)
   - **Smart Enrollment & Navigation Protection**:
     - If prerequisites are incomplete, the primary **Join** button is disabled with an explanatory tooltip (e.g., *"Complete [Course Name] to unlock this course"*).
     - Direct URL navigation to step views or exams (`/courses/step/:courseId/:stepIndex`) evaluates prerequisites and gracefully redirects back to the course overview with an informative notification if prerequisites are incomplete.

### Justification & Practical Impact
- **Structured Pedagogical Pathways**: Enables educators and community managers to build structured learning tracks, multi-grade curricula, and certificate sequences.
- **Referential Integrity**: ID-based tracking guarantees that course renames, multi-lingual translations, and deletions never corrupt student learning paths.
- **Self-Directed Learner Guidance**: Gives students clear, visual visibility into what foundational knowledge they need before tackling advanced subject matter.

The portal should centralize:

- user lifecycle (joiner, mover, leaver, rehire);
- coarse application entitlement (may this person enter app X?);
- supported app roles and scopes (what may this person do in app X?);
- provisioning/deprovisioning and drift reconciliation;
- approvals, audit, connector health, and manual exceptions.

Build a small, permissively licensed **Open Suite desired-state control plane over upstream Keycloak**, not a new IdP and not a universal authorization engine.

Issue #34324: Show recoverable task state when a parent error still has active descendants

Severity: `P2 — Warning`
Type: `Feature`
Evidence state: `Confirmed`
Classification rationale: This is a P2 feature gap because the Codex App presents a terminal-looking task error even though delegated work remains active, creating material operator confusion and a risk of duplicate manual recovery.

## Problem
The Codex App needs a recoverable or degraded-running task state. Today, when a parent response is hidden by the cybersecurity-content safeguard, the task can appear as systemError even while an active descendant continues the same durable workflow. The operator sees neither that progress nor whether intervention is safe.

## Evidence
- **User Report** — The Codex App displayed 'This content can't be shown' with the cybersecurity/Trusted Access notice in the affected task. — `User-provided Codex App screenshot, observed 2026-07-20`
- **Runtime** — The App task inventory reported the parent as systemError while its latest turn was completed and its delegated campaign-manager task remained active with an in-progress turn and active descendants. — `Read-only Codex App thread inventory, observed 2026-07-20`

## Impact
Operators of long-running delegated workflows cannot tell whether work is stopped, safely checkpointed, or continuing. This causes avoidable stress and can prompt manual retries that duplicate workers, consume additional compute, or create competing writers.

## Root cause or gap
Confidence: `Confirmed`

The task-status UX lacks an aggregate recoverability state that incorporates active descendant execution when the parent response is suppressed or marked as a system error.

## Expected behavior
When a parent task cannot display content but one or more descendants remain active, the App should show a non-terminal degraded/recovering state, identify that background work is continuing, and reserve terminal blocked/error presentation for cases where no execution path can progress.

## Likely solution direction
Confidence: `Likely`

Add a derived degraded-running or recovering state based on descendant activity and durable task state. Preserve the safety-hidden content boundary, but expose safe operational facts: whether work continues, whether user action is needed, the last safe checkpoint, and whether resume would duplicate an active execution path.

## Likely affected surface
| Surface | Confidence | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Codex App task-status aggregation and sidebar/detail status presentation | Likely | The mismatch is visible between parent status presentation and descendant execution state. |
| Task resume affordance | Possible | A resume action should warn or remain unavailable while a descendant is actively continuing the same workflow. |

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A parent with a hidden or errored response and at least one active descendant is not presented as terminally blocked.
- [ ] The App visibly distinguishes degraded-but-running, paused/checkpointed, needs-user-action, and system-blocked states.
- [ ] The degraded state exposes only safe operational metadata and does not reveal content that the safeguard withheld.
- [ ] The operator can see whether background work is continuing and whether manual resume risks duplicate execution.
- [ ] When all descendants stop, the displayed state deterministically transitions to completed, recoverable, needs-user-action, or system-blocked.

**Unknowns**

- Whether descendant activity is already available to every App status-rendering surface.

- Changing cybersecurity policy or Trusted Access eligibility.
- Automatically retrying arbitrary failed prompts without durable-state reconciliation.

`codex-cli 0.144.6`

`codex app-server` over stdio with `multi_agent` enabled

An app-server host can need to pause a task while a human resolves blocking feedback (for example, approving or rejecting a plan). The root turn is blocked in the host's MCP tool call, but already-running collaborator turns continue consuming tokens, invoking tools, and mutating the shared workspace.

- Pause the root and all active descendants as one operation.
- Prevent newly spawned descendant work while paused.
- Reference-count or tokenize overlapping pauses so work resumes only after every blocker resolves.
- Resume the same in-flight turns without discarding their progress.
- Define behavior for descendants created or restarted during a pause.

### Current downstream workaround

The only available non-destructive workaround is suspending the entire app-server process group at the OS level. That stops shared-workspace mutations, but it also freezes unrelated runtime work and leaves wall-clock deadlines advancing, so it is much broader and less portable than a protocol-level operation.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. On Codex Desktop for Windows, enable **Full Access** globally.

The active custom permission profile contains the same relative write rules as the original report:

```toml
default_permissions = "repo-dev"

[permissions.repo-dev.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]
"." = "write"
".git" = "write"
".agents" = "write"
```

There were no configuration changes between the two diagnostic snapshots.

| Metric | First snapshot | Second snapshot | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Workspace roots | 2 | 34 | +32 |
| Writable roots | 38 | 102 | +64 |
| Unique root union | 38 | 102 | +64 |
| Minimal `pwd` spawn | 0.061 s | 5.886 s | ~97× slower |

Previously generated writable paths were promoted into the workspace-root set on the next turn. The relative `.git` and `.agents` rules were then applied to those generated roots, producing another suffix layer.

```text
.agents/.git/.git
.codex/config.toml/.agents
.codex/config.toml/.git
```

These were permission metadata entries, not corresponding directories created on disk.

- 2 workspace roots

6. Observe generated write paths being promoted into the next turn's workspace roots and receiving an additional suffix layer.

Relative rules under `:workspace_roots` should be evaluated only against the original runtime workspace-root set. Derived permission paths must not be persisted or promoted as workspace roots on subsequent turns.

Root sets and the serialized permission profile should remain bounded across unchanged turns.

A search of currently open `openai/codex` issues did not find another report covering this exact recursive root-growth and `E2BIG` failure mode.

### What version of the Codex App are you using?

### What issue are you seeing?

A production-style multi-thread orchestration flow cannot reliably continue autonomously from a read-only Planner thread into a workspace-write implementation thread because the write-side thread cannot retrieve the exact final output of the read-only Planner thread through the supported cross-thread/thread-reader path.

In the reproduced workflow:

1. A dedicated read-only planning thread produced the final implementation plan.
2. A separate workspace-write implementation/orchestrator thread was required to retrieve that exact Planner result unchanged, validate it, persist it, and continue implementation.
3. The write-side thread could not retrieve the exact final Planner result through the supported thread reader.
4. The workflow stopped with an explicit blocker equivalent to:

```text

```

5. No product work could continue until the user manually copied the complete Planner output from the read-only thread into the write thread.

This is not a simple UX inconvenience. It breaks unattended / continuous engineering workflows that intentionally separate roles and permissions:

```text
read-only Planner
      ↓ exact result handoff
workspace-write Orchestrator / Implementer
      ↓
implementation → tests → review → next loop
```

If the downstream write-capable thread cannot programmatically read the exact upstream read-only result, the loop requires manual copy/paste at every permission boundary. That prevents reliable 24/7 autonomous engineering even when both threads belong to the same Codex project and the user has already authorized the workflow.

### Why exact retrieval matters

For governed multi-agent workflows, a summary is not sufficient. The downstream thread may need to prove that it consumed the exact upstream result unchanged.

Examples:

- validate a Planner result against a schema;
- compute and compare SHA-256;
- persist the exact plan bytes;
- preserve provenance and auditability;
- avoid reconstructing native/subagent output from prose;
- prevent the implementer from silently rewriting the Planner result before acceptance.

4. In Thread B, use the supported cross-thread/thread-reading mechanism to retrieve Thread A's exact final result.
5. Require exact content rather than a summary, because the next step computes a hash or validates a structured contract.
6. Observe that Thread B may be unable to retrieve the exact result even though the user can open Thread A manually and see it.
7. The orchestration blocks until the user manually copy/pastes Thread A's result into Thread B.

### Expected behavior

Codex should provide a first-class, permission-safe handoff/read mechanism for exact cross-thread result retrieval within an authorized project/workflow.

At minimum, a downstream authorized thread should be able to retrieve:

```text
source_thread_id
source_turn_id
final_result_bytes_or_exact_text
content_sha256
source_permission_profile
result_status
```

with clear provenance and no normalization.

A workspace-write consumer does not need write access to the read-only source thread; it only needs read access to the source result.

The mechanism should preserve exact bytes/text so a downstream validator can verify integrity without requiring user copy/paste.

### Actual behavior

The result is visible to the user in the read-only source thread, but the downstream workspace-write thread cannot reliably retrieve that exact result through the supported reader/handoff path.

The workflow therefore requires a human to manually bridge the threads.

### Impact

This blocks or degrades:

- Planner → Implementer loops;
- Reviewer/Tester → Fixer loops;
- read-only audit → write-side remediation loops;
- role-separated security workflows;
- long-running unattended Codex orchestration;
- 24/7 autonomous engineering loops;
- exact provenance / hash-based governance;
- restart-safe continuation across permission-separated threads.

Issue #41009: Codex Desktop leaves high-CPU grep and Python child processes after an interrupted task on macOS

## Summary

A Codex Desktop task that performed broad local CSV searches was interrupted, but its shell child processes were not cleaned up. Four `grep` processes and one Python process remained running after the task was interrupted, each consuming approximately one CPU core.

## Environment

- macOS on Apple Silicon
- Codex Desktop
- Large local CSV archive

- Task reference: `01a040b8-9e96-7dc3-9882-b51155163f99`
