Issue #498: Benchmark: StructMemEval head-to-head — latent-structure memory + agent goal completion under subconscious vs instructed memory

<!-- draft-owner: pid=79251 ts=1785492928 -->
> **Context.** [StructMemEval](https://github.com/yandex-research/StructMemEval) (Yandex Research; ["Evaluating Memory Structure in LLM Agents"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11243), ICLR 2026 MemAgents workshop) is a memory benchmark built as a deliberate reaction against LongMemEval/LoCoMo-style tests. Its thesis: fact-retention and multi-hop recall "can often be achieved with simple retrieval-augmented LLMs" and do **not** test whether an agent can maintain a *latent data structure*. It therefore builds tasks whose answers are only recoverable if memory is organized as a specific structure — a **ledger** (count-based accounting/netting), a **state machine** (current-state under 0–5 updates), or a **tree/graph** (family/corporate hierarchy traversal). 73 synthetic scenarios, 544 questions, Mem0/Qdrant-based harness.
>
> This issue proposes adding StructMemEval to our benchmark harness **as a head-to-head competitive test** — but with a second scoring axis that no existing memory benchmark measures, and which is the entire point of Popoto's design: **agent goal completion when the memory system is not mentioned in the agent's instructions.**

## Problem

**Current state.** Our external benchmark harness (`tests/benchmarks/run_external.py`, `tests/benchmarks/datasets/{longmemeval_s,locomo}.py`, `tests/benchmarks/scenarios/external_base.py`) targets exactly the two datasets StructMemEval argues are too easy: **LongMemEval-S** (500 questions, PR #436) and **LoCoMo** (1986 QA pairs, PR #439). We have no benchmark that tests whether memory maintains a *latent structure* over a long interaction — the failure mode StructMemEval was built to expose.

**Why it matters.** StructMemEval's published results show retrieval-augmented memory collapsing on structure tasks, and even agentic memory recovering only when handed an explicit hint:

| Task family | Setup | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| State-tracking (gpt-4o-mini) | RAG top-5 | 24% |
| State-tracking (gpt-4o-mini) | RAG top-20 | 40% |
| State-tracking (gpt-4o-mini) | mem-agent **with hint** | 74% |
| State-tracking (gemini-3-flash) | Mem0 agent **with hint** | 95% |
| Count-based @ 50 txns (gemini-3-pro) | RAG top-20 | 0.0% |

The paper's punchline: *"the gap between with-hint and without-hint is often larger than the gap between Mem0 and mem-agent."* Models can **use** the right structure once told to, but do not **spontaneously recognize** they should maintain one.

**Popoto's competitive thesis.** This is precisely the gap Popoto's architecture is designed to close by construction. Popoto's memory is **subconscious**: the structure is chosen at *schema-design time* by the developer via typed primitives, not improvised per-turn by the LLM. In StructMemEval's terms, Popoto is an **always-on structural hint** — the condition under which agentic memory jumps 24%→74%:

| StructMemEval structure | Popoto primitive that provides it as substrate |
|---|---|
| Ledger / count / netting | `PredictionLedgerMixin`, `ConfidenceField` evidence ledger, `FrequencySketch` (Count-Min) |
| State machine / current-state under updates | `MemoryLifecycle` (tier transitions, tombstone states), `EventStreamMixin` |
| Tree / graph traversal | `CoOccurrenceField` (Lua BFS multi-hop), `Relationship` + `graph_traversal.traverse()` |

Critically, **competing systems (Mem0, mem-agent) require the agent's instructions to tell it to store/search/update memory.** Popoto does not — `SubconsciousMemory` injects and extracts around the LLM turn transparently. A benchmark that only scores answer accuracy cannot see this difference. So the head-to-head must score **two** things.

### Desired outcome

A committed StructMemEval adapter that runs a long-running agentic task backed by each memory system and reports, per task family:

1. **Eval score** — StructMemEval answer accuracy (exact-match + LLM-judge, matching their harness), in both **no-hint** and **with-hint** modes.
2. **Agent goal completion** — did the agent finish the long-running task? — measured with **Popoto's memory absent from the agent's instructions**, versus competitors whose memory *requires* instructions to use.

The result worth chasing, and the one the report should headline: **Popoto-native (no hint, memory not in instructions) vs Mem0/mem-agent (no hint).** If the typed-substrate thesis holds, Popoto closes the with-hint/without-hint gap that competitors cannot.

## Definitions

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **StructMemEval** | Yandex Research benchmark for latent-structure memory maintenance. [repo](https://github.com/yandex-research/StructMemEval) · [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11243) |
| **Latent structure** | A data structure (ledger, state machine, tree) that must be maintained across turns; the answer is unrecoverable from snippet retrieval alone. |
| **Memory-organization hint** | An informal prompt in StructMemEval telling the agent how a human would structure knowledge for the task. Their key finding is the size of the hint/no-hint gap. |
| **Subconscious memory** | Popoto's model where store/retrieve/extract happen transparently around an LLM turn without the agent being instructed to use memory. Recipe: `SubconsciousMemory` (`src/popoto/recipes/subconscious_memory.py`). |
| **Goal completion** | Whether the agent finished its long-running task — a task-success metric orthogonal to answer-recall accuracy. |
| **Tier 5 judged harness** | Our existing end-to-end judged-answer harness (`tests/benchmarks/judge.py`, issue #458 / PR #475) — the closest existing scaffold for answer-level scoring. |

## Solution sketch (open questions — root cause / design still uncertain)

This is a **novel harness**, not a mechanical dataset adapter, because of the goal-completion axis. Rather than prescribe an implementation, these are the questions `/do-plan` should resolve:

Issue #139: rule: maintainability/dead-function

## Policy problem

A function nothing calls is a maintenance cost with no benefit: it still has to compile, still
shows up in a search, still gets "maybe this is used somewhere" treatment in review. Reachability is the one
property none of Godlint's current rules can see.

## Blocked

**Needs a repository-wide call graph** — every call site resolved against every declaration,
across files. This is the same class of subsystem as the import graph #57 needs, not a new kind of
difficulty, just the function-level version of it.

## Valid and invalid examples

Invalid: a private function or module-local helper with zero call sites anywhere in the
repository.

Valid: the same function, either called or exported as part of the public API.

## Analysis scope

File-local syntax/fact rule. **Languages:** all four

Public/exported symbols must be exempt by default — a library's public API has no local
caller by definition. That exemption needs the visibility fact, which #94's language declarations partly
motivate.

## Diagnostic and remediation

```
src/util.rs:40:1: error[maintainability/dead-function] normalize_legacy_id has no call sites in this repository.
```

## The false positive to design for

Reflection, dynamic dispatch, test-only helpers referenced by name in a string, and anything called
from outside the analysed tree (a plugin entry point, a CLI subcommand table). All of these look dead and
are not — this rule is only trustworthy after the call graph is real and the exemptions are deliberate.

## Source

[Clean Code F4 Dead Function](https://github.com/janaipakos/Clean-Code-Smells-and-Heuristics)

## Definition of done

Valid, invalid, configuration and suppression fixtures; an expected-output fixture; unit tests declared in the index; a `docs/rules.md` row; a `docs/rule-roadmap.md` row; a changelog entry; dogfooded in `godlint.yaml`; within its coverage budget. Per #88, a fixture per syntactic form that produces the finding — not one per rule.

Issue #57: architecture/no-cycle needs module resolution, and that is a new subsystem

Last rule in Phase 4, deliberately deferred to its own pull request.

## Why it is different in kind

Every rule shipped so far **resolves nothing** — it reads what the source spells, and the roadmap states that boundary repeatedly. A cycle cannot be found that way. To know that `src/a.ts` importing `"./b"` is an edge to `src/b.ts`, something has to map a module spelling to a file.

That makes it the first rule to need module resolution, which is a new subsystem rather than another rule.

## Agreed approach: convention-based resolution per language

Chosen over the two alternatives (relative-only, or repository-declared roots).

- **JavaScript / TypeScript** — `./x` and `../x` probe `x.ts`, `x.tsx`, `x.js`, `x.jsx`, `x.mjs`, `x.cjs`, then `x/index.*`. Bare specifiers are dependencies, not repository edges, and are skipped. `tsconfig` path aliases are explicitly out of scope for a first version.
- **Python** — `a.b` probes `a/b.py`, `a/b/__init__.py`; a relative `from .b import` resolves against the importing file's package.
- **Rust** — `crate::a::b` probes `src/a/b.rs` and `src/a/b/mod.rs`. `self::`/`super::` resolve against the importing module.

An import that resolves to no file in the scan is not an edge. That is the honest failure mode, and it must be observable rather than silent — a resolution that quietly finds nothing would make the rule report no cycles and look like it passed.

## What the rule then does

Build a directed graph over resolved edges, find strongly connected components, and report **the complete edge chain** for each cycle, not just a pair. The finding needs a range, so it should be reported at the import that closes the cycle.

## Where it interacts with what exists

- `ImportFact` already carries the module spelling and the importing file, which is everything resolution needs as input.
- Issue #45's kernel (`report`) takes an iterator of `(source, range, violation)`, so a graph-shaped rule fits the existing driver without a sixth copy of the severity gate.
- This is the first rule whose evaluation is not per-file, so it will need the whole fact set at once — `evaluate` already receives `&[SourceFacts]`, so no signature change.

## Sequencing

Resolution should land as its own reviewed change with its own tests, before the rule that consumes it. A resolver that is wrong is worse than no cycle rule, because it fails quietly.

Issue #4632: [Bug]: cognee.config.set_graph_model() is inert — graph extraction ignores the configured model

## Bug Description

`cognee.config.set_graph_model(MyModel)` is documented as setting the graph
extraction model, but it has no effect on extraction. The setter writes
`graph_config.graph_model`, and no extraction path ever reads that field. As a
result, calling `set_graph_model(...)` silently does nothing — extraction always
uses the hardcoded default (`KnowledgeGraph`) unless a model is passed per call
via `graph_model=`.

The [config docs](https://docs.cognee.ai) list `set_graph_model(model)` as "Set
graph extraction model", and its docstring says "Set the model used for graph
extraction." Neither matches the behavior.

## Steps to Reproduce

```python
import cognee
from pydantic import BaseModel

class MyGraphModel(BaseModel):
    # any custom graph schema
    ...

cognee.config.set_graph_model(MyGraphModel)

await cognee.add("some text")
await cognee.cognify()   # extraction runs under KnowledgeGraph, NOT MyGraphModel
```

## Expected Behavior

After `set_graph_model(MyGraphModel)`, `cognify()` (and other extraction entry
points) use `MyGraphModel` as the graph schema, the same as passing
`graph_model=MyGraphModel` per call.

## Actual Behavior

The configured model is ignored. Extraction uses the hardcoded `KnowledgeGraph`.

Root cause — the write and the read are disconnected:

- **Write:** `cognee/api/v1/config/config.py` — `set_graph_model()` does
  `graph_config.graph_model = graph_model`.
- **Reads of `graph_config.graph_model` across the whole tree:** only that write
  line, plus `GraphConfig.to_dict()` self-serialization. No extraction code reads
  it.
- **How extraction actually picks the model:** `cognee/api/v1/cognify/cognify.py`
  hardcodes `graph_model: BaseModel = KnowledgeGraph` (two signatures) and threads
  that *parameter* down to `extract_graph_from_data` → `extract_content_graph`.
  The parameter chain never consults `GraphConfig`.

So `set_graph_model` stores a value that only the config's own `to_dict()` echoes
back. The only working lever is the per-call `graph_model=` argument.

Verified on tag `v1.5.2` (`df6b549`) and current `main` (`a8f9760bb`): exactly one
occurrence of `graph_config.graph_model` in `config.py` (the write), and
`cognify.py` still defaults to `KnowledgeGraph`.

## Environment

- OS: macOS 15 (behavior is platform-independent)
- Python version: 3.13
- Cognee version: 1.5.2 (also reproduced on `main` @ `a8f9760bb`)
- LLM Provider: provider-independent (config-wiring bug, not provider-specific)
- Database: graph-backend-independent

## Additional Context

Suggested fix, one of:

1. Make extraction read the configured default when no per-call `graph_model=` is
   given — e.g. `cognify()` defaults `graph_model` from
   `get_graph_config().graph_model` instead of a hardcoded `KnowledgeGraph`, so
   `set_graph_model()` becomes the global default it is documented to be.
2. If a global default is intentionally unsupported, remove `set_graph_model` (and
   its docs row/docstring) to avoid advertising a no-op.

Option 1 matches the documented behavior and the pattern already used for other
`set_*_model` setters.

Issue #1383: Guard references and fences through blob deletion

## Problem

The [blob reclamation contract](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/site/content/core/availability/blob-reclamation.md#L8-L9) says a durable decision precedes a storage executor removing bytes, and the [`Ready` state](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/site/content/core/availability/blob-reclamation.md#L44-L48) means "the backend executor may delete bytes". No such executor exists. [`BlobReclamationSelector::reclaim_pass`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-ha-distributed/src/reclamation_runtime.rs#L58-L130) selects candidates and marks them `Ready`, then stops; the previous executor, `reclaim_ready_blob` in `crates/peryx-storage/src/reclaim.rs`, was deleted with the refactor rather than fixed. `Ready` tombstones therefore never release bytes in HA mode.

That executor deleted after unfenced preflight checks: a reference could commit, or a higher epoch could re-arm the tombstone, between the checks and `backend.delete`. The single-node collector closes the reference race with [`compare_and_arm_reclaim_guards`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-storage/src/meta/reclaim_guard.rs#L13-L51), used by [`purge_orphaned_blobs`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-ha-distributed/src/reclaim_guard.rs#L36-L86), and [reference commits](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-storage/src/meta/index.rs#L344-L353) reject a digest with a live guard. Reintroducing the executor without that protocol repeats the race fixed for the collector in [#1084](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/issues/1084) and misses the concurrent-reference and stale-worker acceptance cases in [#572](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/issues/572). [#1382](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/issues/1382) covers readiness before deletion; this issue covers the guarded destructive interval.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Executor reads valid lease and Ready tombstone] --> B[Writer commits reference or new epoch takes lease]
    B --> C[Old executor resumes]
    C --> D[Backend deletes bytes]
    D --> E[Current metadata can point at missing content]
    class C accent
    class A,B good
    class D,E warn
    classDef accent fill:#dbe6f5,stroke:#4a6f9f,color:#16304d
    classDef good fill:#d8ebe1,stroke:#3f8467,color:#14402f
    classDef warn fill:#f6e2d0,stroke:#b06f36,color:#5a3212
```

## Example

An epoch-7 executor passes both preflight checks and pauses before deletion. A writer commits a reference to the digest, or epoch 8 takes the reclamation lease and changes the tombstone. The epoch-7 task resumes and deletes the blob because the backend operation has no guard or fence check.

## Required change

Reintroduce the `Ready`-tombstone executor in `peryx-ha-distributed` with a guarded destructive interval. In one committed transaction, verify the current singleton holder, term, lease generation, `Ready` tombstone generation, and reference revision; then create an owner-specific delete claim and arm the reference guard through the [`ReclaimGuardStore`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-ha/src/store.rs#L81-L95) protocol before `backend.delete`. Reference commits must reject the digest until the claim reaches a committed `Deleted` or `Abandoned` state. The timestamp-only guard expiry used by the collector must not clear a live distributed claim.

Carry the delete-claim generation into the backend. A backend with conditional-delete support must reject stale generations at the point of effect. A backend without that support must keep the reference guard active across lease expiry and transfer; the new owner may inspect the backend and finish recovery, but it cannot expose new references or clear the guard while an old delete can still arrive. Record quota credit and tombstone removal with the terminal claim so retries remain idempotent.

## Acceptance criteria

- A `Ready` tombstone in HA mode leads to a backend delete under an armed reference guard and a fence-checked claim; a reference committed after the claim is rejected until the claim is terminal.
- Lease expiry or transfer during an in-flight delete cannot clear its reference guard; recovery either completes the claimed deletion or proves that the old generation can no longer affect the backend before references resume.
- The blob-reclamation page describes the executor that ships, or drops the `Ready`-means-delete wording until it does.

## Architecture and test boundary

Keep shared code ecosystem-neutral. Shared crates must not depend on concrete `peryx-ecosystem-*` crates or add PyPI/OCI branches. When a shared workflow needs ecosystem behavior, expose a narrow capability trait from the neutral contract-owning crate and implement it in the ecosystem crate.

Use `peryx-plugin-registry` only at binary composition boundaries. Put behavioral tests beside the owning contract or implementation, keep each affected crate independently buildable and testable, and retain system tests for composed behavior.

Issue #1573: Honor reclaim-guard expiry when admitting references

## Problem

A reclaim guard carries a lease.
[`ReclaimGuard::is_expired_at`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-ha/src/reclamation.rs#L7-L16)
defines it, and
[`compare_and_arm_reclaim_guards`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-storage/src/meta/reclaim_guard.rs#L13-L51)
honors it: a lapsed row is available and a new collector may take it. The reference-admission check disagrees.
[`commit_driver_txn_at_with_commit`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-storage/src/meta/index.rs#L344-L354)
rejects the commit whenever a row is present, reading no clock at all, so an expired guard blocks a write exactly like a
live one.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[purge_orphaned_blobs arms 300s guard] --> B[blobs.delete]
    B --> C[disarm guard]
    B --> D[process dies or delete errors]
    D --> E[guard lapses, row remains]
    E --> F[commit_driver_txn_at_with_commit ignores expiry]
    F --> G[MetaError::BlobReclaiming forever]
    class A,E accent
    class F good
    class B,C,D,G warn
    classDef accent fill:#dbe6f5,stroke:#4a6f9f,color:#16304d
    classDef good fill:#d8ebe1,stroke:#3f8467,color:#14402f
    classDef warn fill:#f6e2d0,stroke:#b06f36,color:#5a3212
```

[`purge_orphaned_blobs`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-ha-distributed/src/reclaim_guard.rs#L36-L86)
arms a 300-second guard over each orphan candidate, deletes its bytes, then disarms. Kill the purge in that loop, or let
one `blobs.blocking().delete` return an error, and the guard survives with a timestamp that soon lies in the past.
Nothing clears it:
[`release_absent_expired_guards`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-ha-distributed/src/reclaim_guard.rs#L88-L110)
disarms an expired guard only when `blobs.head` reports the bytes gone, so a failed delete keeps its guard forever, and
a successful delete keeps its guard as soon as a client re-uploads the bytes. No test pins expired-guard admission:
`crates/peryx-storage/tests/unit/tests/meta/reclaim_guard_tests.rs` covers only a live guard.

## Example

A confirmed purge arms the guard over `sha256:9f1c…`, then the node is killed mid-loop. Five minutes later the lease has
lapsed, but a client re-pushing that exact layer gets `MetaError::BlobReclaiming` and is told to "publish the reference
again once its deletion finishes" while no deletion is in flight. The digest stays unpublishable until an operator runs
another confirmed purge that reaches both the delete and the disarm.

## Required change

- Give the admission check the transaction's clock and treat a guard as blocking only while
  `!ReclaimGuard::is_expired_at(now)`, matching the arming side.
- Remove the lapsed row in the same write transaction that admits past it, so an abandoned guard cannot outlive its
  lease.
- Extend `release_absent_expired_guards` to clear an expired guard whose blob is still present; an expired guard proves
  the arming purge no longer holds it.
- Distinguish a collector guard from a claim-backed one before expiry may clear it, so the rule cannot release a live
  distributed delete claim.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A driver commit that references a digest whose guard has a past `expires_at_unix` succeeds instead of returning
      `MetaError::BlobReclaiming`.
- [ ] The same commit against a guard with a future expiry is still rejected.
- [ ] After an interrupted confirmed purge leaves an expired guard over a blob that is still stored, a re-upload of that
      content succeeds without an operator running another purge.
- [ ] A guard past its expiry is either gone or reported as non-blocking after the next `release_absent_expired_guards`
      pass, whether or not its bytes are present.

## Architecture and test boundary

Keep shared code ecosystem-neutral. Shared crates must not depend on concrete `peryx-ecosystem-*` crates or add
PyPI/OCI branches. When a shared workflow needs ecosystem behavior, expose a narrow capability trait from the neutral
contract-owning crate and implement it in the ecosystem crate.

Use `peryx-plugin-registry` only at binary composition boundaries. Put behavioral tests beside the owning contract or
implementation, keep each affected crate independently buildable and testable, and retain system tests for composed
behavior.

## Coordination

Consume the collector-versus-claim distinction from [#1383](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/issues/1383), which
requires that timestamp expiry never clear a live delete claim. This issue owns the single-node expiry rule on the
reference-admission path and the lapsed-guard cleanup; it does not introduce the HA delete executor or its fenced claim.

[#1531](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/issues/1531) fixes the other end of the same reclamation path: the
live-reference set that decides which digests become orphan candidates at all. That issue owns which ecosystems the
reference scan covers; this one owns the guard row's expiry semantics once a candidate has been armed. The two do not
touch the same functions.

Issue #134: postiz: backend dies on host boot — depends_on ordering is ignored by Docker restart policies

## Summary

After a host reboot, the `postiz` container comes up but its **backend (pm2 process on :3000) is dead**, leaving nginx to 502 every `/api` call. The container's healthcheck correctly reports `unhealthy`, but nothing acts on it, so the app stays broken until someone manually restarts the container.

Root cause is **not** the package's compose file — it's that `depends_on` ordering is silently discarded on boot.

## Observed

Seen on a Proxmox LXC host reboot (`hola`, 18 containers). Immediately after boot:

```
hola-postiz-4520f878-postiz-1   unhealthy   fails=9
```

Backend logs:

```
2|backend | [ioredis] Unhandled error event: Error: getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND postiz-redis
2|backend |     at GetAddrInfoReqWrap.onlookupall [as oncomplete] (node:dns:122:26)
```

and nginx, continuously:

```
[error] connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream,
        upstream: "http://127.0.0.1:3000/auth/can-register"
```

Once things settled, redis was fine and DNS resolved — the failure was purely a startup race that the backend never recovered from:

```
ENOTFOUND count in last 3 min:      0
dns.lookup("postiz-redis")       -> OK 172.28.0.2
redis-cli ping                   -> PONG
GET http://127.0.0.1:3000/       -> ECONNREFUSED     <-- backend still dead
```

`docker restart hola-postiz-4520f878-postiz-1` fixed it permanently: `healthy`, backend `HTTP 200`.

## Root cause

`src/postiz/src/compose.yaml` already declares the dependency correctly:

```yaml
depends_on:
  postiz-postgres: { condition: service_healthy }
  postiz-redis:    { condition: service_healthy }
  temporal:        { condition: service_healthy }
```

and this survives into the runtime container labels:

```
com.docker.compose.depends_on=temporal:service_healthy:false,
                              postiz-postgres:service_healthy:false,
                              postiz-redis:service_healthy:false
```

**But `depends_on` is only evaluated by `docker compose up`.** It is metadata; the Docker daemon does not read it. On boot:

```
restart policy:  unless-stopped   (every container)
enabled units:   docker.service, docker.socket — nothing runs `docker compose up`
```

dockerd restarts all containers concurrently in arbitrary order. postiz beats redis, `ioredis` throws on an unresolvable host during NestJS init, the backend pm2 process dies, and pm2 does not bring it back. The frontend and nginx come up fine, so the container stays "running" while `/api` is dead.

This affects **every multi-service package in this repo**, not just postiz — any package relying on `depends_on` for ordering has no ordering guarantee across a host reboot. postiz is just the most fragile because its backend crashes rather than retries.

## Suggested fixes

Roughly in increasing order of effort:

1. **Autoheal (cheapest, highest value).** Run a small autoheal sidecar that restarts containers reporting `unhealthy`. The healthchecks in this repo are already accurate — postiz's deliberately probes `/api/auth/can-register` through nginx specifically to catch a dead backend (per the comment in `compose.yaml`). That healthcheck *correctly detected* this outage; nothing was listening. This turns an existing, working signal into an automatic recovery and fixes the whole class of problem for all packages.

2. **Bring deployments up with compose on boot.** Set `restart: "no"` (or `on-failure`) and have the runtime run `docker compose up -d --wait` per deployment at startup. This makes `depends_on: service_healthy` actually mean something. Likely belongs in the Hola runtime rather than here — see note below.

3. **Make postiz tolerate an absent redis at boot.** `ioredis` supports `retryStrategy`/`lazyConnect`; the crash comes from an unhandled error event during init. This is upstream `gitroomhq/postiz-app`, so probably out of scope here except as a wrapper/entrypoint workaround.

## Note on repo scope

Filing here since `src/postiz/src/compose.yaml` is the artifact that exhibits it, but the actual defect is in **boot-time orchestration**, and that may live in the Hola runtime (`try-hola/hola`) rather than in this package repo. The package's compose file is, as far as I can tell, already correct. Feel free to move or split this — fix (1) in particular is a runtime-level concern.

- Host: Proxmox VE 9.1.11, LXC guest `hola` (unprivileged), 18 containers
- Docker 29.6.1, containerd image store, overlayfs storage driver
- postiz `v2.21.10`, redis `7.4-alpine`, temporal `1.29.7`
- Surfaced during a storage migration that required a clean stop/start of the guest

Issue #4: autodo_kqread recursively locks the knlist mutex (autodo_ring_mtx)

## Summary

`autodo_kqread()` acquires `autodo_ring_mtx`, but that mutex is already held by the caller: `knlist_init_mtx(&autodo_sel.si_note, &autodo_ring_mtx)` makes the ring mutex the knlist lock, and `knote()` (invoked via `KNOTE_UNLOCKED`) takes the knlist lock before invoking `f_event`. This is a recursive acquisition of a non-recursive `MTX_DEF` mutex.

## Details

In `src/mac_do_auto.c`:

1. `autodo_init()` calls `knlist_init_mtx(&autodo_sel.si_note, &autodo_ring_mtx)`, binding the knlist lock to the ring mutex.
2. `autodo_ring_push()` drops the mutex, then calls `KNOTE_UNLOCKED(&autodo_sel.si_note, 0)`.
3. In `kern_event.c`, `knote()` with `KNF_LISTLOCKED` clear does `list->kl_lock(list->kl_lockarg)` — acquiring `autodo_ring_mtx` — before calling `f_event` (`autodo_kqread`).
4. `autodo_kqread()` then calls `mtx_lock(&autodo_ring_mtx)` — same thread, same non-recursive mutex.

Expected behavior on an INVARIANTS/WITNESS kernel: panic (`locking against myself` / witness recursion warning). On release kernels the thread can self-deadlock waiting on a lock it already owns.

The same pattern was identified during BrFS kmod development and verified against `kern_event.c` (`knote()` at the `KNL_ASSERT_LOCK` / `kl_lock` site).

## Fix

`f_event` runs with the knlist lock held — do not re-lock:

```c
static int
autodo_kqread(struct knote *kn, long hint __unused)
{
	mtx_assert(&autodo_ring_mtx, MA_OWNED);
	kn->kn_data = autodo_ring_count * sizeof(struct autodo_event);
	return (kn->kn_data > 0);
}
```

## Notes

- Puzzling that the existing test matrix (43/43, 31/31 on 15.1) never tripped this; presumably the recursive lock on a release kernel happened to be benign in the tested paths, or the knote path was never exercised with an attached EVFILT_READ knote during event delivery. Worth confirming with a WITNESS kernel run before/after.
- BrFS reference fix: pacyworld/brfs commit aacec91 (same pattern, same fix).

Each of these produces a **silently plausible wrong answer** rather than an error, which is what makes them expensive to rediscover.

1. **`events` has no prev_events column.** The DAG lives only in `event_edges`.
2. **`event_edges.is_state` marks legacy state edges.** Synapse's own queries filter `AND edge.is_state is FALSE`, noting the removal "is in a background update, [so] it's not necessarily safe to assume that it will have been completed." 3. **`event_edges.room_id` is nullable.** Added to a table that already had rows, so `WHERE event_edges.room_id = ?` drops every edge predating the backfill and the room reads as disconnected roots. Join `events` and filter *that* `room_id`, as Synapse does.

Issue #8223: Hash DISTINCT with disk spill: O(n²) partition-reload thrash makes a large spilled DISTINCT effectively hang

## Summary

A `SELECT DISTINCT` (or any hash-`DISTINCT`) whose hash table **spills to disk** degrades to **O(rows × partition_size)** — a quadratic **partition-reload thrash** — so a large spilled `DISTINCT` effectively hangs (spins at 100% CPU, no forward progress).

Root cause is in the VDBE hash table (`core/vdbe/hash_table.rs`), **independent of MVCC**. It was originally found via the `whopper` concurrent simulator under MVCC, which is only what supplies a deterministic workload (a `DISTINCT`/join over a seeded table) large enough to spill — see the correction note at the bottom.

## Mechanism

Streaming `DISTINCT` must answer "is this key a duplicate?" for **every** input row, so the target partition must be resident to be checked:

1. On each insert, `insert_distinct` computes `partition_idx = hash % count` and, if that partition was spilled, calls `load_spilled_partition`, which **re-reads and fully re-parses the entire partition from chunk 0** (`parse_partition_chunk` → `HashEntry::deserialize`), rebuilding all its buckets.
2. `evict_partitions_to_fit` (`core/vdbe/hash_table.rs:2669`) keeps only a tiny resident set within the memory budget — it clears a victim partition's buckets back to `OnDisk` and resets `current_chunk_idx = 0`.
3. `DISTINCT` keys are hash-spread across **all** partitions, so consecutive inserts hit **different** partitions. Each insert reloads+reparses its (evicted) partition, which is then evicted again to make room for the next insert's partition.

Net effect: nearly every insert triggers a full re-parse of a partition. Total deserialize work is `O(rows × entries_per_partition)`.

## Evidence

Instrumenting the spill path with counters on the reproducer below (seed 1, ~60s wall):

| counter | value |
|---|---|
| `insert_distinct` calls | **< 1,000,000** (input is bounded) |
| `load_spilled_partition` calls | **300,000+ and climbing** |
| entries deserialized on reload | **40,000,000+ and climbing** |

**~40 entries re-parsed per row inserted, and the ratio grows without bound** — the definition of the thrash. The input is finite (`insert_distinct` never even reaches 1M), so this is a performance collapse, not an infinite loop, but for any non-trivial spilled `DISTINCT` it is indistinguishable from a hang.

## Reproducer

On current `main`, add a small stress mode to `whopper` that uses only existing workloads — one seeded table hammered by concurrent writers + scans (which drives a `DISTINCT`/join large enough to spill), with occasional reopens:

```
SEED=1 cargo run -q -p turso_whopper -- --mode mvcc-livelock --enable-mvcc
```

hangs deterministically (also `SEED=2`). `--enable-mvcc` is needed only because that is what deterministically produces the spilling `DISTINCT` workload in the simulator; the defect itself is in `hash_table.rs` and is not MVCC-specific.

A maintainer on the project tursodatabase/turso (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #8505: PRAGMA max_page_count returns avoidable SQLITE_FULL during index B-tree balancing

## Summary

With 512-byte pages and a secondary index, Turso requires 44 pages for a
database that SQLite fits into 43 pages.

Different valid B-tree layouts do not generally need identical page counts.
However, in this case Turso appears to count a parent divider cell as bytes
resident on a child page. This causes an unnecessary page allocation and makes
the insert fail with `SQLITE_FULL` when `max_page_count=43`.

## Reproduction

```sql
PRAGMA page_size=512;
PRAGMA max_page_count=43;

CREATE TABLE t(
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  k TEXT
);
CREATE INDEX idx ON t(k);

WITH RECURSIVE c(x) AS (
  VALUES(1)
  UNION ALL
  SELECT x+1 FROM c WHERE x<96
)
INSERT INTO t
SELECT x, printf('%080d',x) FROM c;

SELECT count(*) FROM t;
PRAGMA page_count;
PRAGMA integrity_check;
```

## Actual Turso behavior

Turso reports:

```text
max_page_count = 43
Runtime error: Database is full: database or disk is full (13)
```

After reopening the failed database:

```text
SELECT count(*) FROM t;  -- 0
PRAGMA page_count;       -- 3
PRAGMA integrity_check;  -- ok
```

If `max_page_count` is removed or changed to 44, the insert succeeds:

```text
count(*)        = 96
page_count      = 44
integrity_check = ok
```

## SQLite behavior

SQLite 3.40.1 completes the same script with:

```text
count(*)        = 96
page_count      = 43
integrity_check = ok
```

SQLite succeeds at 43 and fails cleanly at 42, so 43 is the boundary for this
workload.

## Note:
- Without a page limit, query results remain correct but one unnecessary page is
  allocated

Issue #156: [backend+product] Model neighborhoods vs. towns — South End's 27 venues are invisible to anyone browsing Charlotte

**Type:** data modeling + product decision · **Parent:** #125 (first live beta) · **Related:** #76 (migration ledger), #75 (PostGIS radius search), #149 · **Surfaced by:** live data review 2026-07-27

### The bug this causes today

`public.cities` currently holds four rows, one of which is not a city:

| name | state | center | radius | venues |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Charlotte | NC | 35.2271, -80.8409 | 8000m | 131 |
| **South End, Charlotte** | NC | 35.2126, -80.8588 | 2500m | **27** |
| Sayville | NY | 40.7359, -73.0821 | 250m | 60 |
| Patchogue | NY | 40.7660, -73.0193 | 2500m | 22 |

South End is a Charlotte neighborhood promoted to a top-level city row. Measured against Charlotte's own center, **all 27 of its venues fall between 1.5km and 4.9km — every one inside Charlotte's 8000m radius.** By contrast Patchogue and Sayville are ~900km from Charlotte and ~6km from each other, with neither inside the other's radius. The data itself draws the line clearly.

Because venue reads filter on a single `city_id`, this produces three user-visible failures:

1. **A user browsing "Charlotte, NC" sees 131 venues and none of the 27 South End ones** — despite South End being one of Charlotte's densest nightlife areas and physically inside the area they selected.
2. **`findNearestCity` snaps to the closest center**, so two users a mile apart get different, non-overlapping lists. Standing in South End selects a different app than standing Uptown.
3. **Boundary assignment is arbitrary.** `google_place_id` is unique table-wide, so a bar near the edge lands under whichever city the sync job reached first. The 131/27 split is an artifact of sync order, not geography.

There's a related smell: 7 of the 131 "Charlotte" venues are up to **17.9km** from its center, well past the declared 8000m. `radius_meters` feeds Google Places as a `locationBias`, which is a bias and not a hard filter — so the radius column doesn't actually bound anything today. Worth settling alongside this, since #75 wants to use that same column for real `ST_DWithin` queries.

### The definitional question

Civic status is the intuitive rule and it does not survive contact with the data:

- **Patchogue** is an incorporated *village* in Suffolk County.
- **Sayville** is an unincorporated *hamlet* in the Town of Islip — not a town at all.
- **Charlotte** is a city.
- **South End** is a neighborhood with no civic existence.

Encoding that faithfully gives four or five categories that vary by state (village, hamlet, township, borough, CDP) and still wouldn't tell the app what to *do* with any of them. The taxonomy the product needs isn't a civic one — it's about browsing.

**Proposed rule — two tests, applied in order:**

1. **Containment.** Is this area geographically inside another area you cover? South End sits wholly within Charlotte's radius → child. Patchogue and Sayville contain neither each other nor anything else → top-level.
2. **Substitution.** Would someone browsing the parent expect these venues in their list? A Charlotte user absolutely expects South End bars → child. A Patchogue user does not expect Sayville bars 6km away — different town, different night out → siblings, even though they're close.

Civic status enters only as a **tiebreaker** when (1) and (2) disagree, not as the rule. The test that actually matters is (2): a child is an area you'd use to *refine* a search, a parent is one you'd use to *start* one.

Applied to today's data: Charlotte (top-level), South End → child of Charlotte, Patchogue (top-level), Sayville (top-level).

alter table cities add column kind text not null default 'city';  -- 'city' | 'neighborhood'

- One table, one FK on venues, no consistency to enforce between two columns.
- Handles the "Uptown inside Charlotte" case without further migration.

**B. A separate `neighborhoods` table** with a `city_id` FK, plus `venues.neighborhood_id`.

**C. A plain `neighborhood text` column on `venues`.**

Not recommended, and worth stating explicitly since "neighborhoods column" reads this way: it is precisely the `venues.city` mistake again. **The portal's entire exposure is one call site** — `lib/compliance/engine/refresh.ex:141-144`:

```elixir

  Drain.run(plan,
    recompute: ReactiveDag.Node.Recompute,

  )
```

becomes:

```elixir
{:ok, %Report{steps: steps}} = Drain.run(plan)
```

That is the whole change. Verified by grep: the portal implements `ReactiveDag.Op` and `ReactiveDag.Source` — both still seams — and nothing else. No `RecomputeStrategy`, no `KeyRule` behaviour, no `SetOp`, no `Job.drain_opts/1`.

## Also worth knowing when you bump

The portal is currently on `0.17.0-rc.35` (branch `reactive-dag-rc23`, with uncommitted work), so rc.36–rc.38 all land at once:

- **rc.36** — `augmented_by` (human edits on a computed node dirty its key) and `lapse` (clearing a human mark when the content it was about moves). Additive.

- **rc.38** — this change, plus `force:` (`Drain.run(plan, force: "cell")` propagates a cell's claimed keys even when the recompute reported nothing changed — for a host that re-ran a cell out-of-band and wants the graph to catch up).

Issue #41: Visualize graph status — a canned route/LiveView the library provides

The engine knows a great deal about itself at runtime, and none of it is visible without writing bespoke code. A dashboard is the natural way to answer "what is stale, what is failing, and what did the last drain actually do?"

## What we already have to render

Nothing new needs computing — the data is all there:

- **Structure** — `%Plan{cells, parents, depths}` from `ReactiveDag.Node.graph/2`: the DAG, its edges, and each cell's depth. `cell.meta` carries `op`, `verdict?`, `leaf?`, the combinator, and the recompute unit.
- **Per-cell status** — `Tuple.status_histogram/2` (counts by status), `keys_by_status/3` (with `:limit`, for a failing sample), `present_keys/2`, `max_observed_at/1` (freshness).
- **Dirtiness** — `Frontier` knows which cells have claimed keys pending.
- **The last run** — `%Drain.Report{steps, passes, duration_us}`, where each step is `{cell, claimed, changed, triggered_by, duration_us}`. That is a full trace of what propagated and why, and it is currently thrown away by most callers.
- **Attestations** — requirement state per gated edge.

## Proposal

A `ReactiveDag.Web` (separate `reactive_dag_web` package, or an optional dep) providing:

- **`reactive_dag_dashboard "/reactive-dag"`** — a router macro in the LiveDashboard idiom, so a host mounts it in one line and gets the page inside its own auth pipeline.
- **The graph** — rendered by depth, each node coloured by its worst status, badged with its key count and freshness. Mermaid is the cheap first cut (we already render it in docs); a force layout is nicer but heavier.
- **A cell drawer** — histogram, a sample of failing keys, last-observed time, and the node's declaration (unit, combinator, inputs).
- **The last drain's trace** — the `Report`'s steps as a waterfall: what was claimed, what changed, what triggered it, how long it took. This is the thing that makes "why did this recompute?" answerable.

## Open questions

- **Packaging.** A hard Phoenix/LiveView dependency in the core library is wrong for hosts that have neither. Options: a separate package, an optional dep with the module compiled only when LiveView is present, or ship the *queries* (a `ReactiveDag.Insights` read API) and let hosts render. Shipping the read API is valuable regardless — it is the part that needs library knowledge.
- **Where the Report lives.** It is returned by `Drain.run/2` and discarded. A dashboard needs the *last* one, so something must retain it (an ETS table? a configurable sink? the `:on_step` hook already exists for streaming).
- **Cost.** Status histograms over large cells are aggregate queries; the page needs sensible limits and probably a refresh interval rather than live-by-default.
- **Auth.** Explicitly the host's job — the macro mounts inside their pipeline; the library should not ship its own.

Related: #40 (install/config) would be the natural place to offer mounting the route.

Issue #17: SQL 也能玩转图数据库？—— 关系型数据库cl.x6j6.com图查询实战全攻略



在数据关系日益复杂的今天，图数据库（如 Neo4j）因其对关联数据的高效遍历而备受瞩目。然而，现实世界中的大量数据仍存储在传统关系型数据库中。难道我们必须迁移数据才能享受图查询的便利吗？答案是否定的。借助 SQL 标准中的递归查询（WITH RECURSIVE）以及新兴的 SQL/PGQ（属性图查询）扩展，我们完全可以在关系型数据库内部构建图模型，并执行强大的图分析。本文将带你走通从建图到查询的全过程，通过 15 个实战代码案例，让你掌握用 SQL 驾驭图数据的能力。
一、为什么要在关系数据库中做图查询？
1.1 图数据的普遍性

社交网络、知识图谱、供应链、权限管理、路径规划……这些场景的核心都是“实体-关系”网络。传统关系模型用外键关联表示关系，但查询多跳关系（如“朋友的朋友”）需要多次自连接，性能差且代码冗长。
1.2 SQL 的进化

SQL:1999 引入了递归公共表表达式（CTE），使得在关系数据库中实现递归遍历成为可能。随后，ISO/IEC 9075-16（SQL/PGQ）标准定义了属性图查询的语法，Oracle、SQL Server、PostgreSQL 等主流数据库已逐步支持。这意味着，我们无需引入新数据库，即可在现有 SQL 引擎上执行图查询。
1.3 适用范围

    存量系统：数据已在关系库中，无迁移成本。

    轻量级图分析：数据量在百万级以下，递归查询性能可接受。

    混合场景：需要同时进行关系型查询和图遍历，统一技术栈。

二、图建模基础：节点表和边表

在图模型中，我们通常用两张表来表示：

    节点表（Node）：存储实体及其属性。

    边表（Edge）：存储关系，包含源节点 ID、目标节点 ID、关系类型及属性。

sql

-- 用户节点表
CREATE TABLE users (
    user_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(50),
    age INT,
    city VARCHAR(50)
);

sql

WITH RECURSIVE path_finder (source, target, path, depth) AS (
    -- 起点
    SELECT user_id, user_id, ARRAY[user_id], 0
    FROM users WHERE name = 'Alice'
    UNION ALL
    -- 扩展路径
    SELECT p.source, f.friend_id, p.path || f.friend_id, p.depth + 1
    FROM path_finder p
    JOIN friends f ON p.target = f.user_id
    WHERE NOT (f.friend_id = ANY(p.path))  -- 避免循环
      AND p.depth < 10
)

FROM path_finder
WHERE target = (SELECT user_id FROM users WHERE name = 'David')
ORDER BY depth
LIMIT 1;

Issue #4498: [NEW] Proposal for a Valkey Radix Tree Data Type

## Abstract

This document proposes adding a general-purpose, binary-safe Radix Tree data type to Valkey. Each Valkey key corresponds to one Radix Tree, and each logical path in the tree maps to a `field -> value` map. The type provides exact lookup, longest-prefix matching, matching of all stored ancestor prefixes, atomic updates, and prefix traversal. It gains persistence and high availability through Valkey's existing RDB, AOF, primary-replica replication, and Cluster capabilities.

The first target use case is a KV Cache placement index for AI inference: Worker KV Cache events continuously update which Workers contain which cached prefixes. A Router queries all reusable prefixes along a request's cumulative block-hash path and then combines the results with real-time load to select a Worker. The type itself does not interpret tokens, models, Workers, or cache tiers. Applications encode those semantics into binary-safe paths, fields, and values, so the type can also serve hierarchical routing, longest-prefix matching, autocomplete indexes, and other prefix-oriented workloads.

## 1. Background and Inference Architecture

### 1.1 Problem Statement

Large-scale model inference services commonly reuse previously computed KV Cache through a prefix cache. When a request reaches a Router, the Router needs to know more than whether the prompt hits the cache. It also needs to know:

1. How deep the request's contiguous prefix matches on each Worker;
2. Whether the same prefix exists simultaneously on multiple Workers or cache tiers;
3. How placement changes continuously as blocks are created, migrated, evicted, and as Workers restart;
4. That multiple Routers must observe the same persistent and recoverable placement index;

A regular Hash can store `block_hash -> workers`, but it cannot express "find all stored ancestor prefixes of this query" in a single query. Storing every prefix as a separate top-level key also inflates the key count, makes atomic updates across keys difficult, and introduces many network round trips. The ordering of a Sorted Set is likewise not equivalent to a byte-prefix relationship.

A Radix Tree compresses paths by their shared byte prefixes, making it naturally suitable for longest-prefix matching and ancestor-prefix enumeration. Valkey already contains a mature internal `rax` implementation that supports path compression, binary-safe keys, values on internal nodes, insertion, deletion, and ordered iteration. Therefore, no new tree implementation dependency is required.

### 1.2 Goals

- Provide a general-purpose, binary-safe prefix-index data type.
- Query the longest prefix or all stored ancestor prefixes with one command.
- Allow multiple fields on the same path to be updated independently.
- Make writes idempotent and support atomic single-key batch application for event streams.
- Use existing Valkey persistence, replication, failover, and Cluster semantics.
- Reuse the path-compression and iteration capabilities of the current internal `rax`.
- Provide stable and explicit response structures for RESP2 and RESP3 clients.

### 1.3 Non-Goals

- The type does not provide vector similarity or semantic-similarity matching; all matching is exact byte-prefix matching.
- The type does not provide a global Radix Tree spanning multiple Valkey keys.
- The type does not replace the inference system's Worker snapshot, live-event, or event-reconciliation protocols.
- The type does not guarantee synchronous replication or zero RPO; data reliability still follows the selected Valkey deployment model.
- v1 does not provide a separate TTL for an individual Radix path; TTL still applies to the top-level Valkey key.

### 1.4 Inference Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Client[Client] --> Router[Router]
    Router -->|prefix query| Valkey[Valkey Radix Tree]
    Router -->|inference request| Worker[Inference Worker]
    Worker -->|KV events| Bridge[KV Event Bridge]
    Bridge -->|atomic batch| Valkey
    Worker -->|load report| Router
```

The data plane has two paths:

- Update path: A Worker produces KV events such as block created, stored, and evicted. The Bridge converts each event into a complete Radix path and writes it idempotently to Valkey through `RSET`.
- Query path: The Router converts a prompt into a cumulative block-hash path, retrieves all matching prefixes and placements in one `RPREFIXES` call, and then combines them with Worker load for routing.

The Valkey Radix Tree is a placement index shared by multiple Routers. The Bridge is responsible for protocol adaptation, event ordering, batch coalescing, retries, generation management, and short-term in-memory buffering rather than serving queries.

### 1.5 Failure and Recovery Boundaries

Radix Tree data is persisted through RDB, AOF, and primary-replica replication. The Bridge uses bounded in-memory buffering and retries for unacknowledged events. If it detects a sequence gap or buffer overflow, it should reconcile against a Worker snapshot before continuing to consume live events.

A Radix placement index is generally rebuildable soft state. Losing an add usually produces a false miss and therefore reuses less cache. Losing a delete can produce a more dangerous stale positive. Applications should therefore include the Worker generation in the value and have the Router accept only the currently live generation. After a Worker restarts, an old generation will not participate in routing even if an old delete was lost; stale records can be reclaimed later by a background scan.

This strategy reduces application-level risk during a failure window but does not change the RPO of Valkey's asynchronous replication itself.

    │   └── field F2 -> value V2
    ├── path P1 || P2
    │   └── field F1 -> value V3
    └── path P1 || P3
        └── field

Issue #14: FuncHub: a Hub whose internals are a comterp FuncObj instead of a nested flowgraph

## Motivation

`GraphHub` (`graphhub.go`) already answers "what gives a `Hub`'s internals substance beyond a builtin transform" one way: a nested `Flowgraph`. `FuncHub` is the sibling answer -- a `Hub` whose internals bottom out in a comterp `FuncObj` (github.com/vectaport/ivtools) instead of more flowgraph. The README already names the destination this package is aimed at ("designed to directly underlie a future HDL for a flowgraph language") -- comterp is the candidate expression/generation layer for that HDL (Flowtran), and `FuncHub` is the concrete bridge component connecting the two: a place in an actual flowgraph graph where a chunk of comterp expression runs.

The deeper motivation, worked out in an ivtools session alongside landing comterp `func()` closures: a DAG of pure operations has two equally valid renderings -- a topological sort (sequential comterp expression) or a spatial graph (Hubs and Pipes). They're the same object described two ways, and free to translate between *exactly* as long as there's no feedback -- feedback is what introduces real time, and a DAG has none. `FuncHub` is where that equivalence becomes a real, working bridge: a feedback-free chunk of comterp expression can sit inside a flowgraph as one Hub's `Transform`, no special handling needed for the combinational part. Where a `FuncHub` needs state across firings (see below), that's the one place the two views genuinely diverge and need explicit design, not free translation.

## Shape

Implements the existing `Transformer` interface (`transformer.go`):

```go
type Transformer interface {
	Transform(h Hub, source []any) (result []any, err error)
}
```

`Transform` would, per firing: marshal `source []any` into comterp positional args (matching comterp's own `arg(n)`/`narg()` convention for a `FuncObj` invocation), run the `FuncObj` (via the two-way proxy layer -- see the paired issue on vectaport/ivtools), marshal the comterp result(s) back into `result []any`.

**Two attrlist lifetimes, matching two things comterp already has, not a new design:**

- **Fresh attrlist per firing** -- no memory, purely combinational. Matches comterp's own bare `FuncObj` call (a fresh per-call locals frame every time).
- **One shared attrlist across firings** -- a `FuncHub` that keeps state between completion-gated firings. Matches comterp's own self-bound `obj.method()` pattern (a persistent attrlist, mutated call over call) -- functionally a register, wearing an object-method costume, sitting in a flowgraph position instead of behind dot-call syntax.

Which lifetime a given `FuncHub` uses should be a construction-time choice (`NewHub` init arg or similar, alongside `AllOf`/`OneOf`), not something inferred -- a `Transformer`'s own comterp body doesn't know it's running inside a flowgraph at all, so the lifetime has to be a property of the `Hub`, not something the `func()` body can express (`local()`/`global()` inside the body remain the ivtools-side escape hatch for cross-firing global/session state, orthogonal to this).

## Open questions

- Exact marshaling for `ComValue`/`AttributeList` <-> Go `any` -- depends on the proxy layer design (paired issue).
- Whether `FuncHub`'s comterp body is supplied as source text (parsed per-`NewHub` call) or as an already-built `FuncObj` value passed in -- affects whether `FuncHub` needs its own comterp parser entry point or just an execution one.
- Naming: `FuncHub` vs `ComboHub` -- `FuncHub` reads more consistently with the existing `GraphHub`/`Transformer`/`Retriever` naming (named for what supplies the internals), leaning that way unless there's a reason to prefer `ComboHub`.

## Related

Paired with an issue on vectaport/ivtools: expose comterp's API to Go through two-way proxy calls -- this issue's `Transform` implementation is the concrete first consumer of that proxy layer.

Issue #293: Follow-on to #167: per-instance objects (member variables, not just methods), and why this is comterp's answer to generics

## Follow-on to #167

#167 defines an interface as an `AttributeList` of `FuncObj`s keyed by verb name -- a per-*type* method table, dispatched on the runtime types of 1-2 operands sitting on the stack. Two extensions came out of tonight's conversation (starting from #291's closure investigation) that build directly on that structure without changing its core mechanism.

## Extension 1: the attrlist also holds arbitrary member variables, not just methods

#167's interface attrlist, as specified, holds only verb-name -> `FuncObj` entries -- a dispatch table, shared across every instance of a type. Nothing stops the *same kind of attrlist* from also holding ordinary data fields alongside those methods -- `(:x 0 :y 0 :incr func(x=x+1; x))` is a single attrlist with two plain data keywords and one method keyword, all in the one structure #167 already specifies.

That's the difference between a per-*type* dispatch table (#167 as written -- one shared table per type, no per-instance state) and a genuine per-*instance* object (data plus methods bundled together, each instance getting its own copy of the data keywords). Both are the same underlying mechanism -- an attrlist mapping keywords to values, where some values happen to be `FuncObj`s -- just at different granularity. Worth specifying explicitly as part of #167's design rather than leaving it as an accidental capability: is an "interface" strictly the shared per-type table, and per-instance objects a separate, related construct built the same way but registered differently (not in the global type-dispatch table, just an ordinary attrlist a script constructs and hands around)?

This is also the thing that makes closures unnecessary as a separate ComTerp feature (see #291): a single-method object built this way *is* a closure -- the data keyword is the captured variable, the method keyword is the function body -- so extending #167 this way subsumes #291's whole investigation as the degenerate one-method case, rather than needing a dedicated `closure()`/`stash()` command built in parallel.

**Directly blocked by #292** (dot access on an attrlist-object returns `nil` instead of the real field when the object arrived via a command's return value rather than a direct variable reference) -- an object system built on attrlists only works if instances can be looked up, stored, and passed around and still reliably support field/method access, which is exactly the case #292 breaks.

## Extension 2: this is also comterp's answer to "why no generics"

Came up independently, worth recording since it's a real argument for the design, not just a tangent. Statically-typed languages need generics because their compilers must know a concrete type in advance; without them, code is either duplicated per type by hand, or falls back to a boxed `interface{}`-style escape hatch that loses both compile-time type safety and performance (Go held out against adding them for a decade-plus on exactly this tension, and added them in 1.18 once a design was found that didn't betray the rest of the language's simplicity). Dynamically-typed languages never had this problem -- duck typing gives "write once, works on any compatible type" for free, no type-parameter syntax needed, which is why Python, Ruby, Lisp, Scheme, Clojure, Erlang never added generics as a core language feature.

#167's DuckType dispatch (`add()` works on whatever type has `add` registered) is comterp's version of exactly that free lunch -- a value is addable if its type's interface has `add`, checked at the moment the call actually runs, no `<T>` syntax required anywhere. This is worth stating explicitly in #167's own writeup as part of its motivation: it isn't just multiple dispatch for its own sake, it's the mechanism that makes comterp's dynamic typing give programmers what generics give statically-typed languages, without ever needing generics-shaped syntax to get it.

One nuance worth keeping precise, not overclaiming: this parity holds against *dynamically-typed* functional/general-purpose languages, not against Haskell/ML-family statically-typed ones. Their use of parametric polymorphism isn't primarily about avoiding duplication (Go's problem) -- it's about proving things about a function purely from its type, before it ever runs (Wadler's "theorems for free": `id :: a -> a` can be proven to be the identity function from its type signature alone). No amount of duck-typing flexibility replicates that, because it depends on the checking happening statically. Interestingly, Haskell's typeclasses (`Eq a => ...`, "generic over any type with these operations defined") are conceptually close to #167's DuckType idea -- both say "works on any type that has the right operations" -- the difference is only *when* a missing operation is caught: Haskell rejects at compile time, #167-style dispatch discovers it by actually running the call and finding nothing registered. Same shape of idea, opposite moment of truth -- worth being honest about that boundary rather than claiming #167 makes generics moot in some absolute sense.

Issue #34: Bidirectional dependency graph: what a file depends on, and what depends on it

## The idea

Search answers "where is X". It does not answer "what does X touch". An agent about to change a function needs both directions: what it relies on, and — far more valuable — what relies on it.

## What is actually differentiating

Dependency graphs are old: LSP, ctags, Sourcegraph, every IDE. Semantic code search is common. What is rare is **fusing them so the graph arrives with the retrieval result, budgeted for a context window**.

And within that, one half carries most of the value: **reverse edges**.

Forward edges an agent gets for free — it has the file, the imports are at the top. Reverse edges require the *whole workspace already indexed*, which is exactly what this is and what a per-project LSP structurally cannot give you. An LSP scoped to one repo does not know that two other repos import this function. We would.

> Before you change this function, here is everything across every repo that will feel it.

Grep cannot answer that (needs the right literal), semantic search cannot (needs meaning, not structure), an IDE cannot (wrong scope).

## Why it is unusually cheap here

Every code file is already parsed with tree-sitter and the AST is then **thrown away**. Import extraction is a second walk over a tree already paid for — and `process()` already accepts `imports=True` / `exports=True`, currently passed as False.

The manifest is already SQLite, which is the right store for edges: relational, queryable in both directions, and it survives a vector-store swap.

`DeclarationScanner` (#28) established the precedent for a supplementary per-language pass.

## The hard part is resolution, and it is where these projects die

Extraction is easy. Knowing which `foo` on disk `import foo` refers to is the whole problem:

- **Python** — `sys.path`, relative imports, namespace packages, and `__init__` re-exports, which this repo does deliberately everywhere. We are our own hard case.
- **Node/TS** — `tsconfig` path aliases, barrel files, extension inference, `node_modules`, monorepo workspaces. The hardest single resolver, but **one** algorithm covering JS, TS, JSX, TSX and Node.
- **C#** — different in kind: resolution is *namespace-based*, not path-based. `using MyApp.Services` names no file. Needs a two-pass workspace symbol table, but is arguably easier than JS once built.
- **CSS family** — `@use`, `@import`, `<link>`, `<script src>` are relative paths. Easiest, lowest value.

**Call graphs are a different order of difficulty from import graphs.** `self._store.upsert(...)` — what is `_store`? That needs type inference, and in Python with protocols and DI it is often undecidable. Symbol-level call edges may never be reliable there, and that is fine.

## Rungs, gated on evidence

The ladder that worked for the classifier — which produced a real "no" for normative+design and a real "yes" for adding `guide`:

| Rung | Cost | Gives |
|---|---|---|
| 1. File imports, unresolved strings | ~free, reuses the parse | "what does this file import" |
| 2. Resolve within a repo | moderate, per-language | real edges, reverse edges work |
| 3. Resolve across repos | harder | **the differentiator** |
| 4. Symbol-level call edges | hard, language-dependent | precision, where tractable |

Rung 1 is a weekend. Rungs 2–4 are the real project, and per-language resolution is never "done" — it accretes edge cases forever. Worth entering with that understood.

## Design notes

**A separate tool, not attached to every hit.** A hub file has hundreds of reverse edges; attaching that to ten search results floods the window, which is what `ResultBudget` exists to stop. Most hits are being scanned, not acted on. So `search_code` returns the location, and the agent calls `impact_of(path)` deliberately when it decides to act — the same reasoning that made `search_code` and `find_guidance` separate rather than one tool with a mode flag.

**The graph needs its own budget and ranking**: direct before transitive, same-repo before cross-repo, truncation declared rather than silent.

**Staleness probably has a clean answer.** If edges are keyed by source file in one table queried both directions, deleting A drops its rows and B's reverse query stops seeing it — reverse edges become a query, not stored state, with no separate invalidation. Worth proving before relying on it.

## The synthesis worth being most excited about

Combine reverse edges with `doc_type: test`, which already exists:

> **3 tests exercise this function: `tests/test_manifest.py:119`, …**

That is the most actionable thing you can hand an agent before it edits code, and it falls out of two things already built. Likewise a `normative` reverse edge means "a spec references this" — the guidance path and the structural path meeting.

## Risk to design against

**Half a graph is worse than none.** If Python resolves and TypeScript does not, `impact_of` on a TS file returns empty, which reads as "nothing depends on this". That is the same silent-empty-result failure already hit three times. It needs the taxonomy treatment: report *which languages have resolvers*, so zero means "no resolver here" and never "no dependents".

- [ ] Import statements extracted for Python, the JS family and C#, stored as raw strings
- [ ] Extraction adds no measurable time to a full index — it reuses the existing parse
- [ ] Coverage is reportable per language, so an empty answer is distinguishable from an unsupported one

Issue #46: [P1] CI: install the way users install, with fresh resolution

## Links
- Epic: #44
- Origin: #40
- Evidence: `docs/audits/2026-08-agent-workflow-audit.md` → Finding 8
- Code: `.github/workflows/ci.yml`

## Problem

CI installs with `uv sync`, which installs the pinned contents of `uv.lock`. Users install with `uvx`, which resolves fresh to the newest version each constraint allows. Only one of those is tested.

```
CI                                  A real user
uv sync  → installs uv.lock         uvx  → fresh resolve, newest allowed
  └─ stayed on mcp 1.x                └─ resolved to mcp 2.0.0 → crash on import
```

**Causality, stated precisely.** The root cause of #40 was the uncapped `mcp` dependency. Lockfile-based CI was a **detection gap**, not the cause. Capping the dependency fixed the bug; this issue closes the detection gap.

## Timeline

| Event | Date |
|---|---|
| mcp 2.0.0 released | 2026-07-28 |
| #40 filed | 2026-07-29 |
| v0.8.2 fix shipped | 2026-07-31 |

The break window was roughly **three days**. An earlier version of this issue claimed eleven months; that was wrong and conflated the outage with a quiet period in the repo.

## An honest limit on the scheduled-job argument

Users reported this within one day. A weekly scheduled check averages 3.5 days and would have been **slower than the community**. So the case for scheduled fresh-resolution testing is not "it would have caught #40 sooner". It is that it gives detection we control, for breaks subtler than a startup crash that users may never report at all.

| Trigger | Catches |
|---|---|
| On PR | breaks we introduce, plus upstream breaks current at that moment |
| On schedule | silent upstream behaviour changes during quiet periods |

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A CI job installs the built artifact with **fresh dependency resolution**, not from `uv.lock`
- [ ] That job completes a real stdio MCP handshake, not a mocked session
- [ ] It runs on PRs at minimum
- [ ] A scheduled variant is added only if the PR-triggered job proves insufficient
- [ ] Any scheduled failure is visible: notification, or an auto-filed issue

## Out of scope

The exact `uv` invocation and the schedule cadence.

## Problem

The three PM-owned bootstrap/shaping workflows are named after Compass-internal vocabulary that (a) doesn't say what the workflow decides, and (b) diverges from the Jira vocabulary the live engagement actually runs on (`source_of_truth: external`, where a bet IS an Epic). ## The three workflows and why all three stay

They share a shape (research → draft → seed DRI → mirror → HITL halt) but differ in **cardinality of the decision** — that's the reason none of them collapses into another:

| Workflow | Artifact | Cardinality | The decision it makes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/setup-product` | `docs/foundation/product.md` | once ever (amend → v2) | why we exist, the moat, the falsifiable hypothesis everything traces to |
| `/create-bet-portfolio` | `docs/foundation/portfolio.md` + 3–6 stub briefs | once ever (refuses after 1st stub promoted) | where the MVP line sits + what depends on what |
| `/create-brief` | `docs/bets/<id>/brief.md` | many, forever | is this one bet worth taking |

The middle one exists because the MVP wedge cannot be decided one-bet-at-a-time — decide serially and "architecture gets decided knowing only bet 1; cross-bet dependencies stay invisible" (`create-bet-portfolio.md`). Confirmed keep.

| Now | Proposed | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| `/setup-product` | `/create-product-brief` | It *is* a brief, at product altitude. Makes the brief shape consistent across all three altitudes. |
| `/create-bet-portfolio` | `/create-mvp-plan` | Names the decision (MVP line + dependency graph + out-of-MVP), not the byproduct. **Deliberately not `/create-epics`** — see hazard below. |

`/create-epics` and `/create-epic` differ by one character. As slash commands that's a live hazard: a typo silently dispatches the wrong workflow, and one of them is bootstrap-only-that-refuses-after-first-use while the other is the everyday path. Names must be semantically distinct, not plural-distinct. Issue #28038: orm: explicit relationship loading with deep select

### Describe the feature

Add explicit relationship-loading control to the ORM Function Call API (`orm.new_query[T]`):

- `include(field)` — load a specific `@[fkey]` relationship.
- `include_alias(field, alias)` — load a relationship and alias it so the existing `where()` can filter it. `field` accepts a dotted path for nested relationships (`children.grandchildren`), with the alias naming the final level.
- `not_include(field)` — exclude a specific relationship from the current implicit loading, keeping the rest unchanged.

Default behavior stays as-is (implicit loading when the primary key is selected), so existing code and tests are not broken.

### Use Case

Today, selecting the primary key implicitly loads every `@[fkey]` relationship, with no way to filter or exclude individual ones. Three common needs are impossible today:

- Load a parent but skip one expensive relationship.
- Load a parent with only the children whose `name` starts with `S` (deep select).
- Load nested relationships (`children` → `grandchildren` → ...) with filters at each level.

### Proposed Solution

```v
// Exclude one relationship, keep implicit loading for the rest.
parents.select('id', 'name')!.not_include('children')!.query()!

// Explicit include with filtering via alias + where().
parents.select('id', 'name')!.include_alias('children', 'c').where('c.name like ?', ['S%'])!.query()!

// Nested: dotted path, alias on the leaf level.
parents.select('id', 'name')!.include_alias('children.grandchildren', 'gc').where('gc.age > ?', [5])!.query()!

// Filter multiple levels by chaining include_alias calls.
parents.select('id', 'name')!.include_alias('children', 'c').include_alias('children.grandchildren', 'gc').where(
	'c.name like ? and gc.age > ?', ['A%', 5],
)!.query()!
```

`where()` must accept alias-qualified fields (`c.name`, `gc.age`). The condition parser already passes tokens containing `.` through unchanged (`v_sql_field_name`, `orm_func.v:338`); what is missing is validating the alias against declared includes and routing the condition to the relationship query for that level.

`include_alias` dotted paths support arbitrary depth (each segment is a `@[fkey]` field on the previous level's struct); the alias names the final level, and `where()` conditions on that alias filter that level.

Signatures (positional only — V has no named args or default param values):

```v
include(field string) !&QueryBuilder[T]
include_alias(field string, alias string) !&QueryBuilder[T]
not_include(field string) !&QueryBuilder[T]
```

### Other Information

### Proposed tests

`feature_include_test.v` covers: `not_include()` excludes one relation while keeping implicit loading for others; `include()` loads a specific relation; `include_alias()` + `where()` filters related rows; `include_alias()` with a dotted path loads nested relationships; `include()` works when the primary key is not selected.

### Implementation notes

- All runtime-side, `vlib/orm/orm_func.v`; no compiler change.
- `not_include()`: add an exclusion set to `QueryBuilder`; `map_row` (lines 1374-1415) skips `@[fkey]` fields in that set while keeping implicit loading for the rest.
- `include()` / `include_alias()`: add an explicit-include set; when non-empty, `map_row` loads only the listed relationships (overrides implicit). `include_alias` stores the alias and the dotted path.
- `where()`: accept alias-qualified fields when the alias was declared by `include_alias()`; route those conditions to the relationship query built for that include instead of the parent query. For nested paths, build a chain of `QueryBuilder` per level, applying alias conditions at the leaf.
- Alias-qualified fields already survive `parse_conditions` (`v_sql_field_name`, line 338, returns tokens with `.` as-is); missing only alias validation and condition routing.

- [x] I may be able to implement this feature request
- [ ] This feature might incur a breaking change

Issue #42: `Maximum call stack size exceeded` on plain objects containing a self-reference (regression in 7.0.3, still present in 8.0.0)

Follow-up to #37, which was closed for lack of a repro snippet. Here is a minimal one. This case differs from the React-component discussion in that thread: no class instances and no functions are involved — only plain objects that pass `ts-deepmerge`'s own `isObject` check.

### Repro

```js
import { merge } from "ts-deepmerge";

// A plain object holding a reference to itself.
const node = { rules: {} };
node.configs = { recommended: { plugins: { self: node } } };
//                                              ^ node.configs.recommended.plugins.self === node

merge({}, { plugins: { self: node } });
```

- **7.0.2** → returns successfully, self-reference preserved.
- **7.0.3** → `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`
- **8.0.0** → `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`

Every object in the graph is a plain object literal whose prototype is `Object.prototype`, so `isObject()` returns `true` for all of them.

### Cause

The branch added in 7.0.3 (`esm/index.js`, present unchanged in 8.0.0):

```js
else if (!isObject(result[key]) && isObject(current[key])) {
    result[key] = merge(current[key], undefined);
}
```

When the destination lacks the key, the source value is now deep-cloned via a recursive `merge()` rather than assigned by reference as in 7.0.2. That recursion has no visited-set, so any cycle in the source graph recurses until the stack is exhausted.

Arrays happen to be immune, since `isObject()` rejects them and recursion stops. Cycles mediated by plain objects have no such brake.

### Why this shape is common

This is the normal structure of an ESLint plugin: a plugin's shareable config has to declare the plugin it belongs to, which produces `plugin.configs.recommended.plugins[name] === plugin`. Any consumer merging ESLint flat configs will hit this. It is not exotic or invalid data — it is plain objects with a cycle.

### Suggested fix

Track visited sources during the clone, e.g. a `WeakMap` threaded through the recursion, returning the already-created clone on revisit. Alternatively, restore 7.0.2's by-reference assignment for this branch, which sidesteps the traversal entirely.

I appreciate the note in #37 that the library targets simple primitives. If cyclic plain objects are considered out of scope, it would help to document that and ideally throw a clear error rather than a stack overflow — the current failure mode is hard to trace back to the merge call.

### Environment

- `ts-deepmerge` 7.0.3 and 8.0.0 (7.0.2 unaffected)
- Node 20 and 24, macOS arm64
