I'm offering some vocabulary from an adjacent field that may let two things the note currently states in prose become typed attributes the KR model can carry. It's a suggestion for the model, with one caveat flagged where the mapping isn't clean.

1. Two typed attributes per artifact (the main proposal). Part I §3 and #7 describe integrity, availability, and "freshness" as prose distinctions. Each could instead be carried as a typed attribute per artifact.

Integrity ∈ {content-addressed | location-bound}. An artifact named by a cryptographic digest of its own bytes carries integrity independently of where it resolves. It verifies offline, with no authority to reach. That takes integrity out of the availability tradeoff. Location then governs only whether you can fetch the bytes, and whether they are current.
Freshness = a staleness bound. "Freshness" (from #7) is the right property, but it isn't representable until it is quantified. The standard quantifier is a bounded-staleness window: the maximum interval in which a revoked or superseded artifact may still verify (for example, "a revocation is observed within ≤ T"). "Bounded staleness" is a named consistency model, so this also connects the note to existing literature.

So {integrity: content-addressed | location-bound, staleness_bound: T} per artifact turns the prose distinction into something the model can reason over. And as #7 notes, the resolvable set is wider than the identity document: the evidence a decision rested on is itself an artifact with these two attributes.

2. Resolution dependency as a PACELC position plus a governance attribute (the framing). Part I §3 says each arrangement "carries a different answer to who can make an agent disappear, a different latency profile at the ninety-ninth percentile, and a different failure mode under network partition or governance dispute." Two of those three are the axes of PACELC (Abadi 2012, extending Brewer's CAP). The p99 latency profile is the latency-vs-consistency trade: fetch-fresh is consistent but slow, serve-cached is fast but possibly stale. The partition failure mode is the availability-vs-consistency trade. The third, who can make an agent disappear, is different in kind. It is a governance property (who controls the resolution authority), and it rides on the availability axis without reducing to it. So resolution dependency could be modelled as a PACELC position plus a separate governance/control attribute, rather than as one dimension. That keeps the technical and governance concerns from being conflated.

3. On §5 Q3 (latency budget under call-chain depth). Minor. The note already asks the right thing, and already frames latency at the ninety-ninth percentile. One name worth attaching: because verification recurs at every hop, per-hop tail latency compounds with chain depth (tail-latency amplification; Dean & Barroso, "The Tail at Scale," CACM 2013). The practical implication is that a budget answering Q3 probably has to be expressed as a tail statistic under realistic depth, since a single-hop p99 understates the chain.

Happy to turn (1) and (2) into a concrete PR against kroftrust.md if that is useful. These are long‑settled problems in the distributed‑systems literature: CAP/PACELC, tail‑latency, bounded staleness. I'm bringing that lens to the note.

Issue #79: Reopen blast radius: answering one open field can silently destroy other answered values

### What and why

Reopening to answer one open field can permanently destroy several answered values, with nothing on screen indicating they ever existed. Found by the reviewer pass on [PR #78](https://github.com/warblersafety/wilson/pull/78) (finding 2), reproduced on the reference-case record `src/lib/end-condition-flow.test.ts` builds.

**The path.** In the Open-fields dialog, clicking "Answer" on suspect product #1's unknown lot number calls `rowForField()` → `reopenReviewRow()`, which walks all six of that curated row's topics and reopens **43 fields**. `nextStep()` then returns the identity topic; `dismissableFieldIds()` bundles `Prod1Name`/`Prod1Strength`/`Prod1StrengthUnit` into one ask; and a single "I don't have that" tap `mark_unknown`s all three. `applyAction()` clears `value` on any non-`answer` action (`src/lib/agenda.ts`), so `amoxicillin` and `875` are gone — not recoverable, and never shown to the clinician as at risk.

**Why it wasn't fixed in #45.** The plan of record chose row granularity explicitly and with a stated reason ("the dialog's per-entry 'Answer' reopens at the same row granularity Review's Edit uses — one reopen mechanism, not two"). Narrowing it is a design change against a fable-reviewed decision, which is not a build session's call.

**Why the obvious fix is probably not the whole fix.** The reviewer's suggestion — have the dialog reopen the entry's own *topic* instead of its row — closes this entrance. But Review's per-card **Edit** is frozen AC and screen 05's own affordance, and it reopens the same 43 fields with the same one-tap consequence. Narrowing only the dialog leaves the hazard wide open at the other door.

The likely real mitigation is the open question already sitting with Steve: whether the re-ask itself shows "you said: {value}". `fieldDisplay()` already resolves retained values (#45 built it), and reviewer-pass finding 5 notes that reminder is currently unreachable in the shipped flow — Review only mounts at `done`, so a reopened-but-unanswered field is never rendered. Answering that question makes the retained value visible exactly where the destructive tap happens.

Related: #47 (repeat-uncertainty machinery), #62 ("Start over" partial reset), #77 (repeat counts unrevisable after decision). This one is about reopen blast radius, distinct from all three.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A decision, recorded in `docs/design.md`, on reopen granularity: whether the Open-fields dialog's per-entry "Answer" reopens the entry's topic rather than its curated row, and whether Review's per-card Edit keeps row granularity.
- [ ] A decision on the deferred open question — does a re-ask show the retained prior value ("you said: 8/20")? — since that is what makes the loss visible at the moment it can happen, wherever the reopen came from.
- [ ] Whatever is decided is implemented so that no single dismiss tap can clear an answered value the clinician has not been shown, or the decision explicitly accepts that and records why.
- [ ] Proof: a test that reopens via the dialog's own path, dismisses the resulting ask, and asserts the surviving record matches the decision — the reference-case record above is a ready-made fixture for it.

Issue #38655: `/download` config/merged.mg requests have no group-membership check

## Summary

`POST /wazuh-manager/download` authenticates the requesting agent (AES-CMAC) but does not authorize what it asks for: any authenticated agent can fetch **any other group's** merged configuration (`merged.mg`) by name, including multigroup selectors, not just its own assigned group(s). This is the `config`/`resource_type` counterpart of the WPK-side gap already being fixed in #38483; that issue explicitly lists `config`/`merged.mg` downloads as "same gap, separate change" and out of its own scope.

## Affected component

`src/remoted/remoted_module/src/endpoints/downloadEndpoint.{hpp,cpp}` (wazuh-manager remoted, HTTPS agent-comms 1517), 5.0.0.

## Root cause

The endpoint's own doc comment states this plainly, `downloadEndpoint.hpp:196-199` (`locateResource()`):

> The manager does NOT check that the requesting agent belongs to what it asks for: per the protocol decision on #38022, `resource_id` is what the agent requests and the group lookup was removed. Any authenticated agent can therefore fetch any group's (or multigroup's) merged configuration.

The resource-id **grammar** is solid, `isValidGroupName()`/`isValidGroupSelector()` (`downloadEndpoint.hpp:102-117`) reject `/`, `.`/`..`, and anything outside `[A-Za-z0-9.:;_=+!@()-]`, so there's no path traversal here. The gap is strictly authorization: `resource_id` is resolved straight to `<sharedDir>/<group>/merged.mg` (or the hashed multigroup directory) with no check that the authenticated agent (`request->agentId`) is actually a member of the group it's asking for.

## Live reproduction

Enrolled a throwaway agent (`005`) in the `default` group only, created a second group `secretgrp` it was never assigned to, then used agent `005`'s own valid AES-CMAC-signed request to fetch it:

```
POST /wazuh-manager/download {"resource_type":"config","resource_id":"secretgrp"}
-> HTTP 200, full merged.mg for secretgrp returned
```

No group lookup, no 403, no indication the agent isn't a member. Test artifacts (agent `005`, group `secretgrp`) were deleted afterward.

## Impact

Any single compromised or low-value agent can enumerate group names and read every other group's shared configuration, custom decoder/rule references, integration settings, internal hostnames, or whatever else operators centralize into group configs, well beyond what that agent should ever see. Multigroup selectors are affected the same way (the selector is hashed, not path-joined, so still no traversal, but still no membership check).

## Relationship to #38483

#38483 implements signed, expiring, agent-bound identifiers for WPK downloads (`S = subject || exp || task_id`, HMAC-verified, checked against `AuthenticatedRequest::agentId`) and explicitly calls out `config`/`merged.mg` as the same class of problem, left out of its own scope. That mechanism doesn't extend to this endpoint as designed: it binds the signature to an upgrade `task_id`, and config requests aren't task-driven, an agent just asks for its (assigned) group by name whenever its `config_hash` changes, with no task in play to bind to.

A workable equivalent for this path: since the manager already knows what group(s) an agent belongs to (it computes `config_hash` per agent for `/control` delivery, per the same doc comment), the simplest fix is reintroducing a membership check at `locateResource()`, comparing `request->agentId`'s assigned group(s) against the requested `resource_id` before resolving the path. A signed-identifier approach analogous to #38483's, binding to `agent_id || resource_id || exp` instead of `task_id`, would also work and keeps the two download paths consistent, but isn't required to close this: a membership check is enough since (unlike WPK filenames) group names aren't intended to be secret, only scoped to their members.

## Expected behavior

`/download` should refuse (404, consistent with the endpoint's existing "unknown resource" response, so as not to disclose which groups exist) a `config`/`resource_id` the requesting agent is not a member of.

## Environment

- Build: 5.0.0 dev packages from the `5.0.0` branch.
- Deployment: single-node manager (Ubuntu 20.04), agent-comms HTTPS reachable on 1517.

## Related

- #38483 — Implement WPK download authorization via signed identifiers (same class of bug, WPK side; explicitly lists this config-side gap as out of scope)
- #38283 — SPIKE: Ephemeral token for WPK downloads (design predecessor to #38483)
- #38022 — Implement `/download` HTTPS endpoint (the protocol decision that removed the group lookup)

This Issue captures the Chatterbox product concept. It does not by itself authorize implementation, branch creation, PR creation, Production changes, or task release.

# Chatterbox

> **Chatterbox — empowering the Agentic workforce because GitHub records the work. Chatterbox communicates the work.**

## Product boundary

**GitHub records the work. Chatterbox communicates the work.**

GitHub Issues and Pull Requests remain the durable system of record for task authority, requirements, implementation evidence, review, merge, verification, and change history.

Chatterbox supplies the missing persistent project-team communication layer for independently hosted agents that may have different check-in cadences, runtimes, notification capabilities, and availability.

## Product analogy

Chatterbox is a persistent asynchronous project conference call.

Agents can join and leave at different times. The conversation persists. Participants returning later can read what changed, see available work, hear peer completions, answer questions, and continue the same program without requiring all agents to be simultaneously online.

The system must support an arbitrary number of participating agents and humans.

## Core operating flow

1. PMO publishes an authorized program/task graph.
2. An agent checks in and reads new conversation/events since its last checkpoint.
3. The agent sees eligible work and atomically claims one task.
4. The agent reads and executes against the authoritative GitHub Issue.
5. The agent records implementation details, status, PR evidence, review, merge, and verification in GitHub.
6. The agent returns to Chatterbox and posts a concise update such as `COMPLETE #7 — Issue/PR updated`.
7. PMO and every participating agent receive the same conversation event immediately or on their next check-in.
8. PMO reviews GitHub evidence, performs required administrative/acceptance updates, and announces successor release or rework in Chatterbox.
9. Other agents see newly unblocked or available work and continue according to the task graph.

A Chatterbox message never substitutes for a required GitHub Issue/PR update.

## Short communication contract

Examples:

```text
CLAIM #7
STATUS #7 — implementation complete; PR review pending.
QUESTION #7 → Claude — does #11 depend on this schema?
ANSWER #7 — yes; #11 can continue after the migration lands.
COMPLETE #7 — PR merged and verification recorded on Issue.
PMO ACCEPT #7 — Issue reconciled. #8 and #9 released.
```

Implementation detail belongs in GitHub; Chatterbox is the spoken team update.

## Dynamic participant model

Participants may include Product Authority, PMO, Cursor, Claude, Grok, Codex, other future agents, and GitHub Actions as a bounded system participant.

Each participant needs:

- identity;
- role/capability eligibility;
- current claims;
- last check-in;
- last-seen and last-acknowledged event;
- unread events;
- unanswered questions;
- optional capacity;
- optional inbound-notification support.

Identity alone does not create task authority.

## Check-in / catch-up

Every participant maintains a durable checkpoint. On check-in, Chatterbox should provide a concise `since you were gone` view including:

- PMO instructions;
- task claims/releases;
- completions;
- questions addressed to the participant;
- peer answers;
- changed gates/dependencies;
- GitHub events;
- newly available work;
- required acknowledgments/actions.

Push notifications are optional enhancements. Pull/check-in is the baseline.

## Task and claim model

Candidate task states:

```text
PLANNED
BLOCKED
AVAILABLE
CLAIMED
IN_PROGRESS
QUESTION
READY_FOR_REVIEW
ACCEPTED
REWORK
COMPLETE
CANCELLED
```

Protected decisions remain separate first-class states:

```text
DECISION_REQUIRED
DECISION_RECORDED
```

Claims must be atomic. A claim is accepted only when the task is available, no conflicting owner exists, the participant is eligible, dependencies are satisfied, protected stops are clear, collision rules permit execution, and participant capacity allows it.

A stale claim must be flagged for reconciliation rather than blindly reassigned because partial work, branches, or PRs may already exist.

## Collision prevention

Tasks may declare collision domains such as paths, migration sequencing, or shared resources. Chatterbox must prevent or visibly flag incompatible concurrent claims according to PMO rules.

## Questions and peer communication

Questions are durable objects and remain visible until answered/dispositioned.

Candidate types:

- INFORMATIONAL
- IMPLEMENTATION_BLOCKING
- PRODUCT_DECISION
- PMO_DECISION
- DEPENDENCY_EVIDENCE

A preferred target may be named, but other eligible participants may answer where appropriate. Peer answers remain visible to PMO and the full team rather than becoming side-channel communication.

## Downstream effects

Chatterbox must distinguish:

1. **Peer unblocking** — one agent's completion allows another already-authorized task to continue.
2. **PMO-controlled successor release** — PMO acceptance is required before the successor becomes claimable.
3. **Protected decision gate** — Product Authority decides, PMO records/reconciles, then eligibility changes.

Conversation alone must not silently create authority.

## GitHub integration

GitHub remains authoritative. Chatterbox should surface factual GitHub events into the room, for example PR opened, review complete, PR merged, or Issue changed, while linking participants back to GitHub for detail.

## GitHub Actions / CI role

GitHub Actions may serve as a bounded Chatterbox clerk for deterministic administration, including:

- ingesting GitHub events into the timeline;
- ACK/last-seen support where practical;
- detecting stale claims or miss

Issue #5: Support shrinking narrative outlines without stale active episodes

## Background

After a chapter outline has already been materialized as episode records, normal editing may reduce the planned episode count. Example:

- Chapter 1 initially has 10 episodes
- The outline is revised to 8 episodes
- Episodes 9 and 10 are no longer part of the active structure

Current Phase 2 narrative tools support `episode_update`, `episode_reorder`, and `canon_status` transitions such as `deprecated`, but there is no `episode_delete`. `chapter_delete` / `scene_delete` are also absent.

This is not necessarily a requirement for physical deletion: marking obsolete narrative nodes as `deprecated` is acceptable if the active narrative view behaves correctly.

## Current problem

`episode_list` currently returns all rows for the chapter ordered by `position`, regardless of `canon_status`. Therefore, after episodes 9 and 10 are deprecated, the chapter still appears to contain 10 episodes in ordinary list/read flows.

This makes routine structural editing awkward and can leak retired outline nodes into later authoring/context workflows.

The same semantic question applies to chapters and scenes.

## Goal

Define and implement a safe way to retire narrative hierarchy nodes so that a structure can shrink cleanly without corrupting references or losing intentional history.

At minimum, a user should be able to revise:

```text
Chapter 1: 10 episodes
```

to:

```text
Chapter 1: 8 active episodes
```

without the retired episodes continuing to behave as active narrative nodes.

## Design options

Physical deletion is optional. Either of the following may be acceptable if implemented consistently:

1. **Retirement / deprecation semantics**
   - Retire obsolete chapter / episode / scene records via `canon_status=deprecated` or an equivalent explicit state.
   - Default list/context/outline operations exclude retired nodes.
   - Historical/debug access remains possible through an explicit include-retired option or dedicated history/read path.
   - Active positions remain contiguous and deterministic.

2. **Guarded delete semantics**
   - Add safe `chapter_delete`, `episode_delete`, and/or `scene_delete` tools.
   - Refuse deletion when protected dependent data exists, or explicitly define cascade behavior.
   - Renumber remaining sibling positions atomically.

A hybrid approach is also acceptable.

## Required investigation

Before implementation, inventory all consumers of chapter / episode / scene rows, especially:

- `chapter_list`
- `episode_list`
- `scene_list`
- `episode_get`
- `episode_outline_get`
- `episode_context`
- episode references
- character states
- reader disclosures
- character knowledge
- drafts / draft history
- canon decision/history behavior

Determine which operations should treat deprecated narrative nodes as inactive and which should continue to expose them for history/debugging.

## Safety requirements

- Do not silently destroy canonical or draft history.
- Do not orphan references, states, disclosures, knowledge, or drafts.
- Structural edits must be transactional.
- Sibling `position` values for active nodes must remain contiguous after retirement/deletion.
- Optimistic version / conflict semantics must remain intact.
- Existing active-node behavior must not regress.
- Do not change migration 001–004.

## Acceptance criteria

A regression scenario equivalent to the following must pass:

1. Create one chapter with 10 episodes.
2. Retire/remove episodes 9 and 10 using the supported workflow.
3. Normal active chapter/episode listing reports 8 episodes.
4. Active positions are `1..8` with no gaps.
5. Retired nodes do not appear in normal outline/context generation.
6. Historical access to retired nodes behaves according to the chosen design.
7. Referenced/dependent data is either protected with a clear error or handled by an explicitly tested safe policy.
8. Existing chapter/episode/scene reorder and update tests continue to pass.

## Scope

This issue is about **safe narrative structure shrink/edit semantics**, not general database cleanup. Broader deletion support for world facts, characters, timeline events, etc. can be handled separately if needed.

Issue #2219: Dependency order depends on `Digraph` vertex-insertion history

I think this is a known limitation @TravisCardwell which may become a problem if we decide to move to a declaration database as single source of truth (#1580).

### Current limitation

At the moment, `toDecls` establishes the ordering of declarations in the frontend:

```haskell
-- hs-bindgen/src-internal/HsBindgen/Frontend/Analysis/DeclUseGraph/Query.hs:34
toDecls index declUseGraph =
    mapMaybe (`DeclIndex.lookup` index) . Digraph.sort $
      Digraph.filterEdges (== NeedsShape) declUseGraph.graph
```

`Digraph.sort` breaks ties by internal vertex index (`Data/Digraph.hs:442`), and internal indices are assigned in *insertion* order:

```haskell
-- hs-bindgen/src-internal/HsBindgen/Frontend/Analysis/DeclUseGraph/Construction.hs:66
-- We first insert all declarations, so that they are assigned vertices. For
-- successfully parsed declarations, we do this in source order. This
-- ensures that we preserve source order as much as possible in 'toDecls'
-- (modulo dependencies).
verticesGraph = foldl' (flip Digraph.insertVertex) Digraph.empty $
  map (.info.id) sortedSuccessfulDecls ++ Set.toList failedDeclIds
```

So the order in the frontend is a function of the *history* of the graph value, not of the graph itself.

This may be problematic, because:

- Two passes mutate the graph afterwards: `ReparseMacroExpansions.updateDeps` deletes and re-inserts a declaration's edges (`Pass/ReparseMacroExpansions.hs:106-112`), and `ResolveBindingSpecs` deletes dependencies and reverce dependencies (`Pass/ResolveBindingSpecs.hs:70-73`). Calling `toDecls` again after those may not reproduce the original order.

- The `DeclDB` design (#1580) turns the declaration list into a view computed on demand, and we run into the above reproducibiliyt problem.

### Suggested fix

Make `dependencyOrder` a function of the graph data only:

```haskell
dependencyOrder :: (C.DeclId -> SortKey) -> DeclUseGraph -> [C.DeclId]
dependencyOrder sortKey g =
    Digraph.sortBy (comparing sortKey) $
      Digraph.filterEdges (== NeedsShape) g.graph
```

and remove the pre-sorting during construction mentioned above.

A maintainer on the project whizbang-lib/whizbang (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #584: Composite fan-out expands unbounded in practice: single composites yielding six-figure child row counts

## Summary

`CompositeInboxFanout` expands a received composite into child inbox rows. Composites carrying
**tens of thousands** of inner events are reaching consumers and being expanded, one of them into
**over 200,000 child rows** from a single parent. A cap exists — `MaxInnerEventsAllowed`, with a
dedicated `MessageFailureReason.CompositeInnerEventLimitExceeded` — but it is evidently not binding
on this path.

Observed on two independent consumers of the same bulk workload:

| consumer | composites observed | largest single expansion |
|---|---|---|
| A | ~170 | ~53,000 child rows |
| B | ~355 | **~200,000 child rows** |

Consumer B's inbox grew to roughly a million unprocessed rows, of which effectively 100% descended
from a small number of these composites. Its inbox climbed for hours **with no producer running and
an empty broker** — the growth was entirely local expansion of work it already held.

## Why this is worse than a large batch

The expansion is a write amplification that happens INSIDE the consumer, after admission control has
already accepted the message. From the outside the consumer looks like it is receiving traffic that
does not exist:

- broker subscriptions empty, no upstream producing, yet inbox depth rising by tens of thousands per
  minute
- the composite row itself remains unprocessed while its children are written, so a depth-based
  health check sees a growing backlog and no obvious source
- a service can be pushed from a manageable queue into a multi-hundred-thousand-row backlog by
  admitting a handful of messages

It also defeats every downstream bound. Claim windows, outstanding-row budgets and lease sizing are
all calibrated against inbox rows, and one admitted message can add six figures of them.

## Where the cap appears not to apply

`CompositeInboxFanout.TryExpand` checks `composite.MaxInnerEventsAllowed` on both the materialized
and raw-inner paths, and the limit is per-composite rather than global. Two things worth checking:

1. whether the default value of `MaxInnerEventsAllowed` on the composite types involved is high
   enough to be effectively unbounded
2. whether the raw-carry path (children built directly from stored JSON) reaches the same check with
   the same value

## Suggested direction

- **A bound that reflects consumer capacity, not just message validity.** A composite whose
  expansion would exceed what the consumer can lease and drain should be rejected or chunked, not
  expanded in one shot.
- **Chunked expansion.** Expanding a large composite incrementally — with the parent retained until
  its children are drained — would keep depth bounded and let backpressure work.
- **A log line at expansion.** Nothing currently reports "expanded composite X into N children",
  which is why a consumer growing by tens of thousands of rows per minute has no attributable cause
  in its own logs. This alone would have made the behavior obvious immediately.

## Note

This compounds with the auto-repair storm in #582: redelivery requests bundle their windows into
composites, so a repair loop produces exactly the oversized composites this issue describes. The two
failures amplify each other — but the composite bounding problem is independent and reproduces on
ordinary bulk domain traffic with repair disabled.

Issue #1047: Run baseline test check before topological sort in coordinator

## Problem

In `src/coordinator/coordinate.ts`, Step 2b builds the dependency graph and topologically sorts every discovered file (`coordinate.ts:352-357`) before Step 2c runs the baseline test check (`coordinate.ts:363-389`), which can abort the entire run if the target project's tests are already failing. Reorder the steps so the baseline test check (Step 2c) runs before the dependency graph construction and topological sort (Step 2b). Issue #159: Server-side GC for staged intermediates after submission completion

Follow-up to #157 / PR #158.

PR #158 makes workers delete their private task dirs after a SUCCESS result is accepted. The **staged copies** of intermediate outputs still live forever:

- `--stage-out file:///path` destinations (e.g. `/scout/wf/data/<taskID>/…`)
- Shock nodes / S3 objects uploaded per task
- server-side uploads via the HTTP stager

Deleting these safely requires submission-level knowledge only the server has: **all consuming tasks are terminal AND the workflow's final outputs have been collected/exported**. A per-shard embedding file (~330 MB) that only feeds the `load` step is dead weight the moment the submission completes, but only the scheduler can prove that.

Sketch:
- On submission terminal state, walk the DAG: any task output NOT referenced by the submission's final outputs is garbage-collectible.
- Respect the `debug` label (#158) — debug submissions keep everything.
- Retention window / `--gc-after` config rather than immediate deletion.
- Needs per-scheme delete support in the staging layer (file, shock, s3); schemes without delete support are skipped with a log line.

Issue #240: migration: the write order cannot handle self-referencing FKs or seeded tables

Found reviewing #227. Neither is a bug in that PR's code — the declared write order is correct for every cross-table foreign key in `backend/migrations` — but both will stop a real run the first time #166 actually moves data, and neither is solvable by ordering tables.

## 1. Four tables reference themselves

`internal/target/verify.go`'s `DeclaredTables()` puts every table after the tables it refers to. That cannot help a table that refers to *itself*:

| table | column | migration |
|---|---|---|
| `users` | `invited_by` | `019_add_invited_by_to_users.sql:2` |
| `categories` | `parent_id` | `003_create_categories.sql:5` |
| `messages` | `parent_id` | `024_add_parent_id_to_messages.sql:2` |
| `forum_posts` | `reply_to_post_id` | `039_create_forums.sql:91,97` |

Foreign keys fire at end-of-statement, so ordering *within* one multi-row INSERT is safe. Across batches it is not. Legacy user 12 invited by user 900, at `BatchSize: 500`: user 12 is in batch 1, user 900 in batch 2, and batch 1 fails with `insert or update on table "users" violates foreign key constraint "users_invited_by_fkey"`. Under `TxPerBatch` the run stops with `users` half written. Same shape for any forum reply whose parent post has a higher id, and any subcategory whose id precedes its parent's.

**Options.** `SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED` inside the transaction is the smallest change and works for `TxPerTable`; it does nothing for `TxPerBatch`, where each batch commits. A NULL-then-backfill second pass works in both modes and is what I would build: write the self-referencing column as NULL, then `UPDATE` it once the table is complete. Sorting each table's rows by id before writing would also work for these four specific cases, but it is luck rather than a property — nothing guarantees a parent has a lower id.

## 2. The seeded tables are in the write order

`DeclaredTables()` includes `groups`, `categories`, `forum_categories`, `countries`, `languages` — and, after #224, `forums`. `target.Seeded` documents those same tables as ones where "the primary keys collide, the unique constraints collide, and an explicit-id insert does not advance the BIGSERIAL". So the same package says write these and says writing these is unsafe, with nothing reconciling the two.

Legacy `categories` ids 1-20 against the target's seeded ids 1-20 fails on the first batch with `duplicate key value violates unique constraint "categories_pkey"`. If the ids happen not to overlap it is worse: 20 duplicate genre names, and every torrent's `category_id` resolving to the wrong genre.

**Options.** The mapping already tells the operator to decide per row whether to merge into the seeded row or insert alongside it — that decision needs somewhere to live in the mapping file and something in the writer that honours it (`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, an id-remapping table, or skipping the table and having the operator reconcile by hand). An id remap is the general answer, since `torrents.category_id` and `users.group_id` have to follow whatever the rows become.

## Acceptance criteria

- A run against a legacy database whose `users.invited_by` points at a higher id than the row itself completes, at any batch size.
- A run against a legacy database whose `categories` ids overlap the seeded ones completes, and every `torrents.category_id` afterwards points at the genre it pointed at before.
- `validate` reports both hazards before the first write rather than the run discovering them — this is the pre-flight's job, and it currently answers "Usable against both databases" for a database that will fail on batch one.
- A test drives the self-reference case with a parent in a later batch than the child, since a single-batch test passes regardless.

## Related

- #166 (resumable runs) shares the batching machinery.
- `NonEmpty` in `verify.go` already answers "does the target already have rows?" and has **no production caller**, so it is not wired into the pre-flight it belongs in. That check is what would catch case 2 early, and it is arguably the second most dangerous question after schema drift — a target with rows is either a half-finished run or a live site, and the second is unrecoverable.

Issue #34: keel trace reports no edges for marker-carried dependencies while marker-census counts 111 in the same model

## Summary

`keel trace <item>` reports `upstream: []` / `downstream: []` for every item tested, in a model where `keel marker-census` AST-counts **111 marker edges**. Two computed views disagree about the same tree.

`keel --help` describes trace as *"every typed edge reaching an item, both directions"*, which promises the marker-authored edges are included.

## Observed

Authored in `.tracking/intake/`, both endpoints declared as parts in the same model:

```sysml
#DerivedFrom dependency from us18 to s8;
```

`keel validate .` — clean, 7 files. Then:

```
$ keel trace us18 .
{"name":"us18","upstream":[],"downstream":[]}

$ keel trace s8 .
{"name":"s8","upstream":[],"downstream":[]}
```

Same empty result for 7 items spanning both trees and four item kinds — `s1`, `s8`, `us18`, `us24`, `us31`, `supplyFlowBucketTest`, `d0230`, plus `d0226` from `.engine/reference/`.

Meanwhile, on the same tree:

```
$ keel marker-census .
DerivedFrom 37 | Supersede 32 | Resolves 17 | DependsOn 11 | JustifiedBy 10
Implicates 2  | Verify 1     | Dispositions 1        (edges, AST-counted)
```

## Name resolution is not the cause

Trace distinguishes an unknown name from an empty result, and the bare names resolve:

```
$ keel trace IntakeReadback::us18 .
keel trace: no item named `IntakeReadback::us18` is declared in this model. An unknown name
exits non-zero rather than answering with an empty result, because an empty result reads as
`this item has no edges` ...
```

So a qualified name errors, a bare name returns the empty result — trace is finding the item and reporting that it has no edges.

## Question rather than a claim

Trace may be scoped to **native** typed edges (`satisfy`, `allocate`, `:>`) by design, with metadata-marker dependencies deliberately excluded. If that is the intent, this is a documentation defect rather than a logic one — but it is still a defect, because the help text says "every typed edge" and the engine's own `relationships.sysml` header documents markers as the edge algebra's carrier wherever no native form exists:

> `verify` -> NO BASE FORM EXISTS for this edge. `#Verify` is a JUSTIFIED last resort (D0140).
> `#DerivedFrom` is a JUSTIFIED last resort (D0140): all 37 of its edges are CROSS-metaclass ...

If the majority of a project's real graph is marker-carried by design, a trace that omits markers shows almost nothing.

## Why it matters

`relationships.sysml:28-30` documents suspicion propagating along `satisfy`, `verify`, `:>`, `allocate` and semantic `dependsOn`. Trace is the natural view for checking that a change actually reaches its dependents before relying on it. In this project the author's stated need is precisely that — every layered assumption verified, with invalidation propagating upward when a layer is overturned. Today the propagation can be authored but not inspected.

## Environment

```
keel 0.3.0
build commit: c444ca5
api contract: 2.0.0 (derived)
guards: 51 (42 hard-blocking, 9 warning-only)
```
Windows 11. Project scaffolded 2026-08-29 via `keel init . --profile strict`. `keel validate` and `keel guard` both green at time of observation.

**Layered, opt-in, capability-free / editor-as-convenience** (matches PRD §17 "path-scoped permissions are later/Pro" and §20 "the capability is always free; the no-code/visual convenience around it is Pro"):

2. **Engine (core, invisible)** — the matrix becomes data-driven: a persisted store of role/permission overrides + custom roles, a resolver that layers overrides on the built-in defaults, injected server-side (`createAuthz`) and admin-side (`ActorProvider`/`useCan`). **Empty store ⇒ byte-identical to the shipped defaults.** No UI.

4. **Rank hierarchy + Maintainer user-management** — ordered roles + "act only below your own rank"; generalizes the last-owner guard to last-Admin.
5. **Advanced-roles editor (opt-in module)** — a permission-matrix UI, hidden unless activated (settings/capability toggle now; architected to migrate to a real plugin later).
6. **Pro / later** — path-scoped roles (Editor for `/blog/*`), role-change audit trail, enterprise SSO.

Issue #1013: feat(navigation): publish the longitudinal healthcare event log

Part of #1006. Depends on stable MHSDS, CSDS and OLIDS domain facts.

Publish the first conformed event log for longitudinal analysis. This PR implements the common contract described in #1006 for MHSDS, CSDS and OLIDS. It does not assign journey IDs or candidate associations.

For OLIDS, emit referral and patient-appointment milestones. Retain encounter IDs as linkage evidence, but do not emit every encounter as a patient-contact event; encounters can also represent letters, texts, reception contacts and other administrative interactions. Clinical history remains reachable through #1016.

OLIDS is currently NCL-only, covering about 1.8 million current patients. MHSDS, CSDS and acute feeds are already at WNL scope. The estimate below scales OLIDS by 2.5× to represent the planned move to WNL's roughly 4.5 million current patients. This is a capacity assumption, not a forecast of record growth or backfill behaviour.

## Existing foundation and effort

Existing: this starts only after the MHSDS, CSDS and OLIDS facts are stable. The cross-system person key, source identifiers and terminology models already exist by that point.

Change: add one narrow adapter per domain, map recorded milestones to the common columns, union the adapters, implement source-aware incremental loading and test branch reconciliation. It does not attempt journey matching or rework the source facts.

Size: Large, about 3–5 engineering days. It owns the shared event contract, source adapters and scale testing. Dependency waits are excluded.

## Proposed design

Create one narrow adapter per source domain, then union them into `fct_person_healthcare_event`. One row represents a recorded milestone such as referral received, appointment booked, care contact, attendance, admission or discharge. A source record may emit more than one milestone; all retain the same source record identifiers.

Core columns cover event identity, pseudonymised person key, source provenance, event date/time and precision, event type/subtype, care setting, status/outcome, service context, provider/site, referral direction and recorded linkage identifiers.

Source-only nulls belong in the union branches. Natural-grain facts remain the drill-down surface for fields that do not conform across sources. CSDS care activities remain child detail linked to a contact; they are not event rows unless a later source model exposes a separate clinical activity time.

## Live size and physical design

Aggregate profiling on 27 August 2026 estimates:

- MHSDS: 27.4 million milestones.
- CSDS: 87.0 million milestones, excluding 55.2 million care-activity child rows.
- OLIDS at current NCL scope: 180.1 million milestones.
- Combined MHSDS, CSDS, OLIDS and acute sources: about 467.2 million rows.
- Combined after OLIDS expands to WNL using the 2.5× capacity assumption: about 737.4 million rows.

`datetime_left` records when the patient left a GP appointment. Keep it on the appointment fact for source fidelity, but do not emit it as a separate event. It does not represent a new care-setting transition or discharge milestone.

Materialise the event log incrementally. The strategy must support OLIDS updates and deletes, MHSDS/CSDS replacement submissions and late acute records; it cannot assume append-only sources. Use source-aware lookback or reporting-period replacement with reconciliation tests.

Production dbt currently runs on `WH_WNL_ENGINEERING_M`. Use `WH_WNL_OLIDS_L` for the initial build and the large periodic model job. Tag the model `large_periodic`. The current daily selector includes all descendants of `source:olids`, so the daily workflow must explicitly exclude `tag:large_periodic`; a separate weekly or agreed-periodic job should select that tag directly.

Benchmark both `(event_date, sk_patient_id)` and `(sk_patient_id, event_date)` as clustering candidates using cohort, date-window and source-filtered journey queries. Record build time, pruning, clustering depth, spill and reclustering cost before choosing a key. Current source widths suggest 50–100 GiB compressed at projected WNL scope, excluding temporary Time Travel and reclustering storage; replace this planning range with the first measured build.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The event taxonomy and mapping from each source fact are documented.
- [ ] An appointment with a supplied booking timestamp emits an `appointment_booked` event, separate from its scheduled time and any attended, cancelled or other outcome event.
- [ ] `event_id` is unique and not null.
- [ ] Every event traces to one natural-grain source record.
- [ ] OLIDS encounters are retained as linkage evidence and are not emitted as patient-contact events by default.
- [ ] CSDS care activities remain contact child detail unless an independent clinical timestamp is available.
- [ ] Branch reconciliations prove the expected milestones emitted per source record.
- [ ] Date-only values are marked as date precision; no midnight timestamp is invented.
- [ ] Placeholder or implausible dates do not drive event ordering; excluded or unsequenced records are reported in aggregate.
- [ ] Unknown, false, not applicable and no recorded evidence remain distinct.
- [ ] Codes and labels are both available for analyst-facing categories.
- [ ] The incremental strategy handles source updates, deletes, replacement periods and late records, with a full-refresh reconciliation path.
- [ ] The daily workflow excludes `tag:large_periodic` and a separate Large-warehouse job builds the selected models.
- [ ] Both clustering candidates are benchmarked on representative queries before the physical key is fixed.
- [ ] Example queries show sequencing and candidate temporal joins without publishing an association rule.
- [ ] The model and affected downstream models build successfully.

Out of scope: SUS/ECDS branches, app/111 branches, journey IDs, matching scores and programme-specific outcome definition

Issue #180: $expand: is-a/descendent-of/child-of/=/regex filter operators return empty results

Part of #179

## Summary

`POST /ValueSet/$expand` for a ValueSet with `compose.include[].filter[]` returns `total: 0` regardless of operator, because the underlying library only implements `is-a`/`descendent-of` against the `concept_closure` table, and even that fails for CodeSystems without closure rows (see finding 2).

## Findings

### 1. Filter operators return empty results instead of filtering

Example (`is-a` filter, `simple-filter-isa`):
```json
"compose": {"include": [{"system": "…/simple", "filter": [{"property": "concept", "op": "is-a", "value": "code2"}]}]}
```
Expected `expansion.total`: 5. Actual: 0.

Operators with no implementation at all: `=` (property/code exact match), `regex` (property/code full-string regex). Example (`=` filter):
```json
"filter": [{"property": "prop", "op": "=", "value": "new"}]
```
Expected `expansion.total`: 3. Actual: 0.

**Root cause:** `terminology_source.bal`, `expandValueSet` - the filter guard is:
```ballerina
if f.property == "concept" && (f.op == "is-a" || f.op == "descendent-of")
```
Only two operators are handled, and only via `closureMembers`, which queries `concept_closure`.

---

### 2. `is-a` hierarchy resolution only works for SNOMED (closure table), not for FHIR-JSON or LOINC uploads

`concept_closure` is populated **only** by the SNOMED RF2 import path (`snomed_import.bal` → `writeClosure`). CodeSystems uploaded via `$upload` as FHIR JSON, or converted from LOINC CSV, only get `concepts.parentConceptId` set, no closure rows.

**Impact:** `is-a`, and `descendent-of` filters will return empty results for any non-SNOMED CodeSystem even after the operator logic is added, unless a `parentConceptId`-walk fallback is implemented alongside the closure-based path.

**Suggested fix:** add a recursive `parentConceptId` walk as a fallback in the same helper that currently only checks `concept_closure`; and/or extend `extractConceptsFromCodeSystemRecursive` (`terminology_source.bal`) to also write `concept_closure` rows at FHIR/LOINC ingest time, so all future non-SNOMED CodeSystems get indexed hierarchy lookups.

## Acceptance criteria

- `$expand` correctly evaluates `is-a`, `descendent-of`, `=`, and `regex` filter operators.
- Hierarchy filters (`is-a`, `descendent-of`) work for CodeSystems both with and without a populated `concept_closure` table.

Issue #57: Epic: CEL functional-paradigm additions - opt-in recursion (rec), non-escaping closures, lambdas, TCO

## Goal
Add a small set of functional-paradigm features to CEL — opt-in recursion, non-escaping closures/lambdas, and guaranteed tail-call optimization — without compromising the no-heap/no-GC guarantee the real-time-audio profile (#56) depends on, and without silently reopening the "loops must be statically bounded" rule that profile establishes.

## 1. Opt-in recursion via a `rec` keyword
By default, a function's call graph must be acyclic — sema statically verifies this. A function must be explicitly marked `rec` to participate in recursion, direct or mutual:

```
func_decl:
    "func" "rec" IDENT "(" param_list_opt ")" "->" IDENT block
  | "func" "rec" IDENT "(" param_list_opt ")" block
  | "func" IDENT "(" param_list_opt ")" "->" IDENT block
  | "func" IDENT "(" param_list_opt ")" block
```

**Mutual recursion rule (confirmed with the user): every function participating in a call-graph cycle must be marked `rec`, not just one of them.** A reader looking at a plain `func b()` should never have to trace into another function to discover `b` is secretly part of a recursive cycle. Sema builds the call graph and rejects any cycle containing an unmarked function, with a diagnostic at the offending call site — same style as the existing domain-gating (`CheckCall`) and return-on-all-paths checks.

## 2. Lambdas (no capture) — free
A lambda with no captured variables is just a function pointer with anonymous syntax. Zero runtime cost, no allocation, no new execution-model concerns.

## 3. Closures — non-escaping only
A closure that captures enclosing variables must not outlive the stack frame it was created in: no returning a closure from a function, no storing one in a global or a field. The captured environment lives on the *caller's* stack; a closure value is a (function pointer, stack pointer) pair. This gets real closure ergonomics (pass a per-element callback into a block-processing intrinsic, a comparator, etc.) with zero heap allocation. Escaping-closure syntax should be a compile-time error, not something that quietly needs an allocator.

## 4. Guaranteed tail-call optimization
Implement TCO as an explicit AST-level rewrite (recognize a `rec` function's self-call in tail position, transform it into a loop at codegen time) rather than relying on LLVM's backend tail-call handling — guaranteed behavior regardless of the target's calling-convention quirks (Windows x64 tail calls are notably unreliable to depend on implicitly). Same category of hand-verified compiler transformation as the existing watchdog-check insertion at loop back-edges.

## Interaction with the real-time-audio profile (#56)
Unbounded recursion (a `rec` function whose recursion depth is only known at runtime) is exactly the same problem as an unbounded `while` loop — it is not a way around the "loops must be statically unrollable" rule, it is the same rule. In the audio-safe profile, `rec` is disallowed entirely, same bucket as unbounded loops, unless a future refinement adds a provably-bounded recursion case. Outside that profile, unbounded `rec` recursion is fine under a watchdog-style fault mechanism analogous to today's CEL9001 loop-budget check, keyed on recursion depth instead of loop iterations.

## Non-goals
- No closures/lambdas that require heap allocation
- No implicit (un-annotated) recursion
- No reliance on LLVM's automatic tail-call elimination as the only mechanism — must be a guaranteed AST-level transform

Issue #529: Self-host guide: the Caddyfile doesn't parse, and its auth depends on line order

The guide is more careful than most of its kind — `:74` warns outright that the raw storage API has no auth, and `:327-329` tells the operator to confirm a tokenless request returns 403. Both matter below: the second is the check that catches the problem I'm reporting, and it's why I think this is narrow.

Two separate things about the Caddyfile in `docs/running-your-own-node.md`: it doesn't parse in `caddy:2-alpine`, and whether `/s/*` is protected depends on which of two adjacent lines comes first. I'm raising them together because one change fixes both. I'm not claiming one causes the other — though I'd note the parse defect forces a hand-reformat of exactly the lines whose order matters, so I can't claim they're unrelated either; I just haven't measured it.

Everything below was run offline, `docker run --network none`, against `caddy:2-alpine` at `v2.11.4` (image `5f5c8640aae0`). Nothing was deployed and no node was contacted, so none of it says anything about `msg.logos.live`. I also don't know whether anyone has followed this guide — I didn't look.

## 1. The recipe doesn't start as printed

`caddy adapt` on `:196-208` exactly as published:

```
Error: Unexpected next token after '{' on same line, at /w/Caddyfile.verbatim:4
exit=1
```

v2.11.4 rejects one-line `{ … }` blocks and the file has four, so I tested each on its own — expanding the other three and leaving one as published. All four are rejected individually: `:199` `log { … }`, `:205` `handle @noauth { … }`, `:206` `handle_path /s/* { … }`, `:207` `handle { … }`.

Expanding all four and changing nothing else gets past that and fails on the domain placeholder instead (`subject does not qualify for certificate: '<your-domain>'`); substituting a real domain and nothing else — your `tls /certs/live/…` paths untouched, `<YOUR_TOKEN>` still literal — adapts cleanly. So the reformat is the whole fix for this part, alongside the substitution the guide already asks for.

## 2. Whether `/s/*` is protected depends on line order

Expanded so it parses, then actually served and queried. Requests come from inside the same network-less container, so `logos-storage:8080` doesn't exist and the proxy can only fail with 502. **That 502 is the signal: the request entered the reverse-proxy handler.** It doesn't mean anything reached an upstream, and I'm not claiming it did.

| request | as published | with `:205`/`:206` swapped |
|---|---|---|
| `/s/api/storage/v1/data`, **no** `Authorization` | **403** | 🔴 **502** |
| same, with `Bearer …` | 502 | 502 |
| `/elsewhere`, no `Authorization` | 403 | 403 |

Row 3 is the limit: other paths stay gated, so this is a `/s/*` bypass rather than a general one. `caddy adapt` on the swapped file exits **0 with empty stderr** — no error, no warning, a config that still validates.

**The mechanism is narrower than "line order matters in Caddy",** which is a known footgun and not my finding. It's that `handle @noauth` and `handle_path /s/*` are *the same directive* once `handle_path` normalises to `handle`. The comparator ties, the stable sort falls back to source order, and the auth decision ends up positional.

**Your guide already contains the check that catches this.** `:327-329` tells the operator a request without the token "should return `403`", so anyone running that step finds the swap immediately.

## Suggested fix — and I had this wrong the first time

My first suggestion was `route { … }`. **That doesn't work**: `route` executes whatever order is written, so a reflow that swaps the two blocks inside it reproduces the bypass exactly. It makes ordering explicit rather than emergent, but it isn't protection.

What does work is making the two ordered things *different* directives, by putting the check inside the only route that reaches the node:

```caddyfile
	handle_path /s/* {
		@noauth not header Authorization "Bearer <YOUR_TOKEN>"
		respond @noauth "unauthorized" 403
		reverse_proxy logos-storage:8080
	}
```

`respond` and `reverse_proxy` have a defined relative order in Caddy's directive list, so the sort puts `respond` first no matter how they're written — there's no tie to fall back on.

Writing `respond` below `reverse_proxy` inside that block changes nothing — same 403, and `caddy adapt` emits a byte-identical config. To be exact about what that does and doesn't show: **the specific edit that breaks the published config can't be performed here at all**, since there's no outer auth handler left to move. And moving the whole `/s/*` handler below the fallback is a no-op by construction — the adapter always sorts the matcher-less `handle {}` last — so treat that one as a demonstration, not a test. What shows the method can detect a reordering effect is your own config, where the same procedure did flip 403 to 502.

I also spent a while trying to get past it: every HTTP method, header-name casing, duplicate and empty `Authorization`, near-miss tokens, `/s`, `/s/`, `//s/x`, `/S/x`, `%2e%2e`, `..%2f`, a 4000-char path, and raw byte-level shapes over `nc` — HTTP/1.0 with no `Host`, absolute-form targets, obs-fold continuations, `CL+TE` and `TE: chunked`, bare-LF. Nothing reached the proxy without the exact token.

### ⚠️ One thing that would undo it

The safety here is emergent, not visible in the block: it comes from `respond` and `reverse_proxy` having a fixed relative order in the directive list. If someone later tidies those same three lines into an explicit `route` with the proxy first —

```caddyfile
		route {
			reverse_proxy logos-storage:8080
			respond @noauth "unauthorized" 403
		}
```

— `route` honours written order and an unauthenticated request gets **502** again. I checked. Worth a comment in the file, because it's exactly the kind of cleanup that looks like an improvement.

Issue #3721: cupy surface_distance stops relaxing after H+W passes and reports reachable pixels as NaN

## Description

The cupy backend of `surface_distance()` solves the shortest-path problem by
repeated parallel relaxation (`_sd_relax_kernel`), and caps the number of
passes at `H + W`:

```python
# xrspatial/surface_distance.py:583
max_iterations = H + W
for _ in range(max_iterations):
    changed[0] = 0
    _sd_relax_kernel[griddim, blockdim](...)
    if int(changed[0]) == 0:
        break
```

One pass propagates distance information roughly one pixel hop. The number of
passes needed is therefore the hop count of the longest shortest path, not the
raster's width plus height. Those two numbers agree on open terrain, but they
come apart as soon as NaN barriers force paths to wind, and the worst case for
a grid graph is `H * W`, not `H + W`.

When the cap is reached the loop exits with no warning and no signal in the
output. Pixels the CPU backend reaches are reported as NaN, meaning
unreachable. A user reading the result cannot tell the difference between "no
path exists" and "we stopped looking."

This affects all three public functions on the cupy backend
(`surface_distance`, `surface_allocation`, `surface_direction`) and the
bounded dask+cupy path, where `_surface_distance_cupy` runs per chunk and the
cap is the chunk's `H + W` rather than the raster's.

## Reproduction

Ran on this host with CUDA available.

```python
import numpy as np, xarray as xr, cupy
from xrspatial.surface_distance import surface_distance

def serpentine(n):
    """NaN everywhere except one winding open corridor from (0, 0)."""
    elev = np.full((n, n), np.nan)
    for r in range(0, n, 2):
        elev[r, :] = 0.0
    for r in range(1, n, 2):
        elev[r, n - 1 if (r // 2) % 2 == 0 else 0] = 0.0
    return elev

def make(data, gpu=False):
    a = xr.DataArray(
        data.astype(float), dims=['y', 'x'],
        coords={'y': np.arange(data.shape[0], dtype=float),
                'x': np.arange(data.shape[1], dtype=float)},
        attrs={'res': (1.0, 1.0)})
    if gpu:
        a.data = cupy.asarray(a.data)
    return a

for N in (8, 12, 16, 24):
    elev = serpentine(N)
    src = np.zeros((N, N)); src[0, 0] = 1.0
    cpu = np.asarray(surface_distance(make(src), make(elev)).data)
    gpu = surface_distance(make(src, True), make(elev, True)).data.get()
    print(f"N={N:3d} cap={2*N:3d}  reachable cpu={int(np.isfinite(cpu).sum()):4d}"
          f" gpu={int(np.isfinite(gpu).sum()):4d}"
          f"  wrongly NaN on gpu={int((np.isfinite(cpu) & ~np.isfinite(gpu)).sum()):4d}")
```

```
N=  8 cap= 16  reachable cpu=  36 gpu=  21  wrongly NaN on gpu=  15
N= 12 cap= 24  reachable cpu=  78 gpu=  29  wrongly NaN on gpu=  49
N= 16 cap= 32  reachable cpu= 136 gpu=  37  wrongly NaN on gpu=  99
N= 24 cap= 48  reachable cpu= 300 gpu=  53  wrongly NaN on gpu= 247
```

At N=16 the GPU finds 37 of the 136 reachable pixels and calls the other 99
unreachable. The last corridor row is the clearest case:

```
row 15, numpy: [126.21   nan   nan ...  nan]
row 15, cupy : [   nan   nan   nan ...  nan]
```

Distances that both backends do report agree exactly (max abs diff 0.0), so
this is purely truncated propagation rather than arithmetic drift.

A serpentine grid is an easy way to make the failure obvious, but nothing
about it is special. Any NaN-masked terrain whose shortest paths wind more
than `H + W` hops (a river network, a canyon system, a coastline with inlets)
hits the same cap.

The numpy and dask+numpy paths run an exact Dijkstra and are correct here. I
also checked the dask iterative sweep cap (`max(n_tile_y, n_tile_x) + 10`)
against the same mazes at several chunk sizes and could not make it produce a
wrong answer, so this report is about the GPU cap only.

## Expected behaviour

The cupy backend should relax until nothing changes, and its result should
match numpy. If some bound must remain as a safety net, it should be the
Bellman-Ford bound for the graph (`H * W`) rather than `H + W`, and reaching
it should warn rather than pass off a truncated answer as a finished one.

The early-exit check on `changed` already means well-behaved terrain costs the
same number of passes as it does today, so raising the ceiling is not a
throughput change for normal input.

## Environment

xarray-spatial `main` @ 069fc13, Python 3.14, cupy with CUDA available.

# URI-as-artifact-keys: explicit `out:` on inputs, URIs as registry keys

## Context

Pipeline YAML `in:` and `out:` maps use URI strings as artifact registry keys (not symbolic names), and the top-level `inputs:` block declares an explicit `out:` so downstream stage references are traceable. The format is always `{<interpolation_key>: <uri_string>}`, with the URI serving double duty as both the artifact identity and the lookup key.

Two sources of pipeline-definition confusion that cause LLM agents to thrash:

1. **The `inputs:` block has no `out:`.** You can't tell what artifacts the inputs stage produces by reading the definition — the bindings happen implicitly in `launcher.py` and `gremlin.py`. Downstream `in:` references are opaque.

2. **Symbolic artifact names.** In `out: { local-review-grok: "file://session/local-review-grok.md" }` the key `local-review-grok` is a redundant indirection. The URI string `"file://session/local-review-grok.md"` should be the key, so `in: { review-one: "file://session/local-review-grok.md" }` is self-documenting — you can trace exactly where `review-one` gets its content without cross-referencing another stage.

## Approach

### Core design: registry values are materialized, not re-resolved

`ArtifactRegistry` stores materialized values, computed once at bind time — not URIs to be re-parsed and re-resolved on every read.

- `ArtifactRegistry.bind(key: str, value: Any)` — `key` is always the URI string from YAML. `value` is whatever the resolver's `materialize()` computed once (a real filesystem path string, a bare ref/sha, an opaque gh URI string, etc). No `Uri` value object is threaded through `bind`/`read`/`resolve` anymore.
- `ArtifactRegistry.read(key)` extracts the key's scheme (`key.split("://", 1)[0]`) purely to pick which resolver's `.read(stored_value)` to call for dereferencing. Keys with no `://` bypass resolver dispatch and return the stored value as-is (this is how loop markers work).
- **`resolve_in_map` never splits the registry key.** The full YAML-declared string is the key, full stop. No `.` splitting, no attribute-path walking.

### `SchemeResolver` protocol (new shape)

```python
class SchemeResolver(Protocol):
    def materialize(self, uri_str: str) -> Any: ...
    def read(self, value: Any) -> Any: ...
    def verify_produced(self, value: Any) -> None: ...
```

- **`FileArtifactResolver`**: `materialize(uri_str)` applies the `session/<name>` convention once and returns the absolute filesystem path as a string. `read(value)` opens that literal path. `verify_produced(value)` checks the literal path exists and is non-empty.
- **`GitResolver`**: `materialize` for `ref/`, `commit/` strips the prefix and returns the bare ref name / sha. For `range` see the `git://range/{unique_name}` design below.
- **`GhOpaqueResolver`**: `materialize(uri_str) -> uri_str` (bare string). `read(value) -> value`. No dict-wrapping.

### `Uri` value object: reduced scope

`Uri.parse()` remains a parse-time validator for YAML authors (rejects malformed/unknown-scheme strings at pipeline-load time) but is no longer threaded through the registry's runtime read/write path. Static helpers like `Uri.is_range()` and `Uri.parse_or_none()` stay.

### `out:` — map form, key = artifact key (URI string)

Each YAML `out:` entry is `{<artifact_key>: <uri_string>}`. The `<artifact_key>` is the registry key. For file URIs, key and value are identical (`"file://session/foo.md": "file://session/foo.md"`). The old symbolic-name-as-key form is gone.

**Normalization at parse time:** `Stage.with_dict` converts list-form `out:` (list of URI strings) into the canonical map `{uri: uri}`. Map form passes through as-is.

### `optional:` sub-block replaces the `?` suffix convention

```yaml
in:
  gloom: file://session/gloom.md
  optional:
    doom: file://session/doom.md

out:
  biz: file://session/biz.md
  optional:
    baz: file://session/baz.md
```

- **`in.optional:`**: if the key is unbound, the resolved value is an empty string rather than raising `MissingArtifact`.
- **`out.optional:`**: if the command didn't actually produce the artifact, skip binding without raising.
- Parsing: `Stage.with_dict`/`Exec.with_dict`/`Agent.with_dict` read `d["in"].pop("optional", {})` and `d["out"].pop("optional", {})` into separate `in_optional_map`/`out_optional_map` dicts.
- Every current `?`-suffixed YAML key across the tree gets rewritten into an `optional:` sub-block.

### `in:` — values are registry keys (URI strings); no key-splitting, ever

`resolve_in_map()` is rewritten to remove all `.`-splitting and attribute-path logic:

```python
def resolve_in_map(artifacts, in_map, optional_map):
    result = {}
    for var, key in in_map.items():
        result[var] = to_str(artifacts.read(key))
    for var, key in optional_map.items():
        try:
            result[var] = to_str(artifacts.read(key))
        except MissingArtifact:
            result[var] = ""
    return result
```

### `GhOpaqueResolver` returns a bare string, not a dict

`GhOpaqueResolver.materialize(uri_str) -> uri_str` and `.read(value) -> value` (bare string, no wrapping). This eliminates both dotted-path call sites:
- `pr-extend.yaml`: `pr_uri: pr.uri` → `pr_uri: pr`
- `github_open_pr.yaml`: `plan_uri: plan-document.uri?` → replaced entirely (see plan-document split below)

`ArtifactRegistry.get_pr_url`'s dict-unwrapping fallback becomes dead code.

### `plan-document` dual-producer split

Split the artifact's two roles into their own fixed keys:
- **content, always:** `file://session/plan.md` — the fixed key `skip_if_exists` and all content consumers target.
- **provenance, sometimes:** `file://session/plan-issue-number.txt` (already present in `plan_gh.yaml`).

`github_open_pr.yaml`'s `compose-pr` drops `plan_uri: plan-document.uri?` and gains `plan_issue_number: file://session/plan-issue-number.txt` under `optional:`. The prompt template updates `{plan_uri}` to `{plan_issue_number}`.

Issue #2244: Proposal: LLGo LLVM-IR escape analysis and heap-to-stack transform

# LLGo LLVM-IR escape analysis and heap-to-stack transform

Status: proposal

## Summary

LLGo should implement its own escape-analysis and heap-to-stack transformation pass over the complete LLVM module produced by LLGo. The pass should be integrated at the same architectural boundary as `internal/cabi`: frontend lowering first emits the complete package module, then an LLGo-owned module transformer analyzes and rewrites that module before the generic LLVM optimization pipeline runs.

The proposed default pipeline is:

```text
Go source
    -> go/ssa
    -> cl lowers the complete package to LLVM IR
    -> LLGo escape analysis and heap-to-stack rewrite
    -> LowerLargeAggregates and C ABI rewrite
    -> generic LLVM optimization passes
```

The escape analyzer operates on LLVM SSA def-use chains, not on Go AST or x/tools `go/ssa`. It starts from LLGo allocation calls and LLVM function parameters, follows their transitive uses, computes allocation escape decisions and parameter leak summaries, and then rewrites proven-local heap allocations into stack allocations.

The work has two phases:

1. Implement a conservative LLVM-SSA use analysis and heap-to-stack rewrite. Unknown uses escape. This phase produces structured `-m` summaries but applies only generic pointer-flow rules.
2. Add LLGo-specific Go semantic rules for channels, maps, interfaces, closures, slices, goroutines, defers, panic/recover, typed memory copies, C declarations, and pointer/uintptr contracts. These rules make the LLGo pass more precise than generic LLVM `AAHeapToStack`.

When detailed diagnostics are requested, the analysis may retain predecessor edges as an explanation graph. That graph exists only to explain the computed `-m` result; it is not the analysis solver.

## Why LLGo needs its own pass

There are three independent reasons.

### 1. Go's escape analyzer is AST/Go-compiler-IR based and tightly coupled

The Go compiler's escape analyzer is not a reusable SSA pass. It walks `cmd/compile` IR, constructs a location graph, and depends on Go compiler concepts including expression nodes, assignment holes, loop depth, closures, pragmas, inlining state, result parameters, and export tags.

Porting it to LLGo would require recreating a large part of `cmd/compile`'s frontend-specific environment and continuously tracking internal Go compiler changes. The analysis difficulty and coupling are disproportionate to LLGo's needs.

### 2. LLVM `AAHeapToStack` cannot produce the required `-m` summaries

`AAHeapToStack` answers a narrow optimization question: can a recognized allocation call be replaced by an `alloca`? A successful rewrite is evidence that one allocation is local. A failed rewrite is only unknown.

It does not expose the source-level information LLGo needs for `-m`, including:

- `p does not escape`;
- `leaking param: p`;
- `leaking param content: p`;
- `p` flowing to result N at dereference level K;
- mutator and called-function effects needed for summary composition;
- an explanation path tied to Go source positions.

These summaries must be computed and retained by LLGo itself.

### 3. LLVM `AAHeapToStack` cannot optimize according to Go semantics

Generic LLVM sees calls, pointers, aggregates, byte copies, and opaque runtime helpers. It does not know LLGo's language/runtime contracts. For example:

- the pointer passed to `runtime.ChanSend` is a temporary transport address borrowed until the call returns, while pointer-containing bytes copied from that address may remain in channel storage;
- a slice value contains a backing-store pointer whose behavior under `append` depends on capacity and possible reallocation;
- an interface payload may be represented directly or copied into an indirect box according to LLGo's ABI classification;
- a closure environment contains captured Go values and escapes according to the closure value's uses;
- goroutine startup data must outlive the caller even when the callee does not retain an argument after startup;
- typed memory moves preserve Go pointer fields in ways that an untyped byte-copy model cannot recover safely;
- `//go:noescape` and uintptr keepalive are Go compiler contracts, not generic LLVM pointer attributes.

An LLGo-owned pass can model these semantics explicitly and conservatively.

## Verified current pipeline

The current repository already has the required transformation boundary.

`internal/build/build.go` calls `cl.NewPackageExWithEmbedMeta`, which returns the generated package and its live `llvm.Module`. For a cache miss, the current order is:

```text
cl.NewPackageExWithEmbedMeta
    -> ModuleHook observes the complete module
    -> llabi.LowerLargeAggregates
    -> cabi.Transformer.TransformModule
    -> LLVM VerifyModule
    -> Module.RunPasses(default<O*>)
```

`internal/cabi/cabi.go` demonstrates the intended implementation shape. `TransformModule` walks LLVM functions, basic blocks, and call instructions, gathers rewrite candidates, and then rewrites function signatures and call sites directly in the completed module.

The escape pass should use the same module-transform pattern. It should not be implemented inside individual `cl` lowering cases and should not require changes to `xgo-dev/llvm` merely to define a normal LLGo pass.

The pass should run before `LowerLargeAggregates` and C ABI rewriting by default. At that point the module is complete, but Go aggregate/function relationships have not yet been obscured by ABI signature changes. The implementation must verify this ordering with C ABI and large-aggregate tests; if a specific rewrite requires a later position, that dependency must be explicit rather than silently inferred from transformed IR.

Issue #44: Transfer LLM self-repair to TFMs — 3-part plan (path-patching DE → CE regression → LN artifact)

## Goal

Transfer LLM self-repair mech-interp (Hydra Effect, McGrath 2023) to TFMs.
Confirm — or falsify — that TFMs do **mechanistic** self-repair (active downstream compensation), not just redundancy or a LayerNorm artifact.

Unit: per (layer, dataset). Primary model: **LimiX-2M**. Ablation: **resample** throughout (zero is settled/legacy).

---

## Core idea: two rulers, one basis

Self-repair = ablate layer `m`, its **direct** write was large, but the **total** effect is small, because downstream **actively compensates**.

- **TE** (`Δ_ablate`) — ablate `m`, downstream free, read final output. *Reuse existing sweep.*
- **DE** (`Δ_unembed`) — freeze downstream at clean, swap `a_m`, read through **native head**. *New: path-patching.*
- **CE** = DE − TE (compensation). Self-repair ⟺ CE > 0.

Both rulers **must go through the same native head** (not per-layer tuned decoders) — else DE and TE aren't comparable.

---

## Confirmation criteria (what "confirmed" means)

A below-diagonal scatter is necessary but **not sufficient**. Must clear 4 impostors:

| Impostor | Looks like self-repair because | Ruled out by |
|---|---|---|
| **Redundancy** | TE ≈ 0 | require **large DE** (not the DE≈0 stripe) |
| **LayerNorm artifact** | ablate → residual norm ↓ → final LN scales up remainder | **fold σ vs no-fold** subtraction (RQ3) |
| **Distribution shift** | off-manifold zero blows up output | **resample throughout** (settled in prior work) |
| **No structure** | a few points below diagonal by chance | **CE~DE regression R²** must be high |

Positive checklist:
- **C1 decoupling** — scatter systematically below diagonal.
- **C2 large-DE** — those points have non-trivial DE (excludes redundancy).
- **C3 systematic compensation** — CE~DE regression: high R², slope 0<k<1 (vs LLM 0.92 / 0.69). *The confirmation number.*
- **C4 localizable** — per-layer CE curve points to *which* layers compensate.
- **C5 robust** — holds after subtracting LN rescaling.

Falsification is a valid result: DE≈0 everywhere → redundancy; CE vanishes after LN subtraction → LN artifact; low R² → no systematic compensation. All publishable.

---

## Three-part split (one verb each: see → confirm → rule out)

### Part 1 — path-patching + scatter — **see the decoupling**
- **New:** path-patching DE (freeze downstream, swap `a_m`, native head).
- **Reuse:** TE from existing sweep — first verify it reads the native head + same scalar.
- Run sweep → per (layer, dataset) `(DE, TE)`.
- **D1:** DE–TE scatter + diagonal (Hydra Fig 2c analog).
- Delivers **C1**; flags the DE≈0 redundant stripe (**C2**).
- Self-contained, cheap, reviewable. Only genuinely new computation in the whole plan.

### Part 2 — CE decomposition + regression — **confirm compensation**
- **New:** CE recompute — after ablating `m`, recompute each downstream layer's DE (red − blue).
- **D2:** CE~DE regression → R², slope (**C3**, the confirmation number).
- **D4:** per-layer CE curve (**C4** — who compensates, where).
- Consistency check: does per-layer-summed CE ≈ DE − TE? (linearity / accounting).
- Regression stays here (not Part 1): the below-diagonal gap `DE−TE` is an identity; the persuasive R² needs an **independently computed** CE.

### Part 3 — LN artifact + writeup — **rule out impostors**
- **RQ3 (LN artifact):** re-run Part-2 CE with σ **frozen at clean** vs recomputed; `CE_LN = CE_nofold − CE_fold`. No new sweep/data — just a σ-freeze toggle on the head's LN.
- **D3:** one-sentence scientific conclusion + final figures.

---

## Head linearity gate (already checked)

`H = norm ∘ decoder`. Determines DE method + who's the clean RQ3 testbed.

| Model | Head | Linear? | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mitra** | LayerNorm + Linear | ✅ (fold σ) | only nonlinearity is LN → **exact TE=DE+IE**, clean RQ3 testbed |
| **LimiX-2M** | LN(no-affine) + GELU-MLP | ❌ | GELU → path-patching required; TE=DE+IE approximate |
| **TabICL** | LayerNorm + GELU-MLP | ❌ | path-patching |
| **TabFM** | RMSNorm + GELU-MLP | ❌ | path-patching |

- Only Mitra's head is linear → `DE_lens = DE_patch` exactly (after folding σ).
- LimiX/TabICL/TabFM have a GELU folding can't remove → **path-patching is mandatory** for the primary unit.

Issue #1689: SandboxDependencyManager caches installed requirements by sandbox name, not instance -- stale on container replacement

## Summary

`SandboxDependencyManager` (`src/xagent/core/tools/adapters/vibe/sandboxed_tool/sandboxed_tool_wrapper.py`) tracks installed pip requirements in a process-wide class-level dict keyed only by `sandbox.name`:

```python
_sandbox_installed_requirements: dict[str, set[str]] = {}
...
sandbox_key = sandbox.name
...
installed = cls._sandbox_installed_requirements.get(sandbox_key, set())
missing = sorted(required - installed)
if not missing:
    return
```

Sandbox lifecycle names are logical/stable (`SandboxManager.make_sandbox_name(lifecycle_type, lifecycle_id)`), not tied to a specific container instance. When a container is evicted (capacity pressure, idle reclamation) or rebuilt (mismatch reconcile) and a *new* container is created under the *same* logical name, `SandboxDependencyManager` still has the old container's "already installed" entry cached. `ensure_requirements()` then skips installation into the fresh container's filesystem, even though it has none of those packages.

## Impact
